en: The Kāśikāvṛtti, First Chapter, First Quarter [1]:
In this commentary (*vṛtti*), as well as in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Dhātupārāyaṇa*, the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*, and so forth, a compendium of the essence of the scattered system is now being composed. //1//

This commentary, named the Kāśikā, includes desired supplementary rules, consists of pure groups [of words], clarifies the meaning of both explicit and hidden sūtras, and establishes the formation of grammatical forms. //2//
The body of grammar consists of this much: the completion of the work of the treatise.
The author of the book now undertakes the remaining preparatory arrangement for it.
(3) Now, regarding the instruction of words: of which words is it the instruction?
Of both worldly and Vedic [words].
How is there instruction?
By means of definitions possessing general and specific characteristics, through the conceptualization of divisions such as roots (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
Now, for what purpose is the instruction of the phonemes?
It is for the sake of abbreviation (pratyāhāra). Abbreviation is for the sake of the concise operation of the treatise.
In the rule *aiuṇ*,
having taught the phonemes in this sequence— *a*, *i*, and *u*— he places the letter *ṇ* at the end for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*.
Its inclusion occurs by means of the single [term] *auran rapraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51).
By means of the vowel *i*:
when the short *a*-vowel is employed, the mouth is contracted;
however, in the case of the long and protracted vowels, there is openness.
For the purpose of establishing their homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), the vowel *a* is declared here in this treatise to be "opened" (*vivṛta*).
For the sake of its practical application, its restoration (*pratyāpatti*) will be effected at the end of the treatise by the rule *a a* (Pāṇini 8.4.68).
Having taught these two phonemes, *ṛ* and *ḷ*, he places the letter *k* at the end of the preceding [section] for the purpose of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
Its inclusion occurs by means of three [terms].
By the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), [substitution] occurs with the vowel *a*; by the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3), [the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* refer to specific phonemes].
By the vowel *i* in the term *iti*,
and by the vowel *u* in the rule *ugitaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6),
the vowels beginning with *a* constitute a domain of extensive usage; therefore, the purpose of their instruction is easily understood.
The sound *ḷ* is employed only in the context of the root *kḷp*;

furthermore, by the rule "that which precedes is not established" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*, Pāṇini 8.2.1), the substitution of *l* for *ḷ* is considered non-existent [for the purposes of the preceding rules].
Since that [substitution] is not established, the operations pertaining to *ac* vowels will apply to the *ṛ* vowel alone; for what purpose, then, is the *ḷ* vowel taught?
It is so that those subsequent operations pertaining to *ac* vowels which are prescribed by the rule for *l* may likewise apply to the *ḷ* vowel.
But what are they?
The protracted (pluta) and the circumflex (svarita) vowels undergo reduplication,
as in *prakḷptaḥ* and *prakḷptavān*.
Furthermore, although an incorrect form of word that arises from incapacity is not itself correct, its correctness is nevertheless accepted when it is an imitation [of a correct form].
For this reason, the instruction of the letter *ḷ* is provided so that even the letter *ḷ* situated therein may be understood as undergoing the grammatical operations applicable to vowels (*ac*).
When one ought to use the word *ṛtakaḥ*, a girl, due to a deficiency in her vocal power, uses the word *ḷtakaḥ*;
another person imitates her and says, "The girl said *kumāry-ḷtakaḥ*."
Having taught these two phonemes, *e* and *o*, he places the letter *ṅ* at the end for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*;
its inclusion occurs by means of a single [subsequent] reference.
By the rule *eṅi pararūpam* (Pāṇini 6.1.94), [the substitution] is with the vowel *e*;
and [there are also] *ai* and *au*.
Having taught these two phonemes, *ai* and *au*, he places the letter *c* at the end of the preceding [section] for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*.
Its inclusion occurs by means of four [rules]:
*acaḥ parasmin pūrva-vidhau* (P. 1.1.57).
By means of the vowel *a* [in the word *iti*],
and by means of the vowel *i* [in the word *ika*] according to the rule *ica ekāco ’m pratyayavat ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.68).
By [the rule] *eco 'y-av-āy-āvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.78), [the substitution] is by means of the vowel *e*;
[and] *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1).
Thus [it is] by means of the vowel *ai*.

[Objection: In a pratyāhāra, how is it that the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are not included when there is a mention of vowels (*aj-grahaṇa*)? [Response: Because of established usage (*ācāra*), because they are subordinate (*apradhānatva*), and because elision (*lopa*) is more powerful.

Among phonemes, those partial phonemes which possess a form similar to another phoneme do not undergo that grammatical operation; for they merely imitate its shadow and are not that very phoneme itself.
Indeed, the teachers maintain that a phoneme is produced by a distinct articulatory effort.
Regarding the rules for the augment *nuṭ*, substitutes, and euphonic changes (*vināma*), one must provide a specific counter-argument concerning the vowel *ṛ*.
In the rule prescribing the augment *nuṭ* (Pāṇini 7.4.71), the mention of the vowel *ṛ* is intended [to prevent its application to other cases].
Thus, we have *ānṛdhatuḥ* and *ānṛdhuḥ*.
The letter ṛ is included in the rule for the substitution of *la* (in the sense of "cutting");
e.g., *kḷptaḥ*, *kḷptavān*. The letter ṛ is also included in the rule for the substitution of *vināma* (nasalization).
Of the agents.
Having taught these phonemes— ha, ya, va, ra, ṭ— and having placed the letter ṭ at the end of the preceding ones, he does so for the purpose of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
Its inclusion occurs by means of a single [term].
By the rule *śaś cho ’ti* (Pāṇini 8.4.63),
this letter *ra* is taught as following the letter *ya*; thus, when there is an inclusion of it through the mention of *yar* and the mention of *yay*, [it is included].
In the cases of *svarnayati* and *prātarnayati*, the rule *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.58) would require the substitution of a nasal for the final consonant.
In the case of *madrahradaḥ* and *bhadrahradaḥ*, the doubling [of the consonant] would apply according to the rule *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (Pāṇini 8.4.46). [As in:
*kuṇḍaṃ rathena*.
In the case of *vanaṃ rathena*, the substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) would apply according to the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58).
This is not a fault.

In this view— that a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) applies once to its entire scope (*sakṛllakṣye*), whether that scope be a form, a word-meaning, or a collection— [the rule] *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45), "when followed by a nasal, a semi-vowel or a stop becomes optionally a nasal," operates in this manner.

Thus, by this [rule], for the sounds beginning with *ga*, those beginning with *ṅa* are respectively the most similar (*antaratama*) in terms of their place of articulation (*sthāna*) and their quality (*guṇa*).
All of those have been explained;
however, those which are neither by way of their locus nor by way of their qualities—

Since all those [substitutes] that are most similar (*antaratama*)—whether by virtue of place of articulation alone or by virtue of phonetic quality alone—have been excluded, the *ṇakāra* is not the most similar to the *repha* by virtue of place alone.

Furthermore, even though the *repha* is included within the *yar* group during reduplication (*dvirvacana*), any grammatical operation (*yak-kārya*) that would apply to it is set aside by the directly taught status of being the cause [of the reduplication]; thus, the *repha* is not reduplicated.
The rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.58) also prescribes a single substitution for the *anusvāra* that is most similar (*antaratama*) to the following sound; however,
since there is no homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound most similar to the *anusvāra* that corresponds to the letter *repha*, the substitution will not occur in the case of *kuṇḍaṃ rathena*.
Regarding the example *vanaṃ rathena*,
here the teaching (*upadeśa*) of the *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, and *upadhmānīya* must also be stated for the [nasal] *aṭ* sounds.
What is the purpose?
*uraḥkeṇa*, *uraḥkeṇa*;
*uraḥpeṇa*, *uraḥpeṇa*. Here, the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is applied so that it occurs even when there is an intervening *aṭ*-vowel. [4]
Having taught the single phoneme *la* as "la," he places the letter *ṇ* at the end of the preceding [section] for the purpose of forming a pratyāhāra.
Its inclusion occurs by means of three [expressions].
By the rule *aṇ-udit-savarṇasya ca apratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), [the term "vowel" (*ac*)] is understood through the letter *a*;
by the rule *iṇ-koḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.57), it is understood through the letter *i*.
By the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), [the term] is [understood] by means of the letter *y*.
All references to *iṇ* are with the subsequent nasal *ṇ*,
whereas references to *aṇ* are with the preceding nasal *ṇ*.
This alone, namely *aṇ-udit-savarṇasya ca apratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), is [the rule] followed by the subsequent one.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *ac* not made here instead?
This is not possible,
for even the semivowels (antaḥsthā) are intended to include their homogeneous counterparts (savarṇa):
*sayam*, *yam*, *yantā*.
Sa-vaṃ,
vaṃ vatsara, ya-laṃ, laṃ.

In the case of *lokam*, *tallaṃ*, *laṃ*, and *lokam*, when the *anusvāra* has been changed to a homogeneous nasal (*parasavarṇa*) before a nasalized semivowel (*anunāsika yay*), doubling (*dvirvacana*) occurs because that [nasal] is included by the term *yar*. Thus [the rule is stated].
In the case of [the letters] beginning with *hakāra*, the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation and is not an *anubandha*;
however, in the case of *lakāra*, it is declared to be nasalized (*anunāsika*).
Therefore, because the term *ra* is used as a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation) in the rule *tena ur-aṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51), there is also the occurrence of *la* following [the vowel].
Having taught these phonemes— ña, ma, ṅa, ṇa, na, and m— and having placed the letter *m* at the end of the preceding ones, he does so for the purpose of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
Its inclusion occurs by means of three [terms].
By the rule *pumaḥ khayy-ampare* (Pāṇini 8.3.6), [the final *m*] is replaced by *a*;
then, by *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.64), [the preceding *y*] is elided.
Thus, [the sandhi] occurs with the letter *y* by virtue of the rule *iti yakāreṇa*;
and it occurs with the letter *ṅ* by virtue of the rule *ṅamo hrasvād-aci ṅamuṇ nityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.32).
The inclusion of this [term] by means of the letter *ñ* is also seen in the rule *ñamantāḍ-ḍaḥ*.
However, some reject the *m* as an *anubandha*, asserting that all these *pratyāhāra* formations should be made with the letter *ñ*.
If that were the case, then [the rule] *ṅamo hrasva-adaci ṅamuṇ nityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.32) would follow accordingly.

In this case, because the substitutes *jha* and *bha* do not exist when the augments are present, one must first understand the absence of the augments before understanding the absence of the substitutes; thus, there is a burden of cognitive effort.
Having taught these two phonemes, *jha* and *bha*, he places the letter *ñ* at the end of the preceding [series] for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*.
Its inclusion occurs by means of a single [term].
Therefore, by [the rule] *ato dīrgho yañi* (*Pāṇini 7.3.101*), [the substitution is made] with the letter *y*.

Having taught these letters— gha, ḍha, dha, and ṣ— and having placed the letter ṣ at the end of the preceding [group] beginning with gha, he does so for the purpose of forming a pratyāhāra (abbreviation).
Its inclusion occurs by means of two [expressions].
By the rule *eka-aco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣ-antasya s-dhvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.37), [the substitution occurs] by means of the letters *bh* and *jh*; [namely:
Having taught these letters—ja, ba, ga, ḍa, da—and the preceding ones, he places the letter śa at the end for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its inclusion occurs by means of six [rules]:
*bho-bhago-agho-apūrvasya yo 'śi* (Pāṇini 8.3.17).
[The substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] by the rule *ity akāreṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), by the rule *haśi ca* (6.1.114),
and by the rule *na-iḍ-vaśi kṛti* (7.2.8).
Thus, [the substitution occurs] by means of the letter *v* [in the rule *vāvasāne*];
and by means of the letters *j* and *jh* [in the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*].
[The substitution of] *bh* for [the final consonant of] a monophthongic root ending in *jhaṣ*, before *s* and *dhv*, according to Pāṇini 8.2.37,
is by means of the letter *b*.
Having taught these letters— kha, pha, dha, ḍha, tha, ca, ṭa, ta, and va— he places the letter *va* at the end for the purpose of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
Its inclusion is accomplished by means of a single [subsequent] reference.
[The rule] *naś-chavy-apraśān* (Pāṇini 8.3.7) [is stated] by means of the letter *dh*. The mention of *kha* and *pha* is for the sake of what follows.
Having taught these two phonemes, *ka* and *pa*, he places the letter *ya* at the end of the former for the purpose of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
Its inclusion occurs by means of four [rules].

The *anusvāra* is replaced by the *parasavarṇa* [the following semivowel] according to Pāṇini 8.4.58, which in this case is the letter *y*; furthermore, according to 8.3.33, the *uñ* [of *u*] is optionally replaced by *v* after *m*.
By means of the letter *m* [in the rule *mo no dhātoḥ*],
and by means of the letter *jh* [in the rule *jhayo ho ’nyatarasyām*].
[The substitution of *u* for *v*] occurs by means of the rule "pumaḥ khayy-ampare" (Pāṇini 8.3.6), which specifies the letter *kh*.
Having taught these phonemes— śa, ṣa, sa, and ra— and having placed the letter *r* at the end of the preceding group [śa, ṣa, sa], he does so for the purpose of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation).
Its inclusion occurs by means of five [rules].
By the rule *yaro 'nynāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45), [the *jha*-class consonant] optionally becomes a nasal before a non-nasal *ya*-class consonant;
by the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65), [it is elided] before a homogeneous *jha*-class consonant.
Thus, by [the rule] *jhakāreṇa*;
by the letter *kh* according to *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55); and by the letter *c* in reduplication according to *abhyāse car ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54).
By the letter *c* [in *cakāra*],
and by the letter *ś* [in *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*] (Pāṇini 8.4.61).
Having taught the single phoneme *ha* as "ha," he places the phoneme *la* at the end of the preceding [section] for the purpose of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
Its inclusion occurs by means of six [terms].

By the rule *alo 'ntyāt pūrva upadhā* (Pāṇini 1.1.65), [the term "upadhā" refers to] that which precedes the final vowel; and by the rule *halo 'nantarāḥ saṃyogaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.7), [consonants] that follow one another without an intervening vowel constitute a "conjunct" (*saṃyoga*).
Thus, [the elision] occurs by means of the letter *ha* [in the rule *haśi ca*];
it occurs by means of the letter *va* [in the rule] *lopo vyor vali*.

By the rule *ralo v-y-upadhad-dhal-ādeḥ saṃś ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.26), [the suffix] *saṃt* is substituted for [the augment *siC*] after a root ending in *r*, provided it has *v*, *y*, or a consonant other than a nasal as its penultimate letter; and by the rule *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26).
Thus, by means of the letter *jha*;
and by means of the letter *śa*, according to the rule *śala ig-upadhād aniṭaḥ kṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.45).

Now, for what purpose is the letter *ha* taught again, even though it has already been taught? It is so that the optional application of *kit*-ness, the substitution of *kṣa*, and the rules regarding *iṭ* may take effect. Thus, in the forms *snihitvā* and *snehitvā*, [the rule] *ralo vy-upadhād dhal-ādeḥ saṃś-ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.26) applies.
Thus, it is so that there may optionally be *kittva*;

or, as in *alikṣat* from the root *lih*, it is so that there may be *kṣa* by the rule "after a root ending in *śal*, having *i* as its penultimate letter, and being *aniṭ*, *kṣa* is substituted" (Pāṇini 6.1.45). [6]

[The rule] "rudihi, svapihi" is for the sake of ensuring that the augment *iṭ*—characterized by beginning with a consonant (*valādi*)—is applied; [the rule] "adāgdhām" is for the sake of ensuring that the letter *ha* is included within the term *jhal*; and [the rule] "ca" is for the sake of ensuring that the letter *ha* is included in the mention of *jhal*.
If that is so, then for what purpose would [the letter] *ha* be taught in the rule *ha ya va ra ḍ*?
For it is great;
it is so that the inclusion of *hakāra* may occur both in the mentions of *aḍ* and in the mentions of *aś*, as in the example *devā hasanti*.

The Brāhmaṇa laughs so that the substitution of *u* (utvam) may occur by the rule "haśi ca" (*Pāṇini 6.1.114*). From one [consonant], there should be *ṅ, ñ, ṇ, N, and Ṭ*; from two, *ṣ*; and from three, *k, ṇ, m, and Ā*.
The letters *jña*, *ya*, and *ca* are to be known as arising from four [consonants]; *ra* from five; and *śa* and *la* from six.
Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the section on *pratyāhāra*. Vṛddhi is [the term for] *āt* and *aic*. (Pāṇini 1.1.1)
The term *vṛddhi* is prescribed as a technical designation (*sañjñā*) for each of the phonemes *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, collectively, when they have been produced by that [process].

And for those [sounds] not produced by that [time-length], the addition of *t* (in *tapara*) is for the sake of *aij*; for according to the rule "that which has *t* after it is *tapara*," there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of three-mora or four-mora durations in words such as *khaṭvaiḍaka*. This is to prevent that occurrence.
Āśvalāyana; Aitikāyana; Aupagava.
Aupamanyava,
Śālīya, Mālīya.
The rules concerning *vṛddhi* substitution— such as "there is *vṛddhi* before *sic* in the case of *parasmaipada* endings" (Pāṇini 7.2.1)—
and so forth.
Adeṅ is termed guṇa.
The word *guṇa* is prescribed as a technical term (*sañjñā*) for each [of the vowels] individually.

This applies generally to the vowels *a* and *eṅ*, whether they have been modified (*tadbhāvita*) or not so modified (*atadbhāvita*). However, the inclusion of the marker *t* (in *tapara*) here serves all purposes.
The one who has crossed over;
the one who perceives; the one who praises.
They are victorious! I shall explain the *guṇa* substitutes: the *guṇa* substitute [is applied] for the root *mid* (Pāṇini 7.3.82).
And so forth.
The terms *iK*, *guṇa*, and *vṛddhi* [are technical names for vowels]. PS 1.1.3.
This *paribhāṣā* is for the purpose of restricting the substituendum (*sthānin*);
when there would otherwise be a lack of restriction, a restriction is now prescribed.
The *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions, when taught under their own specific names, should be understood as occurring only in place of an *ik* vowel.
As he will state: "There is *guṇa* substitution for the *aṅga* [stem] before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes" (Pāṇini 7.3.84).
He alone is to be known as abiding in his place;
he leads;
he exists.
Furthermore, there is also the strengthening (vṛddhi): *akārṣīt*,
*ahārṣīt*, *acaaiṣīt*.
He brought;
he cut; he praised.
The *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions are prescribed by their own technical names; in that context, the term *ikaḥ* should be understood as being supplied. What is thereby accomplished?
By the second [rule], the sixth case is manifested:
in the rules *midimṛjipugantalaghūpadhācchidṛśikṣiprakṣudreṣvaṅgasya* and *jusi ca*, the *ika* vowel is qualified by the *aṅga* (stem).
In the rules concerning *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* *guṇa* substitutions, the *ika* vowel is qualified by the *aṅga*.
*medyate*, *abhighāyuḥ*.
Why [is it said] "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*)? [To exclude cases such as: *madhuraḥ*.
Let it not be [the case] for diphthongs, vowels, and consonants;
as in *yānam* and *glāyati*.
It is bound.
Furthermore, the re-mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*) regarding rules prescribed by their own technical names (*sañjñā*). Let it not occur here: *dyauḥ*.
The path; he; this—so [it is said].
There is no elision of a root-vowel before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

A portion of a verbal root is [itself considered] a root; that *ārdhadhātuka* suffix after which there is the elision (*lopa*) of such a [portion of the] root is called "having a root-elision" (*dhātu-lopa*).
In that case, those [substitutions] which would otherwise undergo *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* do not take place; thus,
[we have] *loluvaḥ*.

The suffix *yaṅ* is elided after roots such as *popu*, *marīmṛj*, and *lolūya* when they end in *yaṅ*, provided that a suffix beginning with a vowel— such as those belonging to the *paca*-class— is subsequently prescribed (Pāṇini 2.4.74).

Thus, when the *yaṅ* suffix has been elided (*luk*), there is a prohibition of those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions that would otherwise apply by depending on that very vowel (*ac*). Why is the term "root" (*dhātu*) mentioned? [Consider: *lūñ*, *lavitā*;
*reḍasi*.
It is like the leaf of a bird;

let there not be [the application of rules] when a suffix following an *anubandha* has been elided. For example, "reṭ" is an instance where the *vic* suffix of the root *riṣ*, meaning "to injure," has been elided.
What is the purpose of the condition *ārdhadhātuke*?
[Consider the example: *tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti*. Let [the substitution] not occur in the *sārvadhātuka* [context].
In the case of *ika* alone—as in *abhāji*, *rāgaḥ*—why is recourse to the *bahuvrīhi* compound necessary? [To answer:
as in *knopayati* and *preddham*.
And [the substitution of Guna and Vṛddhi] does not take place before an affix marked with K or Ṅ.
This is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*):
those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions which would otherwise occur when there is a cause consisting of a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*.
These two do not occur:
*citaḥ* (accumulated) and *citavān* (having accumulated); *stutaḥ* (praised) and *stutavān* (having praised).
*bhinnaḥ*, *bhinnavān*;
*mṛṣṭaḥ*, *mṛṣṭavān*;
and likewise when followed by a suffix beginning with *ṅ*: *cinutaḥ*, *cinvanti*.
*mṛṣṭaḥ*, *mṛjanti*; here the letter *g* is also indicated as having become *c* (through retroflexion). [By Pāṇini 3.2.139] *glā-ji-sthaś ca gstuḥ*: *jiṣṇuḥ*.
The word *bhūṣṇuḥ* [is formed with the suffix *uṇ*]. By the rule *ikaḥ* [it is understood] as follows: *kāmayate*, *laigavāyanaḥ*.
In the case of the root *mṛj*, when followed by an affix beginning with a non-initial vowel, a vṛddhi substitution is optionally desired.
"Saṅkrama" refers to the domain where the prohibition of guṇa and vṛddhi would otherwise apply. [Examples:
*parimṛjanti* (they wipe around), [8]

The suffix *suṭ* is applied to [the verbal root] that is not neuter.
The five case-endings beginning with *suṭ* (the nominative-accusative plural) receive the technical designation *sarvanāmasthāna*, except in the neuter;
for there is no such rule regarding the neuter.
There is no prohibition.
Therefore, by that [rule], the designation *sarvanāmasthāna* applies to *śi*, the substitute for *jas*, precisely by the preceding rule:
*rājā*, *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*.
*rājānam*, *rājānau*.
Why [is the word] *suṭ* mentioned? [To exclude forms such as] *rājñaḥ paśya* ("look at the king").
Why [is the phrase] *anapuṃsakasya* ("not neuter") mentioned?
Sāmanī, Vemanī.
The term *vibhāṣā* means "optionally" or "it may be so, or it may not."
"Na" is a negation;
"vā" is an alternative.
The term *vibhāṣā* is the designation for those two, namely negation (*pratiṣedha*) and option (*vikalpa*). The particle *iti* is used for the purpose of indicating the meaning.
In the rules where *vibhāṣā* is prescribed, negation and option apply.
In that case, once the subject has been rendered uniform by means of a prohibition, a subsequent option (*vikalpa*) then operates;
this is what causes the "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) rules to apply.
For example: *vibhāṣā śveḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30).
*śuśāva*, *śiśvāya*;
*śuśuvatuḥ*, *śiśviyatuḥ*. Rules concerning the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) [of this reduplication]: *vibhāṣā śveḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30).
And so forth.
The *ig* vowels undergo *samprasāraṇa*.
Whatever [sound] occurs in place of *ik*—whether it has already occurred or is yet to occur—is designated by the technical term *saṃprasāraṇa*. For example:
*yaj* + *i* = *iṣṭam*.
*vap* means "sown" (*upta*);
*graha* means "taken" (*gṛhīta*).
Some explain this sūtra in both ways, [stating] that the meaning of the sentence is the technical term (*saṃjñin*).

And regarding the word *varṇa*: that sentence-meaning characterized by the relationship between the substituend (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) which consists of an *ig* vowel in place of a *yaṇ* [consonant] is designated as *samprasāraṇa*; that is, an *ig* vowel occupying the position of a *yaṇ* is designated as *samprasāraṇa*.

In that regard, in the case of a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*), the meaning of the sentence is established by such rules as "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *ṣyaṅ* [suffix] before *putra* and *pati* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound" (*Pāṇini 6.1.13*) and "there is vocalization of *vasu*" (*Pāṇini 6.4.131*).
In the case of a descriptive restatement (*anuvāda*), it is established by such rules as "and after a vowel, there is vocalization" (*Pāṇini 6.1.108*).
It does not apply here due to the enumeration [of specific cases] following the count: *adhitarām*.

In the case of *dyubhyām*, the long vowel does not occur because of the rule *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), where the use of *t* as a marker (*taparakaraṇa*) indicates that only the short vowel is intended.
The rules concerning *samprasāraṇa* include such [sūtras] as "there is *samprasāraṇa* for *vasu*" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 6.4.131),
and so forth.
"Those marked with Ṭ and K are respectively at the beginning and the end [of the element specified in the genitive].
That which is marked with Ṭ becomes the initial element, and that which is marked with K becomes the final element, of that which is indicated by the genitive case.
The [agentive] suffix *tṛc* is applied [to form] *lavitṛ*;
*muṇḍa-* causes fear. The rules concerning the marker *ṭ*: "An augment *iṭ* is added to a *val*-initial *ārdhadhātuka* suffix" (Pāṇini 7.2.35).
These and others are such examples.
The rules concerning *kit* suffixes include: "after the root *bhī*, [the suffix *kta* is *kit*] when fear is caused by a cause" (*bhiyo hetubhaye śuk*, Pāṇini 7.2.40), and so forth.
"Midaco 'ntyāt paraḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.47).
The genitive case in "acaḥ" is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).
Furthermore, this singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*).
When these vowels are in close proximity (saṃniviṣṭa), a *mit* augment follows the final vowel;
this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the position of the suffix (*pratyaya-paratva*). Example:
*viruṇaddhi*.
It releases the waters.
The rules for the suffix *mit* are: *śnam* is applied after roots beginning with *rudh* (Pāṇini 3.1.78).

These and others are such examples. They desire the insertion of *num* before the final letter of the root *masj*, for the purpose of avoiding the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal) and the initial of the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster); thus, [we have] *magnaḥ*.
He has bathed;
one who will bathe;
to bathe.

*Eca ig-ghrasva-ādeśe* (Pāṇini 1.1.48): When a short substitute is to be applied for an *ec* vowel, only the short *ik* vowel is substituted, and no other. [This applies to the forms] *rai* and *atiri*.
Why [is it stated] "of *ec*"? [Consider: *nau-atinu*, *go-uṣa gu*.
*atikhaṭvaḥ* (exceedingly large bed), *atimālaḥ* (exceeding the garland).
Why [is it said] "when there is a substitution of a short vowel"? [Consider: *devadatta*.
"Ṣaṣṭhī sthāne-yogā" (P. 1.1.49). This is a *paribhāṣā* intended to restrict the application of grammatical rules (*yoga-niyama*).
In this treatise, whenever a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is heard that has an unrestricted application, [it is understood as "in place of"].
It occurs through appropriate application,
not through any other application;
when the conditions for appropriate application are present, it is to be realized.

And the word *sthāna* signifies "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). Just as in the expression "one should spread with *śara* grass in place of *darbha* grass," it is understood to mean "on the occasion of the *darbha* grass," so too here, in place of— that is, on the occasion of— the root *as*, *bhū* occurs.
will be; to be; that which is to be.
In the context of verbal activity, the root *vac* becomes *vaci*:
*vaktā* (speaker), *vaktum* (to speak).
It should be stated:

in the context of *prasaṅga*, where it serves as the cause for the relationship, the word *bruva* takes the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For there are many meanings of the genitive—such as owner and owned, immediate proximity, vicinity, collection, modification, part, and so forth.

In that regard, when all those [grammatical operations] which are possible with respect to a word are applicable, the restriction is made: "The genitive [case ending] occurs in the sense of *sthāna* (substitution).
The analysis is: "that which has its connection (*yoga*) in the place (*sthāne*)," which is a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-referential) *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Precisely for this reason, by means of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending.

*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50): When several [substitutes] are applicable in place [of an original], the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute occurs—that is, the one that is most like it. And from what does the similarity of a word arise?
[The application of rules occurs] by way of position, meaning, quality, and measure.
By way of position: *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101); [as in] *daṇḍāgram*.
Regarding the tip of a sacrificial post (*yūpāgra*):
when there are two instances of the letter *a*, the long *a* (ā) becomes a guttural *a* (a).
By way of meaning—for example, she is both a descendant of Vataṇḍa and a young woman, thus "the young woman who is a Vātaṇḍī" (*vātaṇḍī-yuvati*).
By means of the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), the most similar masculine word is extended [to the feminine]; thus,
by virtue of its quality, [the forms] *pākaḥ* and *tyāgaḥ* [are obtained].
Regarding *rāga*:
by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52), the unaspirated,
voiced consonant *c* becomes the corresponding *k*.
For the voiced, weak-aspirated *ja*-sound, there is a corresponding *ga*-sound; by way of illustration:
*anuṣmai*, *amūbhyām*.
By the rule *adaso 'ser dād u do maḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.80), there is a short vowel for a short [vowel] and a long vowel for a long [vowel].
Since the term "sthāne" (in place of) is already understood from the context, why is it mentioned again?
It is so that where multiple types of proximity (*āntarya*) are possible, proximity by position (*sthāna*) alone may be stronger;
as in *cetā* and *stotā*.
By virtue of the rule regarding quantity (*pramāṇa*), the vowel *a* is obtained as the substitute;
therein, by proximity of position (*sthāna*), *e* and *o* arise.
Why is the mention of *tam* (the suffix *ta*) made?
*vāc* becomes *ghas*;
*triṣṭubh* becomes *bhas*. According to Pāṇini 8.4.62, *jha* is optionally replaced by *ha*.
Thus, when the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] is applied to the sound *ha*, the second class consonants (*soṣman*) would be applicable according to the rule "for a *soṣman*, a *soṣman";

the third class consonants (*nādavat*) would be applicable according to the rule "for a *nādavat*, a *nādavat*; and by the inclusion of the superlative suffix *-tamap*, those which are both *soṣman* and *nādavat* become the fourth class consonants (*ūṣman*)."
*uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51): It should be understood that when *aṇ* is prescribed in place of *u*, it is followed by *r*. For example:
*kartā*.
He takes away; he scatters; he swallows.
*dvaimāturaḥ* (son of two mothers), *traimāturaḥ* (son of three mothers). Why [is the rule] restricted by *uḥ*? [Consider: *kheyam* (to be dug).
[This concerns] the *geya* [section].
Why is the mention of *an* necessary? [Because of the rule: "After *sudhātu*, there is also *akaṅ*" (*Pāṇini* 4.1.97).
Saudhātaki: [Enter Saudhātaki.]
*alo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52):
An substitute that is prescribed for what is designated by the genitive case is to be understood as occurring in place of the final *al* (phoneme).

[The suffix *ṭi* is elided after a word ending in the feminine suffix *ī*, when followed by a word beginning with *goṇī* (Pāṇini 1.2.50)—for example: *pañca-goṇiḥ* ("five ox-loads") and *daśa-goṇiḥ* ("ten ox-loads"). And [the substitution of *ṅ* for *n* occurs when a case-ending beginning with *ṅ* follows] (Pāṇini 1.1.53).
Furthermore, a substitute that has the marker *ṅ* (ṅit), even if it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), takes the place of the final phoneme (*alo 'ntyasya*). [For example:
by the rule "ānaṅ replaces *ṛt* in a *dvandva*" (Pāṇini 6.3.25), we have *hotā-potārau*.
Regarding the forms *mātā-pitarau*:

because the substitution of *tātaṅ* for the ending *ta* is intended to prohibit *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* by virtue of its being marked with the *ṅit* indicator, *tātaṅ* becomes a substitute for the entire stem-ending (*sarvādeśa*).
Thus: *jīvatād bhavān*.
May you live!

"Of what follows" (*ādeḥ parasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.54): when an operation is prescribed for something that follows, it should be understood to apply to the first [element] of that which follows. And where is an operation prescribed for something that follows?
Where there is an indication by the fifth case (ablative),
for example: *īdāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.83)—
"he sacrifices while sitting."
The substitution of *ī* for the vowel *a* of the root *āp* occurs after the prefixes *dvi*, *antar*, and *prati*. (Pāṇini 6.3.97): *dvīpam*, *antarīpam*, *pratīpam*.
Nearby.
(1.1.55) *anekāl-śit sarvasya*:
That which is a substitute consisting of more than one *al* (phoneme) and that which is marked with the *śit* designation occurs in place of the entire element specified by the genitive case.
From the root *as* (to be): *bhūḥ* (the imperative), *bhavitā* (the future active participle), *bhavitum* (the infinitive), and *bhavitavyam* (the gerundive).
Furthermore, there is indeed this rule: *śi* replaces *jaś* and *śas* (*Pāṇini 7.1.20*)— for example,
*kuṇḍāni tiṣṭhanti* ("the pots stand") and *kuṇḍāni paśya* ("look at the pots").
*sthānivad ādeśo 'nalvidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56).

Since the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) are distinct, an operation dependent upon the original element would not apply to the substitute; therefore, this extended application (*atideśa*) is commenced.
It functions in the same manner as the original element, and thus it is called *sthānivat*.

A substitute (ādeśa) is treated like the original (sthānivadbhavati) with respect to operations depending on the original, provided those operations do not depend on the phonemes [of the substitute]; that is, excluding operations depending on the phonemes of the original.
"Not an operation concerning phonemes" (analvidhiḥ) means "an operation not concerning phonemes" (na alvidhiḥ).
What is the illustration?

The substitutes for verbal roots (dhātu), stems (aṅga), kṛt suffixes, taddhita suffixes, indeclinables (avyaya), sup suffixes, tiṅ suffixes, and words (pada) [behave like their originals]. A substitute for a verbal root behaves like a verbal root.
*aster bhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52);
*bruvo vaciḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.53);
*ārdhadhātuka-viṣaye prāg evādeśeṣu kṛteṣu dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.91).
Thus, the suffixes beginning with *tavya* occur:
*bhavitā* (he will be), *bhavitum* (to be).
It must be so;
[he is] a speaker;
[he is] to speak.
It should be stated:
that which undergoes substitution of a stem (aṅga) behaves like the original stem— [as in] *kena* and *kābhyām*.
By which [words]?
When the substitution of *ka* is applied to *kimaḥ* by the rule *kimaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.103), the lengthening of the vowel in *ina*, as well as the change to *ais*, occur based on the *aṅga* (stem).
A substitute for a *kṛt* suffix behaves like the original *kṛt* suffix—as in *prakṛtya*.
After the substitution of *lyap* for the suffix *ktvā* in the form *prahṛtya*, the augment *tuk* is applied according to the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71). [23]
A substitute for a *taddhita* suffix is treated like a *taddhita* suffix—e.g., *dādhikam*, *adyatanam*.
And [the categories of] *kṛt* suffixes, *taddhita* suffixes, and compounds [are called "words"]. (*Pāṇini 1.2.46*)
Thus, the designation *prātipadika* applies. A substitute for an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is treated like an indeclinable— e.g., *prastutya*,
*prahṛtya*.
Having offered;
having praised;
[the elision of] *āp* and *sup* suffixes after an indeclinable (Pāṇini 2.4.82).
Thus, there is the elision of *su*; the substitute for *su* behaves like *su*— as in *vṛkṣāya*,
*plakṣāya*.
The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.83).
A substitute for a *tiṅ* ending behaves like a *tiṅ*: *akurutām*, *akurutam*.
By the rule *sup-tiṅ-anataṃ padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14), the designation *pada* is applied.
A substitute for a *pada* behaves like the original *pada*: *grāmo vaḥ svam*.
The word *jana-padaḥ* is our own [example]. By the rule *padasya* (Pāṇini 8.1.16), the substitution of *r* occurs. What is the purpose of employing the term *vat*?
Lest the designation "sthāni" be understood as referring only to the substitute, [the word *sthāne* is used] so that it may also apply to its own original locus (*svāśraya*). For example:
*āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28).
The *ātmanepada* affix occurs in both cases for the forms *āhata* and *āvadhiṣṭa*.
Why is there a mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*)?
It is so that the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) may apply even to a substitute that is inferred (*ānumānika*).
The suffix *eru* is substituted for *pacatu* (Pāṇini 3.4.86).
Why specify "in a rule prescribing an augment"?
[Because] the substitutes *dyu*, *pathi*, and *tad* do not behave as if they were the original bases (*sthānivadbhāva*).
In the case of *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, and *saḥ*,
the elision of *su* does not occur by the rule *hal-ṅy-ābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktam hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

*acaḥ parasmin pūrva-vidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.57). The status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) was previously stated to apply when there is a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme) that precedes [the substitute].
This [sūtra] is now commenced for the purpose of a rule concerning an *al* that follows [the substitute].
The rule "the substitute is like the original" (ādeśaḥ sthānivát) continues to apply.
"Of a vowel" (acaḥ) is the specification of the original element (sthānin). "In respect of what follows" (parasmin) is a locative of occasion (nimitta-saptamī).

In the phrase "pūrva-vidhau," the locative case denotes the scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). A substitute for *aj* (a vowel) which has a subsequent cause (*paranimittaka*) is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhavati*) when a preceding operation (*pūrvavidhi*) is to be performed. For example:
*paṭayati*.
He killed.
*Bahukhaṭvakaḥ*.

When the suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "he speaks articulately" (*paṭumācaṣṭe*), and the *ṭi*-portion is elided, because of the status of that [elision] as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (*Pāṇini 7.2.116*) applies.
Thus, the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] does not occur.

In the case of *avadhīt*, because of the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the elision of the *at* suffix, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by Pāṇini 7.2.7— namely, that which is conditioned by a consonant-final root with a light penultimate vowel (*ato halāder laghoḥ*)— does not take place.

In the case of *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*, by the rule *āpo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 7.4.15), because of the status of the short vowel as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the acute accent does not occur before the final syllable by the rule *hrasvānte 'ntyāt pūrvam* (Pāṇini 6.2.174).
Why is it stated "after a vowel" (acaḥ)? [Consider: praśnaḥ, ākrāṣṭām, āgatya.

In the word *praśnaḥ*, derived from the root *pracch* with the suffix *naṅ*, the substitution of *ś* for *ch* by the rule *c-ch-v-oḥ śūḍ-anunāsike ca* (*Pāṇini 6.4.19*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* when the subsequent condition *tuk* is to be applied.
[Similarly,] in *ākrāṣṭām*, the rule *jhalo jhali* (*Pāṇini 8.2.26*) applies.

Thus, the elision of *s* [in *kṛṣ*] is dependent on a subsequent cause; when the substitution of *k* for the *ṣ* and *ḍh* sounds according to *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* (Pāṇini 8.2.41) is to be applied, it does not behave as if it were the original element (*sthānivat*).
Or, in the case of *lyap*, as in *āgatya* (Pāṇini 6.4.38).
Thus, the elision of a nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) caused by a subsequent element does not behave as if it were the original element (*na sthānivat*) when the augment *tuk* is to be applied.
Why is it said "in the presence of a subsequent element" (*parasmin*)? [Consider:
*yuvajāniḥ*, *vadhūṭījāniḥ*.
Vaiyāghrapadyaḥ;
ādīdhye;
yuvajāniḥ—here, *niṅ* is substituted for the word *jāyā* [by Pāṇini 5.4.134].
It is not caused by what follows;
therefore, when *ya* is elided, it does not behave as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*).
In the case of *vaiyāghrapadyaḥ*, the elision of the final syllable of *pāda*—which is not caused by what follows—does not prevent the substitution of *pad* for *pāda*.

In *ādīdhye*, the substitution of *e* for the final vowel of the root *dīdhīṅ* in the first person singular does not trigger the elision of the *y* and *i* vowels of the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* (by Pāṇini 6.1.19), because that substitution is not caused by a subsequent element.
Why is it stated "in a rule concerning what precedes"? Consider the example: *he gauḥ*.
The followers of Bābhravya say:

in the case of *naidheyaḥ* and *he gauḥ*, the substitution of the *vṛddhi* vowel for the initial [of the suffix] does not behave as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) when the elision of the vocative marker (*sambuddhi*) is to be applied.
In the case of *bābhravīyāḥ*, meaning "these are the pupils of Bābhravya," the suffix *cha* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.114 (*vṛddhāc chaḥ*).

When the elision of the *ya*-sound is to be performed according to Pāṇini 6.4.150 (*halas taddhitasya*), the substitution of *ava* for *av* does not behave as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).
In *naidheya*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), and [the suffix *ḍhak* is applied] by *itaś cāniñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.122).
Thus, in the prescription of an affix characterized by two consonants, the substitute does not behave like the original (sthānivadbhāva).

Not in the rules concerning [substitution at] the end of a word, reduplication, the *vṛddhi* vowel *ai*, elision of *y*, vowels, homogeneous sounds, *anusvāra*, long vowels, and the *jaś* and *car* substitutions (Pāṇini 1.1.58).

The application of the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), which was overextended by the preceding rule, is here prohibited with respect to these rules. Regarding the rule for the end of a word, a substitute beginning with the vowel *a* does not behave like the original.
Who two are? Those two are. Which ones are? Those [many] are.
The elision of *al* in *santi*— which is caused by a subsequent condition (*paranimittaka*) according to the rule *śnasor allopaḥ kṅiti sārvadhātuke*—
would be treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) when the substitution of *āv* and the substitution of *yaṇ* are to be applied in a preceding operation.

On account of this statement, the rule for reduplication does not apply—that is, with respect to the rule for reduplication, it does not behave as if it were the original (sthānivadbhāva). For example:
*daddhy atra*.

In *maddhv atra*, the substitution of *yaṇ* is conditioned by what follows; because that [substitution] is treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), [the rule] *anaci ca* (*Pāṇini 8.4.47*) applies.
Thus, there would not have been a doubling of the letter *dha* [in *yāyādharaḥ*], but by this rule it occurs.

This is a rule concerning a substitute (*vare vidhiḥ*): a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśaḥ*) that occurs in place of a vowel (*vare*) does not behave as the original (*na sthānivat*) with respect to a preceding grammatical operation (*pūrva-vidhim prati*). [Example:
*apsu yāyāvaraḥ pravapeta piṇḍān*.

When *varac* is applied by the rule *yaś ca yaṅaḥ* (*Pāṇini 3.2.176*) after the root *yā* with the *yaṅ*-affix, the elision of the vowel *a* (*ato lopaḥ*, *Pāṇini 6.4.48*) is conditioned by what follows.
Because that [substitute] is treated like the original (sthānivadbhāva), there would be the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *ato lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64); however,
due to this specific statement, it does not occur.
The rule for the elision of *ya*: with respect to the rule for the elision of *ya*, a substitute beginning with *a* is not treated as if it were the original (sthānivat). For example: *kaṇḍūtiḥ*.
When the suffix *ktin* is applied to *kaṇḍūyati*, [the *ya* is elided].

Therefore, an elision (lopa) caused by a subsequent element— such as the elision of *y* according to the rule *lopo vyor vali* (*Pāṇini 6.1.66*)— would otherwise be subject to the *sthānivadbhāva* treatment; however, by virtue of this specific statement, it does not occur.
The rule for vowels (svara-vidhiḥ): with respect to a vowel-rule, a substitute beginning with *a* is not treated as if it were the original (na sthānivat). For example:
*cikīrṣakaḥ*, *jihīrṣakaḥ*. When the suffix *ṇvul* is applied, the elision of the *a* (ato lopaḥ) is conditioned by what follows; thus, by [Pāṇini 6.1.193], the suffix is marked with *li*.
"Before [the application of] a suffix, [the preceding vowel is] udātta";
thus, when an accent is to be applied, it does not behave as a substitute (sthānivat).
Regarding the rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-vidhi*): with respect to a rule concerning homogeneous vowels, a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) does not behave as a substitute.
*śiṇḍhi* and *piṇḍhi*:
after the roots *śiṣ* and *piṣ*, the suffix *śnam* is applied before the second person singular imperative ending (*loṭ*) by Pāṇini 3.1.78.

When the operations of *hitva*, *adhitva*, *ṣṭutva*, and *jaśtva* have been performed, the elision of the *al* of *śna* and *as* before a *sārvadhātuka* affix beginning with a *k* or *ṅ* is dependent on a subsequent cause;
however, this elision does not behave as if it were a *sthānivadbhāva* when the operation of *parasavarṇa* for the *anusvāra* before a *yay* sound is to be applied. [25]
The rule for *anusvāra*: with respect to the rule for *anusvāra*, a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) does not behave as if it were the original (*na sthānivat*). Examples:
*śiṃṣanti*, *piṃṣanti*.
When the substitution of *anusvāra* is to be applied by the rule *naś cāpadāntasya jhali* (P. 8.3.24), the elision of the *a* of *śnas* (i.e., *śnam* and *as*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.
Regarding the rule for long vowels: with respect to the application of a long vowel, a substitute for *ac* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.
[The substitution of *u* for *an* occurs] in place of this *bha*-stem [ending in *an*]: *pratidīvnā*, *pratidīvne*, and *pratidivan* (cf. Pāṇini 6.4.129).

With reference to this, in the third case singular and the fourth case singular, the elision of the vowel *a* in *anaḥ* according to Pāṇini 6.4.134 (*allopo 'naḥ*) is conditioned by a subsequent element;
due to the status of that [elided vowel] as *sthānivadbhāva*, [the rule] *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77) applies.
Thus, the lengthening would not occur,
for this *v* is not followed by a consonant (*hal*); it is only by virtue of this specific rule that it takes place.

The *jaś*-rule: with respect to the application of a *jaś* substitute, a substitute beginning with *a* (an *aj-ādeśa*) does not behave as if it were the original (*na sthānivat*). Examples: *sagdhiś ca me sapītiś ca me*;
*babdhāṃ te harī dhānāḥ*.
By the rule *adeḥ ktini bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.39), there is the substitution of *ghas* for the root *ad*;
and by *ghasi-bhasor hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.100), [the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs].
Thus, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel;
then, by the rule *jhalo jhaṃli* (Pāṇini 8.2.26), there is the elision of the letter *s*.
By the rule *jhaṣas ta-thor dho 'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), *ta* and *tha* are replaced by *dha*;
because the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53) applies.
Thus, the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound for the letter *gh* would not occur; however, by this specific rule, it does occur:
*samanā gdhiḥ*.
The substitution of *sa* for *samāna* results in *sagdhiḥ*.
In the form *babdhām*, the root *bhas* appears in the second person dual of the imperative (*loṭ*), with the elision (*slu*) of the suffix *śap*.

Reduplication, the grammatical operation pertaining to the reduplicated syllable, and [the substitution of *gh* for *han* and *bh* for *bhas*] before a consonant (hal) as well as in the verbal roots *ghas* and *bhas* (Pāṇini 6.4.100).
Thus, there is the elision of the *upadhā* vowel;
then, by the rule *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26), there is the elision of the letter *s*.
By the rule *jhaṣas ta-thor dho 'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), there is the substitution of *dh* for *t*.

Because of the status of the substitute as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) regarding the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), the rule *jhalām jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53) applies.

Thus, the substitution of *jaś* would not occur; however, by this rule, it does occur. Regarding the rule for *car*: with respect to the application of a *car* substitute, the substitute for *ac* is not treated as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhavati*).
They have eaten;
they have eaten; those ancestors have eaten; the ancestors have rejoiced.
In the case of the dual and plural of the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, there is the substitution of *ghas* for the root *ad*; then,

by the rule "there is elision of the penultimate vowel of the roots *gam*, *han*, *jan*, *khan*, and *ghas* before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, except when it is *aṅ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.98), the penultimate vowel is elided.
The doubling [of the root] is the operation pertaining to the reduplication (abhyāsa).
In that case, because the elision of the penultimate vowel (upadhā-lopa) is treated as if it were the original element (sthānivadbhāva), [the rule] *khari ca* (*Pāṇini 8.4.55*) applies.
Thus, the substitution of *c* for the letter *gh* would not occur;
however, it does occur by virtue of this specific rule.
Furthermore, the substitution of *ś* occurs [for *gh*] by the rule "of *śās*, *vas*, and *ghas*" (Pāṇini 8.3.60).
In the form *akṣan*, there is the substitution of *ghas* for the root *ad* in the third person plural *luṅ*;
the suffix *cli* that follows is elided by the rule *mantre ghasa-hvara* (Pāṇini 2.4.80);
and the final consonant of the roots *gam*, *han*, *jan*, *khan*, and *ghas* is elided before a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, except when it is *anaṅ* (Pāṇini 6.4.98).
Thus, there is the elision of the *upadhā* vowel;
because that [elision] is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitution of the sibilant (*cartva*) by rule Pāṇini 8.4.55 (*khari ca*) would not occur.
From this statement it follows:

in the cases of vowel (*svara*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), *yaṇ*-substitution (*ya*), and elision (*lopa*), an elided element or a substitute beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) is not treated as if it were in its original place (*na sthānivat*);
in other cases, it is indeed treated as if it were in its original place (*sthānivad eva*).
Therefore, [the forms] *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*,
*kiryoh*, and *giryoh* [are derived].
In the case of *vāyvoḥ*, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), vowel-quality (*svara*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and elision (*lopa*) do not occur. [P. 1.1.59:

"In reduplication (*dvirvacana*), when *ac* is the cause, a substitute for an *ac* vowel is treated as the original (*sthānivat*). This means that when *ac* is the cause of reduplication, a substitute for an *ac* vowel is treated as the original.
Since the reduplication itself must be performed,
this substitution of form is restricted in its timing;
therefore, once the reduplication has been made, only the substituted form remains.
The elision of *āl*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), the elision of the suffix *ṇi*, and the substitutions of *yaṇ*, *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv* are the purposes [of this rule].
Regarding the elision of *āl*: *papatuḥ*, *papuḥ*.

When the elision of the vowel *ā* is effected by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64), because that [elided element] possesses the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), reduplication occurs according to the rule *eka-aco dve prathamasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.1).

There is elision of the penultimate vowel (upadhā-lopaḥ): *jaghnatuḥ*, *jaghnuḥ*. [This is according to] Pāṇini 6.4.98: "In place of the [vowel] of the roots √gam, √han, √jan, √khan, and √ghas, there is elision before an affix marked with K or Ṅ, except for the augment anaṅ."

Thus, when the elision of the *au* augment (*aupadhā-lopa*) has occurred, there would be no reduplication because of the absence of a vowel (*anackatvāt*); however, by virtue of this specific rule, it does take place.
As for the elision of the *ṇi* suffix: *āṭ-iṭat*.

In the case of the root *aṭ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, when the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is applied and the *ṇi* is elided, because that [elision] is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the rule "the second syllable beginning with a vowel" (*aj-āder dvitīyasya*) applies, resulting in the doubling of the syllable *ṭi*.
After the *yaṇ* substitution, the form is *cakratuḥ*.
They formed [the word] *cakruḥ*.

When the substitution of *yaṇ* has been applied to both the *atus* and the *us* suffixes of the root *kṛ*, reduplication would not occur because [the resulting form] lacks a vowel; however, it does occur by virtue of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
The substitutions *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv*: *ninaya*, *nināya*;
*lulava*, *lulāva*.
When the suffix *ṇal* follows the roots *nī* and *lū*, after the application of *guṇa* and subsequently *vṛddhi*, the substitutions *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv* take place.
Because they possess the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the doubling (*dvirvacana*) occurs according to the rule *ne naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.4).
Why is it said "when doubling is to be performed"? [Consider the examples:
*jagle*, *mamle*.
The substitution of the vowel *ā* does not occur [for the *u* of the desiderative suffix].
Why [is it specified] "when there is a cause for reduplication"? [Consider: *dudyūṣati*.
In this case, the *yaṇ*-substitution [of *u* for *ū*] in the formation of *ūṭ* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*.
Why is it specified that [the suffix] is *aci*? [Consider:
*jeghrīyate*, *dedhmīyate*. [This is by the rule: *ī ghrā-dhmoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.31).

Furthermore, by the rule *yaṅi ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.30), there is the substitution of the vowel *ī*; because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), there would be reduplication of the vowel *ā*.
It does not occur because of the inclusion of the term *aj*.
"Non-appearance is elision" (Pāṇini 1.1.60). Non-appearance means non-hearing,
non-utterance.
Non-apprehension,
non-existence,
and the destruction of color are synonymous.
The designation "elision" (lopa) applies to that meaning which is expressed by these words;
this is a designation for the meaning.
The non-appearance of a sound that has occurred is termed *lopa* (elision). [For example:
from *godhā*, by [the suffix] *ḍhrak* (*Pāṇini 4.1.129*), we get *gaudheraḥ*.
May he be long-lived;
may the giver of life grant us life;
may the seeker of strength attain strength.
The non-appearance of the phonemes *ya* and *va* is the example here;
it refers to another [element], such as an *anubandha*, that would otherwise have been applicable.
The rules for elision (*lopa*) are: "There is elision of *y* and *v* before a consonant" (*lopo vyor vali*).
And so forth.
(Pāṇini 1.1.61): "The elision (*luk*), the *ślu* suffix, and the *lup* suffix [are applied] to an affix (*pratyaya*).
The term "non-appearance" (*adarśana*) carries over [from the previous rule].
The terms *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* are the designations for the non-appearance (*adarśana*) of an affix (*pratyaya*).
And because multiple designations are prescribed here, it is understood that the term refers to that which is permeated by those [designations].
That which is characterized by the designation *luk* becomes designated as *luk*;
that which is characterized by the designation *ślu* becomes designated as *ślu*; and that which is characterized by the designation *lup* becomes designated as *lup*.
Therefore, there is no confusion among technical designations (*saṃjñā*);
furthermore, in the rules and prescriptions (*vidhi-pradeśa*), a designation is understood as being prospective (*bhāvinī*). [For example:
*atti*.
He offers oblations.
*Varaṇāḥ*.

Rules concerning *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup*: *luk* [is applied] when a *taddhita* suffix is elided (*Pāṇini 1.2.49*);
*ślu* [is applied] after roots such as *juhoti* (*Pāṇini 2.4.75*).
The rule "janapade lup" (Pāṇini 4.2.81) and others such as these [apply].
"When there is the elision of an affix, the operation conditioned by that affix [takes place]. (Pāṇini 1.1.62).
This sūtra is commenced so that an operation caused by an affix might indeed take place even when the affix is absent.
When the elision of an affix has been performed, the operation conditioned by the affix—that is, the operation caused by the affix—occurs.

In the case of *agnicit*, *somasut*, and *adhok*, where the nominal suffix (*sup*) and the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) have been elided, the word is defined as that which ends in a nominal suffix or a verbal suffix (Pāṇini 1.4.14).
Thus, the designation *pada* is established.

In the form *adhok*, it is derived from the root *duh* with the suffix *laṅ*, the suffix *tip*, the elision of *śap*, and the elision of *ti*; then, having applied the substitution of *gh* for *dh*, the *bhaṣ*-bhāva, the *jaś*-tva, and the *cartva* substitutions, the form is obtained.
While the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is already understood [from the previous rule], why is the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) mentioned again?
This is so that [the substitution] may occur when there is the elision of the entire suffix (*pratyaya*), but it should not occur here: *āghnīya*,
*saṅgmīya*.

In the case of *han* and *gam*, when the *liṅ* (optative) in the *ātmanepada* occurs, the *sakāra* of *sīyuṭ* is elided by the rule "the *sakāra* of the *liṅ* is elided, except for the final one" (*Pāṇini* 7.2.79). This is an elision of a portion of the affix (*pratyaya-ekadeśa-lopa*).

In that instance, because it is a portion of the affix, the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*)—which would otherwise apply by the rule "before a *jhal* [consonant]" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.37)—does not take place due to the principle of "characterization by the affix" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*).
What is the characteristic of a compound? For example: *rāyaḥ kulam* becomes *raikulam*;
*gave hitam* becomes *go hitam*.
The substitutions of *ā* and *ay* do not occur, because they depend upon the phonemes [rather than the word].
*na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63).
Since the previous rule had over-extended the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix), this specific prohibition is stated.
When a suffix is elided by a word containing the term *lumat*, whatever constitutes the *aṅga* (base) [is not subject to those operations].
For that [suffix], the characteristic of being a condition (pratyaya-lakṣaṇa) does not apply to the effect (kārya). Examples: gargāḥ;
mṛṣṭaḥ.

when the suffixes *yañ* and *śap* are elided by means of the term *lumat*, the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions do not occur for the base (*aṅga*).
Why [is it specified] "by means of *lumat*"? [Consider: *kāryate*.
It is elided.

And so forth.

when there is a reference by means of the locative case (*saptamī*), the grammatical operation applies to the preceding element, not to the following one.
*i* is replaced by *yaṇ* before a vowel (*aci*)— as in *dadhyudakam*,
*madhvidam*,
and *pacatyodanam*.

"From that" (tasmāt), [referring to] the subsequent [element] (uttarasya). The term "nirdiṣṭa" (specified) is understood by way of anuvṛtti.

A word's own form is [meant] when it is not a technical term (aśabda-sañjñā).

and not an external object.
Excluding the designation "word" (śabda-sañjñā).

Since the comprehension of meaning occurs through the word, and because a grammatical operation cannot apply to the meaning itself, this sūtra is commenced so that there may be no application of operations to those words that denote it.
[The rule] *agner ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33): "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni" (*āgneyam aṣṭā-kapālaṃ nirvapet*).

A vowel (ac) having the duration of an *u*-sound is respectively termed short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), or protracted (*pluta*).

The syllable *ū* is a collective designation for the three [vowels] consisting of one mora (*mātrika*), two moras (*dvimātrika*), and three moras (*trimātrika*). Words such as *udātta* and so forth are indeed well-known in both worldly and Vedic usage as accents that are properties of phonemes (*varṇadharma*).

For phonemes are produced in the constituent parts of the articulatory locations, such as the palate and so forth.
Among these, a vowel that is produced in the upper part of a common location is designated as *udātta* (high-pitched).
When it is being uttered, there occurs an extension and tension of the limbs.

The second syllable is *anudātta*. the remainder is anudātta.

This is because, in the rule prescribing the suffix *kyap*— namely, *sañjñāyāṃ samajaniṣadanipatamanavidaṣuñ śīṅbhṛñiṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.99)— the term "acute" (*udātta*) is understood to carry over from the preceding context.

The [vowel] following the words *deva* and *brahman* is unaccented.

furthermore, it becomes a circumflex (svarita) by the rule "an unaccented vowel following an accented one becomes svarita" (*Pāṇini 8.4.66*).

In that case, the single substitute *o* resulting from the combination of two anudātta vowels is itself anudātta; however, when followed by an udātta vowel, it undergoes the substitution of *sannatara* (more deeply depressed).

Because *śutudri* is a vocative at the beginning of a metrical foot (*pāda*), it is not subject to the low pitch (anudātta).
"Everything is unaccented except at the beginning of a metrical foot" (Pāṇini 8.1.18).
Of that [unaccented portion], the first syllable is acute; when that follows, the vowel *i* in *sarasvati* undergoes the substitution of *sannatara*. Example:
*māṇavaka jaṭilakādyāpaka kva gamiṣyasi*.
When the svarita vowel *kva* follows, the anudātta vowel *ka* undergoes the substitution of a more depressed (sannatara) accent.
A single-letter suffix that is not joined [with another element] is called *apṛkta*.
The technical designation *apṛkta* applies to that suffix which consists of a single phoneme (*ekāl*). The word *eka* expresses the sense of "unaccompanied" (*asahāya*).
The suffix *kvin* is applied after the root *spṛś-* when it does not mean "water": *dhṛtaspṛk* ("one who touches clarified butter").
The suffix *ṇvi* is applied after the root *bhaj-*: *ardhabhāk* ("sharing half") and *pādabhāk* ("sharing a quarter").
Why specify "ending in -al"? [Consider] *darviḥ* and *jāgṛviḥ*.
Why specify "an affix" (*pratyaya*)? [Consider] *surāḥ*.
