*vyatihāra* means exchange.
When one person performs an action belonging to another, and another person performs an action belonging to the first,
that is the exchange of actions (*karmavyatihāra*).
The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after a verbal root that expresses an action characterized by that [reciprocity]. For example:
*vyatilunate*, *vyatipunate*.
What is the purpose of [the rule] "in the case of the exchange of actions" (*karma-vyatihāre*)? [Consider: *lunanti* ("they cut").

The mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is for the sake of what follows, namely, [the rule] "from the remainder, the *parasmaipada* occurs when the agent is expressed" (*śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam*, Pāṇini 1.3.78).
Not after [roots] meaning motion or injury. (PS 1.3.15)
By this [rule], the *ātmanepada* which was previously applicable is prohibited.
For roots meaning "motion" (*gaty-artha*) and roots meaning "injury" (*hiṃsā-artha*), the *ātmanepada* does not occur when there is a reciprocal action (*karma-vyatihāra*).
They pass by;
they glide past;
from roots meaning "to injure"—they injure one another.
They strike one another.
Regarding the prohibition [of the *ātmanepada*], there is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *has* and other verbs:
they laugh together.
They converse with one another;
they recite together.
There is no prohibition regarding the root *harati*.
The kings strike one another.
And [the suffix *kṛt* is used] after the prepositions *itaretara* and *anyonya*. (Pāṇini 3.3.16)
After the words *itaretara* and *anyonya* as upapadas, the ātmanepada suffix does not occur after a verbal root when there is a mutual exchange of actions.
They cut each other across;
they cut one another across.
And it should be stated that this occurs when there is a reciprocal prefix.
They cut each other across.
Nor [does he enter] the people. // PS_1,3.17 //

Since the *parasmaipada* would have applied by the rule "after [roots ending in] *śas*, the *parasmaipada* occurs when the agent is expressed" (Pāṇini 1.3.78), the *ātmanepada* is prescribed for the root *viś* preceded by the prefix *ni*.
After the prefix *ni*, the *ātmanepada* endings are used for the root *viś*. For example:
*niviśate*, *niviśante*.
Why [is the word] *neḥ* used? [Consider: *praviśati*.
Since augmentations (*āgama*) are included by the mention of the element they augment, there is no intervention by the augment *aṭ* [in this case]. [But consider:
*nyaviśata*.

In this case, there is no inclusion of the prefix (*upasarga*), because when there is the mention of that which possesses meaning, there is no mention of that which is meaningless. Therefore, it does not occur here.
The bees rest within the honey.
The root √kṛ (to do/make) is used with the prefixes pari, vi, and ava.
The root *ḍukrīñ* is used in the sense of "exchanging goods. Because it bears the marker *ñit*, the *ātmanepada* ending is established when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent.
This undertaking has the sense of "not intending for the agent.
The *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *krī* (to buy) when preceded by *pari*, *vi*, or *ava*. For example: *parikrīṇīte*.
He sells;
he buys back.
The prefixes beginning with *pari* are understood [in this rule]; therefore, it does not apply here: [e.g.,] *paryākaroti*.
He buys the forest for much.
The suffix *ātmanepada* is applied after the root *ji* when preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *parā-*.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam* (Pāṇini 1.3.78).
The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the root *ji* when preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *parā-*. For example: *vijayate*, *parājayate*.
The prefixes *vi-* and *parā-* are understood [here] because of their association;
therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *bahuvi jayati vanam*.
"The army conquers the enemy."
The substitution of *d* for the final *aṅ* occurs except when it refers to the act of moving the nose.
This rule is commenced for the purpose of expressing that the action is not intended for the agent.
The *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the root *dā* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, when it signifies the non-opening of the mouth.
One takes up the sacrificial ladle (*vidhi*). Why [is it specified] "not opening the mouth" (*an-āsya-viharaṇe*)? [Because otherwise one would include:
he opens his mouth (*āsyaṃ vyādadāti*).
A prohibition must also be stated for actions identical to opening the mouth:
"He opens his gouty swelling" (*vipādikāṃ vyādadāti*) and "He opens the house" (*kulaṃ vyādadāti*).

It should be stated that [the rule applies] even when the action concerns one's own body parts (*svāṅga*). This is so that it does not apply here: *vyādadate pipīlikāḥ pataṅgasya mukham* ("The ants open the mouth of the moth").
Also, [the root] *krīḍ* [is ātmanepada] after the prefixes *anu*, *sam*, and *pari*. (Pāṇini 1.3.21)
The root *krīḍ* (to play) is used in the sense of sporting;
after this root, as well as after the same root preceded by *anu*, *sam*, and *pari*, and also when preceded by *ā*, the Ātmanepada voice occurs.
He plays after, he plays together with,
he plays around.
Furthermore, from the prefix *ā*: *ākrīḍate*.
Because of its association with *sam*, the term *upasarga* (preverb) is understood here as beginning with *anv-*.
Therefore, in this case, when used with a *karmapravacanīya* (governing particle), the [suffix] does not occur.
The root *māṇavaka* is used in the sense of "playing.
It should be stated that [the prefix] *sam-* is used in the sense of "not making a sound":
carts play together (*saṅkrīḍanti*).
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) should be prescribed for the root *ā-gam* in the sense of "endurance" (*kṣamā*).
Endurance means indifference,
that is to say, the passing of time.
Wait for the young man for a moment;
you shall learn in your desire to know.
He trains himself in the sciences.
The root *nāth* is used in the sense of "blessing" (*āśis*). He prays for ghee;
he prays for honey.
Why does it say "in the sense of a blessing" (āśiṣi)? [Consider:
*māṇavakam anunāthati* ("he entreats the boy").
[The rule] *harateḥ gata-tācchīlye* ("after *hṛ*, when expressing a habitual action of going") [is also relevant].
Horses imitate their father; cows imitate their mother. Why is it specified "when there is a habitual tendency"? [To exclude cases such as: "The horses imitated their father once."
It follows the meaning of the mother [root].
It should be stated that *kṛ* (kirati) is used in the senses of rejoicing, making a livelihood, and making a dwelling.
"The bull, being joyful, wallows" (*apaskirate*).
In the sense of seeking a livelihood: "The cock scratches for the sake of food. In the sense of making a nest: "The dog scratches for the sake of a dwelling.
Why [is it said] "in cases such as joy and the like"? [To exclude cases not falling under these categories.]
He scatters flowers. An addition [to the rule] should be made for the roots *nup* and *pracch*: the jackal howls.
One asks leave of the teacher. It should be stated that [the root] *śap* means "touching. Touching is the contact of the body with speech.
He curses Devadatta;
he curses Yajñadatta. Why is it said "in the sense of reproaching"? [Because in other cases one simply] curses. [57]
The root *sthā* [takes the ātmanepada endings] after the prefixes *sam*, *ava*, *pra*, and *vi*.
The *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *sthā* preceded by *sam*, *ava*, or *pra*; for example:
*saṃtiṣṭhate*.
It is stated that [the rule] "after *āṅ*, *sthā* [is used] in the sense of promising" should be formulated. *Avatiṣṭhate*; *vitiṣṭhate*.
He maintains the letter *s* as being present;
he maintains that both grammatical operations, namely *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, are present.
And [the same applies] to the faults known as *prakāśana* (exposure) and *stheya* (obstinacy). PS 1.3.23.
*Prakāśana* is the expression of one's own intention.
The designation of the arbitrator is *stheyākhyā*.
That in which one stands is "stheya" (the arbitrator).
One who decides a point of dispute is well-known in the world as "stheya. The mention of the title is for the purpose of identifying him.

The *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the root *sthā* when it means "to be manifest" (*prakāśana*) and when it is called "staying" (*stheya*). First, regarding "to be manifest": *tiṣṭhate kanyā dhātrebhyaḥ* (the maiden stands [manifest] for her suitors);
*tiṣṭhate vṛṣalī grāma-putrebhyaḥ* (the low-caste woman stands [manifest] for the village youths).
The meaning is that it manifests itself.
Regarding the verbal form *stheyā*— it means "it abides in you" or "it abides in me."
He who remains in doubt regarding Karṇa and the others.
The prefix *ud-* is used in the sense of "not upward" (*anūrdhva*) action.
The ātmanepada occurs after the verb *sthā* preceded by the prefix *ud*, provided it does not denote an upward action; here,
the word *karman* signifies "action."
The *ātmanepada* affix occurs after the verb *tiṣṭhati* when it expresses an action characterized by non-ascension; for example:
*gehe uttiṣṭhate* (he remains at home), *kuṭumbe uttiṣṭhate* (he remains with his family).

The meaning is that one exerts effort for that purpose. It should be stated that [the substitution of] *ī* occurs in the sense of striving (*īhā*). Let it not apply here: "A hundred [coins] arise from this village" (*asmād grāmāt śatam uttiṣṭhati*).
The meaning is that one hundred [moments] arise.
The mention of "striving" (*īha*) is a qualification of non-superior karma itself,
not an exception (*apavāda*).
Why is it specified "in an action that is not upward"? [Consider:
He rises from his seat.
The *upā* [prefix] is used when the act of making a mantra is intended. // PS 1.3.25 //

After the root *sthā* preceded by *upa*, when it signifies the employment of a mantra, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs. For example: *aindryā gārhapatyam upatiṣṭhate* ("He worships the Gārhapatya fire with a verse addressed to Indra").
One worships the *ānīghra* fire-altar with a verse dedicated to Agni.
Why [is it specified] "in the case of a mantra being the instrument"? [Consider: "She honors her husband with her youth."
The term *upa* should be stated [as governing the accusative] in the senses of "worshiping a deity," "associating with," and "acting as a friend.
Regarding worshiping a deity: *ādityam upatiṣṭhate* (he worships the sun). Regarding associating with: *rathikān upatiṣṭhate* (he associates with charioteers).
Regarding the making of friends: he attends upon the high ministers.
What is the difference between "making friends" (*mitrakaraṇa*) and "establishing alliances" (*saṅgatakaraṇa*)?
Establishing alliances is close physical proximity.

For example: "The Gaṅgā flows toward the Yamunā. Furthermore, the formation of friendship (*maitrī-sambandha*) occurs even without physical contact, as in the case of making friends. On the road: "This path leads to Strughna. [58]
Or it should be stated [as a rule]: "in the sense of desiring to obtain.
Thus, a mendicant approaches a brahmin family; he approaches (upatiṣṭhate) or he attends upon (upatiṣṭhati).
And [the suffix *ya* is applied] after a verbal root that does not take an object.

The term "upāt" (preceded by *upa*) continues [from the previous rule]. The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the root *sthā* when it is preceded by *upa*, provided that it is intransitive— that is, when it expresses an action that does not take an object.
It remains as long as it has been eaten;
it remains as long as the rice has been eaten.
In the word *bhuktam*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the action (*bhāve*).
The meaning is that it is placed near at every meal.
Why [is the condition] "after an intransitive verb" stated? [Consider:
*rājānam upatiṣṭhati* ("he waits upon the king").
The root *tap* [takes the Ātmanepada suffixes] after the prefixes *ud* and *vi*.
The term "from an intransitive [verb]" (akarmakāt) continues to apply.
The ātmanepada occurs after the root *tap* preceded by *ud* or *vi*, provided that it expresses an action denoting an intransitive state.
It means "it blazes," "it shines forth," or "it is radiant."
The rule "from an intransitive verb" (akarmakāt) applies here as well:
*suvarṇakāra uttapati suvarṇam* ("the goldsmith heats the gold"); *savitā vitapati pṛthvīm* ("the sun heats the earth").
It should be stated that [the verb *tapa* takes the ātmanepada ending] even when its own body part is the object:
*uttapate pāṇim*, *uttapate pṛṣṭham*.
"He fans his hand; he fans his back.
And here, "own limb" (*svāṅga*) is not taken in its technical sense as defined by the rule: "a non-fluid, corporeal own limb."
What then? "One's own limb" means *svāṅga*. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of:
"Devadatta heats Yajñadatta's back."
Why [is it specified] "with *ud* and *vi*"? [Consider: *niṣṭapati*.
The suffix *ātmanepada* is applied after the roots *yama* and *hana* when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*.
The term "from an intransitive verb" (akarmakāt) is understood [to apply here]. The root *yama* means "to cease."

The roots *hana* and *hiṃs* (meaning "to strike" and "to go," respectively) are conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. However, when preceded by the prefix *ā*, they take the *ātmanepada* when expressing an intransitive action.
Examples: *āyacchate*, *āyacchete*, *āyacchante*.
Furthermore, there is the root *han*: *āhate*, *āghnāte*, *āghnate*.
[This applies] only when [the root] is intransitive (*akarmakāt*).
He draws a rope from a well;
he strikes a low-born man with his foot.
It should be stated that [the rule applies] also when the action has one's own limb as its object.
He stretches out his hand;
he strikes his head.
And here, "own limb" (*svāṅga*) is not understood in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense.
What then? "Svāṅga" means one's own limb. Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of: "he strikes another's head."
The roots √gam, √ṛcch, √prach, √svar, √ṛ, √śru, and √vidi (vid) are treated like √sā when followed by the suffixes of the periphrastic future.
The term "from an intransitive verb" (akarmakāt) is understood [from the preceding rule].
From the remainder, the *parasmaipada* endings are used for the agent (*kartari*) [according to Pāṇini 1.3.78].

This being the case, the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] occurs after these roots—*gam*, *ṛcch*, *pracch*, *svar*, *ṛ*, *śru*, and *vid*—when they are preceded by the prefix *sam* and are intransitive (*akarmaka*). For example:
*saṅgacchate*, *amṛddhate*.
He inquires;
he chants together;
his intentions were harmonized.
By the rule *arter luṅ-liṭoś ca ti-śāsty-artistibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.56), the substitution of *aṅ* occurs;
in that context, the phrase "in the parasmaipada" is not taken into account.
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasy amāṅyoge 'pi* (Pāṇini 6.4.75), the augment *āṭ* is prohibited; furthermore,
by *ṛdṛśo 'ṅi guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.16), there is *guṇa* substitution for the vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ* before the suffix *aṅ*.
Thus is the suffix *guṇa*: *samaraṇata*,
*saṃśṛṇute*,
*saṃvitte*.
The term *ṛccher* refers to the substitute [for *ṛch*]; thus, *samṛcchiṣyate* [is formed].
However, for the substitute of *ṛti*, the Ātmanepada is already established by the rule itself (*arti*).
The root *ṛ* is listed in both places:
as *ṛ* in the sense of "motion" and "attaining" in the *bhū*-class (*bhvādi*), and as *ṛ* (or *sṛ*) in the sense of "motion" in the *juhoty*-class (*juhotyādi*).
Since there is no distinction between the two, both are included;
the root *vid* is understood here in the sense of "knowledge" because of its association with roots such as *gam*, which take the *parasmaipada* endings.

It should be stated that [the rule] "of *dṛś*" applies even when it is not for the sake of profit (*lābha-artha*), because it is marked with the svarita accent and is spoken in both ways (i.e., both parasmaipada and ātmanepada). Example:
*saṃpaśyate*.
Only after [the rule] "after an intransitive verb" (akarmakāt):
he perceives the village.
The root *hve* [takes the ātmanepada suffixes] after the prefixes *ni*, *sam*, *upa*, and *vi*.
The phrase "from an intransitive verb" (akarmakāt) has ceased to apply.
From this point forward, the prescription of the middle voice (ātmanepada) is to be understood as applying generally.
With the prefixes *ni*, *sam*, and *upa*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs after the root *hve* (to call); for example:
*nihvayate*, *saṃhvayate*, and *upahvayate*.
He calls out to himself.

This rule is commenced for the sake of meaning where there is no intention directed toward an agent; for otherwise, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would already be established by virtue of the *ñit* marker.
There is an optional rule regarding the prefix *upa* before the roots *as* and *ūh*:
one says either *nirasyati*, *nirasyate*;
*samūhati*, *samūhate*.
The prefix *āṅ* [is used] in the sense of rivalry (*spardhā*).
This undertaking has the sense of "not intending for the agent" (*akartr-abhiprāya*).
When *spardhā* (rivalry) is the object, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs after the root *hvayati* (to call/challenge) preceded by the prefix *ā*.
Rivalry is competition,
the desire to overcome another;
that is the object of the meaning of the verbal root.
The *dhātu*, however, consists of sound alone:
*mallaḥ mallam āhvayate* (the wrestler challenges the wrestler); *chātraḥ chātram āhvayate* (the student challenges the student).
The meaning is that, being in competition, he issues a challenge to him.
Why [is the word] "in competition" (spardhāyām) used? [Consider:
"The cowherd calls the cow."
The verb *kṛ* (to do/make) is used with the locative case when it signifies: smelling, throwing down, serving, violence, effort, speaking, and employment. (Pāṇini 1.3.32)

When the fruit of the action is intended for the agent, the ātmanepada ending is already established. This new rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding cases where the fruit is not intended for the agent.

The *ātmanepada* affix occurs after the root *kṛ* when it is employed in the senses of "hinting" (*gandhana*) and so forth. Here, "hinting" (*gandhana*) refers to an indication characterized by injury that is prompted by another. For instance, [the root] *basti* is used in the sense of "injury" (*ardana*).
The root *ard* is listed in the *cur*-class (the tenth class) in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*).
"Threatening" (*avakṣepaṇa*) means reviling;
"service" (*sevana*) means compliance.
*Saḥasikya* is a rash act;
*pratiyatna* is the imparting of a new quality to that which already exists;
*prakathana* is speaking with excellence.
*Upayoga* is the purpose, such as dharma and so forth; *viniyoga* is the application.
Regarding *gandhana*, first: he elevates (*utkurute*);
he brings forth (*udākurute*).
The meaning is "indicates.
In the sense of "throwing down": *śyena udākurute vartikām*—it means "he threatens. *sevate*—*gaṇakān upakurute*—he serves the accountants.
"He assists the high officials" means he serves them;
"in acts of violence" means he commits adultery with the wives of others. [60]
The meaning is that one engages with them suddenly. Regarding the sense of "preparation" (*pratiyatna*): *edho dakasyopaskurute* (he prepares fuel for the water);
*kāṇḍaṃ guḍasyopaskurute* (he prepares a piece of sugarcane for the molasses).

The meaning is that it effects the addition of another quality to that which already exists. In the case of the sixth case-ending and the suffix *suṭ*, only "effort for improvement" (*pratiyatna*) is prescribed for the root *kṛ*. In the sense of "reciting," as in: *gāthāḥ prakurute* ("he composes verses").
He utters public censure;
the meaning is that he speaks with vehemence.
In the sense of employment: he employs a hundred [pieces].
"He makes a thousand" means he allocates a hundred for the sake of Dharma.
Why [is the word] "in these" used?
He makes a mat.
The root *adhi* is used in the sense of "overpowering."
This undertaking has the sense of "not intending for the agent.
The *ātmanepada* affix occurs after the root *kṛ*, preceded by the prefix *adhi*, when it signifies "overpowering" (*prasahana*).
*Prasahana* means overcoming or being undefeated;
he overcame that,
he surpassed it.
The meaning is that he has not been driven away by him. Why [is it said] "in the sense of overcoming"? [Consider: he devotes himself to wealth.
The formulation of a separate rule is for the purpose of qualifying the prefix.
The root *vi* [is used in the sense of motion] when its object is sound.

The term *kṛñaḥ* (of the root *kṛ*) is understood [from the previous rule]. When preceded by the prefix *vi-*, the root *karoti* takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) when the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent and when sound is the object.
In this context, the word *karman* denotes the grammatical participant (*kāraka*), not the action (*kriyā*). For example: "The jackal modifies its notes" (*kroṣṭā vikurute svarān*).
"A crow utters cries"—why [is this] mentioned under the rule for the action of sound (*śabdakarmaṇaḥ*)? [Because in the following case, it is not so:
"the milk transforms."
And [the suffix *ya* is applied] after a verbal root that does not take an object (*akarmaka*).
The phrase "after the root *kṛ* following *vi*" is understood [from the previous rule].
The ātmanepada occurs after the root *kṛ* preceded by *vi*, provided that it is intransitive—that is, when it expresses an action that does not involve an object.
The Saindhava horses perform transformations;
that is to say, being well-trained, they gallop beautifully.
The students, full of rice, perform transformations.
The meaning is that they act fruitlessly.
The root *ni* is used in the sense of honoring, lifting up, acting as a teacher, knowing, maintaining, counting, and spending. (Pāṇini 1.3.36)
The root *ṇīñ* in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*):
when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartr-abhiprāye kriyāphale*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is already established by rule.
This undertaking has the sense of intending for the non-agent (akartr-abhiprāya).

From this root *ṇīñ* in the sense of "attaining," the ātmanepada [suffix] occurs when there are qualifiers such as "honoring" (sammānana) and so forth. Honoring is worship; for example: *nayate cārvī lokāyate* ("The clever one leads [people] toward the Lokāyata").
The intellect is "cārvī";
because of its connection with that [intellect], the teacher is also called "cārvī. He leads the categories of meaning in the Lokāyata treatise.
Having stabilized [the teaching] through arguments, he causes it to reach the disciples;
being established by means of logical reasoning, they become honored and revered.
"Utsañjana" means lifting up—as in, "he raises up the young student."
The meaning is "he raises up.

*Ācārya-karaṇa* is the act of making someone an *ācārya*—that is, he brings the young student (*māṇavaka*) near to himself by such a procedure that the one who initiates him (*upanetā*) himself becomes the *ācārya*. He initiates the young student (*māṇavakam upanayate*).
The meaning is that one who makes himself a teacher brings the student into his presence.
Knowledge is the ascertainment of the object of cognition (*prameya*); it leads one forward, that is, it causes one to perceive.
In that regard, the meaning is that one ascertains the object of cognition.
*Bhṛti* is wages—[the king] "brings near" (*upanayate*) laborers;
the meaning is that he brings them close by means of the payment of wages.
*Vigaṇanam* is the repayment of debts and so forth—the Madras "bring in" (*vinayante*) tribute.
The meaning is that they hand over [the property]. "Expenditure" (vyaya) is the application [of wealth] toward the Dharma and so forth; for example, "he spends a hundred [pieces of gold]."
"He disciplines a thousand";
the meaning is that he employs a hundred for the sake of religious duties and so forth.
Why [is the word] "in these" used?
"He leads the goat to the village.
And [the same applies when the object] is the body, provided it resides in the agent. (Pāṇini 1.4.52) *Pāṇinīyaśikṣā* 1.3.37.
The agent of the root *nī* (to lead), such as Devadatta and others, is expressed by the *l*-suffixes.
When the object resides in the agent and is not corporeal, the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the root *nī*.
The body is the collection of living beings;
even a single part of it is called "the body.
One subdues anger toward it.
One subdues anger (*manyuṃ vinayate*).
Why specify "when residing in the agent" (*kartṛsthe*)? [Consider:
Devadatta subdues Yajñadatta’s anger (*devadatto yajñadattasya krodhaṃ vinayati*).
Why "without a body" (*aśarīre*)? [Consider:
*gaḍuṃ vinayati* (he removes a goitre);
*ghāṭāṃ vinayati* (he removes a protuberance).
Why is it specified "in the sense of the object" (karmaṇi)? [Because in other cases:
he disciplines by means of intelligence;
he disciplines by means of wisdom.
The sequence [of the powers] occurs in respect to subsistence, creation, and protection. (PS 1.3.38)

When the *śeṣa* (remaining) [roots] would otherwise take the *parasmaipada* in the active voice (*kartṛ*), the *ātmanepada* occurs after a root when used in the senses of "unimpeded progress" (*vṛtti*) and so forth, as well as in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Unimpeded progress (*vṛtti*) means lack of obstruction.
*Sarga* means enthusiasm;
*tāyana* means expansion. Regarding the commentary (*vṛtti*): "The intellect of one who is diligent (*ṛkṣva*) proceeds."
The meaning is that he is not obstructed.
His intellect proceeds toward the *yajus* formulas;
he proceeds toward the *sarga*, that is, toward the study of grammar.
The meaning is "it is capable.
It is extended (*tāyate*): even by means of this treatise, people proceed;
the meaning is that they flourish.
What is the purpose of the phrase "in these"? [It is to exclude:
"he departs."
[The suffix *ghañ* is used after the root *i* when preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *parā*. (Pāṇini 3.3.39)

The phrase "in the senses of livelihood (vṛtti), creation (sarga), and extension (tāyana)" is understood to carry over. The ātmanepada ending occurs after the root *kram* when it is preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *parā*, provided it functions in the senses of livelihood and so forth.
For what purpose, then, is this stated?
It is for the sake of restricting the prefixes:
[the suffix -tva occurs] only after a prefix preceded by *upa* or *parā*.
"Not from one who has been with another" means:
he undertakes;
he exerts himself.
Why [is it specified] "after *upa* and *parā*"? [Consider:
*saṅkrāmati*.
It is only in the case of *vṛtti* and so forth [that the rule applies].
He exerts himself;
he strives with supreme effort.
The prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of rising up. (Pāṇini 1.3.40)
The ātmanepada occurs after the root *kram* preceded by the prefix *ā*, when it signifies rising; for example:
*ākramate ādityaḥ* ("the sun rises").
The moon ascends;
the luminaries ascend. Why [is] *udgamanam* [used as an example]?
The young student steps upon the leather bag.
It should be stated "at the rising of the light"; this is so that it does not apply here: "the smoke steps out from the roof-terrace."
The root *vi* is used in the sense of moving the feet.
The middle voice (ātmanepada) occurs after the root *kram* preceded by the prefix *vi-*, when it signifies "stepping out" (*pada-viharaṇa*).
"Stepping out" (*viharaṇa*) means dispersal (*vikṣepa*).
He strides well;
he strides excellently. "Striding" (vikramaṇa) refers to the specific modes of gait of horses and other such animals.

Although the root *kram* is taught [in grammatical treatises] only in the sense of "stepping with the feet," as in *kramu pāda-vikṣepe*, it is nevertheless stated thus because verbal roots have multiple meanings.
In the case of *pādaviharaṇe*, what is the example?
*vikrāmatyajinasandhiḥ* (he strides with unbent joints).
[62] [The suffix *lyap* is applied after a verb root] when preceded by *pra-* or *upa-*, provided they are semantically connected (*samarthābhyām*). PS 1.3.42.
The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the root *kram* preceded by *pra* and *upa*, provided that those two prefixes, *pra* and *upa*, are semantically capable and synonymous with one another.
And where do these two have the same meaning? In the sense of the beginning of an action: *prakramate bhoktum* (he begins to eat).
He proceeds to eat.
Why [is it said] "by two capable [days]"? [Consider:
He begins on the previous day.
The meaning is "he goes";
on the following day he approaches;
the meaning is "he comes."
Now, regarding the rule *upaparābhyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.39), does the ātmanepada [suffix] not appear here because there is no object?
[The answer is: the mention of *vṛtti* and so forth is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) into that rule.
In another case, this is a counter-example.
Or [the suffix *kyap* is applied] after a verbal root that does not have a prefix (*anupasarga*).
The term *krama* (step) is understood to carry over. This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) that applies where [the step] has not otherwise been established.
The *ātmanepada* suffix optionally occurs after the root *kram*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*). Thus:
*kramate* or *krāmati*.
Why [is it specified] "not preceded by a prefix"? [Consider:
*saṅkrāmati*.
The suffix *jñā* is used when there is a denial.
After the remaining [roots], when the *parasmaipada* would otherwise be prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), the *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *jñā* when it signifies concealment (*apahnava*).
Concealment (*apahnava*) means denial (*apahnuti*) or evasion (*apalāpa*).
And this verb, when accompanied by a prefix, signifies concealment, not when used alone:
*śatam apajanīte* ("he conceals a hundred"), *sahasram apajānīte* ("he conceals a thousand").
The meaning is "he denies. Why [is the word] "apahnave" (in the sense of denial) used? [For example:
"You do not know anything at all."
And [the suffix *ya* is applied] after a root that does not have an object (*akarmaka*).

This [sūtra] is for the purpose of [denoting] that which is not intended for the agent; for when it is intended for the agent, [the rule] "after a root beginning with *jñ* that is not preceded by a prefix" (Pāṇini 1.3.76) applies.
Thus he will say:
the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the root *jñā* when it is intransitive— that is, when it expresses an intransitive action—
as in *sarpiṣo jānīte*.
One knows honey.
And how is this [verb] intransitive?
Because here, ghee and so forth are not intended as the object of knowledge.
What then? [The genitive is used] because it functions as the instrument (karaṇa) in an activity preceded by knowledge.
And thus, by the rule *jño 'vid-arthasya karaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.51), the genitive case is prescribed—as in: *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he knows by means of the ghee").
One knows honey;
the meaning is that one proceeds by means of ghee.
Why [is the condition] "from an intransitive verb" stated?
One recognizes a son by his voice.
The suffix *man* is used after the roots *sam* and *prati*, except when expressing the sense of "thinking about" (*anādhyāne*).
The term "jñaḥ" (of one who knows) is understood [from the previous rule].
This [rule] is for the purpose of including transitive verbs.

The *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the root *jñā* preceded by *sam*, provided it does not mean "thinking about" (*ādhyāna*). "Thinking about" means longing or remembering. Example: *śataṃ saṃjānīte*.
He recognizes a thousand;
he acknowledges a hundred;
he acknowledges a thousand.
What is the purpose of the restriction "not when meaning 'to conceive' (anādhyāne)"? [Examples:
He conceives of his mother;
he conceives of his father.
The meaning is that he yearns.
The verb *vad* is used in the sense of speaking, addressing, knowing, effort, disagreement, and inviting. (Pāṇini 1.3.47)

When the *parasmaipada* endings would otherwise apply to the remaining roots in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), the *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *vad* when it is qualified by [the senses of] "shining" (*bhāsana*) and so forth.
Shining means radiance: *cārvī lokāyate vadate* ("The Cārvāka speaks/shines upon the Lokāyata system").
The meaning is that, shining and blazing, it makes objects manifest therein. *Upasambhāṣā* means consoling; for example, "he speaks to the laborers" means he consoles them.
*Jñānam* is correct understanding—the Cārvāka speaks according to the Lokāyata system;
the meaning is that he knows how to speak.
*Yatnaḥ* is exertion—he speaks on the field.
"He speaks at home" means he manifests enthusiasm for that particular object.
"Dissent" (*vimati*) is a diversity of opinion; they dispute regarding the field.
They quarrel in the house; the meaning is that, having fallen into disagreement, they speak various things. "Upamantraṇa" means secret enticement—namely, he reviles the wife of his own family.
"He speaks ill of another's wife" means "he entices her. Why [is the phrase] "in these cases" used?
Whatever he says.
[The suffix *ktvā* is used] after [roots] whose speech is articulate, when expressing a sequential performance [of actions]. (PS 1.3.48)
The term *vadaḥ* (of speech) continues [from the previous rule]. The simultaneous utterance (*sahoccāraṇam*) of articulated sounds is what is meant by "pronunciation together."

In that context, the *ātmanepada* occurs after the root *vad*. Now, since the root is indeed listed as *vada* with the meaning "in distinct speech," what is the purpose of the qualification "distinct speech"?
This is for the purpose of including what is well-known;
for humans are well-known as those with articulate speech. [The rule] is intended to apply to their pronunciation.
The Brahmins speak together;
the Kṣatriyas speak together.
Why [is the word] "vyaktavācām" (of those with distinct speech) used?
"Cocks crow" (*saṃpravadanti kukkuṭāḥ*). Why [is it] "in the case of simultaneous utterance" (*samuccāraṇe*)? [Consider: "The Brahmin speaks" (*brāhmaṇo vadati*).
The kṣatriya says:
After a root that has no prefix and does not take an object [the suffix *liṭ* is used].
Regarding the rule *vadaḥ*: the terms *vyaktavācām* (of those with distinct speech) and [the previous context] continue to apply.
The ātmanepada (middle voice) occurs after the verb *vadati* when it is preceded by the prefix *anu*, is intransitive, and has distinct speech as its object.
Kaṭha repeats after Kalāpa;
Maudga repeats after Paippalāda. The prefix *anu* is used in the sense of similarity.
The meaning is that "Kaṭha" is so called because he recites [the Veda] just as the Kalāpa school recites it.
Why is it specified "from an intransitive verb"? [Consider:
"He repeats the Yajus which was already uttered previously."
"The lute repeats [the sound] as distinct speech."
Vibhāṣā is [the term for] idle chatter. (PS 1.3.50)
The term "vadaḥ" (of speech) continues [from the previous rule],
as does "in the utterance of articulated speech."

The *ātmanepada* ending optionally occurs after the root *vad*, when it signifies the act of speaking articulately in the form of incoherent speech (*vipralāpa*). This is an optional rule (*prāpta-vibhāṣā*) because the *ātmanepada* is already established by default in this context.
Example: *vipravadante saṃvatsarāḥ* ("the years dispute with one another").
The astrologers dispute;
the moment-observers dispute; the moment-observers dispute.
The meaning is that they speak contradictory things simultaneously by way of mutual negation. Why [is the term] "in idle chatter" used? [For example: "The Brahmins are speaking in harmony."
The rule "of those with articulate speech" applies here as well.
For example: "the birds are quarreling.
The rule "in the case of simultaneous utterance" also applies here.
Gradually, the momentary [cognitions] debate with each other.
[The root] *vad* (to speak) takes the suffix *graḥ*. (Pāṇini 1.3.51)
The root *gṛ*, meaning "to swallow," is listed in the *tudādi* group;
this is its inclusion here.
But it does not refer to the root *gṛ* meaning "to sound," which is listed in the *kryādi* class; for that root is never used with the prefix *ava*.

Since the *parasmaipada* endings would otherwise apply to the remaining roots when used in the active voice (*kartari*), the *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed for the root *gṛ* (to swallow) when preceded by *ava*.
*avagirate*, *avagirete*, *avagirante*.
Why [is it specified] "after *ava*"? [Consider: *girati*.
It is equal in its proposition. (PS 1.3.52)
The term *graḥ* (from the root *grah*) continues [to apply].
The ātmanepada occurs after the root *gṛ*, preceded by the prefix *sam*, when it signifies a formal promise (*pratijñāna*).
*Pratijñāna* is an undertaking;
one pledges a hundred [coins],
or one pledges a word of renunciation.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the sense of promising"? [Consider:
"He swallows the morsel."
The suffix *uda* occurs after a transitive verb meaning "to move."

When the *parasmaipada* endings would otherwise apply to the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of the general rule, the *ātmanepada* endings occur after the verb *car* preceded by the prefix *ud*, provided it expresses an action involving an object (*sakarmaka*). Example:
*geham uccarati*.
It transgresses the family; it transgresses the word of the teacher;
the meaning is that it goes beyond [the bounds].
Why [is it specified] "from a transitive verb"? [Consider:
"He emits steam."
The particle *sam* [is used as a karmapravacanīya] when joined with a word in the third case.

The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the root *car* when preceded by the prefix *sam*, provided it is joined with an instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*). By the term "instrumental," the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-vibhakti*) is understood.
In that case, the connection [of the suffix] with the root *carati* occurs by way of its meaning:
*aśvena sañcarate* ("he moves about on horseback"). Why is it said "after [a word] joined with a third-case ending"? [Consider: *aśvasya sañcāraḥ*.
O Devala, you traverse both worlds, this one and the other;
even though the application of that purpose is possible here,
the instrumental case-ending is not heard.
Thus, this serves as a counter-example.
And [the word] *dāṇ* is [used] in the sense of the fourth case, provided it has that meaning. (Pāṇini 1.4.55)
The root *cāy* (cāṅ) meaning "to give" is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*; however,
when preceded by the prefix *sam* and joined with an instrumental case, it takes the *ātmanepada*.
If that third case occurs in the sense of the fourth case, how then can the third case occur in the sense of the fourth?
This must indeed be explained: it must be stated that in the usage of the unrefined, the third case occurs in the sense of the fourth.
"He gives to a female slave" means that being lustful, he gives to a female slave; "he gives to a low-caste woman" has the same meaning.
Why is it said "in the sense of the fourth case"? [Consider:
*pāṇinā samprayacchati*.
How does the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occur when there is an intervention by the word *pra* after *sam*?
In the case of the qualifier *samaḥ*, the genitive case is used, not the ablative.
[PS 1.3.56] The root *yama* takes the prefix *upa-* when it means "to take for oneself."

When *parasmaipada* endings would otherwise apply to the remaining roots in the active voice (*kartari*), the *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the root *yama-* preceded by the prefix *upa-* when it signifies "taking for oneself. Here, "taking for oneself" is understood as being specifically characterized by the grasping of the hand.
It is not merely by one's own action [that one becomes related].
One marries a wife.
Why is it said "by one's own action"?
Devadatta marries Yajñadatta’s wife.
The suffix *san* is added after the roots *jñā*, *śru*, *smṛ*, and *dṛś*.

The *ātmanepada* ending occurs after these roots— *jñā*, *śru*, *samṛ*, and *dṛś*— when they are in the desiderative (*san*) form. Among them, for the root *jñā*, [the *ātmanepada* is used] in the sense of denial (*apahnava*), as prescribed by Pāṇini 1.3.44.
Thus, the *ātmanepada* has been prescribed by three sūtras;
[the same] is also prescribed for the roots *śru* and *dṛś* in the rule *śrudṛśoḥ samānayoḥ gamyṛcchi* (Pāṇini 1.3.29).
In that case, the *ātmanepada* ending is already established by the rule *sanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62), as before;
therefore, this [present rule] prescribes it for cases other than those.
Furthermore, even before attaining [the goal], he remembers the injunction;
he desires to know the Dharma;
he serves the teacher.
One wishes to remember what has been lost;
one wishes to see the king. Why [is the word] *sanaḥ* mentioned? [To exclude cases such as: *susmūrṣate*.
He knows, he hears, he remembers, and he sees.
The atom is not a knower. (PS 1.3.58)

The *ātmanepada* ending, which would have been obtained by the preceding rule, is prohibited. The *ātmanepada* does not occur after the root *jñā* preceded by *anu*, when it is in the desiderative form (*san*).
And this being the case, this prohibition applies only to transitive verbs:
*putram anujijñāsati* ("he desires to know his son").
Why [is the word] *anoḥ* [stated]? [To exclude cases where the prefix *anu-* is not present.]
He desires to know the Dharma.
The root *śru* [takes the Ātmanepada endings] after the prefixes *prati* and *ā*.
After the prefix *prati*, the *ātmanepada* ending does not occur following the root *śru* when preceded by *ā* and followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*). Example: *pratiśuśrūṣati*.
He desires to hear.
And since this refers to the inclusion of a prefix (upasarga),
therefore there is no prohibition in this case.
He serves Devadatta.
The substitution of *ś* for the root *śad* occurs when followed by an affix marked with *ś*.
The root *śad* (śadlṛ) meaning "to destroy" is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*;
therefore, the *ātmanepada* ending is here prescribed for it.
The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after that which is a *śit*, or that which will become *śit*, or that which is related to *śit*.
*śīyate*, *śīyete*, *śīyante*. Why [is it said] "after *śī*" (*śitaḥ*)? [Consider: *aśatsyat*, *śatsyati*.
The root *mṛ* (to die) takes the augment *iṭ* in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* tenses, as well as in the desiderative (*śiśatsati*).
The root *mr̥ṅ* (meaning "to abandon life") is already established here as being in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) because it is marked with the *ṅit* designation.
This statement is for the purpose of restriction:
the ātmanepada occurs after the root *mṛ* (to die) in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* tenses and before suffixes marked with *śit*,
but it does not occur elsewhere.
Amṛta;
mṛṣīṣṭa;
and also from the root śit—mriyate.
*mriyete*, *mriyante*.
For what purpose is the restriction? [To exclude] *mariṣyati* and *amariṣyat*.
As before, [the suffix] *sana* [is applied]. (PS 1.3.62)
The root *san* (the desiderative suffix), when it is *ātmanepada*, causes the *ātmanepada* endings to occur after a verb ending in that suffix, just as they would after the original root itself.
By whatever cause the *ātmanepada* is prescribed after a verbal root, that same cause applies even when the root is followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*).

According to Pāṇini 1.3.12, "the *ātmanepada* [is used] after a root marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the suffix *ṅ*," as in *āste* (he sits), *śete* (he lies down). That very same cause applies even after a desiderative form: *āsisiṣate* (he desires to sit).
*śiśayiṣate*;
[by the rule] *ner viśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.17)— *niviśate*, *nivivikṣate*.
Regarding *āṅ* in the sense of "rising up" (*udgamane*)— as in *ākramate* and *ācikraṃsate*.
It does not occur here [in other senses].
In *śiśatsati* and *mumūrṣati*, it is not merely the roots *śad* and *mṛ* that cause the middle voice (*ātmanepada`); what then? It is also the suffixes *śit* and so forth.

And that [condition] does not exist here; furthermore, that for which the status as a cause was already prohibited in the preceding section is likewise not a cause in the case of the *sannanta* forms— as in *anucikīrṣati*.
Does he wish to refute [it], or does he feel aversion toward it here, or does he investigate it?
The ātmanepada is already established by the rule *anudātta-ṅitaḥ*;
for a characteristic applied to a constituent part serves to distinguish the whole.
The verb *kṛ* is used as an auxiliary (anuprayoga) after a root that has taken the suffix *ām*, just as it is when *ām* follows [the roots *bhū*, *as*, and *kṛ*].
This undertaking is for the purpose of [expressing] that which does not intend for the agent; "that which has the suffix *ām*" is this suffix *ām*.

The *ātmanepada* affixes occur after the verb *kṛ*, when it is used as an auxiliary following a verbal root that would otherwise take them, just as they do after a root ending in the suffix *ām*. For example:
*īkṣāñcakre* (he looked) and *īhāñcakre* (he strove).

If this [rule] were for the purpose of enjoining [the suffix], then in forms such as *udubjāñcakāra* and *udumbhāñcakāra*, the ātmanepada would result when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāye kriyāphale*).
This is not a fault;
by this [statement], both injunction and restriction are established.
How so? The term "as before" (pūrvavat) is understood [to apply here].
That second effort will be for the purpose of restriction (niyama).
Why [is it said] "after the root *kṛ*"? [Consider: *īkṣāmāsa*.
He looked.

But how is there an application of *anuprayoga* for this, since it is stated that "the root *kṛ* is applied after [a verbal root ending in] *liṭ*" (*Pāṇini 3.1.40*)? In that rule, it should be understood that the term *kṛ* refers to a *pratyāhāra* (a grammatical abbreviation).
Where is the withdrawal [of the *cvi*-suffix] for those situated [in the rules]?
It is from the rule *abhūtatadbhāve kṛbhvastiyoge sampadyakartari cviḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.50) up to the rule *kṛño dvitīyatṛtīyaśambabījāt kṛṣau* (Pāṇini 5.4.58), beginning with the word *kṛ*.
Thus is the letter Ña.
The root *yuj* (to join) following the prefixes *pra-* and *upa-* [forms the Ātmanepada] when used with vessels other than those for sacrifice.
The root *yuj* (to join) is marked with the *svarita* accent.
When the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāya*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established as a matter of course.
This undertaking has the sense of not intending for the agent.
After the root *yuj* preceded by *pra* and *upa*, the ātmanepada occurs when it does not involve the use of sacrificial vessels; for example:
*prayuṅkte*.
He employs [the vessels].
Why say "in non-sacrificial vessels"?
[Because one] arranges the pairs of downward-facing vessels [connected with the gods]. [67]
It should be stated that [the suffix *kyap* is applied] after a root preceded by a vowel and ending in a vowel, when accompanied by a prefix (*upasarga*):
*udyuṅkte*, *niyuṅkte*.
Why is it said "preceded or followed by a vowel or the like"? [Consider:
*saṃyunakti*.
The root *kṣṇu* is also [used] in the same sense.
The root *kṣṇu* (meaning "to sharpen") is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*.
However, when preceded by the prefix *sam*, it takes the *ātmanepada*.
Why was this not read in that very rule [Pāṇini 1.3.29], "samogamyṛcchi"? Because the term "from an intransitive verb" (akarmakāt) is understood to apply there as well.
He sharpens the weapon;
they two sharpen; they sharpen.
The root *bhuja* is used in the sense of protecting.
The root *bhuja* is listed in the *rudhādi* class [of roots] with the meanings "protection" (*pālana*) and "eating" (*abhyavahāra*).
Therefore, when it occurs in the sense of non-protection— that is, not in the sense of protecting— the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed.
*bhuṅkte*, *bhuñjāte*, *bhuñjate*.
Why [is it said] "in the sense of protecting" (*anavane*)? [Because otherwise, as in:
*bhunakti enam agnir āhitaḥ* ("the consecrated fire protects him").

By the prohibition [expressed] as *an-ava-na*, it is understood that only the root belonging to the *raudhādika* class is intended, and not this [root] *bhuja* meaning "crookedness" which belongs to the *tudādika* class.
Therefore, it does not occur here.
He waves his hand.
That which is the object (karman) of a root ending in *ṇic* becomes the agent (kartṛ) when that same root is used with the suffix *ṇi*, provided it does not refer to a state of mind (anādhyāne).
By the rule *ṇicaś ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is already established when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent;
this present rule is commenced for the purpose of cases where it does not accrue to the agent.
The *ātmanepada* ending occurs after a verb in the *ṇic* (causative) form.
How so? If that which was the object (*karman*) in the non-causative (*aṇau*) remains the very same object in the causative (*ṇau*), and that [object] becomes the agent (*kartṛ*).
In the sense of "not causing to mount," excluding the causative meaning:
the elephant-keepers mount the elephant; the elephant mounts by itself.
The elephant-keepers sprinkle the elephant,
and the elephant sprinkles itself by its own accord;
the servants see the king.
The king shows [himself] himself.
Why [is the rule] "after the causative suffix *ṇi*"? [Consider: "the elephant-keepers mount the elephant";
"the elephant, being made to mount [them], mounts well."
Why is it said "in the case of a small number" (aṇau)? [Consider:
*gopālako gaṇaṃ gaṇayati* ("the cowherd counts the herd"), and *gaṇo gaṇayati svayam eva* ("the herd counts by itself").
What is the purpose of including the term *karman* [in the rule]? [Consider:
*lunāti dātrena* ("he cuts with a sickle") and *lāvyati dātram svayam eva* ("the sickle cuts by itself").
The inclusion of the word *cet* (if) is for the purpose of [indicating] a common action: "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant;
being mounted, the elephant douses the frightened [elephant-keepers] with urine.
The inclusion of the word *yat* (which) is for the purpose of [indicating] that there is no other action.
Elephant-drivers mount the elephant;
while being mounted, the elephant causes men to mount onto dry land.
Why is the term "agent" (kartṛ) used?
The elephant-keepers mount the elephant;
the mahout causes them to mount it.
Why does the rule specify "not when there is no mental application" (anādhyāne)?
The cuckoo remembers the mango grove; the mango grove itself brings it to mind.
Indeed, in this case, the examples are those of the reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*).
In that case, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is already established by the very rule of "acting like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*).
For what purpose is this stated?

It is so that the extension of the status of the object (*karmavad-atideśa*) may be understood to apply specifically to those roots whose state resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*) and those whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*).
This undertaking concerns an action residing in the agent (*kartṛstha*).
Accordingly, *ruhi* is cited as having an action residing in the agent (*kartṛstha-kriya*), and *dṛśi* is cited as having a state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*). [68]
The suffixes *bhī* and *smyoḥ* are used when there is a cause for fear.
The term "ṇeḥ" (after the causative suffix ṇiC) is understood [from the previous rule].
This new formulation is intended for cases where the action does not aim at the agent (akartr-abhiprāya).

The *ātmanepada* affix occurs after the causative forms (*ṇyanta*) of the roots *bibhete-* and *smayate-* when the fear arises from a cause (*hetubhaye*). Here, "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*); provided that the fear originates from such an agent, the *ātmanepada* is employed.
The mention of "fear" (*bhaya*) is for the purpose of illustration; "amazement" (*vismaya*) also arises from that very same cause.
One with matted hair (*jaṭila*) causes fear.
The shaven-headed one causes fear;
the matted-haired one causes amazement;
the shaven-headed one causes amazement.
What is meant by "in fear of a cause"?
He terrifies him with a key;
he astonishes him with his form.
In this context, the key is the instrument of fear, not its cause.
The roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* are used in the sense of deceiving.
The term "ṇeḥ" (after the causative suffix ṇiC) carries over [from the previous rule].
This new formulation is intended for cases where the action is not for the benefit of the agent (*akartr-abhiprāya*).
The *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the roots *gṛdh* (in the sense of longing) and *vañc* (in the sense of going) when they are used with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of deceiving;
"deceiving" means misrepresenting or misleading.
The false declaration of a result:
he entices the young brahmin;
he deceives the young brahmin.

What is the meaning of "in the sense of deceiving" (*pralambhane*)? [Example: *śvānaṃ gardhayati* ("he entices the dog"). The meaning is: "he produces greed in him. [Another example: *ahiṃ vañcayati* ("he deceives the snake").
The meaning is that he avoids.
The root *li* is used in the senses of honoring and making someone humble.
The term *ṇeḥ* (after the causative suffix) continues [from the previous rule].
This new formulation is undertaken for the purpose of excluding cases where the action is intended for the agent (*akartr-abhiprāya*).
The root *lī* is listed in the Divādi class as *līṅ śleṣaṇe*, and in the Kryādī class as *lī śleṣaṇe*.
Since there is no distinction between them, both are included.
From the causative (*ṇy-anta*) of *lī*, when it signifies "honoring" (*saṃmānana*) or "making modest" (*śālīnīkaraṇa*), the Ātmanepada [middle voice] occurs.
By virtue of the word "ca" (and), [the rule applies] also in the sense of deceiving.
*Sammānanam* means honoring—e.g., *jaṭābhir ālāpayate*, which means "he attains honor by means of his matted locks. This is the meaning.

*Śālīnīkaraṇa* means making someone humble or submissive; for example, "The hawk makes the quail cry out," which means he humbles it. In the sense of deceiving: "Who is making you cry out? (i.e., who is deceiving you?).
The meaning is "he deceives.
Alternatively, by the rule *vibhāṣā līyateḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.51), the substitution of *ā* for the vowel is prescribed.
Therefore, in this matter, there is always an option [to apply the rule] elsewhere;
for that is indeed a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).
Why [is the phrase] "in the sense of honoring and so forth" (*sammānanādiṣu*) stated?
She addresses the boy.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the prefix *mithyā*, provided that the action is repeated.
The term "ṇeḥ" (after the causative suffix ṇiC) is understood [from the previous rule].
This new formulation is intended for cases where the action does not aim at the agent (*akartr-abhiprāya*).

The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after the causative (*ṇyanta*) of the root *kṛ* when preceded by the prefix *mithyā*, provided there is repetition (*abhyāsa*). Repetition, moreover, means doing again and again, or recurrence. Example: *padaṃ mithyā kārayate* ("he causes the word to be pronounced incorrectly again and again").
The meaning is that one utters [the word] repeatedly with improper conduct, such as being defective in its vowels and so forth. Why say "with a false prefix"? [Consider:
"he causes the word to be well-made."
Why is it said "after the root *kṛ*"? [Consider:
*padaṃ mithyā vācayati*.
Why is it said "in the case of repetition"? [Consider: *abhyāse*.
One causes the word to be uttered falsely;
one utters it once.
[69] [The ātmanepada suffixes are used] after a root marked with svarita or ñ, when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent. (Pāṇini 1.3.72)

The word *ṇeḥ* is no longer applicable. When the *parasmaipada* endings would otherwise apply to the remaining roots by virtue of the agent being the sense expressed, the *ātmanepada* endings occur for those roots that have a svarita accent on their indicatory letter (*ñit*) as well as for those that have an indicatory *ñ*.
If the agent intends the fruit of the action—

where "the fruit of the action" (*kriyāphala*) refers to that which is the primary result for whose sake the action is undertaken— and if that fruit belongs to the agent expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), [then the agent is the principal].
He sacrifices; he cooks;
and also from a root ending in ñi—[as in] he presses [the soma].
It effects [the action]; here, [the rule] intends the agent as the one who receives the primary fruit, such as heaven.
Why [is it specified] "when intended for the agent"?
The sacrificers sacrifice;
the cooks cook;
the laborers work.
Although the sacrificial fee and wages constitute a fruit for the agent in this world, nevertheless, the undertaking of the action is not for the sake of those.
The word *apāt* [is used] in the sense of "speaking. (PS 1.3.73)
The phrase "when intended for the agent" (kartr-abhiprāye) continues [from the previous rule].
When the fruit of the action is intended for the agent, the ātmanepada suffix occurs after the verb *vad* preceded by *apa*.
One desiring wealth denies justice;
he thinks, "I shall acquire wealth by denying justice. Since the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, [the verb] is used in the *ātmanepada*: *apavadate*.
And [the suffixes] beginning with *ṇic*. (Pāṇini 1.3.74)

The phrase "when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent" (kartr-abhiprāye kriyā-phale) continues [from the previous rule]. The Ātmanepada suffix occurs after a causative verb (ṇij-anta) when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent.
He causes a mat to be made;
he causes rice to be cooked—
only when the intention refers to the agent.
He causes another to make a mat.
The suffix *ap* is applied after the root *yam-* when preceded by the prefixes *sam*, *ud*, or *āṅ*, provided it does not mean "to tie."
The phrase "when the result of the action is intended for the agent" (kartr-abhiprāye) continues to apply.
When preceded by *sam*, *ud*, or *āṅ*, the verb *yam* takes the ātmanepada endings when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent.
If the object is a book, there is no application [of the suffix];
as in *vrīhīn saṃyacchate* (he gathers rice) and *bhāram udyacchate* (he lifts a load).
He takes up the garment;
since the verb *ā-yam* is intransitive when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is already established by the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28).
This repetition [of the word *grantha*] is for the sake of including transitive meanings.
Why say "not a book"? [Consider:
"The physician studies medicine."
The rule "when the intention of the agent is expressed" applies here as well:
*saṃyacchati*,
*udyacchati*.
He draws back.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *jñā* when it is not preceded by a prefix.

The phrase "when intended for the agent" (kartr-abhiprāye) continues [from the previous rule]. After the verb *jñā* (to know), when it is not preceded by a prefix (anupasarga) and the fruit of the action is intended for the agent, the middle voice (ātmanepada) occurs.
He knows the cow;
he knows the horse. Why [is it specified] "after a prefix"? [To exclude cases such as: *prajānāti*.
The fool does not know the heavenly world; this is precisely when the agent's intention is involved, as in: "He knows Devadatta’s going. [70]
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, [the suffix] is used when the meaning is understood from a subordinate word (*upapada*). *Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.3.77.
By the five sūtras beginning with *svaritañitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.72), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent.
Since [the reflexive meaning] is not obtained when it is indicated by an *upapada*, this rule is commenced. An *upapada* is another word heard in proximity [to the verb].
When the fruit of the action is understood through that [word] to be intended for the agent, the *ātmanepada* occurs optionally (*vibhāṣā*).
He performs his own sacrifice;
he performs every sacrifice. He performs every Katha-rite.
How does one speak ill of oneself? One speaks ill of one's own son;
one speaks ill of one's own son.
In this manner, it should be cited in the *Pañcasūtrī*.
From the remainder [of roots], the *parasmaipada* ending is used when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
By the preceding section, a restriction regarding the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) has been established, but not a restriction regarding the active voice (*parasmaipada*).
That [rule] applies everywhere;
for that purpose, this is stated:
"The remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to that which is other than those verbal roots for which the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) has been prescribed by a specific qualification.
From the remainder [of roots], the *parasmaipada* (active voice) occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed;
it occurs only from the remainder and not from any other.
It has been stated that the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) follows from those roots marked with an *anudātta* vowel or the suffix *ṅ*; for example, the root *as* (to be).
He lies down;
elsewhere than that, the *parasmaipada* occurs— as in *yāti* (he goes) or *vāti* (he blows).
The *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed for the root *viś-* when preceded by *ni*: *niviśate*. In other cases, the *parasmaipada* endings are used: *āviśati*, *praviśati*.
What is the purpose of the condition "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*)? [Consider: *pacyate* (it is cooked), *gamyate* (it is gone).
Why does the parasmaipada (active voice) not occur in the case of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*)?
Is it that "the rice porridge cooks by itself"?
[In this case], the second mention of the term *kartṛ* (agent) from Pāṇini 1.3.14, *kartari karma-vyatihāre*, is understood to apply here as well.
Therefore, the *ātmanepada* occurs only where there is an agent; it does not occur in the case of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*).
The root √kṛ [takes the ātmanepada endings] after the prefixes anu and parā.

The *ātmanepada* ending has been prescribed for the root *kṛ* when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāya*), as well as in the sense of "hinting" (*gandhana*) and so forth;
this [rule] prescribes the *parasmaipada* as an exception (*apavāda*) to that.
The *parasmaipada* suffix occurs after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *anu* and *parā*:
*anukaroti*, *parākaroti*.
The suffix *kṣip* is applied after the prefixes *abhi*, *prati*, and *ati*.
The root *kṣip* (meaning "to throw" or "to impel") is marked with the *svarita* accent.

Consequently, although the *ātmanepada* would have been expected when there is an intention to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāya-kriyā-phala*), the *parasmaipada* is here prescribed.
In the case of the roots *kṣip* preceded by *abhi*, *prati*, or *ati*, the *parasmaipada* ending occurs; for example:
*abhikṣipati*, *pratikṣipati*.
[The rule applies to] *ati-kṣipati*. Why [specify] "after *abhi*, *prati*, and *ati*"? [Because it does not apply in cases like] *ākṣipate*.
The mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is also repeated for a second time.
Therefore, it does not occur here;
it is itself cast forward.

The term *vaha* is *svarita*-accented when it is applicable. In that case, although the *ātmanepada* would have been required by the desire to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāya-kriyā-phala*), the *parasmaipada* is prescribed instead.
The *parasmaipada* endings occur after the root *vah* preceded by the prefix *pra*:
*pravahati*, *pravahataḥ*, *pravahanti*.
Why [is it specified] "prāt"? [Consider the example: āvahate.
The others are false. (PS 1.3.82)
The root *mṛṣ* is marked with the svarita accent when meaning "to endure.
Consequently, although the ātmanepada would have applied by that very rule, the parasmaipada is here prescribed.
The *parasmaipada* ending occurs after the root *mṛṣ* preceded by *pari*:
*parimṛṣyati*,
*parimṛṣyataḥ*.
They rub [it].
Why say "by another" (pareḥ)? [Because in] "āmṛṣyate," it is not so. Some also carry over the root *vah* here—[as in] "parivahati."
The root *ram* [takes the ātmanepada endings] after the prefixes *vi*, *āṅ*, and *pari*.

Regarding the root *ram* in the sense of "playing": although the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would [otherwise] be prescribed because it is marked with an anudātta vowel, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is here ordained.
The *parasmaipada* occurs after the root *ram* preceded by *vi-āṅ* and *pari-*; for example:
*viramati*, *āramati*.
[The suffix *kyaṅ*] is applied in the sense of "he embraces" (*pariramati*).
Why [is it] said "from these"? [Consider:
"he delights in" (*abhiramate*).
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after a verbal root ending in a long vowel (*upāc*).
Only in the sense of "delighting" (ramaḥ) does the *parasmaipada* [active voice] occur after the root *ram* preceded by the prefix *upa*.
He causes Devadatta to cease; he causes Yajñadatta to cease;
that is to say, he causes them to pass away.
In this context, the root *ram* has its meaning included [within itself].
The separate formulation of the rule is for the sake of what follows;
for he will state that there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) after an intransitive verb.
This [suffix] should occur only after a verb preceded by an upasarga.
According to the Vibhāṣā, [the suffix *ta* is used] after an intransitive verb.
The term *upāt* also carries over from [Pāṇini 1.3.79].
Since the preceding rule would have necessitated the *parasmaipada* (active voice) endings invariably, this optional rule is now introduced.
After the root *ram* preceded by the prefix *upa*, when it is intransitive, the *parasmaipada* endings optionally occur:
*yāvad bhuktam auparamati* or *yāvad bhuktam uparamate*.
The meaning is that it ceases.
The suffix *ṇiC* is elided after the verbal roots *budh*, *yudh*, *naś*, *jan*, *iṅ*, *pru*, *dru*, and *srū*.

By the rule *ṇicaś ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74), when there is a desire to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartr-abhiprāya-tryāphala*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would otherwise be required; however, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is here prescribed.
The active voice occurs after these roots ending in the causative suffix *ṇi*: *budh*, *yudh*, *naś*, *jan*, *iṅ*, *pru*, *dru*, and *sru*.
He awakens; he causes to awaken; he destroys.
He causes to be born;
he causes to study; he causes to put on.
It causes to melt;
it causes to flow.

Regarding those roots which are intransitive (*akarmaka*) here, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] after a root that is intransitive when preceded by *aṇ*, and whose agent (*kartṛ*) possesses consciousness (*cittavat*), according to Pāṇini 1.3.88.
This statement is made for the purpose of [denoting] an agent who lacks consciousness (*acittavat*), even though this is already established:
"The lotus causes itself to bloom" (*bodhyati padmam*); "the pieces of wood cause themselves to burn" (*yodhyanti kāṣṭhāni*).

It destroys suffering and produces happiness; and those [roots] which have the sense of "moving" here [also apply], according to Pāṇini 3.2.87, by virtue of their inclusion among the roots meaning "swallowing" and "moving."
Since this is established, when there is no sense of motion, the statement is for that purpose;
it is understood as "it blows" or "it reaches."
"Iron flows" means it melts; "the water-pot leaks" means it drips.
Examples having that as their object are: *prāvayati*, *drāvayati*, *srāvayati*.
And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after verbal roots meaning "swallowing" (*nigaraṇa*) and "moving" (*calana*).
The term "ṇeḥ" (after the causative suffix ṇiC) carries over from the previous rule.

When there is a desire to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartr-abhiprāya-kriyāphala*), the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is prescribed as an exception to the *ātmanepada*.

*Nigaraṇa* means swallowing; *calana* means moving. After verbal roots meaning "swallowing" and those meaning "moving," when followed by the suffix *ṇi*, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) endings are employed.
He causes to swallow; he causes to eat; he causes to feed.
From roots having the sense of "moving": *calayati*,
*copayati*,
*kampayati*.
This rule (*yoga*) also has the sense of being transitive (*sakarmaka*),
and it refers to an agent who lacks consciousness (*acittavat-kartṛka*).
An exception must be stated regarding the root *ad* ("to eat").
Devadatta eats; Devadatta is made to eat.
In the case of an atom, [the action] arises from an agent possessing consciousness, provided that [the action] is not itself an action.
The term *ṇeḥ* (after the causative suffix *ṇi*) is understood [from the previous rule].
When there is a desire to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartr-abhiprāya-kriyāphala*), the parasmaipada is prescribed as an exception to the ātmanepada.
The *parasmaipada* ending occurs after a causative (*ṇic*) derivative of a root that is intransitive and has a sentient being as its agent; for example:
*āste devadattaḥ* (Devadatta sits), *āsayati devadattam* (he causes Devadatta to sit).
Devadatta lies down; [the master] causes Devadatta to lie down.
Why is it said "in the case of a root that does not have the suffix ṇi"?
Some offer the counter-example, "He causes one who is intending to act to intend," but that is incorrect;
for the rule concerning the causative suffix *ṇic* applies when there is a causal agent (*hetu*).
The prohibition also applies only to that [root] due to proximity;
therefore, in this case, it ought to be *cetayati* with the *parasmaipada* ending.
However, this is a counter-example: one employs someone who is mounting [a horse], as in *ārohayate*.
Why does it say "from an intransitive verb" (*akarmakāt*)? [Consider:
*kaṭhaṃ kurvāṇaṃ prayuṅkte kārayate* ("He causes the Kaṭha student who is making a mat to act").
Why does it say "having an agent possessing consciousness" (*citavatkartṛkāt*)?
The rice grains wither;
the heat dries up the rice grains.
The suffix *kyap* is not applied after the verbal roots *dam*, *yam*, *āyam*, *as*, *pari-muh*, *ruc*, *nṛt*, *vad*, and *vas*.

By the two preceding rules, the *parasmaipada* was prescribed as an exception to the *ātmanepada* when there is an intention to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*kartṛ-abhiprāya-kriyā-phala*). This [present rule] states its prohibition.
That which is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) pertaining to the intention of the agent remains exactly as it is;
it is not prohibited.

After the roots *pā* (to drink), *dam* (to tame), *aṅyama* and *āṅyasa*, *parimuha*, *ruc*, *nṛt*, *vad*, and *vas*—when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*—the active voice (*parasmaipada*) does not occur. [73]
The Ātmanepada ending occurs by the rule *ṇicaś ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74).
In this context, the root *pivati* has the sense of swallowing,
while *dam-* and the others have sentient beings as their agents.
The root *nṛt* also has the meaning "to move," yet these [roots] do not take the *parasmaipada* endings. For example:
*pā*—*pāyayate*.
*dam-i* as in *damayate*;
*āṅ-yam* as in *āyāmayate*. By the rule "the root *yam* [is not designated as *mit*] except in the sense of serving food," the designation *mit* is prohibited.
aṅyasa—āyāsayate; parimuha—parimohayate;
ruci—rocayate.
nṛt—causes to dance (nartayate); vad—causes to speak (vādayate); vas—causes to dwell (vāsayate).
The addition of the root *dheṭ* (to suckle) to the list beginning with *pā* [is required].
"The two mothers-in-law together suckle the single infant."
Or [the suffix *liṅ* is used] after a verb ending in *kyaṣ*.
The author will state [later] that "the affix *kyaṣ* is applied after [roots ending in] *lohitādi* and those ending in *ḍāc*" (Pāṇini 3.1.13).
After that [suffix], the *parasmaipada* ending optionally occurs after the verbal root:
*lohitāyati*, *lohitāyate*.
It makes a crackling sound,
it crackles;
now, since the parasmaipada ending is applied here, how is the ātmanepada obtained?
Is that [the middle voice] restricted by this section beginning with "That which has an anudātta indicatory letter or is marked with ṅ takes the ātmanepada" (Pāṇini 1.3.12)?
If so, then in this case, the ātmanepada alone is prescribed as an option.
And that [rule], having been brought to mind immediately by the prohibition of the *parasmaipada*, is connected here;
therefore, when [the conditions for the *ātmanepada*] are absent, the *parasmaipada* occurs from the "remainder" (*śeṣāt*) in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
The suffix *luṅ* is applied after the verbal roots *dhyai*, etc. (beginning with *dhya*).
It is simply "or" (vā).
[The root] *dyut* means "to shine."
By association with that [term], the roots beginning with *luṭhi* and ending with *kṛpū* are likewise designated in the same way.
Because of the use of the plural number, the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*) is understood.

Since these roots are marked with an indicatory vowel *ṭ* (which is *anudātta*), the *ātmanepada* endings would apply invariably; however, for the *luṅ* tense, the *parasmaipada* endings optionally occur after the roots beginning with *dyut*.
*vyadyutat*, *vyadyotiṣṭa*;
*aluṭhat*, *aloṭhiṣṭa*.
Why "in the *luṅ*" [tense]? [Consider: *dyotate*.
After the roots *vṛt* and those ending in *ṝ*, the suffixes *syat* (the future marker) and *san* (the desiderative marker) are optionally treated as *ārdhadhātuka*.
In the list beginning with *dyuti*, *vṛt* and others are recited; [for example,] *vṛtu* as in "he turns" (*vartate*).
The root *vṛdh* means "to grow"; *śṛdh* means "contemptuous sound"; *syandū* means "to flow";
and *kṛpū* means "capability."
After these verbal roots, when *sya* or *san* follows, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) optionally occurs. For example:
from the root *vṛt*, we have *vartsyati* and *avartsyat*.
He wishes to turn;
he will turn;
he would have turned.
He wishes to turn back; from the root *vṛt*:
he will turn, he would have turned.
He wishes to open;
he will increase;
he would have increased.
It will increase (*vivardhiṣate*). Why [is it said] "in the case of *syasamoḥ*"? [Consider: *vartate*. [Pāṇini 1.3.93:
And in the case of the *luṭ* [future], after the root *klup*.
Since the optionality of *syas* and *san* is already established by their inclusion in the *vṛtādi* group, it is prescribed here for the *luṭ* [future] tense.
In that case, the particle *ca* need not be mentioned for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) *syas* and *san*.
In that case, this *prāpti* (the present rule) would sublate the previous *prāpti* (the preceding rule);
therefore, the particle *ca* is employed for the purpose of carrying over (*anukarṣaṇa*) both *syasanoḥ*.
Thus, in the *luṭ* [future] tense, as well as in the cases of *syasanoḥ*, the *parasmaipada* endings optionally occur after the root *klṛp*.
kalptā, kalptārau, kalptāraḥ; kalpsyati;
akalpsyat.
He wishes to arrange;
it has been arranged;

The *kāraka* which is the object intended to be informed by the verbs *ślāgh* (to boast), *hnuṅ* (to deny), *sthā* (to stand), and *śap* (to swear) receives the technical designation *sampradāna*.
*jñīpsyamānaḥ* means one who is intended to be made known, or one who is meant to be informed;
[as in] *devadattāya ślāghate* (he boasts to Devadatta).
The meaning is that one who praises Devadatta desires to make him aware of that very praise.
Likewise: *devadattāya hnute*, *yajñadattāya hnute*.
He stands for Devadatta; he stands for Yajñadatta;
he curses Devadatta.
"He reviles Yajñadatta. Why say "being informed"? [Because in this case: "He praises Devadatta on the road."
In the case of the root *dhṛ* (to owe), the creditor is [the agent].
In the employment of the verb *dhārayati* ("to owe"), that factor which is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) receives the technical designation *saṃpradāna*.
He who possesses the highest debt is the creditor (uttamarṇa). And whose debt is the highest? That which belongs to him whose wealth it is.
The owner of the wealth, the lender, the creditor—he is designated as the *sampradāna*. Example: *devadattāya śatam dhārayati* ("He owes a hundred to Devadatta").
"He owes a hundred to Yajñadatta.
Why say "having been released" (*uttārṇa*)? [Consider:
"He owes a hundred to Devadatta in the village."
In the case of the root *spṛh* ("to desire"), that which is desired [is called the *saṃpradāna*].
The root *spṛh*, meaning "desire," is listed in the *curādi* group as ending in a long vowel (*adanta*). That object which is desired by it [is the *īpsita*].
That *kāraka* becomes designated as the *sampradāna*.
"Desired" (*īpsita*) is intended here to mean "intended. For example: *puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati* ("he longs for flowers").
He desires fruits.

In the case of roots meaning anger, malice, envy, and censoriousness, the object is that person toward whom the resentment is directed. (Pāṇini 1.4.37)
Impatience is anger;

Envy (*asūyā*) is the revelation of faults in those who possess virtues.
In the employment of verbs meaning anger and the like, [the dative case is used] for the one toward whom the anger is directed.

"Anger" (*krodha*) is simply wrath;

“He envies Devadatta,” “He finds fault with Devadatta. Why [is the rule stated] “toward whom there is anger”?

He is jealous of his wife, thinking, "Let no other see her. Regarding the roots *krudh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to bear malice), when they are accompanied by a prefix, the object is the *karman* (direct object). [PS 1.4.38]
When the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) would have applied by the preceding rule, the designation *karman* (object) is prescribed here.
When the roots *krudh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to bear malice) are *upasṛṣṭa*— that is, connected with a prefix— the person toward whom the anger is directed [receives this designation].

When the roots *śru* (to hear) preceded by the prefixes *prati* and *āṅ* are used, the agent of the preceding action [is called the recipient].
The grammatical factor (kāraka) of the preceding verb *śṛṇoti* [when preceded] by *prati* or *āṅ* is designated as the recipient (*sampradāna*).

The verb *śru* preceded by *prati* and *āṅ* occurs in the sense of acceptance or promise. And that acceptance occurs toward one who exists as an opponent (*para*). "He promises a cow to Devadatta" (*devadattāya gām pratiśṛṇoti*) means "he pledges a cow to Devadatta" (*devadattāya gām āśṛṇoti*); the meaning is that he acknowledges it.

That [agent] becomes designated as the object (*karman*).

The word *artha* is connected with each [of the following]:
roots meaning "to go," roots meaning "to perceive," and roots meaning "to consume."

He causes the boy to go to the village;
