When followed by the causative suffix (*ṇau*), as well as when followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*) or the aorist suffix with the augment *caṅ* (*caṅpare*), the root *iṅ* optionally undergoes the substitution of *gāṅ*.
Thus: *adhijigāpayiṣati*.
And it does not occur [in these cases]:
*adhyāpipayiṣati*;
and also in the case of the *caṅ* [intensive suffix], as in *adhyajīgapat*.
And it did not exceed [the limit].
Aster bhūḥ.
In place of the root *as*, the substitute *bhū* occurs before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. [Example:
*bhavitā*.
Why does [the suffix] *tum* not occur here in the forms *bhavitum* or *bhavitavyam*, and why is it not used?
[The forms] īhāmāsa,
īhāmāsatuḥ, īhāmāsuḥ [are derived from the root īh]. And the root *kṛ* is also employed after it in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), according to Pāṇini 3.1.40.
Thus, by virtue of the inclusion of the root *as* through the mention of *pratyāhāra*,
it is said: "But when used in conjunction with *anu* and *pra*, the wise record that *bhū* does not supersede *as*, because of the specific statement regarding the agent."
The root *brū* is a substitute for *vac*.
In the domain of *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, the root *brū* is replaced by *vac*;
the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.
the speaker / to speak / that which is to be spoken.

By virtue of the substitution of the original element (sthānivadbhāva), when there is an intention to express that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the middle voice (ātmanepada) occurs; as in *ūce* and *vakṣyate*. [166]
For the root *cakṣiṅ*, the substitute *khyāñ* is applied [in place of the root].
The substitute *khyāñ* occurs for the root *cakṣiṅ* before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Example:
*ākhyātā*.
To explain:
it is to be explained that by virtue of the status of being a *sthānin*, the *ātmanepada* ending does not necessarily occur.
By virtue of the inclusion of the phoneme *ñ* as an indicatory suffix (*anubandha*),
[the author] will explain: *ākhyāsyati*,
*ākhyāsyate*.
This substitution is also desired for the root *kṣā* and others:
*ākṣātā*,
*ākṣātum*.
It must be understood that a prohibition regarding avoidance must be stated:
"A wicked person is to be avoided."
The meaning is that they are to be avoided. Furthermore, a prohibition regarding non-existent [beings] must be stated.
Here, *nṛcakṣas* refers to a *rakṣas*, and the root *bhā* has the sense of "to injure."
And furthermore: "The wise one is *vicakṣaṇaḥ*.
It should be stated that [the suffix *khañ*] occurs frequently after the words *sañjñā* and *chandas*.
This is for the sake of forms such as *annavat*, *adhvakat*, *gātravat*, *vicakṣaṇavat*, and *ajiravat*.
Or [the substitution of *sa* for the root *as*] occurs before the *liṭ* suffix.
Since the preceding rule would have made [the substitution] obligatory, an option is now stated:
when the *liṭ* suffix follows, the substitute *khyāñ* optionally occurs for the root *cakṣiṅ*.
He told, they two told, they told;
and it does not occur as [the following]:
he told repeatedly, they two told repeatedly.
They related [it].
The suffix *ya* is applied after a verbal root ending in a vowel, except for those ending in *agh* or *ap*.
The substitute *vī* is applied in place of the root *aj*, when followed by an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, with the exception of the suffixes *ghañ* and *ap*. [Example:
*pravayaṇīyaḥ*.
[The suffix] *ghañ* [is applied in the sense of an agent].
Why [is it said] "except for *agh* and *ap*"? [Consider: *samājaḥ*, *udājaḥ*.
Rather,
[the forms] *samājaḥ* and *udājaḥ* are derived by the rule *sam-udor ajaḥ paśuṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.69), which prescribes the suffix *ap*.
What is the purpose of the long vowel pronunciation? [As in] *pravītāḥ*.
When there is a prohibition regarding the suffixes *bhañ* and *ap*, an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for the suffix *kyap*:
[as in] *samajyā*.
In the case of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with *v*, a choice is desired:
*pravetā* or *prājitā*;
*pravetum* or *prājitum*.
Or those two. (PS 2.4.57)
Since the previous rule would have made [the suffix] obligatory, an option is now stated.
The term *yu* is a reference to the suffix *lyuṭ*.
For the two words *prabhūte* and *aje*, the substitute *vī* occurs; thus,
*pravayaṇo daṇḍaḥ* becomes *prājano daṇḍaḥ*.
Bring the weaving shuttle;
bring the goad.
The suffixes *ṇya*, *kṣatriya*, *ārṣa*, and those ending in *ñi* are elided when forming a patronymic in the sense of "grandson" (*yūni*), provided that the suffixes *aṇ* or *iñ* are elided.
The suffixes beginning with *ṇya* are *gotra*-suffixes.

After a *kṣatriya-gotra* ending in *ṇya*, as well as after one derived from a sage (*ārṣa*) ending in *ñ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* when forming a *yuvan* (descendant) derivative.

First, regarding [a word] ending in *ṇya*: by the rule "after *kuru* and others, *ṇya*" (*Pāṇini* 4.1.151), the suffix *ṇya* is applied; from that, the suffix *iñ* is added for the grandson (*yuvan*), which is then elided (*luk*). Thus, *kauravyaḥ* refers to the father.
The son is Kauravya.
But surely the word *kauravya* is listed among the *tikādi* group; therefore, the suffix *phiñ* ought to apply.
Regarding "Kauravyāyaṇi":
there, a *kṣatriya* lineage is being referred to; [the suffix] *ṇya* is applied after "Kuru" and others (*Pāṇini 4.1.172*).
This [suffix] is prescribed by that [rule], whereas this Brāhmaṇa lineage [is derived] by [the rule] *kurv-ādibhyo ṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.151).

From the rule *kṣatriya-ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.114), the suffix *yaṇ* is applied; from that, the suffix *iñ* is added in the sense of a descendant in the younger generation, which then undergoes elision (*luk*). Śvāphalka is the father.
Śvāphalka is the son.
[The patronymic suffix] *ārṣa-* is applied by Pāṇini 4.1.114 (*ṛṣyaṇ*); from that, the suffix *iñ* is added for a descendant in the younger generation, which then undergoes elision (*luk*).
Vāsiṣṭha is the father.

The son of Vasiṣṭha: by the rule *ñit*—namely, *anṛṣy-ānantarye vida-ādibhyo ’ñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.104), [the suffix] *añ* is applied; from that, the suffix *iñ* is applied for a grandson, and there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix].
Baida is the father;
Vaida is the son.
Furthermore, regarding the suffix *aṇ*: [the suffix] *phiñ* is applied after [patronymic stems] beginning with *tika* (Pāṇini 4.1.154).
Therefore, by the rule *yūni prāg dīvyato ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83), there is the elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]; thus, *taikāyaniḥ* is the father,
and *taikāyaniḥ* is the son.
Why [is it said] "from these"? [Because there are other rules:
*aṇ* after *śiva* and others (*Pāṇini* 4.1.112), and from that, *iñ* after *ataḥ* in the sense of a young descendant (*yuvan*) (*Pāṇini* 4.1.95).
In that case, elision does not occur:
*kauhaḍaḥ* is the father;
*kauhaḍiḥ* is the son.
Why [is the word] "yūni" (in the sense of a youth) used? [Consider:
*vāmarathāḥ*, meaning "the pupils of Vāmarathya.
[This is derived by] the suffix *ṇya* after [words] beginning with *kuru* (Pāṇini 4.1.151).
Thus, there is the suffix *ṇya*; from that, by the rule "from Kaṇva and others in the sense of lineage" (*Pāṇini* 4.2.111), the secondary suffix *aṇ* is applied. Its elision (*luk*) does not occur.
Why [is it specified] "of the suffixes aṇ and iñ"? [Consider:
*dākṣer apatyam yuvā* (the young descendant of Dakṣa) = *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*.
There must be an addition [to the rule] stating that the suffix *yuvan* applies after any [patronymic] suffix, provided it does not denote a Brāhmaṇa lineage (*gotra*).
Baudhi was the father;
Baudhi was the son.
Jābāli was the father.
Jābāli was the son;
Audumbari was the father;
Audumbari was the son.
Bhāṇḍījaṅgha was the father;
Bhāṇḍījaṅgha was the son.
[The suffix] *iñ* is applied here because Śālva is characterized by its constituent parts.
Therefore, there is the suffix *phak*, which undergoes elision (*luk*);
this is established by the observation of the *paila*-class [in the *Gana-pāṭha*].
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *paila* and others. (PS 2.4.59)
The elision of the *yuva*-suffix occurs after [patronymics] such as Paila and others; [alternatively], the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to [Pāṇini 4.1.118]:
"Or [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after Pīlā."
From that [name], by the rule *tasmād aṇo dvyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.156), the suffix *phiñ* is applied; this suffix is then elided (*luk*). Thus, Paila is the father.
Paila is a son [of a Prācya].

Other names such as Paila and others end in the suffix *iñ*; since the elision (*luk*) of that *iñ* would already be established by the rule *iñaḥ prācām* (Pāṇini 2.4.60), this specific listing is for the purpose of including those who are not from the East (*aprāg-artha*).
Paila, Śālaṅki,
Sātyaki.
Sātyakāmi,
Daivi, Audamajji.
Audavraji, Audameghi, Audabuddhi.
The Daivasthas, the Paiṅgalāyanis, and the Rāṇāyanis.
Rauhakṣiti, Bhauliṅgi, Audgāhamāni.
[Auñ] is applied after [the word] aujjihāna; [aṇ] is applied after a word denoting a king (tadrāja). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. [168]
In the opinion of the Eastern grammarians, the substitution of *iña* occurs [for the patronymic suffix *aṇ*].
In the case of a *gotra* [patronymic] stem ending in *iñ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan*-suffix. The mention of "prior" (*prāk*) serves as a qualifier for *gotra*.

It is not for the sake of a grammatical alternative. [In the case of] "the young son of Pānnāgāri," the suffix *phak* is applied by the rule *yañ-iñoś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.101), and there is its elision (*luk*).
Pānnāgāri was the father;
Pānnāgāri was the son.
Mantharaiṣaṇi was the father.
Mānthara is the son of Aiṣaṇi.
Why is it specified "of the Easterners"? [Consider:
Dākṣi is the father.
The son was Dākṣāyaṇa.
Not after [words ending in] *taulvali*. (PS 2.4.61)
The elision (*luk*) that would otherwise apply by the immediately preceding rule is here prohibited.
There is no elision of the secondary suffix (*yuvapratyaya*) following [patronymic stems] such as *taulvali* and others.
Taulvali is the father;
Taulvalāyana is the son;
[and] Taulvali.
Dhāraṇī | Rāvaṇī | Pāraṇī |
Dailīpi, Daivali, Daivamati.
Daivayajñi, Prāvāhaṇi, Māndhātaki.
Ānuhārati,
Śvāphalkī,
Ānumati.
O Āhiṃsi! O Āsuri! O Āyudhi!
O Naimiṣī! O Āsibandhakī! O Baiki!
Āntarahāti,
Pauṣkarasādi,
Vairaki.
Vailaki, Vaihati, Vaikarṇi.
Kāreṇupāli! Kāmāli!
In the case of many [descendants] of a *tadrāja* (patronymic) stem, that same suffix is applied, except in the feminine.
Those [suffixes] are called *tadrāja* (denoting the ruler of that), according to Pāṇini 4.1.172; those beginning with *ñya* are *tadrāja*, according to 5.3.119.
Thus it will be stated:
there is elision (*luk*) of that *tadrāja* suffix when it occurs in the plural and is not feminine,
provided that the plurality is produced by that very same *tadrāja* suffix.
The Aṅgas, the Vaṅgas, and the Puṇḍras.
The Suhmas,
the Magadhas,
and the Lohadhvajās.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [stems ending in] *vrīhimant*.
Why say "of a *tadrāja* [stem]"? [Consider: *aupagavāḥ*.
Why say "in the plural"? [Consider: *āṅgaḥ*.
Why is there a specific mention of that very [term]? [For example: "those for whom a pleasant limb is dear" are *priyavāṅgāḥ*.
Why is it specified "not in the feminine"?
The Āṅgīs are women.
The suffix *yañ* is applied after [names ending in] *yaska* and others to form patronymics (*gotra*).
The entire rule "bahuṣu tenaiva astriyām" (Pāṇini 2.4.63) continues to apply here:
there is elision (*luk*) of a gotra-suffix occurring in the plural, provided it does not denote the feminine gender, when following words such as *yaska* and others.
If the plurality is formed by that very same condition of the *gotra*,
and since the application of the suffix rule excludes the inclusion of the worldly *gotra*, the elision (*luk*) indeed occurs even for the immediate descendant;
thus, [we have] *yaskāḥ*.
[The suffix] *labhya* is applied;
[the rule] "in many" (*bahuṣu*) applies as before, as in *yāskāḥ*;
[the rule] "by that very same [person]" (*tenaiva*) applies as before.
The patronymic suffix *ya* is applied after *priya* and *yāska*; however, this occurs only when not denoting a female: thus, *yāskyaḥ*, but *yāskyaḥ* [with *īn*] for females.
What is the purpose of the term "in the lineage" (*gotre*)? [Example:
*yāskāś chātrāḥ* ("the students of Yaska").
[The base form is] *yaska*.
labhya, duhya, ayaḥsthūṇa.
*Tṛṇakarṇa*:
these five are listed among the *śiva* group and others;
after those, the suffix *iñ* is applied to the next six.
Sadāmatta,
Kambalabhāra, Bahiryoga.
Karṇāṭaka, Piṇḍījaṅgha, Bakasaktha.
Then, from the four subsequent [words] beginning with *gṛṣṭi*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.136:
*basti*, *kudri*.
[Apatya suffixes are added] after *ajavasti* and *mitrayu*; after those following [the aforementioned], the suffix *iñ* is added to twelve [stems].
Rakṣomukha, Jaṅghāratha,
Utkāsa.
Kaṭukamanthaka, Puṣkarasat, Viṣapuṭa.
Uparimekhala,
Kroṣṭumān,
Kroṣṭupāda.
*Kroṣṭumāya* and *śīrṣamāya*:
the suffix *iñ* is applied after the word *puṣkarasat* because it is included in the *bāhv-ādi* group.
The word *kharapa* is listed among the *naḍa*-group; from it, the suffix *phak* is applied:
*padaka*, *varmaka*.
From these two [names], the suffix *iñ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.95;
from the word *Bhalandana*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.112, resulting in *Bhaḍila*.
Bhaṇḍila / Bhadita / Bhaṇḍita.
The suffix *phañ* is applied after these four, beginning with *aśva*, [to form patronymics] (*Pāṇini 4.1.110*).
And [the suffix -tva] is also applied after the words *ya* and *anya*.
In the case of many [descendants], that very same [suffix] is used when not feminine;
and the words "in the lineage" (gotre) also carry over.

The suffix *yañ* and other *aj*-type affixes that denote a lineage (*gotra*) undergo elision (*luṅ*) when they refer to many individuals and are not feminine. For example, from *garga-* etc., by rule 4.1.105 (*gargādibhyo yañ*), we have *gargāḥ*;
likewise, *vatsāḥ*.
Furthermore, there is also the suffix *añ* in the sense of "descendant" after [names of] sages and those for whom no immediate ancestor is known, such as *Bida* and others: *bidāḥ*,
*urvāḥ*.
"Only among many," says Gārgya;
"only by that very [means]," says Baida.
*priyagārgyaḥ*, *priyabaidaḥ*;
[the rule applies] only when not in the feminine.
Gārgyaḥ striyaḥ;
Baidyaḥ striyaḥ.
[The suffix applies] only when referring to a *gotra*.
The suffix *yañ* is applied after *dvīpa* when combined with *samudra*: *dvaipyaḥ*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after words such as *utsa*: *autsāḥ chātrāḥ*.
There is an extension [of the rule] for the application of the genitive case in a *tatpuruṣa* compound when one or two of the suffixes beginning with *yañ* follow.
The family of Gārgya is *gārgyakulam* or *gargakulam*;
the family of the two Gārgyas is *gārgyakulam* or *gargakulam*.
Likewise, the family of Baida is *baidakulam* or *bidakulam*.
*Baidakula* refers to the family of the *baida*s; it may also be *bidakula*. Why [is it specified] "of those beginning with *yañ*"? [Consider] *āṅgakula*.
Why [is it specified] "of one or two"? [Consider] *pāñcālaka*.
The family of the Gargas is the *gargakula*.
Why specify "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound"? [Consider:
that which is near the descendant of Garga is *upagārgya*.
Why is "of the sixth case" (ṣaṣṭhyāḥ) stated? [To exclude cases such as] *paramagārgyaḥ*.
And from Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa, Vasiṣṭha, Gotama, and Aṅgiras. (PS 2.4.65)
The elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix denoting a *gotra* (lineage) occurs when it follows [names] such as Atri and others in the plural.
After the word *Atri*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule "after words ending in *it* and after those not ending in *ini*, [the suffix *ḍhak* is added]" (Pāṇini 4.1.122).
From others, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied:
Atrayas, Bhṛgavas, Kutsas.
The Vasiṣṭhas, the Gotamas, and the Aṅgirasas.
"In many [cases]," so says Ātreya;
"Bhārgava"; "by that very same [person]," so [says] Ātreya.
*Priyātreyāḥ*,
*priyabhārgavāḥ*.
Why does it say "not in the feminine"?
Women who are descendants of Atri are called *ātreyyas*.
[170] After a Bahvṛca-stem ending in *iñ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied when the patronymic refers to people of the East, excluding those from Bhr̥gu. PS_2,4.66.

The suffix *iñ*, which is prescribed after a polysyllabic nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when it denotes a lineage belonging to the Easterners (*prācya*) or the Bharatas, is elided when referring to many descendants.
The Pannāgāras,
the Mantharaiṣaṇas,
and indeed among the Bharatas, the Yudhiṣṭhiras.
Why [is it specified] "having many syllables"? [Consider: *baikayaḥ*, *pauṣpayaḥ*.
Why [is it specified] "among the Eastern Bharatas"? [Consider: *bālākayaḥ*, *hāstidāsayaḥ*.
The Bharatas are indeed Easterners.
Their mention again is for the purpose of making it known that, elsewhere, there is no inclusion of the Bharatas when they were previously included [under the rule *prācām avṛddhāt*].
Consequently, by the rule *iñaḥ prācām* (Pāṇini 2.4.60), there is no elision of the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) for the Bharatas.
The son of Arjuna is the father;
the son of Ārjunāyana is the son.
Not after [names beginning with] Gopavana and so forth. (PS 2.4.67)
After [patronymics] beginning with Gopavana, there is no elision (luk) of the secondary suffix (*gotrapratyaya*) denoting lineage.
This [list] does not belong to the *badādi* sub-group.
Consequently, the elision (luk) that would otherwise apply by the rule *yañañoś ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64) to the patronymic suffix *yañ* and *añ* is prohibited;
thus we have *gaupavanāḥ*.
The Śaiśravas,
Gopavana, and Śigru.
Bindu, Bhājana,
Aśva.
Avatāna,
śyāmāka,
śvāparṇa.
There are exactly these eight, beginning with Gopavana;
the mention of Harita and the others is an error,
for they are recited in the fourth [section] among the Bidas and so forth.
And from those [bases], elision indeed occurs in many instances,
as in *haritaḥ* and *kiṃdāsāḥ*.
In a dvandva compound, [the singular is used] after words beginning with *tika* and *kitava*.
In a *dvandva* compound, the elision (*luk*) of the *gotra* suffix occurs when there are many [descendants] following the *tika*-class and the *kitava*-class. For example:
*taikāyanayaś ca kaitavāyanayaś ca*.
By the rule *tika-ādibhyaḥ phiñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.158), the suffix *phiñ* is applied; its elision (*luk*) occurs, resulting in *tika-kitavāḥ*.
Furthermore, from *vāṅkharayaḥ* and *bhāṇḍīrathayaḥ*, the suffix *iñ* is applied according to *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95).
There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]; thus: Vaṅkharabhaṇḍīrathāḥ.
And Aupakāyanāḥ and Lāmakāyanāḥ, by virtue of the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.99).
There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]; thus, *upakalamakāḥ*.
And from *pāphaka* and *nārakaya*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] the suffix *iñ* is applied, which is then elided; thus, *paphakanarakāḥ*.
From *baka-nakha* and *śva-guda-pariṇaddha*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*, there is the suffix *iñ*; its elision (*luk*) occurs, resulting in *bakanakha-śvagudapariṇaddhāḥ*.
From the word *ubja*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*, [the suffix *iñ* is applied].

From the word *kakubha*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.112] *śivādibhyo ’ṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; there is elision (*luk*) of both [the suffix and its marker], and by [Pāṇini 7.3.18] *tasya luki*, the feminine suffix *īp* is also elided. Thus, *aubjayas* and *kākubhās* become *ubjakakubhāḥ*.
Similarly, from *lāṅkayaḥ* and *śāntamukhayaḥ*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.95] *ata iñ*, the suffix *iñ* is applied.
There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]; thus, *laṅkaśāntamukha*.
The word *urasa* is listed among the *tikādi* group; from it, the suffix *phiñ* is applied.
From the word *laṅkaṭa*, the suffix *iñ* is added; there is elision (*luk*) of those two [suffixes],
and thus *aurasāyana* and *lāṅkaṭaya* become *urasalaṅkaṭāḥ*.

*Bhrāṣṭakayaḥ* and *kāpiṣṭhalayaḥ*: by adding the suffix *iñ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.95, there is its elision (*luk*), resulting in *bhrāṣṭakakāpiṣṭhalāḥ*. *Kārṣṇājinayaḥ* and *kārṣṇasundarayaḥ*: by adding the suffix *iñ* according to Pāṇini 4.1.95...
There is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix]; thus we have *kṛṣṇājina*, *kṛṣṇasundara*, and *āgniveśya* as well as *dāseraka*.

The noble one is a brahmin.
A cow that is fit for breeding is called *kālyā* with respect to procreation.
The form *upasaryā* is an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) when it refers to a woman who is fit for conception; it is formed by adding the suffix *yat* to the root *sṛ* preceded by the prefix *upa*.
*Kālyā* means having reached the proper time.
*Prajana* means procreation,
specifically the first conception of a fetus.
A cow that has reached the time for conception is called *upasaryā*; likewise, a mare that has reached the time for conception is called *upasaryā*.
What is the meaning of "kālyā prajane" (at the time of delivery)? [For example:
"The Madhurā [cow] should be brought near in the autumn."
The association with the undecaying.
The form *ajarya* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) word, provided that it signifies "union."

From the root *jṛ* (to grow old), preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the suffix *yat* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) in the sense of an agent when joined together (*saṅgate*) or in the sense of meeting (*saṅgamane*).
Thus, "it does not grow old" is *ajaryam*.
The association with noble persons (*ārya-saṅgatam*) is *ajarya*.
"May our meeting be ageless.
What is meant by "meeting"?
An aged blanket. [200]
After the root *vad*, when followed by a word ending in a *su*-affix, the suffix *kyap* is applied, as well as [the suffixes previously mentioned].
The term *anupasarge* (in the absence of a prefix) carries over [from the previous rule].
After the verbal root *vad*, when a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is present as an upapada and no prefix (*upasarga*) intervenes, the suffix *kyap* occurs.
From the word "and" (ca), it is understood that there is also the *brahmodya*,
the *brahmavadya*.

[The suffix -ya is applied after the root *vad*] when preceded by *satya*, as in *satyodyam* and *satyavadyam*. Why [is it said] "when followed by a case-ending" (*supi*)? [To show that it does not apply here: *vādyam*.
It is only when there is no prefix (*anupasarge*) [that this applies]; thus, with a prefix, we have *pravādyam*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *bhū* when expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*).
The rule *supy anupasarge* ("after a nominal suffix, provided there is no prefix") is understood to carry over.

After the verbal root *bhū*, when a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) is present as an attendant word (*upapada*) and there is no prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *kyap* occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*).
But that which does not follow [is as follows]:
having attained *brahmabhūya*, having attained the state of Brahman; having attained the state of a god (*devabhūya*).

He has attained the state of a god (*devatvam gataḥ*). The inclusion of the word *bhāva* is for the sake of what follows. [The rule] "when a *sup*-ending word follows" (*supi*) applies here as well; thus, *bhavyam*.
The same applies when there is no prefix:
*prabhavyam*.
And [the suffix] *hanas* occurs after that [root]. (Pāṇini 3.1.108)
The phrase "after a verb meaning 'to sleep' when no prefix is present" is understood [from the previous rule],
as is the phrase "in the sense of an abstract state (bhāva)."

When a word ending in a case-suffix (subanta) is present as an upapada, provided it is not a prefix (anupasarga), the suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *han* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), and the letter *t* is substituted for the final [h]. Example: *brahmahatyā*.
In *aśvahatyā*, [the suffix] *ghañ* is applied by the rule *supi*; thus, *ghātaḥ*.
However, the suffix *ṇyat* does not occur in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), because such a formation is not sanctioned by usage (*anabhidhānāt*).
Only when there is no prefix [is this rule applied];
thus, *praghātaḥ* occurs.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the verbal roots *i*, *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ*.
The rule "after a verbal root [ending in a consonant], when there is no prefix, in the sense of the action itself" is no longer in force;
this is a general prescription.
The suffix *kyap* occurs after these roots: *i*, *stu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, and *dṛ*. Examples:
*ityaḥ* (to be gone), *stutyaḥ* (to be praised).
A disciple; one to be served; one to be honored.
*Juṣyaḥ*.
While the rule for *kyap* was already in effect, the repetition of the term *kyap* is for the purpose of overriding a previous exception.
[The suffix] *kyap* is applied after a root ending in *u* when necessity is implied (Pāṇini 3.1.125).
Thus, setting aside the suffix *ṇyat*, only *kyap* occurs:
*avaśyastutyaḥ*.
When the root *vṛ* is mentioned, it is intended that *vṛñ* (the ninth-class root) is meant, not *vṛṅ* (the fourth-class root).
The suffix *yat* is applied after the roots *vṛ*, *ṛtviñ*, and optionally after *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh*; this should be stated as a rule.
Thus: *śasyam* or *śaṃsyam*.
*duhyam*, *dohyam*, *guhyam*, *gohyam*.
There is an extension [of the rule] for the root *añj* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*).
*Ājyam* means clarified butter (*ghṛtam*). How is it to be understood?
This is the form of the root *ai*, not of *iṇ*. [201]
The suffix *iṇ* is applied after a root ending in *ṛ*, as well as after roots having *ṛ* as their penultimate letter, except for the roots *kḷp* and *cṛ*.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after a verbal root that has *ṛ* as its penultimate letter, with the exception of the roots *kḷp* and *cṛt*. For example:
from *vṛt*, *vṛtyam*.
Regarding the rule *vṛdhu-vṛdhyam akḷpi-cṛteḥ*: why [is it stated] "not after *kḷp* or *cṛt*"? [Examples: *kalpyam*, *cartyam*.
Why is the long vowel marker (*tapara*) used?

The root *kṛ* is used in the sense of making a sound; it takes only the suffix *ṇyat*, as in *kīrtyam*. It should be stated that the suffix *ṇyat* is also applied after the root *sṛj* when preceded by *pāṇau*.
The word *pāṇisargyā* means "a rope for releasing [the sacrificial animal]. And from the root preceded by *sam-ava*, [we have] *samavasargyā*.
And the vowel *ī* [is substituted] for the root *khan*.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the verbal root *khan*, and the vowel *ī* is substituted for the final letter [of the root].
*khe* is a long-term designation for the purpose of *praśleṣa* (conjunction).
Therein, the second *i*-vowel [is understood] by the rule *ye vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.43).
Thus, it is for the purpose of precluding the substitution of *āt*.
The suffix kyac is applied after the root *bhṛ* (to carry) when it does not denote a name.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the verbal root *bhṛ* (to support/maintain) when it does not denote a technical name (*asañjñāyām*). [Example:
*bhṛtyāḥ* = laborers.
The meaning is "those who are to be supported. Why does it say "not when used as a name"? [Consider] *bhārya*, which is the name of a certain Kṣatriya.
After the prefix *sam*, the [suffixes] are optional:
*sambhṛtyāḥ* or *sambhāryāḥ*.
Since the word *sañjñā* is observed to be used in the masculine, your term *bhāryā* is not established [as a feminine noun];
however, since the category of abstract state (*bhāva*) applies to the feminine, the term *bhāryā* is thus established.
The substitution [of *guṇa*] for the root *mṛj* is optional.

The suffix *kyap* is optionally applied after the root *mṛj*. Since the root has *ṛ* as its penultimate letter (*ṛdupadha*), this is an optional rule that applies where [the suffix] was otherwise already required.
*parimṛjyaḥ*, *parimārgyaḥ*.
[202] *rājasūya*, *sūrya*, *mṛṣodya*, *rucya*, *kupya*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, *avyathya*. (Pāṇini 3.1.114)
The words *rājasūya*, *sūrya*, *mṛṣodya*, *rucya*, *kupya*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, and *avyathya* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) with the suffix *kyap*.
[The word *rājasūya* means] that which is to be pressed by a king (*rājñā sotavyaḥ*).

Or, the *rājasūya* sacrifice is so called because a king (*rājan*) is consecrated (*sūyate*) here; [the suffix] *kyap* is applied after the roots *sū* and *sṛ*, and there is *utva* (substitution of *u*) for the root *sṛ*.
Alternatively, the augment *ruṭ* is inserted after the root *sub*.
[The word] *sūryaḥ* is derived from the roots *sṛ* or *sū*.

In the case of the root *vad*, preceded by the prefix *mṛṣā*, although the suffix *yat* would otherwise be applicable, the suffix *kyap* is invariably prescribed as a formal irregularity (*nipātana*).
The word *mṛṣodya* is derived from *mṛṣā* with the suffix *kyap*, meaning "one who speaks falsely. The word *rucya* means "that which is pleasing";
it is formed with the suffix *kyap* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
The suffix *ktvā* is applied after the root *gup* and others when a name is being formed. Thus, *kupyaṃ* (base metal); otherwise, it is *gopyaṃ*.
Those that ripen on plowed ground are called *kṛṣṭapacyāḥ*; this is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) with the agent as the object (*karmakartṛ*). That which does not tremble is *avyathyaḥ*.
The roots *bhid* and *udbhid* denote a river.
The suffix *kyap* is irregularly applied after the roots *bhid* and *ujjh* when "river" (*nada*) is to be expressed;
furthermore, there is the substitution of *dh* for *ujjh*.
*bhidyaḥ* means "that which breaks the bank"; *uddhyaḥ* means "that which abandons the water. Why specify "in a river" (*nade*)? [To exclude cases such as] *bhettā* ("a breaker").
Abandoned.
Under the asterisms Puṣya and Siddhi.
The suffix *kyap* is prescribed after the roots *puṣ* and *sidh* when used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), provided that a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is to be expressed. Thus,
because meanings flourish (*puṣyanti*) in it, it is called *puṣya*.
"Siddhyaḥ" means those things which are accomplished (*sidhyanti*) in this; why "in a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatre*)? [To show: nourishing (*poṣaṇam*), establishing (*sedhanam*).
The suffix *kvi* is applied after the roots *vipūya*, *vinīya*, and *jityā*, as well as after *muñja*, *kalka*, and *hali*.

The words *nipūya*, *vinīya*, and *jitya* are established as irregular forms (*nipātyante*) when the meanings of *muñja*, *kalka*, and *hali* are to be understood respectively. After the roots *pū* preceded by *vi-*, *nī*, and likewise *ji*, the suffix *kyap* is irregularly applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), even though [by other rules] *yat* would have been expected.
Vipūya is muñja grass;
vipāvyam is something else;
vinīya is karka grass.
One thing is to be tamed;
the ploughshare is to be yoked;
another thing is to be conquered.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *grah* following the prefixes *prati* and *apa*.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *grah* preceded by *prati* and *api* in the Vedic domain; for example:
*mattasya na pratigr̥hyam*.
Therefore, it is not *apigṛhya*. Why [is the rule] stated as "in the Veda" (*chandasi*)? [To show that in secular usage it is] *pratigrāhyam*.
Moreover, it should be understood that [the suffix *cha*] is also applied after words meaning "unrestrained," "external," and "adherents of other schools. (PS 3.1.119)

In the case of the word *pada*, when it does not mean "unrestrained" (*asvairin*) and refers to something external (*bāhyā*), the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *grah* in the sense of "a part" (*pakṣya*).
First, regarding *pada*: *pragṛhyaṃ padaṃ*.
That which has been assigned the designation *pragṛhya*;
a word that is subject to *avagraha* (separation) is called *avagṛhya*.
"Without mastery" means dependent;
"these are householders" means they are those who have taken up a home.

Regarding *bāhyāyam*: it refers to an army belonging to a village (*grāma-gṛhyā senā*) or an army belonging to a city (*nagara-gṛhyā senā*); the meaning is that they have come from outside the village or the city.
The feminine gender does not apply except as specifically indicated.
That which exists in a faction is *pakṣya*;
those who are followers of Vāsudeva are *vāsudevagṛhyāḥ*.
"Those who have Arjuna as their leader" means those who have taken refuge in his faction.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is applied after the roots *kṛ* and *vṛṣ*.

The suffix *kyap* optionally occurs after the roots *kṛ* and *vṛṣ*. Since the suffix *ṇyat* would otherwise apply to *kṛ*, and since *kyap* would necessarily apply to *vṛṣ* because it has a short *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel, this rule establishes an option (*vibhāṣā*) for both.
*kṛtyam*, *kāryam*;
*vṛṣyam*, *varṣyam*.
And a vehicle on a leaf. // PS_3.1.121 //
The word *yugya* is derived as an irregular form (*nipātana*) when it refers to a vehicle; for that by which one travels is called a *patra*, meaning a conveyance.
A draft ox;
a draft horse;
a draft elephant.
The suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *yuj*, and the change to the guttural *k* is also prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation).
Why [is it said] "in the sense of 'fit for' (*patre*)"?
[Because] otherwise, it would mean simply "suitable" (*yogyam*).
The word *amāvāsya* may optionally [take the suffix *ṭhak*].
The word *amā* is used in the sense of "together with.
When this word is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *vas* (to dwell) to denote time as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
In this case, the absence of *vṛddhi* substitution for one of the two vowels is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation).
Because the sun and the moon dwell together (*saha vasataḥ*) at this time, it is called *amāvāsya*, or *amāvasyā*.

Alternatively, it is derived from *amāvāsyā* [with the elision of the final syllable], because that which has undergone a modification in one part is not considered different [from the original]. (*Pāṇini 4.3.30*)

Thus, in this context, there is also the inclusion of the word *amāvasyā*. "I shall derive the forms *amāvasya* and *amāvasyam* from the root *vas*, ensuring they lack the *vṛddhi* vowel; likewise, their status as a single compound and their accentuation are established for me."

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the words *niṣṭarkya*, *devahūya*, *praṇīya*, *unnīya*, *ucchiṣya*, *marya*, *starya*, *dhvaryu*, *khanya*, *khānya*, *devayajyā*, *āpṛcchya*, *pratiṣīvya*, *brahmavādya*, *bhāvya*, *stāvya*, and *upacāyyapṛḍa* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*).
The words beginning with *niṣṭarkya* are irregularly formed in the domain of the Vedic language.
Whatever is not established here by means of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) is all established through irregularity (*nipātana*).
In the case of *niṣṭarkyaḥ*, although the suffix *kyap* would have been expected after the root *kṛtī* (meaning "to cut") preceded by the prefix *nis*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied instead,
along with a transposition of the initial and final sounds.
The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is applied as a nipātana (irregular formation):
"One desiring cattle should pile the *niṣṭarkya*.
When the word *deva* is the upapada, the suffix *kyap* is added to the roots *hve* or *hu*.
And there is the state of being long and stout.
[The word] *devahūyaḥ* [is formed] with the suffix *kyap* after the roots *nī-* preceded by *pra-* and *ut-*. [204]
*praṇīyaḥ* and *unnīyaḥ*:
the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *śās* preceded by the prefix *ut*.
*Ucchiṣya*:
from the roots *mṛṅ* (to perish) and *stṛñ* (to spread).
The root *dhvṛ* means "to stagger" or "to reel"; from these [roots], the suffix *yat* is applied.
Thus, *maryaḥ*.
*staryā*:
this is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) specifically for the feminine;
*dhvaryaḥ*.
*khaneryat* / *khanyā*:
from this very [root] *khan*, the suffix *ṇyat* [is applied].
Another [derivation]: when the word *deva* is used as an upapada, the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *yaj*. Thus:
*devayajyā*.
The feminine gender is applied by nipātana.
From the root *prach* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *kyap* is added:
*āpṛcchyaḥ*.
The suffix *kyap* is added after the root *sīv* preceded by *prati*, and there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.
Thus, *pratiṣīvyaḥ*.
When *brahman* is the upapada, the suffix *ṇyat* is added after the root *vad*. Thus, *brahmavādyaḥ*.
The word *brahmavādya* is derived from the roots *bhū* and *stu* with the suffix *ṇyat*, and the substitution of *āv* occurs.
The forms *bhāvya* and *stāvyaḥ* are derived from the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *upa*, with the suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *ā* for the penultimate vowel.
*upacāyyapṛḍam*:
this is a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) when *pṛḍa* is the final member of the compound;
it should be stated that [the first member] is *hiraṇya*.
In *upaceyapṛḍa*, [the suffix] is other than *hiraṇya*.
One should know that in *niṣṭarkya* there is a reversal; the change of *s* to *ṣ* occurs by way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
The suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *āy*—these two are irregularly derived (*nipātita*) in *upacāyya*.

The suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed after one [root], and the suffix *kyap* after four; the suffix *yata* is prescribed after four [roots]. The suffix *ya* occurs after one [root] with *ṇyat*, there are two instances of *kyap*, and the prescription of *ṇyat* occurs four times.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* or a consonant.
The sixth case ending is used in the sense of the fifth case.
The affix *ṇyat* occurs after a verbal root ending in an *ṛ*-vowel as well as after one ending in a consonant.
The task is to be carried out, to be removed, or to be maintained as a statement.
That which is to be cooked.
Or [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after a word denoting a necessary duty (*āvaśyaka*). // PS 3.1.125 //
The state of being inevitable is *āvaśyakam*.
When inevitability is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied after a verbal root ending in the vowel *u*.
From the root *ūh* (to remove): *apavādaḥ*;
from *lū* (to cut): *lāvyaṃ*; from *pū* (to purify): *pāvyaṃ*.
What is the purpose of the condition "when necessity is intended"? [Consider] *lavyam*.
Or, if it is held that the condition applies when necessity is to be expressed (*dyotye*), then there would be the impossibility of forming a *svarasamāsa* (compound with accentual restriction).
Is it that [the forms] *avaśyalāvyam* and *avaśyapāvyam* are incorrect? No, this is not a fault.
The compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-type rule;
furthermore, effort will be made regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member.
[205] The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *ās*, *yu*, *vap*, *rap*, *lap*, *trap*, and *cam*. (Pāṇini 3.2.178)

The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after the root *sunoti* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, as well as after the roots *yu*, *vapi*, *rapi*, *lapi*, *trapi*, and *cam*. This is an exception to [the rule for] *yat*. Example: *āsāvyam*.
To be cooked;
to be sown; to be given.
That which is to be rinsed;
that which is to be protected;
that which is to be sipped for purification.
The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned;
[thus] *dabhi* becomes *dābhyam*.
That which is not to be brought forward [as a probans] is that which is non-eternal. (PS 3.1.127)
The form *ānāyya* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) word when something impermanent (*anitya*) is to be expressed; here,
the suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *āya* for the root vowel are irregularly applied to the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *ā*.
The *dakṣiṇāgni* is not to be fetched [from elsewhere];
this is its conventional etymology.
Therefore, it remains permanently established specifically as the *dakṣiṇāgni*.
And its impermanence is constant because it does not arise from [the original source].
Furthermore, the Dakṣiṇāgni which is brought from the Gārhapatya together with the Āhavanīya has a single origin; in that case, there is the application of that [rule].
Nor [should it be fetched] from the *dakṣiṇāgni* alone;
for its source is considered variable—either from the house of a wealthy Vaiśya, or from a hearth (*bhrāṣṭra*), or from the *gārhapatya*.
If it is argued that the *āhavanīya* is non-permanent, then what has been performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni* would be rendered invalid.
One should know that [the child] belongs to a single womb; otherwise, it would be considered as if born of another.
*Praṇāyya* means "not approved" or "disapproved."
"Non-agreement" (*asammati*) means that there is no agreement (*sammati*) regarding this;
"agreement" (*sammati*) is the act of agreeing (*sammanana*).
The term *praṇāyya* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) used when "consensus" (*saṃmatatā*) or "reverence" (*pūjā*) is to be expressed; for example,
*praṇāyyaś coraḥ* ("a thief who is held in high esteem").
What is the meaning of "not agreed upon"?
For example, "another [person] is to be led.
If this is so, how is the following [to be explained]?
"A father should teach the Veda to his eldest son, or to a beloved pupil, but to no one else whatsoever"?
Here, "consent" (*sammati*) is also said to mean "desire" (*abhilāṣa*).
In the absence of that [desire], through freedom from longing, the disciple becomes one who is not [merely] agreeable;
it is therefore appropriate that one should speak of Brahman to such a disciple—one who is free from desire and striving for the sake of liberation—as to one who is truly worthy.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *pā*, *sā*, *nī*, *ci*, and *dhā* when followed by the words *māna*, *havir*, *nivāsa*, and *sāmidhenī* respectively.

The words *pāyya* and others are derived as irregular forms (*nipātana*) according to their respective order, when the meanings "measuring," "oblation," "dwelling," and "sāmidhenī verse" are to be expressed.
In the case of *pāyya*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *mā*.
The substitution of *p* for the initial [of *mā*] is also prescribed when it means "measuring. Thus, *pāyyam* means "a measure," while anything else is *meyam*.
From the root *nī* preceded by *sam*, the suffix *ṇyat*, the replacement of *ā* for *i*, and the lengthening of the vowel in the prefix are all prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*).
*Sānnāyya* is the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
It is that which is to be brought together (*saṃneya*);
however, due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it remains restricted specifically to a particular type of oblation.

From the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *ni*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, the initial vowel is replaced by *ā*, and the augment *kuṅ* (i.e., *kā*) is also substituted; thus, *nikāyyaḥ* means "a dwelling. Any other meaning is *niceya*.
The word *sāmidhenī* denotes a specific type of *ṛc*;
and among those, it is not every *sāmidhenī* that is called a *dhāyyā*, but rather only a certain one.
For this is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*);
and thus it is seen even in the case of what is not an *āsamidhenī*, in the passage: "He recites the *dhāyyās*: 'Agni is the leader; him with the Soma-sacrifices... [206]
In the sense of a sacrifice, the words *kuṇḍapāyya* and *sañcāyya* are formed with the suffix *kyap*.
The words *kuṇḍapāyya* and *sañcāyya* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when denoting a sacrificial rite (*kratu*).

When the word *kuṇḍa* occurs as a third-case dependent (*upapada*), the suffix *yat* is irregularly applied to the root *pā* (to drink) in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the augment *yuk* is added.
The *kuṇḍapāyya* sacrifice is so called because Soma is drunk from a *kuṇḍa* (vessel) in it;
the accent is that of the *anāvaḥ* group.
From the root *ci* preceded by *sam*, the suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *āya* are irregularly prescribed (*nipātana*).
The sacrificial rite (*kratu*) called *sañcāyya* is so named because Soma is collected (*sañcīyate*) in it. Why "in a sacrificial rite"?
[Consider] *kuṇḍapāna*.
Accumulation.
The words *paricāyya*, *upacāyya*, and *samūhya* refer to types of sacrificial fires.

One who whispers into the ear is a *karṇejapa*, meaning a slanderer.
Why [specify] "of an elephant or a slanderer"? [Consider:
one who delights in a thicket (*stambe rantā*).
The word *maśaka-* is derived from the root *maś* with the suffix *karni*, applied when whispered into the ear.
[214] The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *śam* when used as a technical term (*sañjñā*). (Pāṇini 3.2.14)
When *śam* is the preceding word (*upapada*), the suffix *ac* occurs after the verbal root alone, in the sense of a name (*sañjñā*). Example: *śaṅkaraḥ*.
*śambhavaḥ*,
*śaṃvadaḥ*.
Why is there a mention of the term "dhātu" (root), since the word "dhātoḥ" (of a root) is already understood from the context?

Since the rule is already established by the phrase "when [the word] signifies a name (śami-sañjñāyām)," the explicit mention of the verbal root (dhātu) is for the purpose of prohibiting the suffix *ṭa* after the root *kṛ* when it occurs with causal factors (*hetu*) and so forth; as in:
"A female wandering ascetic named Śaṅkarā," and "A bird named Śaṅkarā."
And she is of such character.
The suffix *lyap* is applied after the root *śī* when it follows a word in the locative case.

The term *supi* is connected [to the rule]. When a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is used as an *upapada* in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the suffix *ac* is applied after the verbal root *śī*.
*khaśayaḥ* means "one who lies in the sky"; *gartaśayaḥ*, "one who lies in a pit.
An addition [to the rule] should be made for *pārśva* and others.
One who sleeps on his sides is a *pārśvaśaya*; one who sleeps on his belly is an *udaraśaya*; one who sleeps on his back is a *pṛṣṭhaśaya*.
And [the suffix *kvin* is applied] after the word *digdha* when it occurs with *saha*. One who sleeps with a poisoned [person] is called *digdha-saha-śayaḥ*.
[This applies] when the agents are those such as *uttāna* and others.
He who lies on his back is *uttānaśayaḥ*;
he who lies head-downward is *avamūrdhaśayaḥ*.
[The suffix] *ḍa* is applied after *giri* in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
He who sleeps on the mountain is Giriśa.
The suffix *ṭa* is applied after a verbal root ending in *care*.

The term "in the locative" (adhikaraṇe) is understood [from the previous rule]. The suffix *ṭa* occurs after the root *car* when a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is present as an attendant word (*upapada*).
One who moves among the Kurus is a *kurucara*; likewise, a *madracara*. A female mover among the Kurus is a *kurucarī*.
The suffix *madra-carī* involves the addition of another affix (*pratyaya*) for the purpose of applying the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
And [the suffix -aṇ] is applied after the words *bhikṣā*, *senā*, and *ādāya*.
This rule is commenced for the sake of [specifying] non-locative meanings. When *bhikṣā*, *senā*, or *ādāya* occur as governing words (*upapada*), the suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *car*.
One who wanders for alms;
one who wanders with an army; one who wanders taking [something].
The suffix *asun* is applied after the root *sṛ* when preceded by the words *puraḥ*, *agratas*, or *agre*.
When *puras*, *agratas*, or *agre* are used as preceding words (*upapada*), the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *sṛ*. Thus, one who moves forward (*puraḥ*) is called *puraḥsaraḥ*.
One who goes at the front;
one who leads.
In the preceding [sūtra], [the suffix] occurs when the agent is expressed.
When the word *pūrva*, signifying the agent (*kartṛ*), is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *sṛ*. Thus,
"one who goes first" is *pūrvasaraḥ*.
Why is it specified "in the sense of the agent"? [Consider: *pūrvasāraḥ*, meaning "one who moves toward the eastern region."
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after the root *kṛ* when expressing cause, habitual action, or conformity.
When *karman* is the upapada, the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *kṛ* when the meanings of cause (*hetu*), habitual tendency (*tācchīlya*), and compliance (*ānulomya*) are understood.
A cause is an absolute instrument.
The state of having that character (*tācchīlya*) is the nature of being that (*tatsvabhāvatā*).
*Ānulomya* is conformity (*anukūlatā*).
First, regarding the causal sense (*hetu*): "A daughter who causes grief."
Knowledge brings glory;
wealth sustains the family. Regarding the formation of nouns from roots expressing habitual action (*tācchīlya*): one who performs ancestral rites is called *śrāddhakaraḥ*.
One who accomplishes the purpose;
in the sense of compliance: one who carries out commands, one who carries out instructions.
What is the purpose of the phrase "in these"? [Examples:
*kumbhakāraḥ* (pot-maker), *nagarakāraḥ* (city-builder).

In the case of *divā-vibhā-niśā-prabhā-bhās-kāra-anta-ananta-ādi-bahu-nāndī-kiṃ-lipi-libi-bali-bhakti-kartṛ-citra-kṣetra-saṅkhyā-jaṅghā-bāhv-ahar-yat-tad-dhanur-aruṣ* [the suffix *ṭa* is applied]. Both rules— *karmaṇi* and *supi*— are understood to carry over [from the preceding sūtras].
In this regard, the connection is as appropriate:
when *divā* and so forth are used as upapadas, the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *kṛ*.
This rule is formulated for the purpose of excluding meanings such as "cause" (*hetu*) and others.
The word *divā* expresses the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and is a qualifier of the rule *supi*.
[Thus: "He makes living beings active during the day" is *divākara*;
"he makes light" is *vibhākara*.
Niśākara (the maker of night),
Prabhākara (the maker of light), Bhāskara (the maker of radiance).
Due to the irregularity (nipātana) of the word *saka*, the visarga and the jihvāmūlīya do not occur;
thus we have *kārakaraḥ* and *antakaraḥ*.
He is the one who brings about the infinite,
the one who initiates the beginning,
and the one who performs much.
A celebrant,
a servant,
and a scribe.
One who performs the libation;
one who performs the offering;
one who performs the devotion.
A maker of mats,
a painter,
a maker of fields.
Number: one-maker, two-maker, three-maker;
shank-maker.
The arm-maker;
the day-maker;
the "what-maker."
*tatkaraḥ*,
*dhanuṣkaraḥ*,
*aruṣkaraḥ*.
Why is the suffix *ac* prescribed after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *kiṃ*, *yat*, or *tat* in the sense of "many"? [Examples: *kiṅkarāḥ*, *yatkarāḥ*.
It is productive of that result;
it is highly beneficial;
or alternatively, its inclusion will be made in the list beginning with "ajā."
The [kṛt] affix *niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) when the action denotes wages (*bhṛti*).
The mention of *karmaṇi* [in the rule] is for the sake of grasping the word-form itself.
When the word *karman* occurs as an *upapada*— that is, when it denotes an object— the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *kṛ*, provided that "wages" (*bhṛti*) is understood.
Wages (bhṛti) mean remuneration; it is the recompense for work.
A "laborer" (karmakara) is one who performs work; the meaning is "a hired servant."
Why is it specified "in the sense of wages"? [Consider: *karakāraḥ*.
Not in sounds, verses, quarrels, songs, enmity, flattery, aphorisms, mantras, or words. // PS 3.2.23 //
When *śabda* and other such words function as *upapadas*, the suffix *ṭa* does not occur after the root *kṛ*.
That which was applicable in the case of *hetu* and other such words is hereby prohibited.
A maker of noise; a maker of verses; a maker of quarrels.
One who composes verses;
one who creates enmity;
one who offers flattery.
A flatterer;
an author of Sūtras; an author of Mantras.
The author of the verses.
The suffix *in* is applied after the words *stamba* and *śakṛt*.
The suffix *in* occurs when the verbal roots *stambh* and *śakṛ* are used as governing objects (*upapada*).
It should be stated that this applies specifically to the [objects] "rice" (*vrīhi*) and "calf" (*vatsa*).
"Stambakari" refers to rice;

Why [is the rule] stated as "of rice and a calf"? [To exclude cases such as: *stambakāri* (one who cuts a pillar).
One who makes a pillar;
one who makes dung.
The suffix *ghan* is applied after the roots *hṛ*, *dṛt*, and *nāth* when the object is an animal.
When the two verbal roots *dṛti* and *nātha* are used as accompanying words (*upapada*) for the root *hṛ*, the suffix *in* is applied to the root *hṛ* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is an animal. Thus,

In *nāthahariḥ*, [the final vowel] is *paśu*.

The *phalegrahi* and the *ātmambhari*. (Pāṇini 3.2.26)

The two words *phalegrahi* and *ātmambhari* are derived as irregular formations (*nipātana*). When the word *phala* is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*), its final vowel is changed to *e*, and the suffix *in* is applied to the root *grah*. Thus, *phalegrahi* is formed. Similarly, *ātmambhari* is formed from the root *bhṛ* with the prefix *ātman*.

A tree that bears fruit is called *phalegrahi*; here, the augment *mum* and the suffix *in* are applied to the root *bhṛ*, with the word *ātman* as its attendant (*upapada*), according to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). One who nourishes oneself is called *ātmambhari*.
The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned:
*kukṣimbhariḥ* (one who fills his belly) and *udarambhariḥ* (one who fills his stomach).
In the Vedic language (chandas), the suffix *kvin* is applied after the roots *vana*, *san*, *rakṣ*, and *math*.
The root *vana* is used in the sense of sharing or distribution; the root *rakṣa* is used in the sense of protection.
The suffix *in* occurs after these roots when *manth* (meaning "to churn") and *vilōḍana* ("churning") are used as governing objects (*upapada*) in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). For example:
*brahmavaniṃ tvā kṣatravaniṃ suprajāvaniṃ rāyaspoṣavaniṃ paryūhāmi*. (I pile you around, O you who win Brahman, who win Kṣatra, who win good progeny, and who win the increase of wealth.)
Let me utter speech that wins cattle;
let the two dogs who guard the path, the seekers of the oblation, turn away from us.
After the root *ej*, the suffix *khaś* is applied.

From the root *ejṛ* "to tremble," when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *khaś* occurs with a noun in the objective case as an upapada. The letter *kh* is for the purpose of adding the augment *mum*.
The suffix *śakāra* is for the purpose of assigning the technical designation *sārvadhātuka*. [Examples:
*aṅgamejayati* (he makes his limbs tremble), *aṅgamejayaḥ* (one who makes his limbs tremble), *janamejayaḥ* (one who conquers people).
An addition to the rule [Pāṇini 2.4.11] should be made regarding the words *vāta*, *śunī*, *tila*, and *śardha* as objects of the verbs *aj*, *dheṭ*, *tud*, and *jahāti*. Examples:
*vātamajā mṛgāḥ* (deer driven by the wind); *śunindhayaḥ* (sucking at a female dog).
One who picks out the sesame seeds; beans that cause flatulence.
The roots √dhmā and √dheṭ take the affix *khaś* after the words *nāsikā* and *stanau*.
When *nāsikā* and *stanau* are used as subordinate words (*upapada*) for the actions [expressed by] the verbal roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ*, the suffix *khaś* is applied.
Here, the correspondence [of the roots to the subordinate words] in their respective order is not intended.
After the root *dheṭ* "to suck," [the suffix *khaś* is applied] when *stanau* ("breasts") is the object;
thus, *stanandhayaḥ*.
But when *nāsikā* ("nose") is the object, it is applied after both *dhmā* and *dheṭ*; thus, *nāsikandhamaḥ* and *nāsikandhayaḥ*.
*nāsikandhamaḥ* and *nāsikandhayaḥ*.
And this is obtained because of the deviation from the rule regarding "the nose and the breast" (*nāsika-stanayoḥ*), specifically by not placing the word with fewer syllables first.
Because the root *dheṭ* has the marker *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine;
thus, *stanandhayī*.
And [the same applies] to the case of a tube and a fist. (PS 3.2.30)
When the words *nāḍī* and *muṣṭi* are used as subordinate objects (*upapada*) for the roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ*, the suffix *khaś* is applied.
Here too, the fact that the word ending in a *ghi* vowel does not appear first is a sign of an exception to the general rule.
Therefore, there is no application of the rule for numbered items [to these]:
*nāḍindhama* ("blowing through a tube") and *muṣṭindhama* ("blowing with the fist").
The tube-sucker; the fist-sucker;
and the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of including those not explicitly mentioned.
One who smelts a pot;
one who drinks from a pot;
one who smelts a khāri-measure [of ore].
Khāriṃdhaya,
Vātandhama Parvata,
and Vātandhaya.
The suffix *u* is applied after the roots *kūl* and *ruj*, when followed by the agentive suffix *vaha*.

From the roots *ruj* in the sense of "breaking" and *vah* in the sense of "carrying," when preceded by the prefix *ud*, the suffix *khaś* is applied when *kūla* (bank) is the object (*karman*) in composition.
A chariot that shatters the bank is called *kūlamudruja*; likewise, one that carries away the bank is called *kūlamudvaha*.
The suffix *liha* is applied after the word *vaha* when followed by *abhra*.
When the two verbal roots *lih* (to lick) and *vah* (to carry) are used as governing words (*upapada*), the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *lih*. Thus,
from *vaham leḍhi* ("he licks the draft-ox"), we derive *vahṃliha* ("an ox that licks the draft-ox").
The wind reaches to the clouds.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *pac* in the sense of measure.
*Parimāṇa* refers to measures such as the *prastha*;
when this is used as a subordinate word (*upapada*) in relation to the action, the suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *pac*.
A cooking pot that cooks a *prastha* is called *prasthapacā*; a vessel that cooks a *droṇa* is *droṇapacaḥ*; a cauldron that cooks a *khārī* is *khāriṃpacaḥ*.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after *mita* and *nakha*.
When *mita* and *nakha* are used as subordinate words (*upapada*) for these two actions, the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *pac*.
This rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *parimāṇa*.
A Brahmin woman who cooks only a small amount is called *mitampacā*; barley-gruel that makes one's nails burn when touched is called *nakhaṃpacā*.
The [root] tud- [is used] with the words vi-dhva and aruṣa.
When the words *vidhu* and *arus* are used as accompanying objects (*upapada*) for the verbal root *tud*, the suffix *khaś* is applied;
[thus] *vidhuntudaḥ* (the moon-devourer), namely Rāhu.
The one who pierces with the dawn.
The word *asūrya* is used before *lalāṭa*, and *dṛś* before *tapas*. (Pāṇini 6.3.145)
When the verbal roots *dṛś* (to see) and *tap* (to heat/suffer) have *asūrya* and *lalāṭa* as their respective governing objects (*upapada*), the suffix *khaś* is applied. [Examples:
*asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ* (the king's wives, who do not look at the sun).
The sun is "scorching the forehead" (lalāṭantapa).
Furthermore, the term *asūrya* is an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound),
because the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the root *dṛś* (to see).
"They do not see the sun. This is intended primarily as a concealment;
it means they are so thoroughly hidden that they do not even see the sun, whose sight is otherwise unavoidable.
And [the suffix -aṇ] is applied after *ugra*, *paśya*, *irammada*, and *pāṇindham*.
The words *ugrampaśya*, *irammada*, and *pāṇindhama* are formed by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
[The compound] *ugrampaśyaḥ* is derived from the sense "he sees what is fierce" (*ugraṃ paśyati*).
That in which one intoxicates oneself is *irammada*;
those paths upon which the hands are blown (puffed up) are *pāṇindhama*.
The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *vad* when preceded by *priya* or *vaśa*.

The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *vad* when the two verbal nouns *priya* and *vaśa* are used as accompanying words (*upapada*). For example, one who speaks what is dear is called *priyaṃvadaḥ*.
*Vaśaṃvadaḥ*.
The *ca* (the letter *c*) is for the purpose of the specific rule: "There is shortening [of the vowel] before a *khac*-affix" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.94).
The suffix *kha* has the sense of "dying" (*mumūrṣu*).

The formation of a separate suffix is for the sake of subsequent rules. In the section on *kha*, there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding the root *gam* when preceded by a nominal stem (*sup*).
*Mitaṅgama* means an elephant;
*mitaṅgamā* means a female elephant. From *vihāyas*, the form *viha* also occurs.
One who moves through the air is a *vihaṅgama*. It should be stated that the suffix *ḍit* is optionally applied after *kha*; thus, [the forms] *vihaṅga* and *vihaṅgama* are derived.
And the substitution of *vihā* for *vihāyas* should be stated; as in *vihaga*. [The suffix *kha* is applied] after the roots √*tap* when preceded by *dviṣat* or *para*. (PS 3.2.39)

When the two objects *dviṣat* (enemy) and *para* (other) are used as accompanying words (*upapada*), the suffix *khac* is applied after the root *tap* (meaning "to heat" or "to torment") belonging to the *curādi* group,
which ends in the causative marker *ch*.
The root *tap* meaning "to heat" belongs to the *bhvādi* class; both [roots] are included here. One who causes an enemy to suffer heat is called *dviṣantapa*.
*Parantapaḥ*:
the rule *dviṣat-parayoḥ* contains two *t* sounds in its formulation;
therefore, it does not apply to the feminine.
One who causes distress to an enemy is called *dviṣatītāpa*.
Restraint of speech in the vow. (PS 3.2.40)
When the word *vāk* is used as the object (*karman*) in composition with the verbal root *yam*, the suffix *khac* is applied provided that a religious observance (*vrata*) is understood.
By "observance" (*vrata*), a rule (*niyama*) prescribed by scripture is meant.
*vācaṃyama* means "he sits observing silence. Why [is it said] *vrate* ("in the context of a vow")? [To show that] *vāgyāmaḥ* ("restraint of speech") is not [used in this sense].
The suffix *kha* is applied after the words *pūḥ* and *sarva*, when combined with the roots *dāri* and *sahi* respectively.

When the two verbal roots *dṛ* (to split) and *sah* (to endure) have *puraḥ* and *sarvaḥ* respectively as their attendant words (*upapada*), the suffix *khac* is applied according to their respective order. [Thus:
he splits the city = *purandaraḥ*.
The word *sarvaṃsaha* means "king"; it should be stated that [the suffix] *dār* occurs after this root.
Thus, *bhagaṃdaraḥ*.
The suffix *kaṣ* is applied after the words *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīṣa*.
When the words *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīra* occur as upapadas, the suffix *khac* is applied to the root *kaṣ*. [Thus:
*sarvaṃ kaṣati* (he scrapes everything) = *sarvaṃkaṣaḥ* (all-scraping) *khalaḥ* (a wicked person).
A river that wears away its banks;
a mountain that scrapes the clouds;
a whirlwind that consumes dried cow dung.
The suffix *kvi* is applied after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the words *megha*, *ṛti*, and *bhaya*.
When *megha*, *ṛti*, and *bhaya* are used as governing words (*upapada*) for these actions, the suffix *khac* is applied after the root *kṛ*. [Examples:
*meghaṃkaraḥ* (one who brings clouds).
*ṛtiṅkaraḥ*,
*bhayaṅkaraḥ*.
In the rule for the formation of secondary derivatives (*upapada-vidhi*), the mention of "fear" (*bhaya*) and so forth implies that the suffix applies to words ending in those terms (*tadantavidhi*).
The bestower of fearlessness.
In the sense of "belonging to," the suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the names of] Kṣema, Priya, and Madra.
When these words— *kṣema*, *priya*, and *madra*— are used as upapadas, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the root *kṛ*; and because of the particle *ca*, the suffix *khac* is also applied.
One who brings security,
one who creates well-being;
one who does what is pleasing.
Priyaṅkaraḥ;
Madrakāraḥ, madraṅkaraḥ.
Although it could have been stated simply as "vā," the mention of *aṇ* again is for the purpose of prohibiting the suffix *ṭa* in the case of *hetu* and others.
The root *bhū* following the prefix *ā-śita-* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the state (*bhāva*).
Here, the term *supi* (in a word ending in a case-suffix) is understood from the previous rule.
When the word *āśita*, ending in a case-suffix, is used as an upapada, the suffix *khac* is applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or an abstract state (*bhāva*).
One becomes satiated by means of this; thus, *āśitambhava* refers to boiled rice (*odana*).
In the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), it is the becoming-satiated of one who has eaten; thus, *āśitambhava* occurs.
The suffix *saN* is applied after the roots *bhṛ*, *tṝ*, *vṛ*, *ji*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, *tap*, and *dam* when *sañjñā* (a name) is to be expressed.
The terms *karmaṇi* and *supi*, which are under discussion, are connected as appropriate according to the requirements of the technical definition (*sañjñā*).
The suffix *khac* occurs after the verbal roots *bhṛ*, *tṛ*, *vṛ*, *ji*, *dhāri*, *sahi*, *tapi*, and *dam*, when they refer to a name (*sañjñā*).
The earth is Viśvambharā, the Vasundharā; it is the Rathantara Sāman;
she is a maiden choosing her own husband.
Śatruñjaya is an elephant;
Yugandhara is a mountain;
[and] Śatruṃsaha.
*śatruṃtapaḥ* (conqueror of enemies), *ariṃdamaḥ* (tamer of foes). Why is it specified "when used as a name"? [To illustrate: *śatruṃ tapati* (he torments his enemy).
One who supports a family is called "the burden of the family" (kuṭumbabhāra).
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the verbal root *gam*. PS_3.2.47.
The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *gam*, when a word ending in a *sup*-case affix is present as an upapada, provided it refers to a proper name (*sañjñā*). For example: *sutaṅgama*.
He whose son was Sautangami;
the division of the rule is for the sake of what follows.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after [the words] *anta*, *atyanta*, *adhva*, *dūra*, *pāra*, *sarva*, and *ananta*.
The term *sañjñāyām* does not carry over [from the previous rule].
When these objects— *anta*, *atyanta*, *adhvan*, *dura*, *pāra*, *sarva*, and *ananta*— occur as *upapadas*, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam*.
One who has gone to the end, one who has gone beyond,
one who has traveled the path,
one who has gone afar.
One who has gone to the further shore; one who goes everywhere; one who goes to the infinite.

The suffix *anantaga* contains the letter *ḍ*; the letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of causing the elision of the *ṭi* portion, because even though it belongs to an *abha* element, the power of its inclusion as an *anubandha* necessitates this. [221]
In the section on the suffix *ḍa*, there is an addition [to the rule] regarding the words *sarvatra* and *panna*:
*sarvatragaḥ* (all-pervading) and *pannagaḥ* (serpent).
There is also elision of *uras*.
[The word] *uraga* is derived from *urasā gacchati* ("he moves with his chest"). [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *su* and *duru* when the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is expressed.
It is called *suga* because one goes easily (*sukhena*) upon it; *durga* [is so called] because it is a difficult place to traverse. *Niro* refers to a location.
