From the root *ni* with the suffix *tṛc*, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the penultimate vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ*; thus, *nayī*. The feminine form is *nayī*. From the root *pi* with the suffix *tṛc*, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the penultimate vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ*; thus, *payī*. The feminine form is *payī*. From the root *di* with the suffix *tṛc*, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the penultimate vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ*; thus, *dayī*. The feminine form is *dayī*. From the root *si* with the suffix *tṛc*, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the penultimate vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ*; thus, *sayī*. The feminine form is *sayī*. From the root *hi* with the suffix *tṛc*, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the penultimate vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ*; thus, *hayī*. The feminine form is *hayī*. From the root *dhi* with the suffix *tṛc*, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the penultimate vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ*; thus, *dhayī*. The feminine form is *dhayī*. From the root *mi* with the suffix *tṛc*, there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the penultimate vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ*; thus, *mayī*. The feminine form is *mayī*. From the root *li* with the suffix *tṛc*,
And from the root *kṣad*,
*kṣattṛ* is formed;
in some instances, it refers to one who is appointed or authorized.
In the Vedic language, there is also the suffix *tṛ*.
[Examples are] *kṣatṛbhyaḥ* and *saṅgrahītṛbhyaḥ*;
the difference lies in the accent.
The suffix *iṣṇuc* is added after the roots *alaṃkṛ*, *nirākṛ*, *prajan*, *utpac*, *utpat*, *unmad*, *ruc*, *apatrap*, *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *sah*, and *car*. (Pāṇini 3.2.136)
The suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied after verbal roots such as *alaṃkṛ* (to adorn) when the agent possesses the habit of performing that action and so forth; for example,
*alaṃkariṣṇuḥ* (one who is habitually inclined to adorn).
nirākariṣṇuḥ (one who is prone to rejecting), prajaniṣṇuḥ (one who is prone to procreating),
utpaciṣṇuḥ (one who is prone to cooking).
One who is prone to fly up; one who is prone to become insane; one who is prone to shine.
*apatrapiṣṇuḥ*, *vartiṣṇuḥ*,
*vardhiṣṇuḥ*.
*Sahiṣṇuḥ* and *cariṣṇuḥ*.
After the root *alaṃkṛ*, when it has the sense of "adorning," the suffix *iṣṇuc* should be stated by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to [the suffix] *yuca*.
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] does not occur after *ṇ*.
In the domain of the Veda (*chandas*), the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied after a verbal root ending in the causative marker *ṇi*, when the agent possesses such a habit and so forth; for example:
*dṛṣadaṃ dhārayiṣṇavaḥ* ("those who have the habit of holding a stone").
The creepers that lead to the further shore.
And after the word *bhuvas*. (Pāṇini 3.2.138)
In the Vedic domain, the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied after the verbal root *bhū* in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Example:
*bhaviṣṇuḥ*.
The analysis of the compound is for the sake of the subsequent term;
the word "and" (ca) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned;
[it refers to] radiant red sandalwood.
And after the roots √glai, √ji, and √sthā, the suffix kṣnu is applied.
The phrase "in the Vedic language" (chandasi) is no longer applicable. [The suffix *kvanip* is applied] after these verbal roots: *glā*, *ji*, and *sthā*.
By virtue of the word "ca" (and), the suffix *kṣnu* is applied after the root *bhū* as well, in the sense of one who habitually performs an action (*tacchīla*) and so forth; for example:
*glāsnuḥ* (one who is prone to languor) and *jiṣṇuḥ* (one who is victorious).
*sthāsnuḥ* (firm) and *bhūṣṇuḥ* (prospering); this suffix *gic* is not *kit*.
Therefore, the vowel *ī* does not occur [in the case of *stha*].
Furthermore, in the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), the letter *g* is also indicated as having undergone the change to *c*;
therefore, *guṇa* substitution does not occur.
In the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), the letter *g* is also specified;
therefore, the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *bhū*.
Because *kṣi* has an indicatory *ṅ*, there is no substitution of *ī* for *sthā*; this is due to the rule that *ṅit* roots do not undergo *ītvam*.

One should remember that there is an absence of *guṇa* in the three [forms]; furthermore, because *śri* and *yuj* have an indicatory *k*, they are *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) after *ga* and *ka*.
An addition [to the rule] should be made for *daṃś* in the Vedic language (*chandas*):
*daṃkṣṇavaḥ paśavaḥ* ("animals with fangs").
After the roots *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*, the suffix *knū* is applied. (Pāṇini 3.2.140)
The suffix *knū* is applied after verbal roots such as *tras* and others to denote those who possess that habit and so forth. For example: *trasnuḥ*.
gṛdhnuḥ, dhṛṣṇuḥ, kṣipnuḥ.
The suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied after eight roots beginning with *śam*.
The word "iti" has the sense of "beginning with.
The suffix *ghinuṇ* occurs after the eight verbal roots beginning with *śam*, when the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*) and the like.
From the root *śam* meaning "to pacify" up to *mad* meaning "to rejoice," the group beginning with *śam* is included within the *divādi* class.
The letter *gh* is for the purpose of the *kutva* substitution [of *g*] in subsequent rules;
the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
The letter *ṇ* serves the purpose of indicating vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*). Examples:
*śamī*, *tamī*.
damī / śramī / bhramī /
One who is weary,
one who is negligent, one who is deranged.
Why "from eight"? [Consider: *asitā*.

The suffix *lyap* is applied after the following verbal roots when preceded by the specified prefixes: *saṃ-pṛc*, *anu-rudh*, *āṅ-yam*, *āṅ-yas*, *pari-sṛ*, *saṃ-sṛj*, *pari-dev*, *saṃ-jvar*, *pari-kṣip*, *pari-raṭ*, *pari-vad*, *pari-dah*, *pari-muh*, *duṣ*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *ā-krīḍ*, *vi-vic*, *tyaj*, *raj*, *bhaj*, *ati-car*, *apa-car*, *ā-muṣ*, and *abhi-ā-han*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.142)

The suffix *ghinuṇ* continues [from the previous rule]. The suffix *ghinuṇ* occurs after verbal roots such as *saṃpṛc* and others, in the sense of "having that as one's habitual disposition" (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
The root *pṛc* in the sense of "contact" is understood as belonging to the *rudhādi* class, and not the [root] of the *adādi* class, because of its having a *luk*-vikaraṇa suffix.
*Paridevi* is understood as belonging to the *bhvādi* class, according to [the rule] *devṛ* in the sense of "sporting.
*Kṣip* in the sense of "impelling" is understood generally as belonging to both the *divādi* and *tudādi* classes.
The root *yuj* in the sense of "concentration" belongs to the *divādi* class, while *yuj* in the sense of "union" belongs to the *rudhādi* class; both are included here.
Regarding the root *rañj* in the sense of "coloring," there is the elision of the nasal due to a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*).
Contacting; conforming; extending.
One who comes, one who wanders about, one who associates.
Lamenting, burning with fever, and wallowing in despair.
One who laments excessively;
one who reviles;
one who suffers from burning anguish.
Deluded, faulty, and hateful.
A traitor,
a milker,
a yogi.
One who sports, one who is discerning, one who renounces.
One who is passionate,
one who possesses a share, and one who transgresses.
One who acts improperly,
one who steals,
and one who commits violence.
The suffix *vau* is applied after the roots *kaṣ*, *las*, *katth*, and *śrambh*.
The root *kaṣ* has the meaning of "injury," and *lasa* has the meanings of "adhering" and "playing."
The suffix *ghinuṇ* occurs after these verbal roots— *ślāgh* in the sense of praising and *srambh* in the sense of trusting— when the word *vi-* is used as a prefix (*upapada*).
One who is boastful, one who is wanton, and one who is self-aggrandizing.
The suffix *visrambhī* is also applied after the root *laṣ*. (PS 3.2.144)
The root *laṣ* means "desire";
from this root, with *apa* as an upapada, [the suffix *khaś* is applied].
By virtue of the word "ca" (and), the suffix *ghinuṇ* also occurs after the root *vā*; thus,
*apalāṣī* and *vilāṣī*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *pra*, *lap*, *sṛ*, *dru*, *math*, *vad*, and *vas*.
When *pra* is the preceding word (*upapada*), the suffix *ghinuṇ* occurs after roots such as *lap*. Example: *pralāpī*.
The one who spreads,
the one who runs away, the one who crushes.
In the words *pravādī*, *pravāsī*,
and *vasaḥ*, there is the inclusion of the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāsa*), and not in the sense of "clothing" (*acchādana*).
Because it has a *luK* vocalization.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the verbal roots *nind*, *hiṃs*, *kliś*, *khād*, *vināś*, *parikṣip*, *pariraṭ*, *parivādi*, *vyābhāṣ*, and *asūy*.
The suffix *vuñ* occurs after verbal roots such as *nind* (to blame) and others, when the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*) and the like;
the nominative case is used here in the sense of the ablative.
The root *kliś* is used in the sense of "afflicting" (*upatāpa*) and *kliś* is used in the sense of "oppressing" (*vibādhana*);
both meanings are included here.
A reviler, a harmer, and a tormentor.
The consumer,
the destroyer, and the one who casts aside.
One who reviles,
one who censures, and one who speaks abusively.

The term *asūyakaḥ* is already established by the suffix *ṇvul* alone; the prescription of the suffix *vuñ* is for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*), namely that among suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do not apply according to the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*asarūpanyāya*).
And [the substitution of *ū* for *u* occurs] for the word *devikā* before the suffix *kraś* and in the case of an upasarga.
When *devayati* and *kruś* have a prefix as an attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *vuñ* occurs; for example,
*ādevakaḥ*.
One who laments,
one who reviles,
and one who reproaches.
Why is it said "in the presence of a prefix"? [Consider: *devayitā* (one who causes to play) and *kroṣṭā* (a jackal).
The suffix *yuc* is applied after an intransitive verbal root whose meaning involves motion.

The suffix *yuc* is applied after verbal roots meaning "movement" (*calana*) and those meaning "sound" (*śabda*), provided they are intransitive (*akarmaka*), when the agent possesses the qualities of habituality (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Example: *calanaḥ*.
Copanaḥ;
from sound and meaning: śabdanaḥ, ravaṇaḥ.
Why [is it specified] "from an intransitive verb"?
[Consider: *paṭhitā vidyām* ("she has studied the science").
And [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a verbal root that begins with a consonant and has an *anudātta* accent on its final vowel.
The suffix *yuc* occurs after a verbal root that is unaccented (*anudātta*), begins with a consonant (*hal-ādi*), and is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
*vartanaḥ* / *vardhanaḥ*.
Why [is it specified] "from a root with an anudātta vowel"? [Consider: *bhavitā*.
Why is it said "of *hal* etc."? [Consider: *edhitā*. Why is the mention of "etc. (*ādi*) made? [Consider: *jugupsanaḥ*.
The suffix *mīmāṃsana* occurs after a verbal root that does not take an object (*akarmaka*). For example: *vastram vasitā*. [244]
The verbal roots *ju*, *caṅkramya*, *daṇḍramya*, *sṛ*, *gṛdh*, *jval*, *śuc*, *laṣ*, *pat*, and *pad* [take the suffix *kyap*].
The suffix *yuc* occurs after the verbal roots *ju* and *praghṛti* when the agent possesses such habitual tendencies (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
*Ju* is a verbal root belonging to the Vedic (Sūtra) tradition.
Swift-moving; walking to and fro; wandering about.
Saraṇa, Gardhana, and Jvalana.
Causing grief; causing desire; causing to fall.
Regarding *padana*: here, the inclusion of both roots meaning "to move" (*calanārtha*) and the root *pad* is for the sake of including transitive verbs;
furthermore, others explain that the inclusion of *padi* is for the purpose of making this known.
Regarding suffixes denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*), there is no rule for the coexistence of dissimilar suffixes (*asarūpa-vidhi*) with one another.
Consequently, the suffix *tṛn* does not apply to the root *alaṃkṛ*, such that *alaṃkartṛ* would not be formed.
For instance, in the case of the root *pad*, because the suffix *ukañ* is specifically prescribed, it would indeed coexist with the general suffix *yuc* due to their being dissimilar forms.
What is the purpose of this rule? It is prescribed again for the sake of making something known;
furthermore, this indicator is general in its application.
In some cases, immersion is indeed desired;
[but] the boastful one goes to Kheṭa.
And [the suffix *ktvā* is used] after verbs meaning "to be angry" (*krudh*), "to adorn" (*maṇḍ*), and those ending in the sense of "for the purpose of" (*artha*).
The suffix *yuc* is applied after the roots *krudh* in the sense of anger, and *maḍi* in the sense of adornment.
One who is prone to anger; one who is irascible; one who is fond of adornment.
An ornament.
Nor that which is not [a cause]. (PS 3.2.152)
The suffix *yuc* does not occur after a verbal root ending in *yakāra*.
That which was obtained by the preceding rule is hereby prohibited.
One who causes to swell;
one who causes to tremble.
And [the suffix *dīkṣ* is applied] after the words *sūda* and *dīpa*. (PS 3.2.153)
The suffix *yuc* does not occur after the roots *sūd*, *dīp*, and *dīkṣ*. Although its application was expected because these roots are marked with an anudātta vowel, it is here prohibited.
Slaughtered / Illuminated / Consecrated.

But surely, the suffix *ra* is seen to be specifically prescribed for the root *dīp* by the rule "After the roots *nam*, *kamp*, *smi*, *ajas*, *kam*, *hiṃs*, and *dīp*, the suffix *ra* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 3.2.167); that very rule will therefore be the sublater [of the general rule].
What is the purpose of the prohibition?
For otherwise, even the suffix *yuc* would apply by virtue of the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpa*).

Furthermore, it has been stated that among suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), the rule of optional application for dissimilar forms does not exist; thus, this [prohibition] is merely a general tendency.
And thus the inclusion is observed:
"a desirous young woman," "a longing young woman."
Thus it is understood through the division of the rules (*yoga-vibhāga*).
Alternatively, *madhusūdana* and others will be seen among the roots beginning with *nandi* (Pāṇini 3.1.14).
[The suffix] *kṛtya* and *lyuṅ* are used diversely (*bahulam*) [in these cases] (Pāṇini 3.3.113).
Thus, they may end in *lyuṭ*. [245] After the roots *laṣ*, *pat*, *pad*, *sthā*, *bhū*, *vṛṣ*, *han*, *kam*, *gam*, and *śṝ*, the suffix *ukañ* is applied. (Pāṇini 3.2.154)
The suffix *ukañ* is applied after verbal roots beginning with *laṣ* when the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*) and the like; for example:
*upalāṣukam vṛṣalasaṅgatam* (one who is habitually fond of associating with low-caste people).
The embryos become prone to miscarriage;
the being is born spontaneously;
and animals become his attendants.
The food becomes potent;
the rain-clouds pour forth rain;
and the urine of a Pākalika is caustic.
Women become enamored of him;
they say that the *vārāṃsī* plant brings one near,
and that the *kiṃśāruka* is sharp.
The suffix *ṣākan* is applied after the verbal roots *jalp*, *bhikṣ*, *kuṭṭ*, *luṇṭ*, and *vṛṅ*.
The suffix *ṣākan* occurs after verbal roots such as *jalpa* and others, when the agent possesses the qualities of habit (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*.
A chatterer;
a beggar;
a cutter.
A plunderer;
a wretch; a wretched woman.
The suffix *ini* is applied after the word *praja*.
The suffix *ini* is applied after the root *ju* preceded by *pra*, when the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*) and the like; for example:
*prajavī*, *prajavinau*.
And [the suffix *kan* is added] after the verbal roots *ji*, *dṛkṣi*, *viśri*, *iṇ*, *vama*, *avyatha*, *abhyama*, *paribhū*, and *prasū*.
The root *ji* means "to conquer"; *dṛṅ* means "to respect."
Both *kṣi* in the sense of "destruction" (*kṣaye*) and *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling and going" (*nivāsagatyoḥ*) are included;

*prasū* is the inclusion of the root *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*). The suffix *ini* occurs after roots beginning with *ji* when the agent possesses such habitual tendencies (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
Victorious,
cavernous, decaying.
One who takes refuge;
one who has passed beyond;
one who vomits.
Unperturbed, unassailable, and unconquerable.
The progenitor.
The suffix *āluc* is applied after the words *spṛh*, *gṛhi*, *pati*, *dayi*, *nidrā*, *dandrā*, and *śraddhā*.
*spṛh* in the sense of longing for;
*grah* in the sense of seizing.
The root *pat* in the sense of "going" is listed among the roots ending in *-a* in the *curādi* (denominative) class; *day* is used in the senses of "giving," "going," and "protecting."
The root *drā* means "to go";
when preceded by *ni* and *tat*,
its final *t* is also changed to *n*, and this form is thus established as an irregularity (*nipātyate*).
The root *ḍudhāñ* preceded by *śrat*: after these roots, when the agent possesses the sense of habitual practice (*tacchīla*) and so forth, the suffix *āluc* occurs. Example: *spṛhayāluḥ*.
gṛhayāluḥ (one who desires to seize),
patayāluḥ (one who desires to fall), dayāluḥ (compassionate).
Sleepy; languid; full of faith.
In the case of the suffix *āluc*, the root *śīṅ* must be included [in the rule].
Thus: *śayāluḥ*.
The suffix *ru* is applied after the roots *dā*, *dhā*, *si*, *śad*, and *sad*. (Pāṇini 3.2.159)
The suffix *ru* is applied after the roots *dā*, *dhā*, *dheṭ*, *si*, *śad*, and *sad*. [Examples: *daruḥ*.

In the case of *dhāruvatsaḥ* (the calf that drinks milk), the genitive case does not occur because of the elision of the vowel *u* [in the rule] *la-ukāra-avyaya-niṣṭhā-khalartha-tṛnām* (Pāṇini 2.3.69).
[Another example is] *seruḥ*.
śadruḥ / sadruḥ //
The suffix *kmarac* is added after the verbal root √sṛj when followed by the word *ghas*.
The suffix *kmarac* occurs after the verbal roots *sṛ*, *ghas*, and *ad*, when the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*) and the like; for example,
*sṛmaraḥ*.
Ghasmara means a glutton; adbhara means one who eats voraciously.
The suffix *ghurac* is applied after the verbal roots *bhañj*, *bhāṣ*, and *mid*.

The suffix *ghurac* occurs after the roots *bhañj*, *bhās*, and *mid* when denoting an agent characterized by such habitual tendencies (*tacchīla*) and so forth; for example, *bhaṅguraṃ kāṣṭham* ("wood that breaks easily").
Because the suffix is marked with the letter *gh*, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*) takes place.
"Bhāsura" means light;
"medura" means a fat animal.
The suffix is applied to the root *bhañj* in the sense of the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*), by its very nature.
The suffix *kurac* is applied after the roots *vidi*, *bhidi*, and *cchid*.
The inclusion of the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāna*)— and not in the sense of "obtaining" (*lābha*) and so forth— is due to its inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
The suffix *kurac* occurs after roots such as *vid* when the agent possesses the habit (*tacchīla*) or similar qualities.
Vidura is wise;
*bhidura* is wood that splits;
*chidurā* is a rope that breaks.

The construction with *bhid* and *chid* is used in the sense of the agent being also the object (*karmakartṛ*). Regarding the root *vyadh*, it should be stated that there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the suffix *kurac*;
thus, *vidhuraḥ*.
The suffix *kvarap* is applied after the verbal roots √i, √naś, √jī, and √sṛt.

The suffix *kvarap* is applied after the verbal roots *iṇ*, *naś*, *ji*, and *sṛt* when the agent possesses the qualities of habit (*tacchīla*) and so forth; the letter *p* is for the purpose of [causing] the insertion of *tuk*. Example: *itvaraḥ*.
transient; perishable (masculine); perishable (feminine).
*jitvaraḥ*, *jitvarī*,
*sṛṭvaraḥ*.
In *sṛtvarī*,
there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *neḍvaśi kṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8). [247]
And [the suffix] *gatvara* [is applied after a verbal root]. (Pāṇini 3.2.164)
The word *gatvaraḥ* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) term; it is derived from the root *gam* with the elision of the nasal and the suffix *kvarap*.
gatvaraḥ / gatvarī //
The suffix *ūka* is applied [after a verbal root] to form a word meaning "one who habitually performs that action."
The suffix *ūka* is applied after the root *jāgarti* when the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*) and the like;
[thus] *jāgarūkaḥ*.
The suffix yaṅ is applied after verbal roots ending in -yaj, -jap, or -daś.

The suffix *ūka* is added to verbs beginning with *yaja* when they are in the intensive (*yaṅ*) form, provided that the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*) and the like; for example:
*yāyajūkaḥ*.
One who mutters repeatedly;
one who bites fiercely.
The suffix *raḥ* is applied after the verbal roots *nam*, *kam*, *sma*, *yaj*, *as*, and *hiṃs*.
The suffix *ra* is applied after verbal roots such as *nam* and others when the agent possesses the qualities of habit (*tacchīla*) and so forth; for example, "wood that bends" (*namraṃ kāṣṭham*).
The branch is trembling;
the face is smiling;
he offers oblations incessantly.
*Hiṃsra* means a predatory demon (*rakṣas*).
*Dīpra* means wood.
Regarding *ajasram*: the root *jasu* means "to release"; preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, it takes the suffix *-ra* and is used in the sense of uninterruptedness (*āsātatya*) of action.
The suffix *u* is applied after the verbal root *bhikṣ* when it is preceded by the prefix *san* and conveys the sense of hope (*āśaṃsā*).
The term *san* refers to that which ends in the suffix *san*, and not to the verbal root *san*, because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*) or according to the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*).

The suffix *u* is applied after verbal roots ending in the desiderative suffix *sa(n)*, as well as after the roots *āśaṃs* and *bhikṣ*, when the agent possesses that habit or similar quality; for example:
*cikīrṣuḥ* (one who desires to act), *jihīrṣuḥ* (one who desires to take).
"Āśaṃsuḥ" refers to the [root] "āṅ-śas," meaning "to desire," which is included here.

First, regarding the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*): "I do not consider it possible."
I do not conceive it possible,
nor do I believe it, that your honor would officiate as a priest for a low-born man; yet your honor will indeed officiate as a priest for a low-born man.
Who indeed is this *vṛṣala* whom your honor would cause to sacrifice?
Who indeed is this *vṛṣala* whom your honor will cause to sacrifice?
In the sense of indignation (*amarṣa*): "I cannot tolerate that your honor would cause a *vṛṣala* to sacrifice."
He will perform the sacrifice.
What kind of outcaste indeed is he that your honor would perform a sacrifice for him?
He will perform the sacrifice.
However, when there is a desire to speak of a past fact, or when there is a failure of an action, the conditional suffix (lṛṅ) occurs;
in the future tense, it occurs invariably:
"I do not believe that your honor would indeed have caused a low-born man to sacrifice."
The suffix *lṛṭ* is used in the sense of "it is said that" (*kiṃkila*) when referring to things that exist.
The phrase "in the senses of disbelief and indignation" continues [from the previous rule].
The word *kiṃkila* is a composite form that serves as the *upapada*.
The words *asti*, *artha*, *asti-bhavati*, and *vidyate* signify existence (*astyartha*).

When these words signifying existence are used as attendant words (*upapada*) for the sense of "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) or "intolerance" (*amarṣa*), the suffix *lṛṭ* is applied after the verbal root;
this is an exception to the rule for *liṅ*.
Is it indeed true that His Honor will officiate at a sacrifice for a *vṛṣala*?
It is said that His Honor will officiate at a sacrifice for a *vṛṣala*. It is certain that His Honor will officiate at a sacrifice for a *vṛṣala*.
It is said that the honorable one intends to officiate at a sacrifice for a *vṛṣala*;
I do not believe it, nor can I tolerate it.
The cause for the conditional suffix (liṅ) does not exist here; therefore, the conditional suffix (lṛṅ) does not occur.
The suffix *liṅ* is used after the particle *jātu* when expressing possibility.
The same rule applies when there is a sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*) or intolerance (*amarṣa*).
When *jātu* or *yadā* function as attendant words (*upapada*), the suffix *liṅ* is applied after a verbal root provided that the senses of impossibility or intolerance are understood.

This is an exception to the future tense suffix *lṛṭ*. [Examples: "Perhaps His Honor might officiate at a sacrifice for a low-caste man," or "If indeed His Honor should officiate at a sacrifice for a low-caste man."
I do not believe it; I do not tolerate it.
[Vārttika: An addition should be made to the rule for the conditional suffix (liṅ) [to include] *jātu* and *yadā*, as well as *yadi* and *yadā*.
If one like you were to officiate as a priest for a kṣatriya,
or if one like you were to cause a kṣatriya to perform a sacrifice,
I would not believe it.
I do not tolerate it. The conditional (lṛṅ) is used for the past when there is a failure of action; it is used invariably for the future.
The suffix *yat* is used after the words *yad* and *yatra*.
Only with regard to "impossibility" (anavaklṛpti) and "impatience" (amarṣa).
When the words *yat* and *yatra* function as governing particles (*upapada*), the suffix *liṅ* occurs after a verbal root when "impossibility" and "impatience" are implied.
This is an exception to the *lṛṭ* suffix.
The division of the rule (*yoga-vibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows; it is not intended to apply according to the respective order of enumeration (*yathāsaṅkhyam*).

And regarding the cases "that the honorable one might cause a *vṛṣala* to sacrifice" and "where the honorable one might cause a *vṛṣala* to sacrifice," the conditional (*lṛṅ*) occurs according to the respective rules when there is a failure of action. [286]
And [the suffix *kha* is used] in the sense of reproach. (Pāṇini 3.3.149)
The phrase "in the sense of impossibility and intolerance" is no longer applicable. [The suffix *kyaṅ* is used] in the senses of reproach (*garhā*) and censure (*nindā*).

*Kutsā* (censure) is synonymous with *anarthāntara* (the same meaning). When the two subordinate words *yat* and *yatra* are present, the suffix *liṅ* occurs after a verbal root when censure is implied; this is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).
And as for that wherein your honor might cause a *vṛṣala* to sacrifice, or wherein your honor, being a prosperous and aged Brāhmaṇa, might cause a *vṛṣala* to sacrifice— we censure this.
Oh, this is unjust! When there is the non-occurrence of an action, the conditional suffix (lṛṅ) is applied according to the respective rules.
And [the suffix *ka* is used] in the sense of treating as something wonderful. (PS 3.3.150)
It is precisely because of the [use of] *yacca* and *yatrayoḥ* that the making into four is marvelous.
It is wonderful,
that which is to be marveled at; when the two words *yat* and *yatra* function as adjuncts (*upapada*) and a sense of wonder is implied, the suffix *liṅ* occurs after the verbal root.
This is an exception to all verbal suffixes (lakāras):
"If Your Honor were to cause a low-caste man (vṛṣala) to sacrifice," and "Where Your Honor might cause a low-caste man to sacrifice."
This is remarkable:
when there is a failure of action, the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* occurs according to the respective circumstances.
In the remaining cases, the suffixes *lṛṭ* and *ayad* [are used].

*Yaccayatrābhyām anyatra* (Pāṇini 3.3.151): When the sense of "wonder" (*citrīkaraṇa*) is conveyed other than by the words *yad* and *yatra*, it is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). When the word *śeṣa* is the governing term (*upapada*) and the sense of "wonder" is understood, the suffix *lṛṭ* occurs after a verbal root.
If the word *yadi* is not employed, it is an exception (*apavāda*) to all verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). [The words] *āścaryam*, *citram*, and *adbhutam* [are used].
"One named Andha will climb a mountain; one named Badhira will study grammar.
Why [is the word] *ayādau* used?
"It would be a wonder if he were to eat; it would be a wonder if he were to study"—
in these cases, because the condition (*liṅ-nimitta*) is absent, the conditional mood (*lṛṅ*) does not occur.
The optative suffix (liṅ) is used after the particles *uta* and *api* when they have the same meaning [of possibility].
When the two particles *uta* and *api* are used in conjunction with a verbal root, the suffix *liṅ* occurs;
this is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).
In the sense of "certainly" (*bāḍham*), these two [particles] have the same meaning;
[as do] *uta kuryāt* and *api kuryāt*.
"Furthermore, he might study;
even he might study;
indeed, he will certainly study"—this is the meaning.
Why specify "of two capable [actions]"?
Consider: "Will the staff fall? or "Will he close the door?"
Both "question" (praśnaḥ) and "concealment" (pracchādanam) are understood;
the optionality [prescribed] by *vā ā udāttoḥ* (*Pāṇini 3.3.141*) is here set aside.

From this point forward, even when the cause for the conditional suffix (liṅ) exists, the periphrastic future (lṛṅ) is used invariably to express the non-occurrence of an action; however, in the case of the future tense, it is invariably used in all instances.
The particle *akaccit* is used in the expression of a desire to know.
The manifestation of one's own intention is the expression of desire (*kāmapravedana*).
Desire (*kāma*) is longing (*icchā*).

*Abhilāṣaḥ* (desire) is synonymous with *anarthāntaram* (no other meaning). Its *pravedanam* is its manifestation. When that [manifestation] is understood, provided that the word *akaccit* is used as an attendant (*upapada*), the suffix *liṅ* occurs after a verbal root.
This is an exception to all verbal suffixes:
"It is my wish that you eat"; "It is my desire that you eat."
What is the purpose of using *kaccit*? For example:
"I hope your mother is alive; I hope your father is alive.
O messenger, I ask you: "I hope Pārvatī is alive? [287]
When expressing a possibility, if the word *alam* is used, [the genitive case is employed] provided that the verb is not actually present. (PS 3.3.154)
The term *liṅ* alone [is used]. *Sambhāvanā* (possibility) is the determination of the suitability of actions.
This is the conviction regarding capacity;
it is now qualified by its object.
And if that conviction is sufficient and not false, [it constitutes right view].
In the expression "siddha-aprayoge," *alamba* is the qualifier; that is, the non-employment (*aprayoga*) of *alamba* is established (*siddha*). And where is this established?
When a meaning is intended but that [meaning] is not actually expressed,

the suffix *liṅ* occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting such a sense characterized by the condition of possibility (*sambhāvanopādhika*). This is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).
One might even break a mountain with one's head;
one might even eat a meal cooked in a large cauldron.
What is the meaning of "enough"?
Devadatta, residing abroad, will likely go to the village. Why is it said "when used with *siddha*"? [Consider:
Devadatta is capable of killing the elephant.
In the case of the non-occurrence of an action, the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is always used for both the past and the future.
The term *vibhāṣā* [is used] when there is a statement of possibility regarding a verbal root, provided that the word *yadi* is present. (PS 3.3.155)

When *alam* is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvana*), the entire rule "when there is no usage of a *siddha*" (*siddha-aprayoge*) is understood to carry over. That by which possibility is expressed is called "a word expressing possibility" (*sambhāvana-vacana*).

When a verbal root expressing possibility (*sambhāvanā*) is the attendant word (*upapada*), provided it is not the word *yat*, the suffix *liṅ* optionally occurs after that root. Since [the suffix] was necessarily required by the preceding rule, this statement is for the purpose of providing an option. Example: *sambhāvayāmi bhuñjīta bhavān* ("I think it possible that you might eat").
I expect that you will eat;
I am certain that you will eat,
you will eat.
One should say: *śraddadhe*, *bhuñjīta*, *bhavān*, *bhokṣyate bhavān*.
Why [is it specified] "not *ayadi*"? (i.e., why exclude forms containing *yadi*)?
I trust that you will partake [of it].
The indicative mood is used for both the cause and the effect.
They say that the cause is the possessor of the effect;
the effect is that which possesses the cause.

The suffix *liṅ* occurs after a verbal root when it denotes an action that serves as a cause (*hetu*) or an effect (*hetumat*). This is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*). For example: "If he were to go by the southern road, the cart would not overturn."
If one calls out "kamalaka," the cart will not overturn;
if it goes toward the south, the cart will not overturn.
In this regard, the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) continues immediately from the preceding rule.
While the term *liṅ* was already in effect, the repetition of *liṅ* is for the purpose of indicating a specific time;
therefore, it does not apply here:
"He flees because [the enemy] kills."
"He runs because it rains";
in the case of the non-occurrence of an action, the conditional (lṛṅ) is used.
The suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* are used after a verb when expressing a wish (*icchā*).
When verbal roots meaning "desire" are used as attendant words (upapada), the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* occur after the root;
this is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).
I wish that you would eat;
I wish that you would eat;
I desire it.
I request that it should be stated: "the making known of a desire. This is so that it does not apply here: "he acts while desiring."
The suffix *tumun* is used when the agents of the action expressed by the verbal root and the action expressed by the infinitive are the same.
When verbal roots meaning "desire" (icchārtha) have the same agent as their attendant words (upapada), the suffix *tumun* is applied after the root.
The identity of the agent (*samāna-kartṛkatva*) is determined solely with respect to the base of the *tumun* suffix itself.
He wishes to eat;
he desires to eat; he intends to eat.
He desires to eat.
Why [is it specified] "when the agents are the same"? [Consider:
Yajñadatta desires Devadatta while he is eating.
Why does [the suffix] not occur here:
*icchan karoti*?
Because it is not so expressed.
And [the suffix] liṅ [is used]. (Pāṇini 3.3.159)

When verbal roots expressing desire (*icchārtha*) having the same agent (*samānakartṛka*) are used as attendant words (*upapada*), the suffix *liṅ* is applied to the root. For example: *bhuñjīya itīcchati* ("he desires that he might eat").
When one desires "I would study," the conditional (lṛṅ) occurs in the case of the non-actualization of the action. The separation of the rule (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of what follows.
The suffix *liṅ* is optionally used after verbal roots expressing desire when referring to the present time.
After verbal roots expressing desire (*icchārtha*), the suffix *liṅ* optionally occurs when the present time is intended.
This rule is stated because the suffix *laṭ* would otherwise have applied by default.
icchati, icchet;
vaṣṭi, uśyāt;
kāmayate, kāmayeta.

The suffix *liṅ* is used in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), permission (*āmantraṇa*), entreaty (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*saṃpraśna*), and request (*prārthana*). (Pāṇini 3.3.161)
*Vidhi* is an instigation;
*nimantraṇa* is the performance of a duty.
Addressing is the act of granting permission to act as one desires.
A request is an activity preceded by honor.
Inquiry is thorough deliberation.
*Prārthanā* means a request.
The *liṅ* suffix occurs after a verbal root in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth;
it is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*).
And the optative and other [moods] are qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix.
The *liṅ* suffix occurs when the agent and other [grammatical participants] are qualified by the optative and so forth.
First, regarding the optative: "One should make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kuryāt*).
"May you come to the village.
In an invitation: "May you eat here;
may you sit here."
In the sense of invitation: "May your honor sit here"; "May your honor eat here. In the sense of entreaty: "We entreat your honor [to teach] the boy"; "May your honor initiate the boy."
In the sense of inquiry: "O sir, what indeed should I study—grammar? In the sense of a request: "I have a request that I might study grammar."
And the imperative suffix [is also used]. (Pāṇini 3.3.162)
The suffix *loṭ* occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth.
The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows.
In the sense of injunction (*vidhi*): "May you, sir, please make a mat";
"May you, sir, please come to the village.
In the sense of invitation (*nimantraṇa*): "May you, sir, please sit there."
"May you eat there" (*amutra bhavān bhuṅktām*);
in an invitation: "May you eat here" (*iha bhavān bhuṅktām*);
in a request: "We wish for you to [teach]; may you teach the young brahmin" (*adhīcchāmo bhavantam māṇavakam bhavān adhyāpayatu*).
"May you initiate the young student.
Regarding inquiry: "O sir, shall I indeed study grammar? Regarding request: "I have a request that I study grammar."
The suffix *chandas* is used in the sense of "to study";
and the *kṛtya* suffixes are also used in the senses of "command," "permission," and "proper time. [PS 3.3.163]
*Prēṣaṇa* is an injunction (*praiṣa*).
*Atisarga* is permission for acting according to one's own will.
The term *prāptakālatā* refers to the arrival of the proper time (*avasara*) for that which has become the occasion (*nimitta*).
In these senses, affixes designated as *kṛtya* occur after a verbal root; and by virtue of the word "ca" (and), the *loṭ* affix also occurs.
The mat must be made by you;
it is to be made, it is to be done, it is to be performed.
Furthermore, regarding the imperative (*loṭ*): "May you make a mat here, having been sent; you have been authorized; it is the proper time for you to make a mat."

For what purpose are the *kṛtya* suffixes prescribed specifically for the *praiṣa* (command) and so forth, rather than generally? Since those suffixes are already prescribed for the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*), they would apply to the *praiṣa* and other cases as well as elsewhere. [The answer is: They are superseded by this *loṭ* suffix, which is prescribed for these specific instances.
Will they occur by means of the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*)?
If so, then it indicates that after the section governing feminine suffixes (*stry-adhikāra*), the rule regarding optional forms does not necessarily apply.
What is the distinction between *vidhi* (injunction) and *praiṣa* (direction)?
Some say that *vidhi* is the making known of what was previously unknown, while *praiṣa* is the act of directing.
And the optative suffix (liṅ) is used [after a root] when the action occurs after a muhūrta.
The [terms] *praiṣa* and so forth occur.
When *praiṣa* and so forth are implied, the suffix *liṅ* occurs after a verbal root denoting an action that takes place more than a *muhūrta* in the future.
By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is also understood as it occurs [in common usage]:
"After a muhūrta," meaning "above a muhūrta, you must indeed make the mat."
It is to be done; it is a task. You should indeed make a mat; you should indeed do it.
You have been sent here; you have been authorized; the time has come for you.
The suffix *loṭ* is used in the sense of *sme*.
In the case of *praiṣa* (commands) and so forth, the term *ūrdhva-mauhūrtika* (referring to a time after one muhūrta) is understood to carry over.

When the word *sam* is used as an *upapada* (governing word), and when *praiṣa* and so forth are implied, the suffix *loṭ* occurs after a verbal root denoting a meaning that takes place after one muhūrta.
This is an exception to the *liṅ* and *kṛtya* suffixes:
"After a moment, you should indeed weave the mat; you should indeed go to the village."
He taught the young brahmin students.
And also when one has been commissioned. (PS 3.3.166)
The term *sme* is understood [from the previous rule].
*Adhīṣṭa* has been explained.
When the word *sma* is used as an attendant word (*upapada*) and a request (*adhīṣṭa*) is implied, the suffix *loṭ* occurs after a verbal root;
this is an exception to the rule for *liṅ*. Example: *aṅga sma rājan māṇavakam adhyāpaya* ("Please, O King, teach the boy").
Come now, O King, perform the Agnihotra sacrifice.
The suffix *tumun* is used after verbal roots when expressing time, occasion, or specific junctures.
When words such as *kāla* (time) and others are used as *upapada*s, the suffix *tumun* is applied to the verbal root. Example:
*kālo bhoktum* (it is time to eat).
[The word] *velā* [is used] in the sense of "time for eating.
Why is it not so here [in the case of] "Time cooks all beings" (*kālaḥ pacati bhūtāni*)?
The mention of *praiṣa* and so forth is connected here.
Why does it not occur here:
*kālo bhojanasya* ("it is time for eating")?
By the rule of *vāsarūpa*, the suffix *lyuṭ* also occurs;
this has been stated: that after the section on feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*), the *vāsarūpa* rule is not invariably applicable.
The optative suffix (liṅ) is used when [the word] "yadi" (if) occurs. PS_3.3.168.

The [categories] beginning with *kāla* (time) continue to apply. When words such as *yad* are used as *upapada*, the suffix *liṅ* occurs after a verbal root when [words] beginning with *kāla* are present.
"Sir, it is time for you to eat; sir, please eat. This is a reproach regarding hunger.
Please eat at the proper time.
The kṛtya suffixes and the tṛc suffix are also used in the sense of the dative case (arha).
The word *arha* means "one who deserves" (*arhati*), that is, one who is fit for it.
When the sense of "deserving" (*arhe*) is to be expressed as the agent (*kartari*) or is merely implied (*gamyamāne*), the *kṛtya* suffixes and the suffix *tṛc* are applied after a verbal root.
By virtue of the suffix *ca*, the optative (*liṅ*) is also [employed]:
"The maiden must indeed be married by you," or "she is to be carried away," or "she is to be wed."
"You are indeed the bridegroom of the maiden;
you should indeed marry the maiden;
you are worthy of this."

Now, why are the *kṛtya* suffixes and the *tṛc* prescribed for the sense of fitness (*arha*), when they will also apply to fitness because it has already been prescribed by the general rule? This *liṅ* which is prescribed here—
Therefore, so that there may be no contradiction,
the rule regarding optional forms (vāsarūpa-vidhi) is considered non-obligatory (anitya).
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root to express necessity (*āvaśyaka*) or debt (*ādhamarṇya*).
The state of being inevitable is "inevitability" (āvaśyakam);
this is a limiting condition (upādhi).
Not [applying] when there is an upapada.
When the agent is to be expressed as qualified by necessity or qualified by debt, the suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root. Example:
*avaśyaṃkārī* ("one who necessarily acts").
The compound is formed because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group.
Furthermore, regarding debt (*ādhamarṇya*): "one who owes a hundred," "one who owes a thousand," "one who owes a *niṣka*."
And [the suffixes] kṛtya. (PS 3.3.171)

The phrase "in the sense of necessity (āvaśyaka) and debt (ādhamarṇya)" carries over [from the previous rule]. Furthermore, affixes designated as *kṛtya* occur after a verbal root when necessity and debt function as the limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
Indeed, you must certainly make a mat;
it is necessarily to be made,
it is necessarily to be done.
It must necessarily be done. Regarding debt: "A hundred must be paid by you," or "A thousand must be given."
For what purpose is this [rule],
since those [suffixes] prescribed by the general rule will also apply to this subject?
They would be superseded by the suffix *ṇini*, which is prescribed as a specific exception.
The suffix *ṇini* occurs in the sense of the agent,
while the *kṛtya* suffixes occur in the senses of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*); so how could there be any possibility of conflict between them?
Regarding this, some say that the kṛtya suffixes such as *bhavya* and *geya* denote the agent (*kartṛ*), and these are the examples here. [291]
The suffixes *śaki* and *liṅ* [are used] in the sense of possibility (*śakti*).

The word *śaki* is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). The suffix *liṅ* occurs when the meaning of the verbal root is conditioned by the sense of "being able" (*śaknoty-artha*).
By the inclusion of the word "ca" (and), the *kṛtya* suffixes are also included:
indeed, the burden must be carried by you; it is to be carried (*voḍhavya*), it is to be borne (*vahanīya*), it is to be conveyed (*vāhya*).
"You indeed should carry the burden;
you are capable in this matter.
This restatement of what is already generally prescribed is intended so that there may be no sublation by the optative suffix (*liṅ*).
In the sense of benediction, the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* are used.
*Āśīḥ* is the act of wishing; it is the desire to obtain an object that is desired but not yet attained.

And this [word *āśis*] is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). The suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* occur after a verbal root when it denotes a meaning qualified by a benediction (*āśis*). For example: "May you live long! (*ciraṃ jīvyād bhavān*).
"May you live long!
Why [is it specified] "in a benediction"? [Consider:
"Devadatta lives for a long time."
The suffixes *ktic* and *kta* are also used to form names (*saṃjñā*).
"In the sense of a benediction" (āśiṣi) [is understood] from the previous rule.
In the domain of a benediction, the suffixes *ktic* and *ktau* occur after a verbal root.
If the designation is understood through the aggregate as a whole:
from *tanu* comes *tanti*;
from *sanu* comes *sāti*.
Let there be prosperity (*bhūti*); let there be destruction (*manti*). Indeed, the suffix *kta* is also used: one to whom the gods should give (*deyāsuḥ*) is Devadatta.
The suffix *kta*, which is prescribed generally, is stated again so that it may not be superseded by *ktic*;
the particle *ca* serves the purpose of specification.
And there is no lengthening [of the vowel] before the suffix *ktic* (Pāṇini 6.4.39).
The aorist is used after the particle *māṅ*.
When *māṅ* is used as an upapada, the *luṅ* suffix is applied to the verbal root;
this is an exception to all other verbal suffixes (*lakāra*s).
May he not do it; may he not take it;
how might his evil not come to pass?
"Will it not be?"—
this [form] is simply incorrect.
Some say that there exists another word *mā* which is not followed by the augment *iṭ*.
This is its formal application:
In the sense of "sma," the suffixes *laṅ* and *liṭ* are also used.
When the word *māṅ* follows after the word *sma*, the suffix *laṅ* is applied to the verbal root; furthermore,
by virtue of the word *ca* [in the rule], there is also elision (*luk*).
Let him not do;
let him not have done; let him not take.
Let him not take it away.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Kāśikā* commentary composed by the venerable Jayāditya.
The Fourth Pāda of the Third Adhyāya. [292] Suffixes [are introduced] when there is a connection between verbal roots (dhātu). (Pāṇini 3.4.1)
The word *dhātu* [is used] in the sense of "verbal root" (*dhātvartha*).
The "connection of verbal roots" (*dhātusambandha*) is the connection between the meanings of verbal roots, namely the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
When that [future tense] exists, even conditions expressed at an improper time are valid:
"The son of one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice will be born"; "The mat made will exist tomorrow."
The action to be performed was yet to come;

When an indeclinable (avyaya) expresses something contrary to what was intended, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied after the root *kṛ*.

When an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is used as an accompanying word (*upapada*), and a statement contrary to one's desire is implied, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied to the root *kṛ*. Example:
"O Brāhmaṇa, a son has been born to you."
What then, O Vṛṣala?
Having lowered [my voice], I shall speak; having lowered [my voice].
One should speak with humility; a name should be addressed respectfully. "O Brāhmaṇa, your daughter is pregnant."
What then, O Vṛṣala?
I speak having raised my voice;
having made it loud.
In a loud voice;
in a low voice; and an unpleasant name should be mentioned.
[The rule applies] when mentioning something contrary to one's desire—what is the purpose of this?
He says aloud, "A son has been born to you.
Why is the mention of *ktvā* made,
given that it has already been stated that throughout this entire section, the *ktvā* suffix occurs by way of the *vāsarūpa* rule?
The statement is for the sake of the compound meaning;
thus, in the rule "ktvā ca" (Pāṇini 2.2.22), the rule "tṛtīyā-prabhṛtīny-anyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 2.2.21) [is understood to apply].
Thus it continues.
The re-mention of *ṇamul* within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *ṇamul* is for the purpose of indicating that [the two] are of equal status;
by this, both will be carried forward (*anuvṛtti*) in what follows.
And in the case of animals, [the result occurs] at the time of death.
When the word *tiryak* is used as an upapada, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* occur after the root *kṛ*, provided that completion (*apavarga*) is understood.
Apavarga means completion. Having gone by turning sideways, or having turned sideways and gone.
*tiryak-kāram gataḥ* means "having gone across" or "having completed [the journey]";
what is the purpose of the term *apavarge*?
Having placed the wood crosswise, he went;
"tiryaci" is an imitation of sound.
And an imitation need not necessarily conform to the original form.
Because it would follow that the form being imitated would be destroyed,
as stated in the rule *etado 'ś, adaso māt* (Pāṇini 7.1.12).
When the suffix *tas* follows a word denoting one's own limb (*sva-aṅga*), it is added after the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*.

The suffix *tas* is used when [the action] proceeds from one's own limb (*svāṅga*); thus it is so stated. When the suffix *tas* follows, with a word denoting one's own limb (*svāṅga*) as the attendant word (*upapada*), the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied to the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*.
Here, a correspondence according to the order of enumeration is not intended,
because there is no *svarita* accent;
it has proceeded by making [the preceding] the primary subject.
Having placed it at the front, he went;
he went making it the foremost.
He stands having become the foremost.
Having come to the front, he stands; he stands facing forward. Having gone behind, he remains there.
Having placed [it] behind, he went; having gone with it behind him; having gone by being behind [it].

[The suffix -vati is applied] after the word *pṛṣṭha*, [forming] *pṛṣṭhatobhāva*. Why [is it specified] "in reference to one's own body"? [To exclude cases such as: *pṛṣṭhato bhūtvā* ("having stood behind").
[The suffix] *ktvā* is applied after [the verb] *gam* when preceded by *sarvataḥ*. Why is the mention of *tas* (i.e., *sarvatas*) necessary?
[Consider: *mukhīkṛtya gataḥ* ("having turned toward the front, he went").
He went having become face-to-face.
Why is the mention of *pratyaya* (suffix) used?
[Because] from *mukha* with the suffix *tas* we get *mukhataḥ*, meaning "from the mouth."
Having placed it at the front, he departed.
In the sense of the suffix *cvī*, [the substitution of *na* for *an* occurs] before a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a word ending in a suffix having the sense of "becoming" (*bhavārtha*).
That [suffix] from which neither the meaning of *na* nor the meaning of a verbal root (*dhā-artha*) is understood is referred to in this way.
When a word containing a suffix with the sense of *na* is used as a co-occurring word (*upapada*) in the sense of *cvi*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* occur after the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*.
Having made the non-different different, he has gone; having gone by making a distinction, he has gone; having made it different, he has gone;
he has gone in a manifold manner.
He has gone having separated [from it],
he has gone having made [it] separate,
he has gone in a state of separation.
Having become manifold, he has gone;
having become manifold, he has departed;

He has gone having become separated,
he has gone having become apart,
he has gone to a state of being split asunder.
He went having made [it] twofold;

Having become twofold he went;
having become divided into two he went;
he went into a state of being twofold.
He went having created a division; he went having made a division;
he went by means of creating a division.
He has gone into a state of duality; having become divided, he has gone; he has entered into a state of duality.
What is the purpose of including the term *pratyaya*? [Examples: *hiruk kṛtvā* / *pṛthak kṛtvā*.

Why is it said "for the sake of [obtaining] wood" (*cavy-arthe*)? [Consider: "Having split the pieces of wood, he has gone. The mention of the word *artha* is for the purpose of expressing the sense of "purpose" (*dhā*).
Furthermore, it is not just the single [suffix] *na*;
rather, according to the rule "from the roots *vi* and *nañ*, the suffixes *nān* and *ña*" [are applied].
One should remain silent. // PS_3.4.63 //
When the word *tūṣṇīm* is used as an upapada, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied to the root *bhū*. For example:

"Having become silent" means silence (*tūṣṇīṃ-bhāva*).
The inclusion of the root *bhū* is for the purpose of excluding the root *kṛ*.
The suffix *anvac* is used in the sense of following in order.
When the word *anvak* is used as an upapada, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied after the root *bhū* in the sense of compliance (*ānulomya*).
Compliance (*ānulomya*) means being in accordance with or favorably disposed toward.
Conformity is the adaptation to the minds of others;
it remains in a state of following along.
Having become compliant, he remains;
he remains in a state of compliance. Why specify "in the sense of compliance"? [To exclude cases such as: *anvaga gataḥ* ("he has gone after").
Having become a follower, he remains.

[307] The suffix *tumun* is used after the roots *śak*, *dhṛṣ*, *jñā*, *glā*, *ghaṭ*, *rabh*, *labh*, *kram*, *sah*, and *arh*, as well as after a verb meaning "to exist" (*asti*), when followed by another verb. (Pāṇini 3.4.65)

When words such as *śaka* (to be able) and others are used as co-occurring elements (*upapada*), or when words expressing existence (*asty-artha*) are present, the suffix *tumun* is applied after the verbal root alone.
This rule is formulated because its purpose is not already covered by the meaning of the co-occurring element.
He is able to eat; he dares to eat; he knows how to eat.
He is weary of eating;
he strives to eat;
he begins to eat.
He obtains to eat;
he proceeds to eat;
he endures to eat.
He is worthy to eat.
Furthermore, regarding the sense of existence: "there is to eat" (asti bhoktum) and "it happens that he will eat" (bhavati bhoktum).
In the case of words expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti*), when they have the sense of "enough" (*alam*). (Pāṇini 3.4.66)
*Paryāpti* means sufficiency (*anyūnatā*).
When words expressing sufficiency (*alam-artha*) are used as *upapadas*, the suffix *tumun* is applied to the verbal root.
He is sufficient to eat;
he is able to eat;
he is capable of eating.

What is the purpose of the phrase "in the case of words meaning 'sufficiency' (paryāpti)"? [Example: *alaṃ kṛtvā* ("having done enough"). What is the purpose of the phrase "in the sense of 'enough' (alam-artha)"? [Example:
*paryāptaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats sufficiently").
In the preceding sūtra, the inclusion of the term *śaki* is for the purpose of expressing incapacity, as in "it is not possible to do it thus."
A *kṛt* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The suffixes designated as *kṛt* occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*).
This is a supplementary rule (*śeṣa*) for the rules governing the derivation of *kṛt* suffixes.
In those cases where there is no explicit statement of the meaning, this [rule] applies because of the expectancy for meaning; however,
it does not apply to sentences such as "khyun" and so forth.
Because when the meaning is directly indicated, they are free from expectancy;
[thus we have] *kārakaḥ* and *kartā*.
Nandana; Grāhin; Paca.
Or [the suffix *ya* is applied] after words meaning "suitable for," "to be sung," "to be spoken," "to be attended to," "to be produced," "to be flooded," or "to be cast down. (PS 3.4.68)
Words such as *bhavya* and others are optionally prescribed as being formed with the agentive sense (*kartari*).

By the rule "The senses of the kṛtya, kta, and khal suffixes apply only to those two [the action and the object]" (Pāṇini 3.4.70), [these suffixes would otherwise denote the action and the object]. However, for these specific words, they are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) to denote the agent.

Thus, while the states of being the object (*karman*) or the action (*bhāva*) would [otherwise] apply, the agent (*kartṛ*) is also optionally expressed; for he is called *bhavya* because he comes into being (*bhavati*),
or because he is capable of coming into being (*bhavyam anena*).
The young brahmin is one who should chant the Sāmans, or the Sāmans are those to be chanted by the young brahmin;

The teacher may say, "Recite your lesson," or the resident pupil may attend upon the teacher,
or the teacher may be attended upon by the student.
He is born, thus he is "janya," or alternatively, he is that by which [something] is produced;
he floats, thus he is "āplāvya."
Or, it is that by which one is immersed;
or, he falls upon it, thus it is "to be fallen upon" (āpātya), or it is that by which one is caused to fall upon it.
The suffix *la* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) and in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) after intransitive roots.
In the rule "laḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the general term "la" is understood as being without an indicatory marker (anubandha), and the word "at" is taken as ending in the nominative plural.

The *lakāra*s occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) as the grammatical participant (*kāraka*); by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), they also occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); and from intransitive roots (*akarmaka-dhātu*), they occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), and again by virtue of the word "and," in the sense of the agent as well.
"The village is being gone to by Devadatta"; "Devadatta goes to the village.
From intransitive verbs: "It is sat by Devadatta."

Devadatta sits. The kṛtya suffixes, the past passive participle (*kta*), and the suffixes having the sense of *khal* do not occur in the impersonal (*bhāva*) voice after roots that require an agent (*sakarmaka*). [308] The functions of the kṛtya, *kta*, and *khal*-type suffixes belong to those two [the agent and the object] alone. (Pāṇini 3.4.70)
Only for those two— namely, the state (bhāva) and the object (karman)— the affixes designated as *kṛtya*, as well as those with the sense of *kta* and *khal*, occur.

In the sense of the action (*kṛtyāḥ*): "A mat must be made by you" (*kartavyaḥ kaṭo bhavatā*);

In the sense of the state of being (*bhāve*): "You must eat" (*āśitavyaṃ bhavatā*).
"You must lie down.
The *kta* suffix is used in the sense of the object: "The mat was made by you";
"The rice was eaten by you."

In the sense of state (bhāva): *āsitaṃ bhavatā* (you have sat), *śayitaṃ bhavatā* (you have lain down). Words having the sense of *khal* (suffixes expressing difficulty or facility) are used in the object (karman): *īṣatkaraḥ kaṭo bhavatā* (the mat was easily made by you).
It is easy;
it is difficult.
In the sense of the abstract state (bhāve): "You have become somewhat wealthy."

The suffix *kta* occurs after roots meaning "to become" (*bhū*) when used intransitively; however, because of the continued application of the rule "after transitive [roots] [the suffix denotes] the state (*bhāva*"), these suffixes do not occur in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) after transitive roots.
The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*) and also in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

The *kta* suffix prescribed after a root in the sense of the inception of an action (*ādikarman*) occurs in the sense of the agent; by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), it also occurs as prescribed [elsewhere] in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).

The first moment of an action is "initial action" (*ādikarman*); this is the explanation of the meaning of that *kta* suffix which is prescribed when that initial action is intended to be expressed as having already occurred (*bhūtatva*).
Devadatta made a mat; the mat was made by Devadatta;
it was made by Devadatta.
Devadatta ate the rice;
the rice was eaten by Devadatta; it was eaten by Devadatta.
And [the agent is designated as the *kartṛ*] after verbs meaning "to go," after intransitive verbs, and after the roots *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.72)
The *kta* suffix that follows verbal roots meaning "motion" (*gaty-artha*) when they are intransitive (*akarmaka*), as well as those beginning with *śliṣ*, occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
By the word "and" (ca), the [application of the suffixes] as they are otherwise prescribed for the agent and the object [is also included]:
*devadatto grāmaṃ gataḥ* (Devadatta went to the village) and *devadattena grāmo gataḥ* (the village was gone to by Devadatta).
The village was gone by Devadatta;
it was gone by Devadatta.
From intransitive verbs: you have become ill.
You have become ill;
you have sat down,

With the root *śliṣ* (to embrace): you have embraced the teacher; the teacher has been embraced by you;
[the teacher] was embraced by you.
śīṅ—You have rested near the teacher; the teacher has been rested near by you; [the act] was rested near by you.
You have attended upon the teacher;
the teacher has been attended upon by you; [the teacher] was attended upon by you.
You have attended upon the teacher; the teacher was attended upon by you;
[the act of] attending was performed by you.
You have dwelt with the teacher; the teacher has been dwelt with by you; it has been dwelt with by you.
The young man is born after the measure;
the young woman is born after the young man; [the offspring] is born after the young man.
You have climbed the tree;
the tree was climbed by you; it was climbed by you.

*jīryati* (to grow old): *anujīrṇo vṛṣalīṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta has grown old after [having lived with] a low-caste woman), *anujīrṇā vṛṣalī devadattena* (the low-caste woman has grown old after [having lived with] Devadatta), *anujīrṇaṃ devadattena* (it has grown old after [having been with] Devadatta).
Verbs such as *śliṣ* become transitive when accompanied by prepositions; it is for this purpose that they are included here.
The words *dāśa* and *goghnau* are used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*).
The two words *dāśa* and *goghnau* are irregularly formed (*nipātana*) when they function as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) kāraka.
[The root] *dāśṛ* means "to give," from which [the word *dāśa* is derived] by adding the suffix *ac* according to the rule for roots beginning with *pac*.

Since it would have applied to the agent by virtue of its being designated as *kṛt* [suffix], it is here prescribed as an irregular form (*nipātana*) for the recipient (*sampradāna*). One gives to him, thus he is a *dāśa*.
A *goghna* is one who kills a cow (*gām*) to give it to a guest (*atithi*) who has arrived and is worthy of honor (*arghārha*);
the suffix *ṭac* is applied here as an irregular formation (*nipātana*).
Precisely by the force of the grammatical derivation (nipātana), the term *goghna* refers to a priest (*ṛtvij*) and others, but not to a *caṇḍāla* or similar persons;
even in the absence of an actual killing of a cow, he is designated as a "cow-killer" (*goghna*) on account of his fitness for that role. [309]
The words *bhīma* and others [function as the first member of a compound] when used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).
The words *bhīma* and others are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).
These are derived from *uṇādi* suffixes.
The suffix *mak* is added after the roots *iṣ*, *yudh*, *indh*, *das*, *śyā*, *dhūs*, and *bhī*; the suffix *ṣuk* is added after *gras* and *vas*. Such are these [rules].
Elsewhere than by those two, there are the *uṇādi* suffixes (Pāṇini 3.4.75).
Since this would result in the exclusion [of the suffix], the following irregular formation (nipātana) is commenced:
*bhīmaḥ*,
*bhīṣmaḥ*.
The terrifying one;
Varuṇa;
the earth.
Rajas;

The *uṇādi* suffixes occur after those two [roots] and others.
The words formed by the *uṇādi* suffixes occur in grammatical relations other than those of the ablative (*apādāna*) and dative (*sampradāna*).
Since they are *kṛt* suffixes, they would primarily apply to the agent (*kartṛ*); however, they are here stated to occur in the roles of object (*karman*) and so forth as well.
The reference "by those two" has the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*);
otherwise, only the ablative (*apādāna*) would be excluded, because it is the most proximate.

that which is stretched is a "thread" (tantu);
that which has occurred is a "path" (vartma).
*Caritam* means skin.
The locative case is used for the agent (kartṛ) as well as for the locus (adhikaraṇa), after verbs denoting stasis, motion, or consumption.
Roots whose meanings consist of endurance are intransitive;
those whose meanings consist of consumption and eating are likewise so— this is the established doctrine within our own school.
The *kta* suffix prescribed after roots meaning "stability" (*dhrauvya*), "motion" (*gati*), and "consumption" (*pratyavasāna*) occurs in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*);
by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), it also occurs as otherwise established [in other senses].
After roots meaning "stability," it occurs in the senses of the agent (*kartṛ*), the state of being (*bhāva*), and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

After roots meaning "motion," [the locative case is used] for the agent, the object, the abstract state (bhāva), and the locus; after roots meaning "consumption" (pratyavasāna), for the object, the abstract state, and the locus. First, regarding those meaning "stability" (bhrauvya): *devadatta āsitaḥ* ("Devadatta has sat").
He has sat;
this is their sitting.
From roots meaning "motion": Devadatta has gone to the village.
"The village has been gone to by Devadatta," "It has been gone by Devadatta," or "This going belongs to them."
From roots meaning "eating" [the following forms are derived]: *odanaḥ bhuktaḥ devadattena* (rice was eaten by Devadatta),
*devadattena bhuktam* (it was eaten by Devadatta),
*idam eṣāṃ bhuktam* (this was eaten by them).
In the expressions "the Brahmins have eaten" (*bhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ*) and "the cows have drunk" (*pītā gāvaḥ*),
the vowel *a* functions as a suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*).
"They have eaten; they have drunk."
Of the *las* [suffix]. (PS 3.4.77)
This [rule] beginning with *lasya* is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). The vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇa-artha*).
The mere letter *l* is designated as the substituendum (*sthānin*).
That which we shall subsequently enumerate under the heading "of *la*" (*lasya*) should be understood in this way.
Furthermore, what is this "of *la*" (*lasya*)?

The ten *lakāras*, specified by their respective *anubandhas*, are prescribed for specific meanings and specific times. Having discarded the *anubandhas* that serve as qualifiers, that which is common [to them] is taken.
Six have the marker *ṭ*, and four have the marker *ṅ*.
They are taught according to their sequence, like the traditional recitation of the alphabet:
*laṭ*,
*liṭ*.
The *luṅ* (aorist), *lṛṭ* (periphrastic future), and *leṭ* (subjunctive).
The imperative (loṭ), the imperfect (laṅ), and the optative (liṅ).
The conditional (luṅ) and the conditional past (lṛṅ).
Thus.
Now, why is there not the inclusion of the letter *l* alone [in the term *lakāra*], as in the cases of *lunāti* and *cūḍālaḥ*?
The governing rule for the verbal roots (*dhātu*) continues to apply, and the agent (*kartṛ*) and others serve as qualifiers.
[310] *tip*, *tas*, *jhi*, *sip*, *thas*, *tha*, *miP*, *vas*, *mas*, *ta*, *ātām*, *jha*, *thās*, *āthām*, *dhvam*, *iṭ*, *vahīM*, *mahīṅ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.78)
In the place of *las*, the substitutes beginning with *ti* occur.
The letter *p* in *tip*, *sip*, and *mip* is for the sake of accentuation (*svara*).

*pacati*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*;
*pacasi*, *pacathaḥ*, *pacatha*.

*pacāvahe*, *pacāmahe*; in this same way, examples may be cited for the other suffixes (*lakāras*) as well.
In place of the *ṭe* (the final vowel and following consonant) of the *ātmanepada* affixes marked with *ṭ*, there is *ṭi*.
In place of the *lakāra* marked with *ṭ*, those *ātmanepada* suffixes that follow undergo the substitution of *e* for their final *ṭ*.
This has already been illustrated accordingly.

The suffix *thās* is used for the second person singular.
By the rule "ṭitaḥ" [itself],

In place of the *ta* and *jha* suffixes of the perfect tense (*liṭ*), *eś* and *irec* are substituted respectively.
In place of the substitutes *ta* and *jha* of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], there are the substitutes *eś* and *irec*, respectively.

*Pece*, *pecāte*, *pecire*;

The letter *l* is for the sake of [indicating] a vowel;

The rule "of the parasmaipada [endings]" applies here as well.
In the sense of "knowing," from this root *vid*, there are nine optional substitutes—*ṇal* and so forth—for the *parasmaipada* endings that follow the *laṭ* [present tense] affixes.
veda, vidatuḥ, viduḥ; vettha, vidathuḥ, vida;
veda, vidva, vidma.
And it does not exist; [the forms are] vetti, vittaḥ, vidanti;
[and] vetsi, vitthaḥ, vittha.
*vedmi*, *vidvaḥ*, *vidmaḥ*.
[311] For the five [verbal roots] beginning with *brū*, [the substitute] *āha* is used in place of *brū*. (Pāṇini 3.4.84)
[The rule] "of the parasmaipada [terminations]" applies as before,
and [the rule] "or of the present indicative (laṭ)" also applies.

From that, by the rule *iñaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112), the suffix *aṇ* occurs.
Phāṇṭāhṛtaḥ.
Bhāgavitti is the descendant of Bhāgavitta;
his youthful descendant [is Phāṇṭāhṛta].
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *vṛddhāṭ ṭhak sauvīreṣu bahulam* (Pāṇini 4.1.148), resulting in *bhāgavittikaḥ*.
His pupils [are called...]
As before, when the suffix *yu* has been elided, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *iñaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112), resulting in *bhāgavittāḥ*.
[The word *taikāyaniḥ* means] the descendant of *Tika*.
From *tika* and other such words, the suffix *phiñ* is applied [to form patronymics] (Pāṇini 4.1.154): *taikāyaniḥ*.
The young descendant of that person is formed by adding *cha* after the suffix *pheḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.149).
Thus, from *cha*, [we derive] *taikāyanīyaḥ*.
Its student: when the suffix *yuva* has been elided, by [Pāṇini 4.2.114], *cha* is applied after a *vṛddha* [stem].
The Taikāyanīyas. Kāpiñjalādi is the descendant of Kapiñjalāda; his youthful descendant [is called] a Kāpiñjalādi-yuvan.
The suffix *ṇya* is applied after words such as *kurū-* (Pāṇini 4.1.151), as in *kāpiñjala*. [The suffix *cha* is applied] to form *tasya chātrāḥ* ("his pupils").
Since the other [names] have ceased [to apply], the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "and after *iñ*" (*Pāṇini* 4.2.112), resulting in *kāpiñjalādāḥ*.
[The word *glaucuki* means] the offspring of Glucuka.
*Glucukāyaniḥ* is formed by the suffix *phin* according to Pāṇini 4.1.160, *prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam*;
it denotes the youthful descendant (*yuvan*) of that [lineage].
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *prādīvyat* (Pāṇini 4.1.83); [for example:
*glaucukāyanaḥ*.
His pupils: [glaucukāyanāḥ].
When the *yuva*-suffix has been elided, that same *aṇ* [applies], as in *glaucukāyanāḥ*. Only when an *ac* vowel follows does this apply, as in *phāṇṭāhṛtarūpyam*.
[The suffix] *mayaṭ* is applied after *phāṇṭa* and *āhṛta*.
This applies even before the scope of *prādīvyataḥ*;
for example, that which is beneficial for Bhāgavittika is *bhāgavittikīyam*.
The substitution of *phak* or *phiñ* occurs optionally [after a word denoting a place of origin].
Only when [the descendant] is young (yūni).
Since the previous rule would have mandated compulsory elision (nitye luki), an option is now stated.
When a suffix beginning with a vowel is intended after a *prāgdīvyatīya* derivative, there is optionally an elision (*luk*) of the two suffixes *phak* and *phiñ*.
For instance, when the suffix *yañ* has been applied to the *garga*-class words, the suffix *phak* is added by the rule *yañiñoś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.101), resulting in *gārgyāyaṇaḥ*.
His students are the Gārgīyas and the Gārgyāyaṇīyas;
the Vātsīyas and the Vātsyāyanīyas.
Furthermore, regarding *phiñ*: the offspring of Yaska is Yāska, by virtue of [the rule] *śivādibhyo ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.112).
The youthful offspring of that [Yāska]—
From *Aṇu*, by [Pāṇini 4.1.156] *dvyacaḥ* [the suffix] *phiñ* is applied, resulting in *Yāskāyaniḥ*. His pupils are the *Yāskīyāḥ*.
The Yāskāyanīyas.
The suffix *yañ* is applied after [the word] "tasya" (of him) to denote offspring.
This is a statement of meaning,
which is connected with both preceding and subsequent suffixes.

After that [word] expressed in the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhīsamartha), a suffix is applied as prescribed when the meaning is "offspring" (apatyam). Here, the genitive sense qualified by the meaning of the base is understood as "offspring," and only the suffix -aṇ is taken; gender, number, and all other such factors are not intended to be expressed.
The offspring of Upagu is Aupagava;
likewise Āśvapata and Daitya.
Belonging to oneself (autsaḥ), belonging to women (straiṇaḥ), belonging to men (pauṃsnaḥ).
This [rule] might be intended to exclude even his offspring;
however, this is merely a general statement (*utsarga*), and its purpose is simply to indicate that [the suffix *vṛddhi*] applies to the remainder.
The offspring of Bhānu are the Bhānavas; [the offspring] of Śyāmagu are the Śyāmagavas.
One [is established] in the lineage. // PS 4.1.93 //

*Apatya* (offspring) beginning with the grandson is called *gotra* (A 4.1.162). When that [term] is intended to be expressed with distinction, and there arises the contingency of the production of suffixes for each individual offspring, a restriction is made.
In the case of a lineage (*gotra*), there is only a single suffix;
all [members] are connected by means of "offspring" (*apatya*). It is called "offspring" because of not falling away (*apātana*) from the lineage.
Even that which is produced through an intervening [generation] is indeed the offspring of the original progenitor; for example,
the offspring of Garga is Gārgi.
The offspring of Gārgi is Gārgya; even his son, though born from one removed by an intervening generation,
is indeed the offspring of the original progenitor.
The descendant of Garga is Gārgi;
the descendant of Gārgi is Gārgya;
his son also is Gārgya.

In all cases of lineage descendants (*gotrāpatya*), even when there is an intervention [of generations], only the suffix *yañ* occurs after the word *garga*; thus, the suffix is restricted. Alternatively, when the lineage descendant is intended to be expressed, only one word is the primary base (*prakṛti*) that produces the suffix; thus, the base is restricted.
[The result is] *gārgyaḥ*.

The suffix *yañ* is applied after a word denoting a lineage (*gotra*) to form a patronymic (*yuvan*), provided it does not end in the feminine suffix *ī*.
This is also a restrictive rule (*niyama*):
when a young descendant is intended to be expressed, the suffix is applied only from the *gotra* [stem].
Not after those who are not immediate descendants of the original progenitor. For example, Gārgyāyaṇa is the young descendant of Gārgya;
Vātsyāyana [is likewise].
Dākṣāyaṇa, Plākṣāyaṇa, Aupagavi.
Nāḍāyaniḥ. Why [is it specified] "not feminine"? [Consider: dākṣī, plākṣī.
What, then, is being prohibited here?
If it is a restrictive rule (niyama), then the absence of restriction would follow in the case of a woman.

Now, if the *yuvan* suffix were applied, the designation of a female by means of the *gotra* suffix would not be obtained, because the technical name *gotra* is superseded by the technical name *yuvan*.
Therefore, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made.
A suffix occurs after a *gotra* [patronymic] stem to denote a descendant in the younger generation (*yuvan*).
From that [suffix], when not feminine (*astriyām*), [the following applies]:
what has been stated regarding the younger generation does not apply to the feminine.

*ata iñ*]

This is an exception to the rule regarding *aṇ*. [For example:

The *haritādi* group is a sub-group within the *bidādi* group.

This is an exception:
the descendant of Harita is Hāritāyana;
[the descendant of Kindāsa is] Kaindāsāyana.

But is it not the case that the word *gotre* (in the locative) continues [from the previous rule], and that no other suffix for *gotra* occurs after [a base meaning] *gotra*, because of the statement: "Only one [suffix is applied] when *gotra* is to be expressed" (*Pāṇini 4.1.93*)?
This is true;
however, here, even though the context concerns the lineage (*gotra*), by virtue of the underlying implication, the suffix is understood to apply to the younger generation.
The mention of the context of the lineage, moreover, is for the sake of what follows.
And [the substitution of *ya* occurs] for *yad* and *iña*.
