*gārgyāyaṇaḥ*.
Vātsyāyana: from a stem ending in *iñ*— Dākṣāyaṇa,
Plākṣāyaṇa.
Regarding the form *dvīpānusamudram*, the suffix *iñ* [prescribed] by the rule *sutaṅgamādibhya iñ* (*Pāṇini* 4.2.80) does not apply here.

By the mention of *gotra*, the suffixes *yañ* and *iñ* are specified; however, this suffix [the *phak*] occurs only after a word ending in those [suffixes] when denoting a younger generation (*yuvan*), because of the rule stating, "The suffix occurs after a *gotra* [name] when denoting a person of the younger generation."
The [final] vowel of *śaradvat*, *śunaka*, and *darbha* becomes long before the patronymic suffixes *-vatsa* and *-āgrāyaṇa*.
Under the heading "in the sense of a lineage" (gotre),
the suffix *phak* is applied after the words *śaradvat*, *śunaka*, and *darbha*, respectively, to denote a descendant in the specific lineages of Bhṛgu, Vatsa, and Agrayaṇa.
If he is a Bhārgava, he becomes a Śāradvatāyana; otherwise, he is a Śāradvata. If he is a Vātsya, he becomes a Śaunakāyana.
Śaunaka is one;
if [the lineage] is Āgrāyaṇa, it is Dārbhāyaṇa;
otherwise, it is Dārbhi.
The words *śāradvata* and *śaunaka* belong to the *bidādi* group;
from these two, the suffix *phak* is applied as an exception to *añ*.
The suffix *cha* (forming a feminine in *ī*) is optionally applied after the words *droṇa*, *parvata*, and *jīvantā*.
The rule "in the sense of a lineage" (gotre) applies here as well.
After nominal stems such as *droṇa* and others, the suffix *phak* optionally occurs in the sense of a descendant in the lineage.

if this is the meaning,

In that case, this is not established:
that Indrabhūti was the seventh of the Kāśyapas. Rather, the designation [Indrabhūti] will occur by means of the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* applied to the form of his immediate descendant.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way:
if the prohibition were understood to apply to the offspring of sages (*ṛṣyapatya*) in the sense of uninterrupted lineage, then [the name] Kauśika Viśvāmitra would be faulty;
therefore, [the rule] says "in the *gotra*," as in Baidi.
But should it not be formed with the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*?

the territory [is] other than the Kṣaudrakas and Mālavas. What is the purpose of the rule "aṇ-suffix after a word beginning with an udātta vowel" [in the case] of Kṣaudrakamālava? It is for the sake of [the form] Kṣaudrakamālavī.

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after a word denoting a lineage (*gotra*), provided that the word is not itself a lineage-name; furthermore, it is not applied after every such word ending in that [suffix].

That would be an indicator (jñāpaka) for the fact that [the suffix] occurs after such forms; and likewise, there is a rule for *śali*. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of restriction regarding the army (*senā*), so that [the suffix] *añ* might be applied instead of *vuñ*.
The words *khaṇḍikā*,

Words such as *kaṭhaka* and *kalāpa*, which denote [Vedic] recensions (*caraṇa*), take suffixes in the sense of a collection (*samūha*)— just as they do in the sense of a religious duty (*dharma*)— when they are in grammatical apposition with a word in the genitive case.

Beginning with the rule "vuñ after *gotra* and *caraṇa*," suffixes will be explained; in that context, if it is stated "after *caraṇa*, [the suffixes apply] to *dharma* and *āmnāya*," by that, an extension (*atideśa*) is made such that [the suffixes] are applied as they are to *dharma*.
The suffix *vati* has the sense of complete similarity.
*Kāṭhakam* is the dharma of the Kaṭhas; *kālāpakam*.
The Chandogya, the Aukthikya, and the Atharvaṇa.
Likewise, in the case of a collection as well— such as the Kāṭhaka, the Kālāpaka, and the Chāndogya.
The Aukthikya; the Ātharvaṇa.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *acitta*, *hastin*, and *dhenu*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words denoting non-living things and after the words *hastin* and *dhenu*, in the sense of "a collection thereof";
this is an exception to the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ*.
A collection of cakes is *āpūpika*;
[a collection of] *śaṣkuli* cakes is *śāṣkulika*; [a collection of] elephants is *hāstika*.
The suffix *ka* is applied after *dhenu* to form *dhainuka*. It should be stated that this applies when the negative particle *nañ* does not precede; thus, from *adhenu*, one forms *ādhenava*.
The suffix *yañ* and the suffix *cha* are optionally applied after the words *keśa* and *aśva*.
After the words *keśa* and *aśva*, by virtue of these two, the suffixes *yañ* and *cha* respectively occur optionally in the sense of "a collection thereof" (*tasya samūhaḥ*).
A collection of hair is *kaiśyam* or *kaiśikam*.
A collection of horses is *aśvīyam* or *āśvam*.
The suffix *ya* is applied after words beginning with *pāśa*.
When the suffix *ya* occurs after words such as *pāśa*, it denotes "a collection" (*samūha*); for example,
a collection of ropes is *pāśyā*.
A grassy place,
a snare, and grass.
Smoke, wind, and embers.
infant / child / basket

A thicket of reeds.
The suffix *ṭac* is applied after the compound *khala-goratha*.
Regarding the suffix *ya* that occurs after the words *khala*, *go*, and *ratha* in the sense of "a collection" (*samūha*), [the following applies]:
a collection of threshing-floors (*khala*) is *khalyā*.
*gavyā* and *rathyā*:
their non-inclusion among *pāśa* and the others is for the sake of subsequent rules.
And [the suffix] kaṭyac follows the verbal roots *ini* and *tra*.
After the words *khala*, *go*, and *ratha*, the suffixes *ini*, *tra*, and *kaṭyac* respectively occur in the sense of "a collection thereof" (*tasya samūhaḥ*). [Examples:
*khalinī*.
The suffix *ini* should be stated [as applicable] after *gotra*, *rathākaṭya*, *khala*, and so forth.
Ḍākinī / Kuṇḍalinī / Kuṭumbinī.

Kumuda, saroja, padma.
*nalinī*,

*kamala*, and so forth, constitute a class of words based on their form (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
The condition for hell-beings, elephants, and horses is the shoulder; thus,
there is the "shoulder of a man" (*naraskandha*) and the "shoulder of an elephant" (*kariskandha*).
The suffix *kāṇḍa* is applied after [words] such as *pūrva* and others; for example, *pūrvakāṇḍa*. *Turaṅgaskandha*.
The suffix *kāṇḍa* occurs after *pūrva* and other words. *Pūrvakāṇḍa*.
The word *kāṇḍa* [is used] in the sense of "grass" and in the sense of "section of ritual action" (*karmakāṇḍa*). [PS 4.2.52] The word *viṣaya* [is used] in the sense of "country. [PS 4.2.52]
The term "collection" (*samūha*) is discontinued. The genitive case as the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*) continues to apply.
From that [word] ending in the sixth case (genitive), when the sense is "the domain" (*viṣaya*), an affix occurs as prescribed;
provided that this "domain" is a place (*deśa*). The word *viṣaya* has many meanings.
In some cases it exists as a collection of villages, [as in the thought] "a region has been acquired";
in other cases it refers to that which is graspable by the sense faculties.
The eye has form as its object; in some cases, when the object of knowledge is extremely familiar, one says, "Devadatta’s object is this Vedic hymn."
In some other cases, it refers to non-existence, as in "water is the domain of fish.
In that context, the mention of "place" (deśa) is for the purpose of understanding a collection of villages.
The country or region of the Śibis is *śaiba*;
[the derivative] *auṣṭra* [is likewise formed].
Why is it specified "in the sense of a country"?
The section of the Veda is the domain of Devadatta.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words such as *rājanya* and others [to form patronymics].
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the words *rājanya* and others in the sense of "a region that is the domain" (*viṣaya*) of those [people];
this is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
The region or country of the Rājanyas is *rājanyaka*;
[the country] of the Daivayānas is *daivayānaka*.
This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words).
The country or region of the Mālavas is *Mālavaka*; likewise,
*Vairāṭaka* and *Traigartaka*.
Rājanya, Devayāna, Śālaṅkāyana.

Vasāti,

The suffixes *vidhal* and *bhaktal* are applied after the group beginning with *bhauriki* and the group beginning with *aiṣukāri*.

After the group beginning with *bhairikī* and after the group beginning with *aiṣukārī*, the suffixes *vidha* and *bhakta* respectively occur when the sense is "a region that is the object [of their activity]";

The *bhaurikividha*,
the *vaipeyavidha*,
and those from *aiṣukārī* and so forth— such as the *aiṣukāribhakta*.
The descendants of Sārasyāyanabhakta are the Bhaurikis and the Vaipeyas.
Bhauliki,
Caiṭayata,
Kāṇeya.
Vāṇijaka, vālija, vālijyaka.
Śaikayata, Vaikayata, Aiṣukāri.
Sārasyāyana,
Cāndrāyaṇa,
Dvyākṣāyaṇa.

Śayaṇḍa, Tārkṣyāyaṇa, Śaubhrāyaṇa.

That [first verse] of this [hymn] is the *ādi* (opening) in the case of *pragāthas*, according to the Vedic rule.
The word *sa* (he/that) is the case ending expressing capacity (*samarthavibhakti*). The word *asya* (of this) is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*).

The word "ādi" (beginning) is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). The particle "iti" is used for the purpose of indicating the intended meaning. The word "chandasaḥ" (of the Veda) is a specification of the base.

In the case of *pragātheṣu*, it is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix. From that which is expressed in the nominative case (*sa*), a suffix occurs in the sense of the genitive (*asya*) according to the rules prescribed; provided that the base in the nominative case is a *chandas* [Vedic meter], it becomes the initial element [of the formation].
If those which were designated by "yat tadasya" are *pragāthas*, then the use of the particle *iti* indicates that intention; thus,
a *pragātha* beginning with a *paṅkti* verse is called *pāṅkta*.
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after [words denoting] the *ānuṣṭubha* and *jāgata* meters.
Why say "at the beginning"? [To exclude cases where it does not apply when the word is not at the beginning.]
The middle of this *pragātha* is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. Why [specify] "of the meter"?
[To exclude cases such as: the word *ud u tya* is the beginning of this *pragātha*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the *pragāthas*"? [Consider:
"The *paṅkti* is the beginning of this *anuvāka*.
The word *pragātha* is based on an action and applies only to certain specific mantras.
Where two *ṛc*s are made into three by means of *pragrathana*, that is called a *pragātha* because of being *pragrathita* (interwoven) or because of its superior singing (*prakarṣagāna*).
Regarding the application of suffixes to a *chandas* [noun], there is an addition [to the rule] for the neuter gender in its own sense (*svārthe*).
The *triṣṭubh* is indeed the *traiṣṭubha*;
[the *jagatī*] is the *jāgata*.
In battle, [the suffix *cha* is used] after words meaning "purpose" and "warriors. (PS 4.2.56)
The genitive case ending in *so 'sya* expresses the sense of capability (*samarthavibhakti*),
and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) also carries over.

The qualifiers [of the base] are the *prayojana* (purpose) and the warriors (*yoddhṛ*), while the qualifier of the meaning of the suffix is the battle (*saṅgrāma*). From words expressing a *prayojana* and from words expressing warriors, when they are in the first case (*prathamā*) and in syntactic agreement, a suffix is applied as prescribed when the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) meaning "belonging to this" is to be expressed in reference to a battle.
The purpose of this battle is Bhadra; it is the Battle of Bhadra,
the Battle of Saubhadra, or the Battle of Gaurimitra.
Regarding the suffix *yoddhṛ* (fighter): one whose fighters in this battle are from Āhimālā is *āhimālayoddhṛ*;
likewise *syāndanāśva* and *bhārata*.
Why [is it specified] "in battle"? [Consider:
"Subhadrā is the purpose of this gift.
Why [is it specified] "from those who fight for a purpose"?
Subhadrā was a spectator of this battle.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied [to a word denoting a weapon] in the sense of "this is his weapon" when referring to a sport (krīḍā). (Pāṇini 4.2.57)

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after a word in the first case (*prathamā*) in construction with it, in the sense of the seventh case (*saptamī*), provided that what is designated by "that" (*tat*) is a weapon (*praharaṇa*).

If that which is specified by the word "in this" (asyām) is a game (krīḍā), and if that [game] exists, then the particle *iti* indicates the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*). In the case of *daṇḍā*, the staff (*daṇḍa*) is the weapon (*praharaṇa*) used in this game; thus, it is called *dāṇḍā*.
*mauṣṭā*.
Why [is it specified] "it is a weapon"? [Consider:
*mālā bhūṣaṇam asyāṃ krīḍāyām* ("A garland is the ornament in this game").
Why does it say "in play"? [Consider: "In this army, a sword is the weapon."
The suffix *ñ* is applied after a word ending in the *ghañ* suffix to form a feminine noun meaning "that in which this action occurs."
*sa-* is the case ending expressing the required syntactic relation (*samarthavibhakti*). *Asyām* is the meaning of the suffix, expressed in the feminine gender.
"Kriyā" (action) is a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*); "of *ghañ*" is a specification of the verbal root;
the particle "iti" is used for the purpose of indicating the intended meaning.

The suffix *ñ* occurs after a word ending in *ghañ*, denoting an action (*kiyāvācin*), which is in syntactic agreement with a word in the nominative case, to express the sense of the locative case (*asyām*) in the feminine gender.
The mention of *ghañ* here is a reference to the entire class of primary derivatives (*kṛt*); therefore, it includes those preceded by prefixes (*gati*) or objects (*kāraka*).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied when the sense is "the swoop of a hawk occurs upon this," resulting in *śyainaṃpātā*;
and [the suffix] *tailaṃpātā* [is formed] by the rule *ghañ*. Why [is the restriction] stated? [To exclude cases such as: *śyenapatanam asyāṃ vartate* ("the falling of a hawk occurs upon this").
What is the purpose of [specifying] "action" (*kriyā*)? [Consider:
"A rampart exists in this [place]. Furthermore, why are the case-ending denoting the governing relationship (*samarthavibhakti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) mentioned again?
Since both [terms] are indeed under discussion,
that [term] is connected with "in play" (*krīḍāyām*); therefore, if that were to recur, the recurrence of "play" would also be possible.
And this rule applies generally:
when the falling of a staff occurs on a particular lunar day, that lunar day is called *dāṇḍapātā*; [likewise] a lunar day on which the falling of a club occurs is called *mausalapātā*.
One who studies that knows it. (PS 4.2.59)

The suffix *tat*—provided it is in syntactic agreement with a word in the accusative case—is applied according to the rules prescribed when the meanings "studies" or "knows" are intended. For example: *chando 'dhīte* (he studies the Veda) = *chāndasaḥ* (one who has studied the Veda).
A grammarian; an etymologist;
one who knows the omens is an omen-knower.
The *mauhūrta* [astrological] and the *autpāta* [portentous].
The mention of these two is for the purpose of establishing them separately from those who merely recite and those who possess knowledge. [378]
The suffix *ṭhak* is added after words ending in *kratu*, *uktha*, and so forth, as well as those ending in *sūtra*.

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words denoting specific sacrifices such as *uktha*, and after words ending in *sūtra*, in the sense of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*.
One who studies or knows the Agniṣṭoma is called *āgniṣṭomikaḥ*; one who studies or knows the Vājapeya is called *vājapeyikaḥ*.
From the words beginning with *uktha*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied]: *aukthikaḥ*.
A materialist;
according to the Sūtras: one who follows the Vārttika-sūtra, one who follows the Sāṅgraha-sūtra.
It is accepted that [the suffix -aṇ] occurs after *sūtrānta* and so forth;
for example, one who studies the *Kalpasūtra* is called a *kālpasūtra*.
Only the suffix *-aṇ* is applied.
The word *uktha* is conventionally restricted to certain *sāmans* alone;
it is not intended to apply to those [verses] which are chanted after the *yajñāyajñīya*, even though they are studied [as such].
Rather,
the word *uktha*, when occurring in the sense of the *Sāmavedic* *Aukthikya*, produces a secondary derivative (*pratyaya*):
one who studies the *uktha* is an *aukthika*.
The meaning is "he studies the Aukthikya"; furthermore, the suffix does not occur after the word *aukthikya* at all, because there is no such conventional designation (*anabhidhāna*).
It should be stated as "from the Kalpas and Sūtras characterized by [mundane] sciences":
one who practices the science of crows (*vāyasavidyika*), one who practices the science of serpents (*sārpavidyika*).
One who specializes in the characteristics of cattle;
one who specializes in the characteristics of horses;
one who specializes in the Mātṛkalpa.

One who follows the *Pārāśara-kalpa* is a *pārāśarakalpika*. Furthermore, the science (*vidyā*) is not preceded by three [prior births] when it involves contact with the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), the Kṣatriya dharma, or [other fields].
One who studies the auxiliary science (*aṅgavidyā*) is an *āṅgavidyaḥ*.
One who knows the science of the warrior class;
one who knows the science of dharma; one who knows the science of social interaction.
The suffix *ṭhak* should be prescribed after the words *traividya*,
as well as after *ākhyāna*, *ākhyāyikā*, *itihāsa*, and *purāṇa*.
In the case of *ākhyāna* and *ākhyāyikā*, there is the inclusion of their meaning.

The formation of nouns from the names of the *Itihāsa* and *Purāṇa*, as well as from the names of works such as the *Yāvakrīta*, the *Praiyaṅgava*, and the *Vāsavadattā*, is accomplished by means of the suffix -ika. For example:
*yāvakrītikaḥ*, *praiyaṅgavikaḥ*, and *vāsavadattikaḥ*.
One who specializes in the Sauma-uttara,
one who specializes in historical accounts, and one who specializes in ancient lore.
The suffix *la* is applied after a compound beginning with *sarva* and after a *dvigu* compound; for example:
*sarvavedaḥ*, *sarvatantraḥ*.
After a word beginning with *sad-*— as in *savārttikaḥ* and *sasaṅgrahaḥ*;
after a *dvigu* compound— as in *dvivedaḥ*.
The fivefold exposition;
and the *anusū* regarding the object and its characteristics.
The *anusū* is a work consisting of names.
One who studies that [work] is called *ānusukaḥ*,
*lākṣikaḥ*,
or *lākṣaṇikaḥ*.

The suffix *ika* is applied diversely after a compound whose final member is *pathin*; it is applied regularly after a compound whose first member is *śata* or *ṣaṣṭi*. Thus, we have *pūrvapathikaḥ* and *śatapatheyaḥ* or *ṣaṣṭipatheyaḥ*.
One who travels a hundred paths; one who travels a hundred paths (feminine);
one who travels sixty paths.
*Ṣaṣṭipathikī*;
because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*), the suffix *aṇ* also occurs,
as in *śātapathaḥ*.
The sixty paths:
the Uktha and the Lokāyata.

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words denoting narrative (*ākhyāna*), tale (*ākhyāyikā*), history (*itihāsa*), and ancient lore (*purāṇa*).
The suffix *la* is applied after a compound beginning with *sarva* and after a *dvigu* compound.

In the two-footed Jyotiṣa:

The suffix *an* is added in the sense of "conforming to" (*anuguṇa*), with the addition of *ik* being frequent; it is applied after a word that is the second member of a compound, and the suffix *ṣikan* is applied after the words *śata* and *ṣaṣṭi*.
The path is manifold.
The suffix *vun* is applied after words such as *krama* and others.
The suffix *vun* is applied after words such as *krama* and others in the sense of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that";
this is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
One who knows the Krama; one who knows the Padas; the Krama.
The study of words, training, and investigation.
The suffix *ini* is applied after the word *sāman* and after words designated as *anubrāhmaṇa*. [PS 4.2.62]
The suffix *ini* is applied after the word *anubrāhmaṇa* in the sense of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that";
this is an exception to [the application of] the suffix *aṇ*.
This text is similar to a Brāhmaṇa; it is an *anubrāhmaṇa*. One who studies that is called *anubrāhmaṇī*, or *anubrāhmaṇinī* (dual: *anubrāhmaṇinī*).

Is [the formation of] *anubrāhmaṇinaḥ* established by the suffix *ini* according to Pāṇini 5.2.115, "The suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are used in the sense of possession (*mattvartha*) after [stems ending in] *at*?"
In that case, the suffix *ṭhan* would also apply here. [Objection: It will not occur because of the lack of expression (*anabhidhāna*).
[Response: Then the statement is for the purpose of excluding *aṇ*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [words beginning with] *vasanta* and others.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words such as *vasanta* and others in the sense of "one who studies that" or "one who knows that";
this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*.
This treatise is accompanied by spring;
one who studies it is called a *vāsantika* (a student of the spring) or a *vārṣika* (a student of the rains).
Spring,
summer and autumn, winter.
The first quality of the cool season.
Final;
conformable;
not at a joint.
Atharvan.
The elision (*luk*) [of the case-ending] is prescribed for those [words] that have been mentioned [in the preceding rules]. *Pāṇini Sūtra* 4.2.64.

A suffix denoting one who has studied (prokta) is called *prokta*. There is elision (*luk*) of a suffix that occurs after a word ending in a *prokta* suffix, when it denotes a student or a knower (*adhyetṛ-veditṛ*).
That which was proclaimed by Pāṇini is the *Pāṇinīya*.
One who studies that is a *Pāṇinīya*;
likewise, an *Āpiśala*.
There is a distinction regarding the feminine gender and the accent:
[the word] *brāhmaṇī* according to the followers of Pāṇini.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after a stem ending in *u* or *ṛ*, provided it has *k* as its penultimate letter, according to the Sūtra. (Pāṇini 4.2.65)

There is elision (*luk*) of a suffix that follows a word denoting a *sūtra* and which has *ka* as its penultimate letter (*upadhā*). This rule is commenced because its meaning has not been previously stated.
The grammatical aphorisms of Pāṇini consist of eight sections;
those who study them are called the Aṣṭakas or the Pāṇinīyas. Those who study the ten sections are the Vaiyaghrapadīyas.

The Trikās are the followers of Kāśakṛtsna. It should be stated that [the suffix] applies after a word denoting a number; this is so that it does not apply here: *māhāvārttikaḥ*, meaning "one who studies the Mahāvārttika-sūtra."
One who studies the *Kālāpa* is a *Kālāpaka*. Why [is it said] "from a word containing the suffix *ka*"?
[Consider: one who studies the *Catuṣṭaya* is a *Cātuṣṭaya*.
And the Vedic hymns and Brahmanas have those [objects] as their domain.

The term "prokta" (declared) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Vedic meters (*chandāṃsi*) and Brāhmaṇas ending in suffixes that denote "declared by" (*prokta-pratyaya*) apply only to those specific subjects.
[The suffixes] have as their domain those who study and those who know, beyond [the mere word].

But in the case of *asañjñā*, only suffixes such as *ṭhañ* and others apply according to what has been previously established.
The word *pathin* becomes *pantha*.
The suffix *vun* is applied after the word *pathin* in the sense of "born there," serving as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*.
By the rule of conjunction with the suffix *pratyaya*, the substitution of *pantha* for *path* occurs;
thus, one born on the path is *panthaka*.
[406] Or, [the suffix is applied] to *amāvāsyā*. (PS 4.3.30)
The suffix *vun* optionally occurs after the word *amāvāsyā* in the sense of "born there," provided that [the rule] *sandhivelādy-ṛtu-nakṣatrebhyo ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.16) does not apply.
Because of such readings, this [suffix] is an exception to *aṇ*. Thus, we have *amāvasyakaḥ* and *āmāvāsyaḥ*.
Since that which is modified in one part remains essentially the same, the suffix also occurs from the word *amāvasya*.
amāvasyakaḥ, āmāvasyaḥ.
And also [the suffix] *a*. (Pāṇini 4.3.31)

The suffix *a* is applied after the word *amāvāsyā* in the sense defined by [Pāṇini 4.3.25]: "born there. [START JKv_4,3.31] *amāvāsyā-śabdāt akāraḥ pratyayo bhavati tatra jātaḥ (4,3.25) ity etasmin viṣaye /* [END]
Since the suffixes *vuñ* and *naṇ* would have applied previously, this third [suffix] is now prescribed:
*amāvāsyaḥ*, *amāvāsyakaḥ*, *amāvāsyaḥ*;
*amāvasyaḥ*, *amāvasyakaḥ*, *āmāvasyaḥ*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *sindhu* and *apakara*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *sindhu* and *apakara* in the sense of "born there" (*tatra jāta*), as prescribed by rule 4.3.25.
The word *sindhu* belongs to the *kacchādi* group; therefore, this rule provides for the suffix when both the suffix *aṇ* and the suffix *vuñ* (denoting a human) would otherwise apply.
It also applies to the word *apakara* when the general suffix *aṇ* is to be applied.
Sindhuka;
Apakāraka.
And [the suffixes] aṇ and añ [are applied after a word ending in the sixth case]. (Pāṇini 4.3.33)
The suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* are applied respectively after the words *sindhu* and *apākara*, in the sense of "born there" (*tatra jātaḥ*), as prescribed by rule 4.3.25.
This statement is made because [the previous rule] would have applied even to the word *kani*; for example:
*saindhavaḥ* and *āpakaraḥ*.
The suffix *luk* (elision) is applied after the names of the nakṣatras Śraviṣṭhā, Phalgunī, Anurādhā, Svāti, Tiṣya, Punarvasu, Hasta, Viśākhā, Aṣāḍhā, and Bahulā.
After words denoting lunar mansions beginning with *śraviṣṭhā*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix expressing birth (*jātārtha*) that has been added;
when that [suffix] is elided, there is also elision of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) due to the elision of the secondary derivative (*taddhitaluki*).
Thus it occurs:
one born under Śraviṣṭhā is Śraviṣṭha;
[one born under Phalgunī is] Phalguna.
Anurādhā, Svāti, Tiṣya.
Punarvasu, Hasta, and Viśākhā.
Aṣāḍhā;
Bahulā.
In the section concerning elision (luk), there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) stating that [the suffix] is added after Citrā, Revatī, and Rohiṇī when the feminine gender is intended.
Born under Citrā, she is Citrā;
Revatī;
Rohiṇī.
When the feminine suffix is elided, the *ṅīṣ* is applied because [the stem] belongs to the *gaura*-class.
Regarding the words *phalgunī* and *aṣāḍhā*, it should be stated that the suffixes *ṭāp* and *ṅīṣ* are applicable;
thus, *phalgunī*.
From *aṣāḍhā* and *śraviṣṭhāṣāḍhā*, the suffix *chaṇ* may also be stated:
*śrāviṣṭhīya*.
The suffix *cha* (forming *āṣāḍhīya*) is applied after the words *sthāna*, *ananta*, *gośālā*, and *kharaśālā*. (Pāṇini 4.3.35)
After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the locative case, such as the words *gośāla* and *kharaśāla*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting "born therein" (*jāta*). [For example:
born in a cow-pen (*gosthāna*) is *gosthāna*.
A horse stable; a cow shed; a donkey stall.
Or [the asterisms] Vatsaśālā, Abhijit, Aśvayuj, and Śatabhiṣaj. (PS 4.3.36)
The suffix denoting "born there" (*jāta*) following [words] such as *vatsaśālā* optionally undergoes elision (*luk*).
One born in *vatsaśālā* is called *vatsaśāla*.
Vātsaśāla; Abhijit, Ābhijita;
Aśvayuk, Āśvayuja.
*śatabhiṣak*, *śātabhiṣajaḥ*;
this is an elaboration of the inclusion of the term "bahula" (variously).
The suffix *cha* is frequently applied after words denoting lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) [to form a word meaning "born under that"].
The suffix following the word *nakṣatra* (constellation) is frequently elided when it occurs in the sense of "born under" (*jāta-artha*). Examples:
*rohiṇaḥ*, *rauhiṇaḥ*.
Mṛgaśiras, Mārgaśīrṣa.
Those who have acquired skill through practice, by receiving instruction, or by purchase. // PS_4.3.38 //
In that case, [the suffix] *iti* itself [is used]. From a word having the sense of the locative case, a suffix occurs as prescribed when the meanings beginning with "done" (*kṛta*) are intended.
Whether born in Sṛughna, found there, purchased there, or being skilled [in its dialect],
one is called a *sraughana*; likewise, a *māthura* or a *rāṣṭriya*.
But surely, when something is produced in a certain place, it exists in that very place;

and when something is purchased or obtained in a certain place, it likewise exists in that very place. Why, then, is a distinction made in their mention, given that the word and its referent are non-different?
That which is purchased by means of the mere object is indeed obtained,
yet the meaning of the word remains distinct.
Birth for the most part. // PS 4.3.39 //
In this context, the word *tatra* (there) [is understood].

After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī* or *āp* that is in syntactic agreement with a locative case, a suffix is applied as prescribed when the sense is "mostly existing there" (*prāyabhava*).
The word *prāya-* expresses a slight deficiency relative to totality (*sākalya*). For example:
"A native of Srughna (*sraughana*) or Mathurā (*māthura*) generally (*prāyeṇa*), that is, for the most part, resides in Srughna."
Regarding the term *rāṣṭriya*: the inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāya*) would be redundant, because [the state] there is already established by the very fact of being born (*bhava*).
If it is argued that "mostly born" means "not permanently born," [that too is incorrect].
It is equivalent to *mukta-saṃśaya*.
[408] The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *upajānu*, *upakarṇa*, and *upanīvi*. PS 4.3.40.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words such as *upajānu* when they are in the locative case and signify "mostly existing there";
this is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
aupajānukaḥ, aupakrṇikaḥ, aupanīvikaḥ.
In the case of *sambhūta*. // PS_4.3.41 //
In this context, [the word] *tatra* is used.
After a nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*) or *ā*, being in the seventh case (locative), the prescribed suffixes are applied in the sense of "produced therein."
In this context, "possibility" (sambhava) is understood as the determination [of a measure] and the non-excess of that measure;
it is not [mere] origination or existence, because those are already covered by the terms "born" (jāta) and "come into being" (bhūta).
One who is born in Srughna is a Sraughana; likewise,
a Māthura and a Rāṣṭriya.
The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the word *kośa*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after the word *kośa* in the sense of "produced therein";
this is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
*Kauśeya* refers to silk cloth produced from a *kośa*; this is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*),
for which reason it does not apply to a worm, nor to a sword-sheath.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [words denoting] time, when [the action] is well-flowering or ripening.

In this context, after words expressing specific times that are used in the locative case, a suffix is applied according to the rules prescribed for the senses of "proper" (sādhu) and so forth. For example:
*hemante sādhuḥ* = *haimantaḥ prākāraḥ* ("a wall suitable for winter").
The unguent is for the cool season. In spring, the vernal *kunda* creepers flower;
the *pāṭala* trees flower in summer.
In autumn, the śāradā rice crops ripen;
in summer, the barley crops [ripen].
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *vap*. (PS 4.3.44)
In that case, [the rule applies] only when [the word] "there" (*tatra*) is used, and also when [it follows] a word denoting time (*kālāt*).

From a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting time that is in the seventh case (locative) construction, a suffix is applied as prescribed when the sense is "sown. For example: *haimantā yavāḥ* ("barley sown in winter") and *graiṣmā vrīhayaḥ* ("rice sown in summer").
The division of the yoga-rule is for the sake of what follows.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the word *āśvayujī*.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the word *āśvayujī* in the sense of "sown," as an exception to the suffix *ṭhañ*.
"Māṣa beans sown in Āśvayujī" are called *āśvayujaka*.
The full moon day conjoined with the two Aśvinī constellations is *āśvayujī*.
The word *aśvayuk* is a synonym for *aśvinī*. [409]
[The suffix *śas* is used] in other cases than the summer (*grīṣma*) and the spring (*vasanta*).
The suffix *vuñ* optionally occurs after the words *grīṣma* and *vasanta* in the sense of "sown," as an exception to the suffix *ṛtvaṇ*.
*grīṣmam* (autumnal crop), *graiṣmakam*;
*vāsantam*, *vāsantakam*.
In the case of a debt, [the word] *deya* is used [in the sense of "to be paid"]. (Pāṇini 5.1.47)
In that case, [the rule applies] precisely as stated, and also from a word denoting time.

A suffix is applied, as prescribed, to a nominal stem denoting time in the sense of the seventh case-ending when the meaning is "to be given," provided that what is to be given is a debt (*ṛṇa*). For example:
*māse deyam ṛṇam* (a debt to be paid in a month) = *māsikam*.
"Fortnightly" and "yearly.
Why [is the word] "debt" mentioned? [To exclude cases such as: "Alms are to be given every month."
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the words *kalāpī*, *aśvattha*, and *yavabusā*.
The rule "from [words denoting] time" (kālāt) applies here as well.
From the words *kalāpi*, *aśvattha*, and *yavabus*, when they denote time and are in the locative case, the suffix *vun* is added in the sense of "a debt to be paid."
Words such as *kalāpin* and others denote time through association (*sāhacaryāt*).
That time in which peacocks possess their plumage is called *kalāpin*;
that [time] in which the *aśvattha* trees bear fruit is called *aśvattha*.
That in which barley chaff is produced is designated by the term "barley-chaff" (*yavabusaka*).
A debt to be paid at the time of sheaves is called "sheaf-debt" (*kalāpaka*);
likewise, "aśvatthaka."
[It is] like chaff from barley.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after [a word ending in] *grīṣma* and *avara-samā*.
The suffix *vuñ* occurs after the words *grīṣma* and *avarasama* in the sense of "a debt to be paid" (*deyam ṛṇam*).
This is an exception to [the application of] the suffixes *aṇ* and *ṭhañ*.
A debt to be paid in summer is "graiṣmaka";
likewise, it is "āvarasamakam.
Making a different agreement for the sake of interest is "pratyayāntarakaraṇam."
The word *samā* is a synonym for *varṣa* (year).
After the words *saṃvatsara* and *āgrahāyaṇī*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is also applied.

The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after the words *saṃvatsara* and *āgrahāyaṇī*, and by virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *vuñ* is also applied, in the sense of "a debt to be paid"; for example, a debt to be paid in a year is called *sāṃvatsarika*.
*Sāṃvatsarakaṃ* (pertaining to a year); *āgrahāyaṇikaṃ*,
*āgrahāyaṇakaṃ* (pertaining to the Āgrahāyaṇī festival).

Although it would have been sufficient to say simply "vā" (or), the specific mention of the suffix *ṭhañ* is for the purpose of ensuring that *ṭhañ* alone is applied—rather than the suffix *aṇ*—when the rule "saṃvatsarāt phalaparvaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.50) is recited within the *sandhivelādi* group, and the fruit (*phala*) is intended to be expressed as a debt (*ṛṇa*).

From a nominal stem expressing time, when it is in the seventh case (locative) and is used in connection with the sense "the animal cries out," a suffix is added as prescribed; for example:
"the deer cries out at night" (*niśāyāṃ vyāharati mṛgaḥ*) results in *vaiśaḥ* or *naiśikaḥ*;

[Because] the owl cries out at night.

From the word "kālāt" (time), it is understood that [the rule applies] from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting time which is in the first case (*prathamā*) and is semantically connected; the suffix occurs in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), as prescribed, when that which is in the first case is something that has been endured (*soḍha*).
It means that which has been endured, conquered, or practiced. "Niśā" refers to study accompanied by the night.
That [pleasure] was endured by this student during the night;
it was *vaiśika*, *prādoṣa*, or *pradoṣika*.
That which exists therein [is called *tatra-bhava*]. (Pāṇini 4.3.53)

The suffix *yat* is applied after words such as *diś* (direction) and others.

*Diśyam* means "belonging to a direction.

The commander of the army, the rear guard of the army;
the direction.

belonging to the five peoples.
And [the suffix *śas* is applied] after an *avyayībhāva* compound.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that bears the technical designation *avyayībhāva*, in the sense of "that which exists therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*);
this is an exception to [the application of] the suffix *aṇ*.
And it does not occur after every *avyayībhāva* compound;
rather,
it occurs after those beginning with *parimukha*.
This is precisely the purpose of the inclusion of *parimukha* and the others in the list of gaṇas:
their specific qualification is the mention of the term *avyayībhāva*.
That which exists facing the face (*mukha*) is *pārimukha*.
The suffix *vyat* is applied in the sense of "surrounding" (*pārihanavya*). It does not occur after words such as *parimukha*, as in *aupakūla* and *parimukha*.
Parihanu / Paryoṣṭha / Paryulūkhala.
parisīra / anusīra / upasīra /
upasthala, upakalāpa, anupatha.
Anukhaḍga, anutila, anuśīta.
Anumāṣa, anuyava, anuyūpa.
In accordance with the lineage.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a compound whose prior member ends in *anta*.
[The rule] "from an *avyayībhāva*" applies as before. The word *anyataḥ* is compounded when it expresses the sense of a case ending (*vibhakti*).

The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after an *avyayībhāva* compound that does not have *atapa* as its prior member, in the sense of "that which exists therein"; this is an exception to the rule for the suffix *aṇ*. Example: *āntarveśmikam*.
Regarding *āntargehika*:
it should be stated that the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *samāna*.
That which exists in the same [place] is *sāmānika*.
And from that [prefix],
there are the forms *sāmānagrāmika* (belonging to the same village) and *sāmānadeśika* (belonging to the same place).
And from "adhyātma" and so forth:
internal (*ādhyātmika*),
pertaining to the divine (*ādhidaivika*).
*Ādhibhautika*.
*Adhyātma* and so forth constitute an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
It should be stated that the suffix *ṭhañ* is also applied after *ūrdhvanda*.
Aurdhvandāmika:
the word *aurdhvandama* has the same meaning as the word *ūrdhva*;
it also means "after the body."
Pertaining to the afterlife,
pertaining to the supramundane state,
and pertaining to this world.
Regarding the word *pāralaukika*:
the suffix *īya* should be stated after the words *mukha* and *pārśva* when they end in the suffix *tas*. [Thus:
*mukhatīya*.
The suffix *cha* (forming *-īya*) is applied after *pārśva*; furthermore, the augment *kuk* is added after *jana* and *para*.
Thus: *janakīya*.
The suffix *īya* is added after the word *madhya*;
furthermore, it should be stated that the two suffixes *maṇ* and *mīya* are also applied [after *madhya*]. Thus, *madhyīyaḥ*, *madhyamaḥ*, and *madhyamīyaḥ*.
*Mādhyama*, *mādhyamīya*,
and *madhya* [are derived from the word *madhya*]; and [the suffix] *dinan* is added after this [word].
That which occurs in the middle is *mādhyandina*. It should be stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *stha* [in the formation of] *aśvatthāman*.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the word *ajina*. For example:
*vṛkājinakaḥ* (one who wears a wolf-skin) and *siṃhājinaḥ* (one who wears a lion-skin). [413]
The suffix *samāna* and its substitutes are desired in the sense of "internal" (*adhyātma*) and so forth,
as well as after the words *ūrdhvanda*, *deha*, and the word *lokottara*.
The suffix *īya* should be applied after the words *mukha*, *pārśva*, *tasa*, *kujjana*, and *para*;
furthermore, the suffixes *maṇ* and *mīya* are likewise to be applied after the word *madhya*.
The middle [day] and the midday, as well as the elision of the suffix *lugañjin* from this position.
[The suffix *cha* is applied after *grāma*] when preceded by *pari*, *anu*, or *pūrva*.

[The rule] "from an *avyayībhāva*" remains in force. The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in the word *grāma*, provided that it is preceded by *pari* or *anu*, in the sense of "that which exists therein."
An exception to the rule [concerning] the atom:
that which pertains to a village (*pārigrāmika*) and that which pertains to the vicinity of a village (*ānugrāmika*).
The substitution of *cha* occurs for the letter *jha* at the end of a word when followed by the root *jihvāmūlīya* (the visarga before *k* or *kh*) or the letter *a*.
The suffix *chaN* occurs after the words *jihvāmūla* and *aṅguli* in the sense of "that which exists therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*),
as an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule] beginning with *yat*.
jihvāmūlīya (the guttural sibilant) / aṅgulīya (a finger-ring) //
And [the substitution of *ṣ* occurs] after a consonant at the end of a word-group (*vargānta*).
The suffix *cha* is applied after a nominal stem ending in the word *varga* in the sense of "that which exists therein";
this is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
Belonging to the *ka*-group; belonging to the *ca*-group.
When the word *aśabda* is present, the suffix *yat* is optionally used for the sense of *khā*.
The rule "after a word ending in a consonant group" (vargāntāt) applies here as well.

When a suffix other than *śabda* is intended, the two suffixes *yat* and *kha* optionally occur after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a consonant group, in the sense of "that which exists therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*).
When [the suffix] *cha* is applied,
that [suffix] also occurs as an alternative:
*vāsudevavargyaḥ*.
Belonging to the group of Vāsudeva, belonging to the group of Vāsudeva;
belonging to the group of Yudhiṣṭhira.

*yudhiṣṭhiravargīṇaḥ* (belonging to Yudhiṣṭhira’s group), *yudhiṣṭhiravargīyaḥ* (belonging to Yudhiṣṭhira’s group). Why does the rule specify "not when [the following word] is not *aśabda*"? [To illustrate: *yudhiṣṭhiravargaḥ*.
A letter belonging to the ka-group.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *karṇa* and *lalāṭa* when an ornament is meant.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *karṇa* and *lalāṭa* in the sense of "that which occurs there" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), when an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is to be expressed;
this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the general rule].
*karṇikā* and *lalāṭikā* [are formed with the suffix *kan*] when referring to ornaments; why [is this stated]? [Because otherwise they would form] *karṇyā*.
Pertaining to the forehead.
And [the suffix] *cha* occurs after a word denoting the name of that which is to be explained, in the sense of "its commentary. (PS 4.3.66)
That by which something is explained is an "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*);
the name of that which is to be explained is the "name of the object to be explained" (*vyākhyātavyanāma*).

From that [word] ending in the sixth case, namely from a nominal stem whose name is to be explained, a suffix is applied as prescribed when "explanation" (vyākhyāna) is to be expressed, as well as when "that which exists therein" (tatra bhavaḥ) is to be expressed. The particle *ca* ("and"), being heard in proximity to the meaning of the sentence, conjoins only the sense of the preceding rule, namely "that which exists therein" (Pāṇini 4.3.53).
An explanation of the *sup*-case endings is a *saupa* treatise.
*Taiṅaḥ* [means "after the affixes of the third person"];
*kārttaḥ* [means "after the affix *kṛt*"];
*saupam* [means] "that which occurs after case-endings (*sup*)."
*taiṅam* / *kārtam*.
Why [is it said] "of that which has the name 'to be explained' (*vyākhyātavya*)"?
Sukośalā is the expounder of Pāṭaliputra; Pāṭaliputra is explained by Sukośalā;
thus, Pāṭaliputra is [defined] by its configuration.
But *Pāṭaliputra* is not the name to be explained [here].
The simultaneous mention of *bhava* and *vyākhyāna* is for the purpose of formulating an exception (*apavāda*),
for those two have already been defined.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a polysyllabic word that has an udātta accent on its final syllable.

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after a polysyllabic nominal stem (*prātipadika*) whose name is to be explained and which has an udātta accent on its final syllable, in the senses of "belonging to" (*bhava*) and "explaining" (*vyākhyāna*). This is an exception to [the application of] *aṇ*.

The suffixes -ṣa, -tva, and -an have the acute accent on their first syllable; the suffixes -na and -ati have the acute accent on their last syllable; and the bases [ending in these] are oxytone by virtue of the accent of the compound.
Why does it say "having many syllables"?
[Because] he will state that for a word with two syllables, the suffix *ṭhak* is used;
therefore, a one-syllable example is being cited.
The suffix *saup* (nominative singular), the suffix *taiṅ* (optative),
and the suffix *kārt* (past passive participle).
Why does it say "after one that has an udātta accent on another syllable"? [Consider:
*saṃhitāyāḥ sāṃhitam*.
For the word *saṃhitā* has an udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the accent rule for *gati* prefixes.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words denoting *kratu* and *yajña*. (Pāṇini 5.1.73)

After nominal stems (*prātipadika*) meaning "sacrificial rites" (*kratu*) and "sacrifices" (*yajña*), as well as those denoting things to be explained (*vyākhyātavya*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the senses of "that which comes into being" (*bhava*) and "that which explains" (*vyākhyāna*).
This is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
Regarding the sacrifices (*kratubhyaḥ*): there is the exposition of the *agniṣṭoma*; that which pertains to it is *āgniṣṭomika*.
[Likewise] *vājapeyika*.
*rājasūyikaḥ* (pertaining to the Rājasūya sacrifice);
*pākayajñikaḥ* (pertaining to the cooked-sacrifices) and *nāvayajñikaḥ* (pertaining to the boat-sacrifice) from *yajñebhyaḥ*.
The undertaking [of this rule] is for the sake of an infinite number of examples with the udātta accent.
Although the result would have been established by the word *kratubhyaḥ* alone, the inclusion of the word *yajña-* is so that the suffix may also apply after non-Soma sacrifices; for example:
*pāñcaudanikaḥ*.
*Dāśaudanikaḥ*. The plural number is used for the purpose of excluding the rule that [the suffix] applies to the word-form itself.
In the case of the seer's [name], it occurs only within the chapters. // PS_4.3.69 //

Words denoting seers (*ṛṣi*) are names of lineages; from those words denoting seers, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the two senses of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*) and "explanation thereof" (*vyākhyāna*), as an exception to *aṇ*, provided that the suffix refers specifically to chapters (*adhyāya*) which serve as qualifiers for the meaning of the suffix.
The term "of that which is to be explained" (*vyākhyātavya-nāmnaḥ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule];
by association with that, the word *ṛṣi* refers to a treatise (*grantha*). Thus, a chapter belonging to Vasiṣṭha, or one occurring therein, is called *vāsiṣṭhika*.
[Vaiśvāmitrikaḥ].
Why [is it specified] "in the chapters"? [Consider:
vāsiṣṭhī ṛk (a verse belonging to Vasiṣṭha).
The suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied after the word *puroḍāśa* when it means "made of sacrificial cake."
After the words *paurāḍāśa* and *puroḍāśa*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs in the senses of "originating from" (*bhava*) and "explaining" (*vyākhyāna*).
*Puroḍāśas* are balls of ground flour.
The mantra that prepares them is the *pauroḍāśa*; that which explains it, or that which pertains to it, is *pauroḍāśika* (masculine) or *pauroḍāśikī* (feminine).
The term *puroḍāśika* (or *puroḍāśikī*) refers to a text that accompanies the *puroḍāśa* [oblation], its commentary, or that which exists therein.
The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of [introducing] the suffix *ṅīṣ*. According to the Vedic usage (*chandasaḥ*), the suffixes *ya* and *aṇ* [are applied]. (PS 4.3.71)

From the word *chandas*, when the meanings of "origin" (*bhava*) and "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*) are intended, the suffixes *ya* and *aṇ* occur. This statement is made because [otherwise], by the rule for words consisting of two syllables, the suffix *ṭhak* would have applied.
chandasyaḥ means "one who belongs to the Veda" (chāndasaḥ).
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word ending in *dvyañ*, *ṛd*, *brāhmaṇa*, *ṛc*, *prathama*, *adhvara*, *puraścaraṇa*, or a name or a verb (*nāmākhyāta*).

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) consisting of two or more syllables that denote the name of something to be explained, in the senses of "originating from" (*bhava*) and "explaining" (*vyākhyāna*). This is an exception to [the application of] *aṇ* and other such suffixes.
First, from words consisting of two syllables: *aiṣṭikaḥ* (pertaining to the iṣṭi) and *pāśukaḥ* (pertaining to the animal sacrifice).
From a word ending in the vowel ṛ: *cāturhotṛkaḥ* (pertaining to the four hotṛ priests).
*pāñcahotṛkaḥ* / *brāhmaṇa-brāhmaṇikaḥ* / *ṛk-ārcikaḥ* /
*prathama*—*prāthamika*; *adhvara*—*ādhvarika*;
*puraścaraṇa*—*pauraścaraṇika*.
The mention of "noun" (nāman) and "verb" (ākhyāta) is for the purpose of including both compounds and their analyzed forms:
*nāmikaḥ* and *ākhyātikaḥ*.
It is that which is expressed by names.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words] beginning with *ṛgayana*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after nominal stems such as *ṛgayanā-* and others, in the senses of "originating from" (*bhava*) and "expounding" (*vyākhyāna*). This is an exception to [the application of] *ṭhañ* and other suffixes.
The term *ārgayana* [is formed with the suffix *aṇ*];
it is an explanation of the word *pāda*. The mention of the suffix *aṇ* is for the purpose of setting aside a potential sublater.
The science of architecture, the method of Vedic recitation,
and the explanation of words.
Metrics,
Prakrit languages,
and prosody.
Logic, rhetoric, and grammar.
Etymology, architecture,
and the science of bodily marks.
The science of the Kṣatriyas; portents;
arising.
Year / Moment / Sign.
The Upaniṣads, the Śikṣā, the Ṛg-veda and so forth.
Thence he has come. (Pāṇini 4.3.74)
After a word ending in the fifth case, in the sense of "come from," an affix is applied as prescribed; for example:
*srughnāt āgataḥ* (come from Srughna) = *sraughanaḥ*.
"Māthuraḥ" (a person from Mathurā),
"rāṣṭriyaḥ" (a person from a kingdom).
Here, that which is intended as the primary *apādāna* (ablative point of departure)— namely, "from there"— is what is understood in this context.
It is not necessarily concomitant;
for example, one might say, "I am coming from Srughna," or "I have come from the foot of a tree."
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words meaning "places of income" (*āyasthāna*).
The term *āya* refers to the portion to be taken by the owner; that in which it arises is the source of income (*āyasthāna*).
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) that denote a source (*āyasthāna*) in the sense of "come from that";
it is an exception to *aṇ*,
but it is superseded by *cha* due to its later occurrence in the sequence of rules.
One who has come from a customs house is a *śaulkaśālika*.
[The term] *ākarika* [is also used]. The plural number is for the purpose of excluding [the restriction to] the specific form [of the singular]. [416]
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *śuṇḍika*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after nominal stems such as *śuṇḍika* and others in the sense of "come from that";
this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhak* prescribed for places of business (*āyasthāna*).
One who has come from a *śuṇḍika* (liquor-seller) is a *śauṇḍika*.
[Similarly,] a *kārkaṇa*.
The inclusion of the suffix *aṇ* is for the purpose of overriding what would otherwise be an exception.
A well, a tavern-keeper, and a crane.
A sacrificial mound, a well, and a stone.
ford / ground / grass
The group beginning with *parṇa* and *śuṇḍikā*.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied [to form patronymics] after words denoting branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) and sources of birth (*yoni*).
Those whose relationship is based on learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*) are called *vidyā-yoni-sambandha*.
From words expressing such [relationships], the suffix *vuñ* is applied in the sense of "come from that" (*tata āgataḥ*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*; however, the suffix *cha* supersedes it due to its higher status. First, regarding its connection with *vidyā*: that which has come from a teacher (*upādhyāya*) is *aupādhyāyaka*.

The suffix *ka* is applied after words denoting a teacher (*ācārya*) and after words denoting maternal relations (*yoni-sambandha*), such as *mātāmaha*. Thus: *śauṣyaka*, *ācāryaka*, and *mātāmahaka*.
The son of a paternal grandfather;
the son of a maternal uncle.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a word ending in *ṛta*.
The rule "from [words denoting] relations of learning or of birth" (vidyā-yoni-sambandhebhyaḥ) applies here as well.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is added to nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in the vowel *ṛ* that denote relations of learning or of birth, in the sense of "come from that."
*vuñ* is the suffix for denoting derivation (*apavāda*).
First, regarding those expressing a connection with knowledge (*vidyā-sambandha*): that which has come from a *hotṛ* priest is *hautṛka*;
[that which has come from a *potaṛ* priest is] *pautṛka*.
From words expressing blood relationship: *bhrātṛkaṃ*,
*svasṛkaṃ*,
*mātṛkaṃ*.
The addition of the long *ā* (taparakaraṇa) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.
Except in the case of [the suffixes] *vidya* and *yoni*, it is *sāvitra*.
And that which belongs to the father. (PS 4.3.79)
The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *pitṛ*, and by virtue of the particle *ca*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is also applied, in the sense of "come from that" (*tad-āgata*).
That which has come from the father is *pitrya*, [also] *paitṛka*.
From the lineage, like a mark. (PS 4.3.80)

Apart from the context concerning offspring (*apatya*), the term "lineage" (*gotra*) in common usage is understood here as mere offspring. From a nominal stem ending in a lineage-suffix, a secondary suffix is prescribed in the sense of "come from that," just as in the case of the suffix *aṅka*.
By the mention of the "marker" (aṅka), this general meaning of that [suffix] is indicated;
therefore, the suffix vuñ is extended by analogy,
not aṇ.

According to the rule *saṅgha-aṅka-lakṣaṇeṣv añ-yañ-iñām aṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.127), [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after [words ending in] *añ*, *yañ*, or *iñ* when followed by *aṅka*. Thus, the mark of the Aupagavas is *aupagavakaḥ*;
[the mark of the Kāpaṭavas is] *kāpaṭavakaḥ*.
*Nāḍāyanakaḥ*,
*cārāyaṇakaḥ*;
likewise, that which has come from the Aupagavas is *aupagavakam*.
The Kāpaṭavaka, the Nāḍāyanaka, and the Cārāyaṇaka.
The suffix -rūpya is optionally applied after the words *hetu* and *manuṣya*.
The suffix *rupya* optionally occurs after words denoting causes (*hetu*) and after the word *manuṣya*, in the sense of "come from that," provided that [the cause] is not a human being.
The mention of *manuṣya* is for the purpose of excluding [the application of this rule when the cause] is a human being.
The cause is the reason (*kāraṇa*). From the causes, first: that which has come together is *samarūpya*, *samīya*; that which is of uneven form is *viṣamarūpya*, *viṣamīya*.
After the word *gahāditya*, the suffix *cha* is applied.
From *manuṣya*: *devadattarūpya*, *yajñadattarūpya*, *daivadatta*.
"Yājñadatta";
the plural number is for the purpose of excluding a rule regarding the specific form [of the name].
And the suffix mayaṭ [is also used in this sense]. (Pāṇini 5.4.21)
The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied after words meaning "cause" (*hetu*) and after the word "man" (*manuṣya*), in the sense of "come from that," as in the example *samamayaṃ*.
This is full of poison;
from among humans— this is full of Devadatta,
this is full of Yajñadatta.
The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of [introducing] the suffix *ṅīp*.
[The example is] *samamayī*.
The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of avoiding [the application of] the respective order (*yathāsaṅkhya*).
It prevails. // PS_4.3.83 //
From that very [word],

namely, after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī* or *āp* which is in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), the suffix prescribed [by the rules] occurs in the sense of "originates from" (*prabhavati*).
It means that it originates, shines forth,
or is perceived for the first time; for example,
the Gaṅgā originating from the Himavat is called "Gaimavatī."
The Sindhu is the giver of wealth.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after [a word ending in] *vidūra*.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after the word *vidūra* in the sense of "originating from that";
this is an exception to [the application of] *aṇ*.
The vaidūrya gem originates from Vidūra;
yet, it actually originates from Bālavāya,
not from Vidūra.
But is it refined there?
If that is so, then: "Either *vālavāya* or *vidūra*, or indeed something else of similar nature;
if one should say, 'It is certainly not there,' one should apply [the treatment] as in the case of *jitvarī*."
That [suffix] occurs after the words *pathin* and *dūta* when they are in the locative case. // PS_4.3.85 //

After a word in the second case in construction, the suffix prescribed by the rules is applied in the sense of "he goes," provided that the path he goes upon is either a *dūta* (messenger) or [a specific type of road].
The path or the messenger belonging to Srughna goes to Srughna; [likewise] one belonging to Mathurā. When those residing there are going, it is said that "the path goes."
Alternatively, "attaining Srughna" means traveling on the road.
Why say "of the road and the messenger"? [Consider: "The caravan goes to Srughna. [418]
He goes forth through the gate.

*tad*—thus indeed. From the word *tad*, when it is in the second case (dvitīyā-vibhakti) and in agreement with another, the suffix prescribed [by the rules] occurs in the sense of "he goes out through," provided that which he goes out through is a door (*dvāra*).
He goes forth, he goes out;
he goes forth toward Srughna, toward the gate of Kānyakubja, toward Sraughna, toward Mathurā.
The gate (dvāra) is well known as the instrument (karaṇa) in the act of going forth;
here, however, it is intended to be expressed as being independent.
For example: "The sword cuts.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "the door"? [Answer:
"A man goes out toward Srughna."
[The suffix -aṇ] is applied to a word denoting the subject matter when it forms the title of a work composed concerning that subject.
[The word] *tat* is used precisely for this purpose;
the accusative case is employed with reference to that which is being governed."

"Adhikṛtya" means having introduced or having set forth; "āgūrya" is its meaning. From a word in the second case (accusative) in construction with "tad," when the sense is "made with reference to that," an affix occurs as prescribed, provided that what is made is a literary work (grantha).
Having studied under Subhadra, the work composed is the Saubhadra;
likewise the Gairimitra and the Yāyāta.

Why does the word "in a work" (granthe) [occur in the rule]? [Consider: "A palace built with reference to Subhadrā. There is frequent elision (lub) of the suffix when it signifies a narrative (ākhyāyikā).
The narrative composed concerning Vāsavadattā is called *Vāsavadattā*; likewise *Sumanottarā* and *Urvaśī*.
And Bhīmarathī does not exist.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the compounds *śiśukranda*, *yamasabha*, *dvandva*, *indrajana*, and so forth.

The suffix *cha* is applied after words such as *śiśukranda*, when they are in the second case and signify "with reference to," provided that the word refers to a work composed with reference to that subject. This applies specifically to the rule beginning with *tad ity eva* and the rule *adhikṛtya kṛte granthe*.
This is an exception to the [previous] rule.

[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the words *bhikṣu* and *naṭasūtra* alone; thus, from *kārmaṇḍa* [comes] *kārmaṇḍam*, and from *kārśāśva* [comes] *kārśāśvam*. [425]
By that, [the suffix] ekadiK [is applied]. (Pāṇini 5.3.112)

The suffix prescribed [by the rules] occurs after a word in the third case (instrumental) in construction with *tena*, in the sense of "being in the same direction" (*ekadik*). "In the same direction" (*ekadik*) means having an identical direction (*tulyadik*) or a common direction (*samānadik*).
Saudāmanī is lightning that comes from the same direction as Mount Sudāmā;

the repeated mention of the "case-ending expressing semantic competency" (*samarthavibhakti*) in this context, despite the topic being already established by "by that" (*tena*), is for the purpose of terminating the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "Vedic" (*chandas*).
For in the preceding rule, because of the governing heading of "Vedic," its scope was established as being restricted to that domain.
And [the suffix] *tasi* [is used in the same sense]. (Pāṇini 5.4.47)

The suffix *tasi* also occurs when the sense is "in the same direction as that. Since the suffixes *gha* and others, as well as *aṇ* and others, would have applied by the preceding rule, this other suffix is now prescribed.

In this context of "in the same direction," this [suffix] is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*. From *uras* (chest), we have *urasyaḥ* (belonging to the chest) and *urastaḥ* (from the chest).

By that very [rule],
namely *tena*, when [the word] *upajñāta* (invented) follows a word in the third case-relationship (*tṛtīyā-samartha*), the suffix occurs as prescribed.
That which is known without instruction is *aupajñātam*, meaning that which has been understood by oneself;
for example, the grammar without temporal distinctions (*akālaka*) known by Pāṇini is called *pāṇinīyam*.
The system of Kāśakṛtsna concerns the relative weight of grammatical rules;
that of Āpiśali concerns difficult formations.
[The suffix -ṭhak is applied] after a word denoting a work when it signifies "composed by. // PS_4.3.116 //
By the word "tena" (by that) alone;
when the sense is "made by that," a suffix occurs as prescribed after a word standing in the third case.
If it is a work composed by him, then it is so called;

*bhaikurāṭaḥ* is a book; *jālūkaḥ* [is another example]. Why does the rule specify "in a book"? [To exclude cases such as: *bhaikurāṭaḥ* [as a person's name].
A palace is "made by a carpenter" (*takṣakṛta*);
that which is produced is "done" (*kṛta*), while that which is already existing and merely known is "invented" (*aupajñāta*)— this is the distinction between these two.
In the case of *sañjñā*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied]. (PS 4.3.117)
After a word in the third case in construction, a suffix is applied as prescribed when the meaning is "made by," provided that a name is understood from the whole compound; for example,
*makṣikābhiḥ kṛtam* (made by bees) becomes *mākṣikam*.
Bowstring resin from the *kārmuka* tree;
honey from the *sāragha* bee; honey from the *pauttika* bee.
These are the designations for honey.
[426] The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words such as *kulāla* and others. (Pāṇini 4.3.118)

The words "tena" (by that), "kṛte" (made), and "sañjñāyām" (when a name is understood) all continue to apply here. The suffix *vuñ* occurs after words such as *kulāla* and others in the sense of "made by that," provided that a name is understood.
The craft of the potter;
the craft of the snake-charmer; the potter.
Varuḍa / Caṇḍāla / Niṣāda.
Blacksmith, army, head of the hair.
With the senses,
O King of Gods, and the assembly.
Vadhū, Ruru, Dhruva.
O Rudra, O bull, O Brahman!
A potter,
a dog-cooker, a potter, and so forth.
From the small bee, the wasp, and the banyan tree. (PS 4.3.119)

The entire rule "tena kṛte sañjñāyām" (Pāṇini 5.1.101) continues to apply here. The suffix *añ* occurs after the words *kṣudra* and others in the sense of "made by that," provided that a technical name (*sañjñā*) is understood to be conveyed.
This is an exception to the rule [regarding the suffix *aṇ*];
there is a distinction in accent.
That which is made by those beginning with *kṣudra* is called *kṣaudra*.
Relating to bees, relating to the enclosure, and relating to trees.
This [suffix] occurs after that [word]. (Pāṇini 4.3.120)
The word *tasya* (of that), being in the genitive case, [governs] this context: when the sense is "this belongs to that," an affix occurs as prescribed.
The five [affixes] beginning with *aṇ* are the great general rules (*mahotsarga*).
And suffixes such as *gha* and others are prescribed according to the rules.
Of the base (*prakṛti*) and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), only the sense of the genitive case and merely their mutual relationship are intended to be expressed;
whatever else there may be—such as gender, number, perceptibility, or imperceptibility—all that is not intended to be expressed.
This belongs to Upagu: *aupagava*; [this belongs to Kapaṭu:
*kāpaṭava*;
this belongs to Rāṣṭrin: *rāṣṭriya*.]
The suffix *īna* is applied to form *avārapārīṇa*.
It does not occur after words such as *anantara*, because it is not prescribed there; for example, one says *devadattasya anantaram* (the immediate succession of Devadatta).
And after the root *vah* preceded by *sam*, there is also the suffix *tṛn*.
The property (*sva*) of one who carries [it] together is *sāṃvāhitram*.
Here, the suffix *aṇ* is already established.
An addition [to the rule] for the sake of the sense of "place":
after *āgnīdha*, when meaning "a shelter," there is the suffix *raṇ* and the replacement of the final vowel with *bhaṃ*.
Thus: *āgnīdhram*.
The suffix *ṣeṇyaṇ* is applied after the word *samidh* in the sense of "that by which fuel is placed.
Thus, *sāmidhenyaḥ* refers to the mantras,
and *sāmidhenī* refers to the *ṛc* verses.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *ratha* and others.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *ratha* in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*),
as an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
The term *rathya* refers to a part of the chariot— whether it be the wheel or the yoke—
it is intended to mean a component of the chariot itself.
It is not otherwise than because of the non-statement [of the rule];
for in the rule "after *ratha*, *sītā*, and *hal*, when *ya* is prescribed," the extension of the rule to include that which ends with these words (*tadantavidhi*) is supplied.
Thus: *paramarathyam*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the words *uttamaratha* and those preceded by *patra*. PS_4.3.122.
That by which things fall is called a *patra*, meaning a vehicle such as a horse and so forth.
From the word *ratha* preceded by that [word], the suffix *añ* occurs in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*).
Since this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule:
*āśvarathaṃ cakraṃ* (the wheel of a horse-chariot), *auṣṭrarathaṃ* (of a camel-chariot).
A donkey-chariot.
And [the same applies] to the assembly of the Adhvaryu priests. (PS 4.3.123)

The suffix *añ* is applied after a nominal stem denoting a vehicle (*patra-vāhana*), as well as after the words *adhvaryu* and *pariṣad*, in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*). This occurs in the domain of the [general] topic of possession.
This is an exception to the [rule on] *aṇ*.
It is applied when [the object] is external to the leaf (*patra*). That which is to be carried by a horse is *āśva*.
Pertaining to camels; pertaining to donkeys; pertaining to the Adhvaryu priest.
The assembly.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the compound *hala-sīra*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *hala* and *sīra* in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*),
as an exception to [the application of] *aṇ*.
This belongs to a plowman: *hālikam* / *sairikam*.
The suffix *vun* is added after a copulative compound (*dvandva*) to denote enmity or sexual union.

The suffix *vun* is applied after a term having the designation *dvandva*, in the sense of "belonging to this," provided that enmity (*vaira*) and sexual union (*maithunika*) qualify the meaning of the suffix.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *aṇ*; however, because it occurs later in the sequence, it supersedes that rule. For example, in the case of *vaira*, we have *bābhravya-śālaṅkāyanikā*.
The *kākolūkikā* [is used] in the sense of sexual union— as in *atribharadvājikā* and *kutsakuśikikā*.
*Vivahana* means sexual union.
Although *vaira* (enmity) is neuter, these [words] are feminine by nature.
A prohibition must be stated regarding enmity arising from gods, asuras, and so forth.
The enmity between the gods and the asuras; the enmity between the rākṣasas and the asuras.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after [a word denoting] a *gotra* (lineage) when it signifies the practice [of that lineage]. (Pāṇini 4.3.126)

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) denoting lineages (*gotra*) and those denoting Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), in the sense of "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*); this is an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
However, because it is taught later in the sequence, it supersedes the suffix *cha*.
First, from the [name of a] lineage: *glaucukāyanaka*, *aupagavaka*.
From the name of a school (*caraṇa*), it is accepted in the sense of the Dharma and the traditional teaching (*dharmāmnāya*).
The Kāṭhaka, the Kālāpaka, and the Maudaka.
The *Paippalādaka* [is derived from Paippalāda].
According to Pāṇini 4.3.127: "In place of the suffixes *añ*, *yañ*, and *iñ* when they follow a word denoting a member of the Saṅgha or a mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the suffix *aṇ* is substituted."

[The suffix -matup is applied] after words ending in the suffix yaÑ, when they denote a specific quality that serves as the cause for [the designation of] the Saṅgha and so forth, provided that [the quality] is not already expressed by another word.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a nominal stem ending in *iñ* in the sense of "belonging to this," as an exception to the previous rule for *vuñ*. The mention of *ghoṣa* should be included here.
Because of this inequality, there is no correspondence according to the respective order. The *baida* is the Saṅgha; the *baida* is the *aṅka*.

A mark of the Gārgyas; a characteristic of the Gārgyas;
a hamlet of the Gārgyas.

the Dākṣa limb,

The sound [of the word] *dākṣa* [is an example].
What is the difference between a *lakṣaṇa* (mark) and a *liṅga* (sign)?
A *lakṣaṇa* is that which serves as a mark belonging specifically to that which is marked (*lakṣya*), such as knowledge is the *lakṣaṇa* of the learned (*vidvāṃsaḥ*).
However, even though "aṅka" (mark/sign) resides on a cow or other such things, it does not constitute the property (*sva*) of the cow or those things.
The addition of the marker *ṇ* is for the purpose of applying the suffix *ṅīp* and for the purpose of prohibiting the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).
[Thus,] *vaidī* means "knowledge," and one who possesses that knowledge is called *vaidīvidyaḥ*.
Or from Śākala. (PS 4.3.128)

From the word *śākala*, when the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*) is to be expressed, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of a community (*saṅgha*) and so forth, which serve as qualifiers for the meaning of the suffix;
this is an exception to *vuñ*.
Those who study what was proclaimed by Śākala are the Śākalas;
their assembly is the Śākala or Śākalaka.
The mark is Śākala.
The mark is from Śākala; the characteristic is Śākala,
the characteristic is Śākalaka.
The hamlet of Śākala; the hamlet belonging to Śākala.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after the words *chandoga*, *aukthika*, *yājñika*, *bahvṛca*, and *naṭa*.
The [rules concerning] the *saṅgha* and so forth have been concluded; now follows the general injunction.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after words such as *chandoga* and others in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*),
as an exception to the suffixes *vuñ* and *aṇ*.
[This applies] when referring to the religious duties (*dharma*) or the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*) of a Vedic school (*caraṇa*).
By association with that [suffix], it occurs after the word *naṭa* only in the sense of "dharma" or "scripture" (*āmnāya*). For the Chāndogas, the dharma or the scripture is *chāndogya*;
likewise, *aukthikya*.
The sacrificial science, the Rigvedic science, and the dramatic art.
"Except for a family of Chāndogas," and so forth.
Nor [should one use the vocative] with respect to staff-bearers, novices, or pupils. (PS 4.3.130)
"Daṇḍamāṇavāḥ" refers to those Māṇavas for whom punishment is primary;
they are resident pupils or disciples.
The suffix *vuñ* does not occur after those [words] as denotable objects (*abhidheya*). The mention of *gotra* is understood to carry over here; therefore, the prohibition of *vuñ* is understood.
The Gaukakṣas, the Daṇḍamāṇavas, the Antevāsins,
the Dākṣas,
and the Māhakas.
The suffix *cha* is applied after [the names] beginning with Raivatika.
The suffix *cha* occurs after words beginning with *daivatika* in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*). These [words] end in a *gotra* suffix.
Therefore, since the suffix *vuñ* would have applied by the preceding rule, this statement is made for the purpose of prescribing *cha*:
*raivatikīyaḥ*,
*svapiśīyaḥ*.
Raivatika,
Svāpiśi, Kṣaimavṛddhi.
O Gauragrīvi!
O Audameyi! O Audavāhi!

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *kaupiñjala* and *hāstipada* in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*),
as an exception to the *vuñ* suffix used for *gotra*.
Because of the context of the *gotra*:
Kaupīñjala and Hāstipada.
In the case of the word *ātharvaṇika*, there is also the elision of the suffix *ika*.
"Aṇ" alone [is understood].
The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *ātharvaṇika*.
And by virtue of its proximity, there is the elision of the suffix *ika* in this context of "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*);
it is an exception to the suffixes *caraṇa* and *vuñ*.

This is the *dharma* or the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) of the *Atharvaṇika*; it is called *Ātharvaṇa* because of its connection to the *caraṇa* (school), according to the rule that the suffix *aṇ* is applied to denote both *dharma* and *āmnāya*.
The suffix *cha* is applied to denote a modification thereof.
After the word *tasya* (of it), which is in the genitive case and is semantically connected, a suffix is applied as prescribed in this context to denote a *vikāra* (modification).
A *vikāra* is a different state of the original material (*prakṛti*).
What is the illustrative example here?
It is a word beginning with a non-living being that is udātta-accented on its first syllable and not containing a vṛddhi vowel,
for which there is no other specific rule of application.
A derivative of *aśman* is *āśmanaḥ* or *āśmaḥ*. Regarding the sense "a modification of stone," the elision of the suffix *ṭi* is optional.
*bhāsmanaḥ* and *mārttikaḥ*:
these are udātta on the first syllable by virtue of the *nitsvara* rule.

In this context, the repetition of the word "tasya" (of it) is for the purpose of excluding the *śaiṣika* suffixes; thus, suffixes such as *dhak* and others do not apply to denote either a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*). For example: *hālaḥ*.
Saira.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after words denoting parts of living beings, medicinal herbs, and trees.

A suffix, as prescribed, occurs after words denoting living beings, medicinal herbs, and trees when they are in the genitive case and possess a word in syntactic agreement with them, provided it signifies a part;
and by virtue of the word "ca" (and), it also occurs when signifying a modification (*vikāra*).
In that context, he will state the suffix *añ* after words denoting living beings:
*kāpotaḥ* means a modification or a part of a pigeon;
likewise, *māyūraḥ*.
From the *taittira* comes the plant;
from the plants comes the *maurva* stalk;
from the *maurva* stalk comes the ash.
From trees— *kārīraṃ kāṇḍam* (a stalk of millet),
*kārīraṃ bhasma* (ash of millet). From this point onward, the suffixes apply to living beings, herbs, and trees in the senses of "modification" (*vikāra*) and "part" (*avayava*).
But in other cases, it applies merely to a derivative form (*vikāra*).
How, then, is both [the rule] "its derivative" (*tasya vikāraḥ*) and the rule "from animals, herbs, and trees regarding their parts" (*avayave ca prāṇy-oṣadhi-vṛkṣebhyaḥ*) simultaneously applied?
The simultaneous mention of "modification" (vikāra) and "part" (avayava) is for the purpose of an exception (apavāda) to the rule;
for those two have already been defined.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words beginning with] *bilva* and others.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words such as *bilva* and others in the sense of a derivative product (*vikāra*) or a constituent part (*avayava*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the application of *añ* and *mayaṭ* as appropriate.
*Bailva* means a modification or a part of the *bilva* tree.

The word *gavedhukā* is recited here; since it would already be established by the rule for words ending in a *ka*-suffix (*kopadha*), its inclusion is for the purpose of precluding the suffix *mayaṭ*.
bilva,
vrīhi,
kāṇḍa.
mung beans / lentils / wheat /
sugarcane, bamboo, and wild millet;
Karpāsī,
pāṭalī, karkandhū.
The suffix *ka* is applied after words beginning with *kuṭīra* and *bilva*, etc., when they are used as upapadas. [PS 4.3.137]

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that has *ka* as its penultimate letter, according to the appropriate application, in the senses of a modification (*vikāra*) or a constituent part (*avayava*). This is an exception to [the rule for] *añ*.
*tarku*—*tārkava*;

*māṇḍūka*.
Dārdurūka;
mādhūka.

by virtue of that [suffix], the augment *ṣuk* is added to those two.
An exception to the rule for gold:
a derivative of tin is *trāpuṣa*;
[a derivative] of lac is *jātuṣa*.
Because it does not begin with a living being, the suffix [ṭhak] is not applied to a part.
Or [the suffix] añ. (Pāṇini 4.3.139)

The suffix *añ* is applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the vowel *u*, in the senses of "modification" (*vikāra*) and "part" (*avayava*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ*.
The following are examples other than those beginning with anudātta:
*daivadāram* and *bhādradāravam*.
And [the suffix] after a root that begins with an anudātta vowel [is ṅit].

The suffix *añ* is applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that begins with an anudātta vowel, in the senses of a modification (*vikāra*) or a constituent part (*avayava*). This is an exception to [the application of] the suffix *aṇ*.
Dādhitya,
Kāpitya, Māhitya.
Or [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *palāśa* and other such words. *PS_4.3.141*
The suffix *añ* optionally occurs after nominal stems such as *palāśa-* and others in the senses of a derivative product (*vikāra*) or a constituent part (*avayava*). [Example:
*pālāśam*.
