This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases.
In the case of *palāśa*, *khadira*, *śiṃśipā*, and *spandana*, [the rule] applies because they do not begin with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*); whereas for others, it does not apply.
*Palāśa*. *Khadira*.
Śiṃśapā,
spandana,
karīra.
Śirīṣa, yavāsa, vikaṅkata.
The *palāśa* and other [trees].
The suffix *ṭlañ* is applied after the word *śamyā*.
The suffix *ṭlañ* is applied after the word *śamī* in the senses of a product (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*); it is an exception to [the application of] *añ*.
The word *śāmīla* means ash;
*śāmīlī* means a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*).
[431] The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied after these two words in common speech (*bhāṣā*), except when referring to food or clothing. (Pāṇini 4.3.143)

The suffix *mayaṭ* optionally occurs after a mere base (*prakṛti*) in the sense of a product (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*), excluding food and clothing, within the scope of the common language (*bhāṣā*). Since various other suffixes would otherwise apply according to the specific case,
[the rule provides for] *aśmamayam* and *āśmanam*.
[The suffix -maya- forms] *mūrvāmayam* or *maurvam*.
Why [is it specified] "in common usage" (*bhāṣāyām*)?
[Because otherwise] the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) might be made of *bilva* or *khadira* wood.
Why [is it specified] "of non-edible food and clothing"? [Consider:
*maudgaḥ sūpaḥ* (bean soup);
*kārpāsam ācchādanam* (a cotton garment).
By the phrase "of these two," what is meant? Since the modification and the component are indeed included within the base (*prakṛti*),
[the rule] should apply even in the domain of those specific suffixes such as *añ* prescribed by the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.154), and so forth.
It may be made of clay,
earthenware, metal, or iron.
The suffix *nitya* is applied after the words *vṛddha*, *śara*, and so forth.
In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), [the suffix *mayaṭ* is used] only when referring to things that are not edible or not clothing.

From *vṛddha* nominal stems and from [stems beginning with] *śara*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is invariably applied in the domain of the spoken language to denote a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*), provided they are neither edible nor clothing.
From the elders, first: made of mango wood; made of *śāla* wood;
made of *śāka* wood.
From *śara* and so forth: *śaramayam*, *darbhamayam*, *mṛnmayam*.
What is the purpose of including the word "nitya" (always), since it will necessarily be permanent by the very force of its initial formulation?
They desire that *mayaṭ* be always applied after a single vowel;
that is what is accomplished by this [rule].
That which consists of skin,
that which consists of strings, and that which consists of speech.
Reeds, *darbha* grass, and earth.
Kuṭī, Tṛṇa, Soma.
Balvaja grass,
reeds, and so forth.
And [the suffix -matup is applied] after the word *go* when it means "cow dung."

[thus] *gomayaṃ*.
Why [is it specified] "in the case of *purīṣa*"? [Consider:
*gavyam payaḥ* ("cow's milk").
Here, *purīṣa* is neither a derivative (*vikāra*) nor a constituent part (*avayava*).
This is the rule regarding its object;
however, he will state the suffix *yat* for *go* and *payas* when they denote a modification or a part.
And also from flour. (PS 4.3.146)
The suffix *mayaṭ* is invariably applied after the word *piṣṭa* in the sense of "a modification thereof" (*tasya vikāraḥ*).

The suffix *ya* is applied after the word *sodara*, when it is in the seventh case (locative), in the sense of "lying upon"; this is optional according to Pāṇini 6.3.88.

Having anticipated the elision (*luk*) of the *matup* suffix in the case of "mind" (*citta*), [the rule applies]: "The suffix *mat* is used in the sense of 'thinking' and 'deserving', as well as for 'a month' and 'body'. (Pāṇini 5.2.94) [PS 4.4.128]

In the Vedic domain, when the suffix *matup* is prescribed for a particular meaning, the suffix *yat* occurs in place of it within that same Vedic context, provided that "month" (*māsa*) and "body" (*tanu*) serve as qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix.

The suffix *yat* occurs after a word in the first case that is semantically connected to the sense of "existence" (*asti*) and functions as an attribute, in the sense of the sixth case (genitive) and the seventh case (locative).
This is an exception to the suffixes used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
For example: *abhasyo māsaḥ*, meaning "a month in which clouds exist."
Sahasya; Tapasya; Madhavya.
The word *nabhas* occurs in the sense of "clouds.
Furthermore, it is used in the sense of "body" (*tanu*): for example, *ojasyā tanūḥ* ("a body possessing vigor") and *rakṣasyā tanūḥ* ("a demonic body").

And [the suffix] *ñya* is applied after the word *madhu*.

"Yaśobhagyaḥ" means one who possesses glory and fortune.

One who possesses that is called *veśobhagya*.

The suffix *kha* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *bhaga*, such as *veśoyaśas* and others, in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). By virtue of the word "ca" (and), [the suffix] *yat* is also applied:

The augment *iṭ* is applied after the roots *ina* and *yā* when preceded by preverbs.

From the word *pūrva*, when it is in the third case (instrumental) and has the sense of "done by," the suffixes *ina* and *ya* are applied;

Those two are equal to a thousand.

The case ending is applied according to what is appropriate;

After a word in the first case in construction (*prathamāsamartha*), the suffix prescribed [by the rules] occurs in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe*), provided that the word in the first case in construction denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*). For example:

and by virtue of the word *ca* [in the sūtra], the suffix *yat* is also applied.

*kaḍaṅkaryaḥ*.
A monk who is worthy of a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) is *dakṣiṇīya*; a Brahmin is *dakṣiṇya*.

By not placing the word *dakṣiṇa* first—despite it having fewer syllables—which serves as a sign of a deviation from the general rule, it indicates the absence of a sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*). [483] From *sthālībilāt* (PS 5.1.70).
The two suffixes *cha* and *yaṭ* are understood [to follow]. From the words *sthālī* and *bila*, the suffixes *cha* and *yaṭ* occur in the sense of "he deserves that" (*tad arhati*),
serving as exceptions to the suffix *ṭhak*.
The rice grains that are fit for the pot are called *sthālībila* or *sthālībilya*;
the meaning is "suitable for cooking in a pot."
The suffixes *gha* and *khañ* are applied after the words *yajña* and *ṛtvij* respectively.
From the word *yajña* and from the word *ṛtvij*, the suffixes *gha* and *khañ* respectively are applied in the sense of "he deserves that" (*tad arhati*),
as exceptions to the suffix *ṭhak*.
"A Brāhmaṇa who is fit for sacrifice" (*yajñiyaḥ brāhmaṇaḥ*); "a Brāhmaṇa who is fit for officiating at a sacrifice" (*ārtvijīnaḥ brāhmaṇaḥ*).
There is a supplementary rule stating that the suffix *cha* (forming *-ya* and *-īna*) is applied after the words *yajña* and *ṛtvij* when one is entitled to perform those respective acts.
A sacrificial site (yajñiya-deśa) is that which deserves a sacrificial rite;
a Brahmin family (ārtvijīna-brāhmaṇakula) is that which deserves the work of officiating priests (ṛtvik-karma).
This marks the full extent of the suffixes beginning with *ṭhak* for words ending in *arha*.
From this point onward, only the suffix *ṭhañ* applies as before.
He performs the Pārāyaṇa, Turāyaṇa, and Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
The term "samarthavibhakti" (the case-ending of semantic competency) continues [to apply];
the term "arhati" (deserves/is worthy of) has ceased [to apply].
The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after words such as *pārāyaṇa* when they are in the second case and denote the sense of "causing to perform" (*vartayati*). For example:
*pārāyaṇaṃ vartayati adhīte* ("he performs the complete recitation; he studies it thoroughly") results in *pārāyaṇikaś chātraḥ* ("a student who performs the complete recitation");
*taurāyaṇiko yajamānaḥ* ("a sacrificer who performs the Taurāyaṇa sacrifice").
The ascetic who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having fallen into doubt. // PS_5,1.73 //

From the word *saṃśaya* (doubt), when it is in syntactic agreement with an accusative case, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of "having fallen into" (*āpanna*). One who has fallen into, or reached, doubt is *sāṃśayikaḥ*— a pillar [mistakenly perceived as a man].
He travels a yojana. // PS_5.1.74 //
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after the word *yojana*, when it is in the second case and denotes the sense of "going"; for example,
one who goes a *yojana* is called *yaujanika*.
The addition of "hundred *krośas* and hundred *yojanas*" [is required]. One who goes a hundred *krośas* is called *krauśaśatika*; one who goes a hundred *yojanas* is called *yaujanaśatika*.
Furthermore, there is the addition of the rule: "He deserves to be visited. This applies to distances of a hundred *krośas* and a hundred *yojanas*.
A monk who is a hundred *krośas* away deserves to be visited;
likewise, a teacher who is a hundred *yojanas* away.
The suffix *ṣkan* is applied after the word *pathin*.
After the word *pathin*, when it is in the second case (accusative) construction, the suffix *ṣkan* occurs in the sense of "one who goes";
the letter *n* is for the sake of the accent.
The letter *ṣ* is for the sake of the suffix *ṅīṣ*. One who goes on a path (*panthānam*) is a traveler (*pathikaḥ*);
[the feminine form is] *pathikī*.
The word *pantha* does not necessarily [retain its original accent]. 5.1.76.
The inclusion of the term *nitya* (always) serves to qualify the meaning of the suffix:
in this context, the substitution of *pantha* for *patha* occurs, and the suffix *ṇa* is applied always when the sense is "one who goes."
"The traveler always goes on the road; he always begs for alms.
Why say "always"? [Consider: "the wayfarer" (*pathikaḥ*).
And that which has been brought from the northern region. PS_5.1.77.
The case ending expressing the required syntactic relation is established by the very statement [of the rule].
From the word *uttarapatha*, when it is in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) expressing the sense of "brought from" (*āhṛta*), the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in this context.
The particle *ca* serves to conjoin the meaning of the suffix with "gacchati" (he goes);
here too, the third case alone is the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*).
*Auttarapathika* means "brought by way of the northern road" (*uttarapathena-āhṛtam*).
One who goes by way of the northern road is *auttarapathikaḥ*.
Regarding the section on "brought," there is an extension [of the rule] for compounds preceded by *vāri*, *jaṅgala*, *sthalaka*, and *kāntāra*.
That which is brought by way of water is *vāripathika*; one who goes by way of water is *vāripathika*. That which is brought by way of a desert path is *jāṅgalapathika*.
One who travels by a forest path is a *jāṅgalapathika*;
that which is brought by a land route is *sthālapathika*;
one who travels by a land route is a *sthālapathika*.
That which is brought by way of a forest path is "forest-path-brought" (*kāntārapathika*);
one who goes by way of a forest path is a "forest-path-goer" (*kāntārapathika*).
There is also an extension [of this rule] for the compounds *ajapatha* and *śaṅkupatha*.
That which is brought by way of a path of goats is *ājapathika*; or, that which goes by way of a path of goats is *ājapathika*.
That which is brought by way of a path of stakes is *śāṅkupathika*.

Or, one who travels by way of a path with stakes is a *śāṅkupathika*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *madhuka* and *marica* when preceded by *sthalapatha*; thus, honey brought by way of land is called *sthālapatha* honey.
From time. // PS_5.1.78 //
"From time" (kālāt) is the governing heading (adhikāra). Whatever we shall set forth hereafter, that should be understood as being governed by the term "from time."
He will say: "By that, it is excluded" (PS 5.1.79).
That which is completed in a month is *māsika*;
that which is completed in half a month is *ārdhamāsika*.
"Annual" (sāṃvatsarika). The governing rule is "from time [expressions]" (kālāt), extending as far as "the suffix -aṇ after vyuṣṭa and others" (*Pāṇini 5.1.97).
By this, [the sense of] "accomplished by that" (*tena nirvṛttam*) is understood (*Pāṇini 5.1.79*).

The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting time that ends in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), in the sense of "completed by that. For example: *ahnā nivṛttam* (completed in a day) becomes *āhnikam*;
*ārdhamāsikam* (completed in half a month).
The annual [offering].
He is one who has been requested, one who has been supported, one who has existed, and one who will exist.

After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting time that is in the second case (*dvitīyā-samartha*), the suffixes prescribed [by the rules] occur in the sense of "commissioned" (*adhīṣṭa*), "hired" (*bhṛta*), "past" (*bhūta*), or "future" (*bhāvī*).
"Commissioned" (*adhīṣṭa*) means treated with honor and assigned a task.
*Bhṛtaḥ* means one purchased for wages;
*bhūtaḥ* means that which pervades time by its own existence;
and *bhāvī* is the same kind [of entity] in the future.
The second case ending is used here by the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). Thus, one who has been commissioned for a month is called a *māsika* teacher.
A laborer hired for a month is "monthly" (*māsika*);
a disease that has lasted for a month is "monthly";
a festival that will occur after a month is "monthly."
But surely, the request and the maintenance are performed for only a moment; how then can the month be pervaded by them? [The answer is:
The request and the maintenance have action as their purpose; therefore, when the month is pervaded by the action which is the result, it is said that it is pervaded by those two [very acts].
In the sense of age, [the suffixes] khañ and ñyaṅ are applied after the word *māsa*.
When the word *māsa* denotes an age, the suffixes *yat* and *khañ* are applied;
these are exceptions to [the application of] *ṭhañ*.

Although the four suffixes beginning with *adhīṣṭa* fall under this governing rule (*adhikāra*), by virtue of the contextual force (*sāmarthya*), only those denoting duration already elapsed (*bhūta*) are connected here. For example: *māsaṃ bhūtaḥ* [one who has been for a month] results in *māsyaḥ* and *māsīnaḥ*.
Why is the condition "in reference to age" (*vayasi*) specified? [To exclude cases like: *māsikam* (monthly).
The suffix *yaP* is applied after a *dvigu* compound [ending in a consonant].
The term "in age" (*vayasi*) continues [from the previous rule]. The suffix *yap* occurs after a *dvigu* compound ending in *māsa* when age is to be expressed.
One who has become two months old is *dvimāsyaḥ*;
[one who has become three months old is] *trimāsyaḥ*.
And also [the suffix] ṇya after [the word] ṣaṇmāsa.
The rule "in the sense of age" (vayasi) applies here as well.
When the word *ṣaṇmāsa* denotes age, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, and *yap* is also applied.
The general suffix *ṭhañ* is also intended here; it is to be conjoined by the word "ca" (and),
and because it is marked with the svarita accent, it will carry over from the immediately preceding rule.
By that, there is a threefold form:
*ṣāṇmāsyaiḥ*, *ṣaṇmāsyaḥ*, and *ṣāṇmāsikaḥ*.
And [the suffix] ṭhañ is applied after words denoting age.
The suffix *ṭhaṇ* is applied after the word *ṣaṇmāsa* when a period of life (*vayas*) is to be expressed;
by the inclusion of the letter *ca*, there is a conjunction with the immediately preceding suffix *ṇyat*.
A disease lasting six months is called *ṣaṇmāsikaḥ* or *ṣāṇmāsyaḥ*. [486] After the word *samā*, the suffix *kha* [is applied]. (Pāṇini 5.1.85)
The four meanings beginning with *adhīṣṭa* (being requested) continue to apply.
From the word *samā*, when it denotes the second case (*dvitīyā*), the suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of being requested (*adhīṣṭa*) and so forth.
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhañ*. [The word] *samāmadhīṣṭaḥ*, *bhṛtaḥ*, *bhūtaḥ*, or *bhāvī* [is formed with the suffix *ini*] as *samīnaḥ*.
However, some maintain that the rule *tena nirvṛttam* (Pāṇini 5.1.79) applies everywhere [in these cases].
That which has arisen from the *samaya* is the *samīna*.
Or [the suffix *ṅīp*] is optionally applied after a *dvigu* compound.

Regarding the rule *samāyāḥ khaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.85), it is as follows: after a *dvigu* compound ending in the word *samā*, the suffix *kha* optionally occurs in the five senses beginning with "produced" (*nirvṛtta*) and so forth.
By the preceding rule, [the suffix] *nitya* (always) was already established; it is now being subject to an option.

Indeed, there is already an application [of the rule] by virtue of *Pāṇini 7.3.17*: "In the absence of elision (*aluk*), there is the inclusion of that which ends in a numeral as the prior member, when a word ending in *vati* follows."
When the suffix *kha* is elided, the suffix *ṭhañ* also occurs:
*dvisāminaḥ*, *dvaisamikaḥ*.
trisamīnaḥ,
traisamikaḥ.
And [the suffix -vat] is applied after the words *rātri*, *ahan*, and *saṃvatsara*.
The suffix *kha* optionally occurs after a *dvigu* compound ending in *rātri*, *ahaḥ*, or *saṃvatsara*, in the sense of "completed" (*nirvṛtta*) and so forth.
When *kha* is not applied, the suffix *ṭhañ* also occurs in that alternative case.
One who has fasted for two nights,
a two-nighter; one who has fasted for three nights, a three-nighter.
Lasting for three nights;
lacking two days, or lasting for two days; lacking three days, or lasting for three days.
Two years old,
biennial;
three years old.
*Trisāṃvatsarikaḥ*:
by the rule "of a numeral and a word denoting a number of years," there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member.
After the word *varṣa*, [the suffix] *luk* is also applied.
Under the rule "dvigoḥ" (after a *dvigu* compound), specifically after a *dvigu* ending in *varṣa*, the suffix *kha* optionally occurs in the senses of "produced therefrom" (*nirvṛtta*) and so forth.
In this case, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; furthermore, there is optionally elision (*luk*) of those two.
Thus, three forms are produced.
A disease lasting two years, two-year-old, two years old;
three-year-old.
*trivārṣikaḥ*, *trivarṣaḥ*:
there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the subsequent member by [Pāṇini 7.3.16] *varṣasyābhaviṣyati*.
But when [the pregnancy] is expected to last three years, [the penance is] that lasting for three years.
It is always present in that which possesses consciousness.

When a word meaning "endowed with consciousness" (*cittavat*) is to be expressed as the object of the suffix, there is always elision (*luk*) of the suffix produced after a *dvigu* compound ending in the word *varṣa*, in the sense of "completed" (*nirvṛtta*) and so forth.
This rule is stated because the previous [sūtra] would have allowed for an option.
"A two-year-old boy.
Why [is it specified] "in a conscious being"?
[Consider: "a two-year-old illness."
The sixty-day rice ripens in sixty nights.
The word *ṣaṣṭika* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). The plural number is not restrictive.
From the word *ṣaṣṭirātra*, when used in the third case, the suffix *kan* is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the sense of "they are cooked," and the word *rātri* is elided. Thus,
those which are cooked in sixty nights are called *ṣaṣṭikāḥ*.
This is a designation for a specific type of grain;
therefore, there is no over-extension of the term to mung beans and the like.
[487] *vatsarāntāc chaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.1.91).
After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *vatsara*, the suffix *chan* is applied in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) in the sense of "ceased" (*nivṛtta*) and so forth;
this is an exception to [the suffix] *ṭhañ*.
idvatsarīyaḥ / idāvatsarīyaḥ //
After the prefix *sam-pari*, [the suffix] *kha* is also applied.
In the Vedic domain, the suffix *kha* is added after a nominal stem ending in *vatsara* when preceded by *sam*, *pari*,
or *vi*, in the sense of "completed" (*nirvṛtta*) and so forth.
By virtue of the word "ca" (and), there is also "śa":
*saṃvatsarīṇāḥ*, *saṃvatsarīyāḥ*.
Annual;
pertaining to the annual cycle.
Therefore, it is easily accomplished through mastery.

From that [word] ending in the third case, namely from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting time, [the suffix *yat* is applied] in the sense of "conquerable" (*parijayya*) or "obtainable" (*labhya*).
The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of "body," "easy," and these other meanings; for example,
"to be mastered within a month."
A disease lasting one month can be conquered;
so too one lasting a year.
A cloth obtainable in a month is "monthly" (māsika);
a Cāndrāyaṇa penance to be performed in a month is "monthly";
a palace easy to construct in a month is "monthly."
That constitutes his practice of celibacy.
The word *tat* [in the rule] is a case ending in the accusative, and it denotes continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
The word "of this" (asya) refers to the object of the cognition;
"celibacy" (brahmacarya) is connected with both [the preceding and following terms];
it pervades the duration of time.
And regarding the word *svam* (one's own) as the meaning of the suffix:

from a second-case-inflected nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting time, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of the genitive case (*asya*), provided that the meaning "celibacy" (*brahmacarya*) is understood.
One who observes celibacy for a month is a *māsika* celibate;
one for half a month is *ārdhamāsika*; one for a year is *sāṃvatsarika*.

Another rule: after a word in the nominative case ending in *tad* (meaning "that"), the suffix *ṭhañ* is added in the sense of the genitive case (*asya*, "of this"), provided that what is indicated by "this" is a period of studentship (*brahmacarya*). For example, when the studentship lasts for a month, it is called *māsika-brahmacarya* ("a month's studentship").
[The penance lasts] for half a month or for a year;
in the former case, the status of a celibate student (brahmacārī) serves as the qualifying condition.
In the latter case, it is simply celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Both are authoritative,
because the Sūtra was composed in both ways.
An addition [to the rule] is made for words such as *mahānāmni* when they are in the sixth case in construction:
*māhānāmikam*,
*gaudānikam*.
It is the Ādityavrata;
and it is that which one performs.
These are the Mahānāmnī verses.
The vow associated with that [deity] is expressed by the word "tat" (that). One who performs the Mahānāmnī vow is a *māhānāmika*;
one who performs the Āditya vow is an *ādityavratika*.

[Gaudānikaḥ: By the rule *bhasyāḍhe* (Pāṇini 7.3.44), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is removed through the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*); then, by the rule *na staddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144), there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion [of the suffix].
The suffix *ḍini* should be prescribed after words such as *avāntaradīkṣā*. One who performs the intermediate initiation is an *avāntaradīkṣī*; one who observes the sesame vow is a *tilavratī*.
The suffixes *ḍvuñ* and *ḍini* should also be stated [after the word] *aṣṭācatvāriṃśat*.
One who performs the vow for forty-eight years is called *aṣṭācatvāriṃśakaḥ* or *aṣṭācatvariṃśī*.
Regarding the word *cāturmāsya*, it should be stated that there is elision of the *y* sound and that the suffixes *ḍvuñ* and *ḍini* are applied:
from *cāturmāsyāni carati* [one who performs the four-month rites], we derive *cāturmāsakaḥ* (with *ḍvuñ*) and *cāturamāsī* (with *ḍini*).

The suffix *ṇya* occurs after the word *caturmāsa* in the sense of "a sacrifice" (*yajña*) performed therein. [The term] *cāturmāsyāni* means "those occurring in four months. It should be stated that the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of a technical name (*sañjñā*).
The full moon day occurring in four months is called *cāturmāsī*; it refers to the full moon days of Āṣāḍhī and Kārtikī.
Phālgunī.
And its sacrificial fee consists of those [gifts] known as belonging to the sacrifice.

After words denoting sacrifices that are in the genitive case (understood as being in the sixth case), the suffix *ṭhañ* is added in the sense of "sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*). For example: the sacrificial fee of the *agniṣṭoma* is *āgniṣṭomikī*.
The suffix -ika is applied to denote the *vājapeya* sacrifice and the *rājasūya* sacrifice.

The mention of the term "name" (*ākhyā*) is so that it may apply even when the word does not refer to the specific time [of the sacrifice], provided it denotes the sacrifice itself. Thus, for example: *vājapeyikī*.

Otherwise, due to the governing rule of "time" (kāla), only sacrifices lasting one day, twelve days, and so forth would be included. Even though the governing rule of "time" applies, there is still the possibility of inclusion for terms such as *dvādaśāha* because of the rule: "In the absence of elision (*aluk*), words preceded by a numeral are understood to include those ending in that [numeral]" (*Pāṇini* 2.1.51). [489]
And in that case, the operation is applied as if it were present.

In this context, the suffixes prescribed for *bhava* occur after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) denoting time that are in the seventh case (*saptamī*), provided they signify "given" (*dīyate*) or "a duty/task" (*kārya*).
For example: that which occurs in a month is *māsika*; that which occurs in a year is *sāṃvatsarika*; that which occurs in the rainy season is *prāvṛṣeṇya*.
The springtime [rite],
the vernal [rite], the winter [rite].
The winter [robe], the wintry [robe], the autumn [robe].
The suffix *vati* has the sense of "complete similarity. Furthermore, a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) must be made here; and in that [first part], there is the sense "it is given therein."
"From those called sacrifices": this refers to the portion belonging to the Agniṣṭoma and that belonging to the Rājasūya.
The section concerning the Vājapeya sacrifice is concluded;
this marks the final limit of the rules governing time. Hereafter follows the general prescription of suffixes.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words beginning with *vyuṣṭa*.
In this context, after the words *vyuṣṭa* and others used in the locative case (*saptamī-samartha*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied to form the meanings "given" (*dīyate*) and "to be done" (*kāryam*).
*Vaiyuṣṭa* refers to that which is given or performed at dawn (*vyuṣṭe*). It is obligatory (*nitya*).
In the section on the suffix *aṇ*, there is an addition [to the rule] for words beginning with *agnipada*.
The station of Agni;
the root of the Pilu tree.
What more needs to be said?
It need not be stated;
they should be recited right here:
*vyuṣṭa*.
Constantly entering and exiting.
Holy ford; agitation; rug.
Battle, slaughter, and the path of fire.
Pīlumūla, Pravāsa, Upasaṅkramaṇa.
The *vyuṣṭa* sacrifice and others.
By that [suffix], the suffixes *ṇa* and *yat* are applied after the word *yathākathāc*, with the elision of the final syllable.

The words "is given" (dīyate) and "to be done" (kāryam) carry over from the previous rule. Thus, from the two words *yathākathāca* and *hasta*, which are in the third case (instrumental), the suffixes *ṇa* and *yat* respectively occur.
The connection is made with each of these two meanings— “is given” and “is to be done”—
but a correspondence according to their respective order (yathāsaṅkhyam) is not intended.
The indeclinable compound *yathākathāca* occurs in the sense of disregard.
And here only the sense of the third case is possible,
but not the third case as a case-ending expressing capability (*samartha-vibhakti*). Thus, *yāthākathācam* means "given or performed in whatever manner."
That which is given by the hand, or that which is performed by the hand, is called *hastyam*.
[The suffix *ini* occurs] in the sense of "one who accomplishes" (sampādini). // PS_5.1.99 //
By that very [rule],
namely *tena*, when the sense of "accomplishing" (*sampādin*) is to be expressed, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after a word standing in the third case.
*Guṇotkarṣaḥ* means excellence;
the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). A face that is brought about by two ear-ornaments is called a *kārṇaveṣṭakika* face.
The body is "possessing a pair of garments" (*vāstrayugika*);
the meaning is that it is especially beautified by a pair of garments. [That which arises] from the action of clothing is [expressed by the suffix *ṭhan*]. (PS 5.1.100)

The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *karman* and *veṣa*, when they are in the third case (instrumental) and possessive construction (*samartha*), in the sense of "one who accomplishes" (*sampādini*). This is an exception to [the application of] the suffix *ṭhañ*.
Through action one becomes fit for action;
through dress one becomes a dress-wearing actor.
The suffix *thak* is applied after that [word] when it means "heating" and so forth, provided that the word ends in *saṃtāpa* or similar forms.

The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after words such as *santāpa*, when they are in the fourth case (*caturthī*) in construction, in the sense of "he prevails over" (*prabhavati*). One who is capable or able is said to "prevail."
The fourth case is used in the sense of "for the sake of" (alamarthe). For example: *santāpāya prabhavati* means *sāntāpikaḥ*;
*sānnāhikaḥ*.
santāpa (affliction), sannāha (armor), saṅgrāma (battle).
Union,
the next world,
and crushing.
Crushing / Natural emission / Non-emission.
visarga, upasarga, upavāsa.
Departure; assembly; mutual greeting.
Even from flour, meat, and boiled rice taken separately.
And that which [arises] from yoga. (PS 5.1.102)
The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *yoga*, and by virtue of the particle *ca*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is also applied.
In this context,
regarding the sense of "he has power over that," one who has power for yoga is "yogya" (fit) or "yaugika" (suitable).
The suffix *ukañ* is applied after a verbal root to form a noun denoting the instrument of an action.
The suffix *ukañ* is applied after words denoting an action (*karman*) in the sense of "he is capable of that," as an exception to [the rule for] the suffix *ṭhañ*.
The bow is capable of the action [of shooting];
it does not exist apart from the bow, because [the action] would not be denoted [otherwise].
Therefore, that [consequence] has been reached by him. (PS 5.1.104)

From the word *samaya*, when it is in the first case and in grammatical agreement with another word (*tat-prathamā-samartha*), the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), provided that what is expressed by that first-case word is something that has been reached (*prāpta*).
The occasion has arrived for his occasional duty; the meaning is that the time has come. The indication of the case-ending in "samaye" is for the sake of what follows.
The suffix *raṇ* is applied after a word denoting a season (*ṛtu*) [to form a feminine derivative].
The phrase "that has been obtained by him" (tad asya prāptam) is understood to follow here.

From the word *ṛtu*, when it stands in the nominative case in construction with "that" (*tat*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of the genitive "of him" (*asya*) in this context: "that has been obtained by him."
The season has arrived for him; the seasonal flower is his. In this context, there is an addition [to the rule] from "upavasta" and so forth: the fast-day has arrived for him; it is his *aupavastra*.
The *prāśitra* is that which has been eaten (*prāśita*) by him; [the suffix -tra is applied here].
In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the root *ghas* [is used for *pra-aś*]. (Pāṇini 5.1.106)
In the Vedic language, the suffix *ghas* is applied after the word *ṛtu* in the sense of "that has been obtained by him," serving as an exception to the suffix *aṇ*.
This is your seasonal womb.
That which [is derived] from time (kālāt). // PS 5.1.107 //
The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *kāla* in the sense of "that has arrived for him"; for example,
*kālyaḥ tāpaḥ*, meaning "the heat that has arrived for him."
In the morning, it is cold.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a word denoting excellence (*prakṛṣṭa*).
[The rule] "from time" (kālāt) remains in force,
as does "that belongs to this" (tad asya).
The word *prāpta* is excluded.
Time is qualified by excellence (*prakarsa*).
From a word denoting time that expresses excellence, when it is in the first case (nominative) construction, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*asya*).

That which has a long, extended duration is *kālikam* (temporal); for example, *kālikam ṛṇam* (a debt lasting over time) or *kālikam vairam* (enmity lasting over time). The inclusion of the suffix *ṭhañ* is for the sake of clarity.
The purpose [of the treatise]. (PS 5.1.109)
*tad asya*—thus [it is said].
From a word in the first case (*prathamasamartha*) meaning "that," the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*), as in *asya*.
When that which is incapable of being expressed in the nominative case serves as the purpose (*prayojana*), [the suffix -ika is applied].
For example: *aindramahikam* ("that which has the festival of Indra as its purpose") and *gāṅgāmahikam* ("that which has the festival of Gaṅgā as its purpose").
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *viśākhā* and *aṣāḍhā* when [the derivative] signifies a *mantha* (a stirred drink) or a *daṇḍa* (a staff).

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *viśākhā* and *ṣaḍhā* in the sense of "this is its purpose," provided that the objects denoted are respectively a churning-stick (*mantha*) and a staff (*daṇḍa*). For example:
*vaiśākho manthaḥ* ("a churning-stick for which the *viśākhā* constellation is the occasion").
The word *āṣāḍha* is used in the sense of a staff (*daṇḍa*).
There is an extension of the rule to include words such as *cūḍā* and others:
that for which the tonsure (*cūḍā*) is the purpose is called *cauḍa*.
That which has faith as its purpose is *śrāddha*.
The suffix *cha* is applied after words such as *anupravacana*.
The suffix *cha* is applied after nominal stems such as *anupravacana* and others in the sense that "this is its purpose"; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhañ*. For example:
that for which the purpose is *anupravacana* is called *anupravacanīya*.

The suffix *anīya* is added [to form gerundives]. An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made for roots whose nature involves entering, filling, falling, or climbing, when preceded by a prior member [in a compound]: that which has "entering the house" (*gṛhapraveśana*) as its purpose is *gṛhapraveśanīya*.
It is that which fills a water-station;
it is that which causes one to fall from a horse;
it is that which leads one up to a palace.
That which is to be expressed after words such as *svarga* [is formed with the suffix -ya]:
that for which heaven is the purpose is *svargya*; likewise, *yaśasya*.
It bestows long life; it fulfills desires; it brings prosperity. [492]
The elision [of the suffix] should be stated after words such as *puṇyāhavācana*. That which has the recitation for auspiciousness (*puṇyāhavācana*) as its purpose is called *puṇyāhavācana*;
likewise, *svastivācana*.
The recitation for peace,
the subsequent recitation,
and the rite of rising.
Entry, thorough entry,
and establishment.
Entering together, entering after, and reciting after.
Exposition / Anointing / Commencement.
Ascending;
growing forth;
following after in ascent.
The recitation of the scriptures and so forth.
[The suffix *ka* is applied] after a word ending in *samāpanna*, provided it is preceded by another word [forming a compound].

The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *samāpana* when it is preceded by another word— that is, when it has an existing prior member— in the sense of "this is its purpose. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhañ*.
That which has the completion of the *chandas* as its purpose is "to be completed by the *chandas*" (*chandaḥsamāpanīya*). It is "to be completed by grammar" (*vyākaraṇasamāpanīya*).

And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after copulative compounds and after words such as *manojña*.

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after words that form *dvandva* compounds and after the group beginning with *manojña*, in the sense of state (*bhāva*) or action (*karman*). For example, the state or action of cowherds and shepherds is *gaupālapaśupālikā*.
*Śaiṣyopādhyāyikā*; *kautsakuśikikā*;
from *manojña*, *mānojñaka*.
Auspicious;
pleasing; beautiful.
O one of pleasing form!
O follower of the Vedic meters!
O student!
O wise one! O handsome one! O wealthy one!
Noble son,
learned brahmin,
thief.
O rogue!
O one belonging to the Viśvedevas!
O youth!
Village youth! Village lad! Village boy!
Son of such-and-such a person; of such-and-such a family;
hundred-petaled one.
Wholesome; [it is] that which is agreeable to the mind and so forth.
Praise and censure regarding one's lineage or conduct [are used] when referring to those very things. // PS 5.1.134 //

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) denoting a lineage (*gotra*) or a conduct (*cāraṇa*), in the sense of either an action or an object, when [verbs such as] *ślāgh* (to praise) and others constitute the context for each case.
In this context, *ślāghā* means boasting;
*atyākāraḥ* means reviling others;
and *tadavetaḥ* means one who has attained that, or one who knows that.
The word *tat* refers here to the states (*bhāva*) and actions (*karman*) belonging to a lineage (*gotra*) or a school (*caraṇa*).
One who has attained or understood that is said to "know" (*veda*) it.
First, regarding praise (*ślāghā*): *gārgikayā ślāghate* ("he praises himself by means of his Gārgya-ness").
"He praises with the *kāṭhikā*" means he boasts of being a Gārgya and a Kaṭha. Regarding "insulting":
"He insults with the *gārgikā*."
"He reviles excessively with the *kāṭhika*" means that he insults others by virtue of their being Gārgyas or their being Kaṭhas.
"He knows that" means he knows the state of being a Gārgya (*gārgikām avetaḥ*).
"Endowed with the Kaṭha lineage" means that he has attained the status of being a Gārgya and the status of being a Kaṭha;
or, it means that he has understood that [truth].
Why [is it specified] "in the sense of praise and so forth"? [Consider:
*gārgyatvam* (the state of being a Gārgya) and *kaṭhatvam* (the state of being a Kaṭha).
The suffix *cha* is applied after words denoting the offices of the *hotṛ* priests.
The word *gotra* denotes a specific kind of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
The suffix *cha* is applied after words denoting specific kinds of officiating priests to express the sense of an action or an object.
The state or function of the Acchāvāka is the *ācchāvākīya*;
[likewise] the *maitrāvaruṇīya* and the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsīya*.
The Āgnīdhrīya, the Pratiprasthātrīya, and the Tvaṣṭrīya.
The term *potrīyam* [is used];
the plural number is for the purpose of excluding a rule regarding the specific form [of the word].
Thou art indeed of Brahman.

The term *hotrābhyaḥ* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. The suffix *tva* occurs after words denoting *hotrā* (sacrificial offices) that contain the word *brahman*, in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
The suffix *cha* expresses censure (*apavāda*).
*Brahmatvam* means the state or activity of a *brahman*.
Although one could have simply said "not" (*na*), the fact that it was not so stated is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *tal*.
However, as for the word *brahman*, which is a synonym for *brāhmaṇa* and denotes a genus (*jāti*), the suffixes *tva* and *tal* do indeed occur after it:
*brahmatvam*, *brahmatā*.
The governing rule for the suffixes *nañ* and *tañ*, which have *bhavana* as their limit, is concluded.

Thus ends the first quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Kāśikā-vṛtti*. **The second quarter of the fifth chapter:** [498] *dhānyānāṃ bhavane kṣetre khañ* // Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.1 // The suffix *khañ* is applied after words denoting grains to form a word for a field where those grains grow.
From the very statement [of the rule], the governing case is established:
after words denoting specific types of grain that end in the genitive case and are semantically capable, the suffix *khañ* occurs when the sense of "growing" (*bhavana*) is to be expressed.
If that field is a dwelling place (*bhavana*),
it is called a "dwelling place" because beings (*bhavanti*) are born (*jāyante*) therein; thus,
a field for mung beans is *maudgīna*.
*kaudravīṇam*, *kaulatthīnam*.
Why [is it specified] "of grains" (*dhānyānām*)? [To exclude cases such as: *māṣāṇām* (of beans).
In the case of "a field for grass" (*tṛṇānāṃ bhavanam kṣetram*), [the suffix] does not occur. Why is it said "a field"? [Consider: "a granary for mung beans" (*mudgānāṃ bhavanam kusūlam*).
The plural number is used for the purpose of excluding an injunction regarding the essential nature [of the word].
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *vrīhi* and *śāli*.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *vrīhi* and *śāli* when the field (*kṣetra*) where they grow is to be expressed; this is an exception to [the rule for] *khañ*.
A field that is the place of growth for rice is called *vraiheya*.
This is from Śālīya.
[The suffix -mayaṭ is used] after the words *yava*, *yavaka*, and *ṣaṣṭika*.
The suffix *yat* is applied after words such as *yava* and others when "field" (*kṣetra*) is to be expressed in the sense of "growing there";
this is an exception to [the application of] *khañ*.
The field that is the place of growing barley is called *yavyam*,
*yavakyam*,
or *ṣaṣṭikyam*.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* is applied after the words *tila*, *māṣa*, *umā*, *bhaṅgā*, and *aṇu*.

The suffix *yat* is optionally applied after *tila*, *māṣa*, *umā*, *bhaṅgā*, and *aṇu* when the field (*kṣetra*) where they grow is to be expressed. This statement is made because the suffix *khañ* would otherwise have been required by rule.
In that case, it also occurs [with the suffix -ya].
Even in the instances of *umā* and *bhaṅgā*, the status of being a grain (*dhānya*) is indeed relied upon.
The field where sesamum seeds grow is *tilya* or *tailīna*.
māṣyam, māṣīṇam;
umyam, aumīnam;
bhaṅgyam, bhāṅgīnam.
atomic, not derived from atoms.
The suffixes *kha* and *khañ* are applied after the word *sarvacarman*.

From the word *sarvacarman*, when used in the third case (instrumental), the suffixes *kha* and *khañ* are applied in the sense of "made. Furthermore, in this context, the word *sarva* is connected with the meaning of the suffix— namely, that which is made— and not with the word *carman* (skin).
In this regard, this should be understood as an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound):
the formation occurs in the sense of the sentence "made entirely of leather," namely,
*sarvacarmīṇaḥ*.
[The suffix] *cha* (forming *sārvacarmīṇa*) is used after [the word *sarvacarman*].
[The suffix] *kha* (forming *yathāmukhasammukha*) is used after [the compound] *yathāmukhasammukha*. PS 5.2.6.
From the words *yathāmukha* and *sammukha*, when they are in the sixth case (genitive) and possessive sense, the suffix *kha* occurs in the meaning "that which is seen.
That in which something is seen is called *darśana*, such as a mirror or other substratum for a reflection.
By means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of similarity:
*yathāmukha-darśanaḥ* becomes *yathāmukhīnaḥ*;
*sarvasya mukhasya darśanaḥ* becomes *sammukhīnaḥ*.
That [wind] pervades everything from the beginning of the path to the leaf and vessel that serve as the instruments for wholesome action.
The word *tat* is the case ending in the accusative, which expresses the sense of the object; the meaning of the suffix is "to pervade."
The remainder is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti-viśeṣaṇa*).

From a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) beginning with *sarva-* and ending in *pathin*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, or *pātra*, when it is in the second case (*dvitīyā-samartha*), the suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of "pervading" (*vyāpnoti*). For example: that which pervades all paths is a "universal-path chariot" (*sarvapathīna rathaḥ*).
One who suffers throughout his entire body;
a man capable of all actions;
a charioteer who reaches every part of the path.
The rice is for all the vessels.
He reaches up to his ankles. // PS_5.2.8 //
"Prapada" refers to the tip of the foot; the prefix "ā" is used here in the sense of a limit (maryādā).
The *avyayībhāva* compound of those two [words] is as follows:

from the word *āprapada*, when it is in the second case in construction (*samartha*), the suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of "reaching up to" (*prāpnoti*). Thus, "a cloth that reaches up to the toes" is *āprapadīnaḥ paṭaḥ*.
The measurement of even a cloth that is not connected with the body is stated.
One who follows the track of all food—whether right or wrong—consumes it among those things that are bound and those that are not to be eaten. // PS_5.2.9 //

After the words *anupada* and others, when they are in the second case in construction, the suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of "bound," "eaten," or "to be led," respectively. [In this context,] *anu* signifies either length (*āyāma*) or similarity (*sādṛśya*).
A sandal that is bound to every footstep is called *anupadinā*;
the meaning is that its size conforms to the foot. A monk who eats all kinds of food is called *sarvānnīna*.
*Ayas* is clockwise; *anayas* is counter-clockwise.
When the footprints of arrows moving clockwise and counter-clockwise do not coincide with those of other arrows, that is *ayānaya*.
*Ayānaya* means "to be led back and forth"; *ayānayīna* refers to the shuttle (*śāra*).
The meaning is that it is situated at the head of the loom-board (*phalaka*).
One experiences [the results] through a succession of descendants, from son to grandson, higher and lower.

The suffix *kha* occurs after the words *parovara*, *paramparā*, *putrapautra*, and so forth, when they are in the accusative case (*dvitīyāsamartha*) and the sense is "he experiences" (*anubhavati*).
In the word *parovara*, the substitution of *u* for the final vowel of *para* is prescribed by way of its connection with the suffix.
One who experiences both the higher and the lower is called *parovarīṇa*.
The state of being a succession of those that are higher and further is expressed by the derivative form;
one who experiences both the higher and the further is called *paramparīṇa*.
One experiences sons and grandsons; [the suffix] *īna* is used for "sons and grandsons. The word *paramparā* is seen even without a suffix, as in the expression:
"a succession of ministers (*mantriparamparā*) betrays the secret counsel."
That should be understood as a distinct word [ending in -gāmin].
[PS 5.2.11] One who goes to the near shore, the far shore, the beyond, or according to desire.
The suffix *kha* occurs after the words *avārapāra*, *atyanta*, and *anukāma*, when they are in construction with an accusative case and signify the sense of "one who goes" (*gāmī*).
[One who will go] is "a goer" (*gāmī*).
Regarding the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.3),
the prohibition of the genitive case applies by the rule *aka-inor bhaviṣyad-ādhamarṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70).
One who goes from this shore to the other shore is *avārapārīṇa*;
and by reversal,
one is *pārāvārīṇa*.
The suffix *ini* is also desired after a word ending in *vigṛhīta*; for example, *avārīṇaḥ*.
After a word ending in *atyanta*, the suffix *inaṅ* is applied; for example, *atyantīnaḥ*.
The meaning is "one who goes excessively. *Anukāmīnaḥ* means "one who goes according to desire";
the meaning is "one who goes as he wishes."
She gives birth every year.
In the expression *samāṃsamām*, the repetition (*vīpsā*) is indicated; the collection of nominal stems (*subanta-samudāya*) constitutes the base form (*prakṛti*).
The meaning of the suffix is "she brings forth" and "she bears a fetus.

Because she pervades the entire year by means of bearing a fetus, the second case ending is used to express continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Thus, *samāṃsamāṃ vijāyate* means "a cow that brings forth [a calf] every year," which is expressed as *samāṃsamīnā gauḥ*.
The word *samāṃsamīnā* means "a mare that brings forth a foal every year.
It should be stated that there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) in the first member of the compound.
However, some analyze it as "one who gives birth in the same year" (*samāyāṃ vijāyate*).

Regarding the release of the fetus, they say that "birthlessness" (vijaniḥ) occurs; in their case, only the elision of the *y* in the first member is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), while the non-elision (*aluk*) of the remainder must be stated.
In the case of *anutpatti*, it should be stated that there is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of the *ya* of the subsequent member:
*samāṃsamāṃvijāyate*, or alternatively, *samāyāṃ samāyāṃ vijāyate*.
The two forms *adyaśvīnā* and *avaṣṭabdhe*.
The term "is born" (*vijāyate*) continues [from the previous rule].
The form *adyaśvīna* is an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) meaning "one who has recently given birth" when referring to a secluded woman.

When the delivery is near, the suffix *mūrdhanya* (the cerebral ṇ) is prescribed by the rule "after [the word] *ava*, it is used in the senses of proximity and non-proximity" (*avyād-ālambanāvidūryayoḥ*, Pāṇini 5.4.49). Thus,
a cow that will give birth today or tomorrow is called *adyaśvīnā*.
The term *adyaśvīnā* refers to a mare.
Some, however, do not apply the rule "she gives birth" (*vijāyate*), stating instead that this is a nipātana (irregular formation) applied merely to the state of being impregnated.
Death is imminent,
separation is imminent;
thus ends [the section on] *āgavīna* (PS 5.2.14).

The form *āgavīna* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) word. From the root *go* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *kha* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*) to denote a person who performs labor until the completion of the payment for that cow.
An *āgavīna* is a laborer;
one who performs work for wages in exchange for a cow, until that cow has been returned.
One who follows along with the anus. // PS 5.2.15 //
After the word *go*, the suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of "one who follows" (*anugu*), specifically meaning "one who goes after."
The cowherd who goes after the cows until they have gone far enough is called *anugavīnaḥ*.
The suffix *yat* is applied after a word denoting time (*adhvan*) when followed by the locative case ending *-khau*.
The word *tat* (that) follows as the case ending in the accusative (*dvitīyā*) expressing semantic competency;
and *alaṅgāmī* (one who goes beyond) is the meaning of the suffix.

From the word *adhvan* (road), when it is in the second case construction, the suffixes *yat* and *kha* are added in the sense of "one who goes along" (*alaṅgāmī*). [Examples: one who goes along the road is *adhvanyaḥ* or *adhvanīnaḥ*.
And by the rules "ye ca abhavakarmaṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.168) and "ātma-adhvānau khe" (Pāṇini 6.4.169), there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
And [the suffix *cha*] is applied after the word *abhyamitra*.
The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) meaning "capable of overcoming an enemy" (*abhyamitra-śad*), in the sense of "one who goes to meet [that enemy]";
by virtue of the word *ca*, the suffixes *yat* and *kha* are also applied.
*abhyamitram alaṅgāmī*, *abhyamitrīyaḥ*, *abhamitryaḥ*,
and *abhyamitrīṇaḥ* mean one who goes well toward the enemy; that is, one who advances directly against the foe.
The suffix *khañ* is applied after the word *goṣṭha* when expressing that which formerly existed there.
A *goṣṭha* is that in which cows stand;
by the word *goṣṭha*, a location containing a herd of cows is denoted.
The inclusion of the term *bhūtapūrva* (formerly being) serves as a qualification for that very [word].
From the word *goṣṭha*, when it has the adjunct of "having formerly been," the suffix *khañ* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). An area where there was formerly a cow-pen is called *gauṣṭhīna*.
What is the purpose of including the term "bhūtapūrva" (formerly existing)? [For example:
*goṣṭho vartate* ("the cow-pen exists").
The distance traveled by a horse in one day [is called *aśvīna*]. PS_5,2.19.

The case ending is determined by the very statement [of the rule]. From the word *aśva*, when it is in the sixth case (genitive) expressing capability, the suffix *khañ* occurs in the sense of "one who traverses in a single day."
That which is traveled in one day is "one-day-travel" (*ekāhagama*).
The road that is a horse's one-day travel is "equine" (*āśvīna*).
Having flown for a hundred equine distances.
The words *śālīna* and *kaupīna* denote, respectively, one who is timid and an improper act.

The words *śālīna* and *kaupīna* are irregularly derived (nipātita) respectively when denoting one who is "timid" (*adhṛṣṭa*) and an "improper act" (*akārya*). One who is timid is one who lacks confidence (*apragalbha*).
*Akārya* means that which is improper to do or contrary to what should be done.

*Śālīna* and *kaupīna* are synonyms for "timid" and "that which should not be done," respectively, though their etymologies must be explained in some way or another. [The former] is so called because it deserves entry into the house (*śālā*).
The suffix *khañ* is prescribed [after the word *kūpa*] in the sense of "deserving to descend into," and there is the elision of the final member of the compound; thus,
*śālīna* means "dull-witted" and *kaupīna* means "sin."
He lives by means of a troop.
By the very statement [of the rule], the third case is the governing case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*).
From the word *vrāta*, when it is in the third case and possesses the required semantic relation, the suffix *khañ* occurs in the sense of "he lives by means of that."
"Guilds" (saṅghāḥ) and "associations" (vrātāḥ) are groups of various kinds with不定 (aniyata) modes of livelihood who subsist by bodily labor (utsedhajīvinaḥ).
"Bodily labor" (utsedhaḥ) refers to the body; those who live by means of it are "those who subsist by bodily labor."
Their collective activity is the *vrāta*;
one who lives by that collective activity is a *vrātīna*. He is said to be one belonging to any one of those very *vrātas*.
But in the case of another who lives by means of that [wealth], it is not desired there.
Friendship is formed by walking seven steps together.
The word *sāptapadīna* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) term when friendship (*sakhyam*) is to be expressed;
it means that which is obtained by seven steps (*saptabhiḥ padaiḥ*).
People say that friendship is established by walking seven steps together.
How is it that one becomes a friend by walking seven steps, or that a friend is defined as "one who has walked seven steps"?

When the word *sāptapadīna*—in which the quality (*guṇa*) is primary—is used in the sense of friendship or its activity, then it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "friendship" (*sakhyam*); but when it is used through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then it stands in coreferentiality with the word "person" (*puruṣa*).
The word *haiyaṅgavīna* is [an irregular formation] when it denotes a specific name.
The form *haiyaṅgavīna* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the sense of a specific name;
it is the substitution of *hiyaṅgava* for *hyogodoha*.

The suffix *khañ* is applied after [the word] *tasya* (of that) in the sense of its modification (*vikāra*), when it is a proper name (*sañjñā*). For example, the modification of *hyogodoha* (the milk of a cow that has recently calved) is *haiyaṅgavīna*;
this is a name for clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Therefore, it does not occur here:
*udaśvit* is a modification of yesterday’s milk (*hyogodoha*).
The suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are added after the word *pākamūla* and after words beginning with *pīlu* and *karṇa*, respectively.

The suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are applied respectively after the words *pīlu* and others, as well as *karṇa* and others, when these are used in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) to denote the meanings of "ripening" (*pāka*) and "root" (*mūla*). For example:
the ripening of *pīlu* fruits is *pīlukuṇa*.
*karkandhukuṇaḥ*. From words such as *karṇa*: the root of the ear is *karṇajāham*. *pīlu*.
Jujube, Śamī tree, and Karīra fruit.
kuvala, badara, aśvattha;
The *khadira*, *pīlu*, and so forth; the *karṇa*.
eye / nail / mouth /
Sacrifice / Hair / Foot
Ankle, frown, and tooth.
Lip / Back / Thumb.
The suffix *ti* is applied after a word denoting a side (*pakṣa*) to form the name Karṇādi. (PS 5.2.25)
*tasya* (of that) indeed.
From the word *pakṣa*, when it is in the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the suffix *ti* occurs when the root is to be expressed.
The mention of *mūla* continues,
not the mention of *pākṣa*;
for even among those [terms] taught in a single grammatical rule (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*), it is only one part that continues.
The root of the fortnight is the *pakṣati*, which is the first day (*pratipad*).
The suffixes *cuñcup* and *caṇap* are added after that [word] when it means "wealth. (Pāṇini 5.2.26)
The suffixes *cuñcup* and *caṇap* occur after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyāsamartha*), in the sense of "known" (*vitta*). "Known" (*vitta*) means recognized or understood.
One who is rich in knowledge is *vidyāvittaḥ*, *vidyācuñcuḥ*, or *vidyācaṇaḥ*.
When the negative particles *vi-* and *nañ* are used with [a word ending in] *na*, the suffixes *nā* and *nāñ* respectively are applied, provided that they do not co-occur with the word *saha*.
After the two [prefixes] *vi-* and *nañ*, the two suffixes *nā* and *nāñ* respectively occur.
The term *nasaha* is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*).

The suffixes *na* and *nāñ* occur in the sense of "being with" (*saha*) after the words *vi-* and *nañ*, which here function in the sense of "separation" (*asahārtha*) or "distinctness" (*pṛthagbhāva*). [Thus:
*vinā*;
*nānā*.
After the word *vi*, the suffixes *śālac* and *śaṅkaṭac* are applied.

The suffixes *śālac* and *śaṅkaṭac* occur after the prefix *viśada*. These two suffixes occur after a preposition (*upasarga*) that expresses an action accompanied by its means, in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
When the horns have fallen away, they are "broad" (*viśāla*) and "wide-spreading" (*viśaṅkaṭa*);
because of that connection, the cow itself is also called "broad" and "wide-spreading."
From the perspective of ultimate reality, however, these are words for qualities (*guṇa-śabda*) that are derived through some conventional etymological analysis;
herein there is no dogmatic adherence to the meanings of the root or the suffix.
The suffix *kaṭac* is applied after the verbal roots *saṃ*, *pra*, and *ud*.
The suffix *kaṭac* is applied after the words *sam*, *pra*, and *ud*; by virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), it is also applied after *vi*.
Confined; manifest; intense.
Regarding the word *vikaṭa*:
in the section on *kaṭa*, there is an addition [to the rule] concerning *alābu*, *tila*, *ūma*, and *bhaṅga* when used with the word *rajas*.
Thus, the dust of *alābu* plants is *alābūkaṭa*.
A load of sesame,
a load of linseed,
a load of hemp.
An addition to the rule is that words such as *goṣṭha* ("cow-pen") and others are used with the locative case and so forth when denoting the place of animals, starting from "cows. For example:
*gavāṃ sthānaṃ gogoṣṭham* ("the place of cows is a cow-pen"), *mahiṣīgoṣṭham* ("a buffalo-pen").
The suffix *kaṭac* should be stated after the word *saṅghāta*. Thus, a collection of sheep is *avikaṭam*.
The suffix *paṭac* should be stated after the word *vistāra*.
Without the suffix *apaṭa*:
when there are two, it is *goyuga*; an ox-yoke (pair of oxen) and a camel-yoke (pair of camels).
A pair of horses and oxen (*aśvagoyugam*).
When the meaning of the base word is six, [the suffix] *ṣaṅgava* is applied:
six oxen (*hastiṣaṅgavam*).
