*ekaviṃśatitama*, *ekaviṃśa*;
*triviṃśatitama*, *triviṃśa*.
The thirtieth, the thirtieth;
the thirty-first,
the thirty-first.
The worldly numerals beginning with "twenty" (viṃśati) and so forth are intended here, not those arranged in the grammatical sūtras such as *paṅkti* and the rest;
for if those were taken, [the formation] would not occur from words such as *ekaviṃśati*.
Because there is a prohibition against the application of the rule regarding what ends with that (tadantavidhi) when a nominal stem (prātipadika) itself possesses the suffix [in question],
this being the case, the exclusion (paryudāsa) in the rule *ṣaṣṭyādeś ca asaṅkhyādeḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.58) is indeed appropriate.
The [suffix *ṭhañ*] is used after [words meaning] "hundred" and so forth, as well as after "month," "fortnight," and "year," to express "constant" (*nityam*).

The words beginning with *śata* are understood here as worldly (laukika) numerals. After these, as well as after the words *māsa*, *ardhamāsa*, and *saṃvatsara*, the augment *tamad* is invariably inserted before the suffix *ḍaṭ*.
Words such as *māsa* and others are not numerals;
from this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied after them. For example, "that which completes a hundred" is *śatatamaḥ*.
The thousandth; the hundred-thousandth;
the day that completes the month, the "month-ending" day.
The suffix -tama follows [the words] *ardhamāsa* and *saṃvatsara*,
as well as [words ending in] *ṣaṣṭi* and so forth, provided they do not begin with a numeral (*asaṅkhya*). (Pāṇini 5.2.58)
Since this is already established by what is about to be stated, the inclusion of "hundred" (*śata*) and so forth is for the purpose of including numbers and the like;
[examples are] *ekaśatatamaḥ* (the one hundredth) and *dviśatatamaḥ* (the two hundredth).
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after words beginning with *ṣaṣṭi*, provided they are not numerals (*asaṃkhyā*).
The augment *tamaṭ* is invariably added after the suffix *ḍaṭ* following a numeral beginning with sixty (*ṣaṣṭi*) that does not begin with another numeral.
This is for the purpose of making the rule compulsory, as it would otherwise have been optional by the rule "after *viṃśati* and so forth."
The sixtieth;
the seventieth.
Why [is it said] "of *asaṃkhya* and so forth"? [To exclude cases such as: *ekaṣaṣṭitamaḥ*.
Sixty-first, the sixty-first;
seventy-first, the seventy-first.
And the *mata* [suffix] occurs after the words *sūkta* and *sāman*.
Regarding the word *matau*: the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is expressed here.
The suffix *cha* occurs after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in the sense of possession when a *sūkta* or a *sāman* is to be denoted.

By the inclusion of the sense of possession (*matvartha*), everything is implied: the case-ending expressing semantic competency (*samarthavibhakti*), the qualification of the base (*prakṛtiviśeṣaṇa*), and the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*).
The hymn in which the word *acchāvāka* occurs is the *acchāvākīya* hymn; [the hymn] addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa is the *mitrāvaruṇīya*;
[and] the *yajñāyajñīya* is the *sāman*.
The word *vāravantīyam* and onomatopoeic words produce a suffix when their own form alone is the primary element;
therefore, [the formation] is established even from a multi-word compound.
The suffix *luk* (elision) is applied to the names of chapters (*adhyāya*) and sections (*anuvāka*) [of the Ṛgveda], as in *asyavāmīyam* and *kayāśubhīyam*. (Pāṇini 5.2.60)

The rule "in the sense of *matau*" applies here as well. There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cha* when it occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), provided that the subjects denoted are chapters (*adhyāya*) or sections (*anuvāka*).
But by what means is there an affix for *adhyāya* and *anuvāka*? This very mention of elision (*lug-vacana*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for its application. This elision is intended to be optional.
Because the word *gardabhāṇḍa* occurs in it, the chapter or the section (*anuvāka*) is called *Gardabhāṇḍīya*. [Likewise,] *Dīrghajīvitaḥ*.
Dīrghajīvitīya;
Palitastambha, Palitastambhīya.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words such as *vimukta* and others.
[The rule] "in the case of *mati*" applies as before,
and also [the rule] "of chapters (*adhyāya*) and sections (*anuvāka*)."

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after nominal stems such as *vimukta* and others in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), when the referents are chapters (*adhyāya*) or sections (*anuvāka*). For example, an adhyāya or anuvāka in which the word *vimukta* occurs is called *vaimukta*;
likewise, one containing [the words] *deva* and *asura* is called *daivāsura*.
O liberated one!
O lord of gods and asuras!
O possessor of the earth!
Satvat, Upasat, Daśārhapaya.
Havirdhāna, Mitrī, Somāpūṣan.
Agnāviṣṇū;
Vṛtrahatye;
Iḍā.
O Rakshasa, O Asura,
O existent and non-existent,
O purifier!
Vasu, Marutvat, Patnīvat.
O Mahīyala! O Daśārha! O Vayas!
O winged one!
O Soma! O great mother!
The cause is liberation and so forth.
The suffix *vun* is added after words such as *goṣada*.
[The rule] "in the case of *mati*" applies,
as does [the rule] "of chapters and sections."

The suffix *vun* is added to nominal stems such as *goṣada* and others in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), when referring to a chapter (*adhyāya*) or a section (*anuvāka*). For example: "In this [chapter or section] there is the word *goṣada*" results in *goṣaḍaka* (a chapter or section containing the word *goṣada*). Similarly, *iṣetvaka*.
Mātariśvaka; Goṣad;
iṣe tvā.
O Mātariśvan!
By the impulse of the god!
O divine waters!
Thou art Kṛṣṇa, the most excellent;
[thou art] divine intelligence;
O slayer of Rākṣasas.
Añjana,
Prabhūta, Pratūrta.
*Kṛśānu* belongs to the *goṣad*-class and so forth.
In that regard, the wholesome path is as follows: // PS_5.2.63 //
*vun* indeed.
In this context, the suffix *vun* occurs after the word *pathin*, when it is in the seventh case (*saptamī*) and signifies the sense of "skilled in."
One who is skilled on the road is a guide.
The suffix *kan* is applied after [the verbal roots] *ākarṣa-* and others.
In that regard,
it is simply "there" and also "skilled."

The suffix *kan* is applied after nominal stems such as *ākarṣa* and others when they are in the locative case, in the sense of "skilled in. For example: one who is skilled in *ākarṣa* is an *ākarṣaka*;
[one skilled in] *tsaru* is a *tsaruka*.
Ākarṣa!
Tsaru! Pippasā!
picaṇḍa,
aśani,
aśman.
Investigation,
accumulation,
and victory.
Accumulation,
coming, leading.
Nipāda, Gadgada, Dīpa.
lake / sound / delight
*Śakuni*, *ākarṣa*, and so forth; [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words for wealth and gold in the sense of "desire for. (PS 5.2.65)
In this context, there is the suffix *kan* after the word *tatra*, and also after the word *kan*.
From the words *dhana* and *hiraṇya*, when they are in the seventh case (*saptamī*) in construction with *tatra*, the suffix *kan* occurs in the sense of "desire for that."
*Kāma* means desire or longing. *Dhanakā devadattasya* means Devadatta’s desire for wealth; *hiraṇyakā devadattasya* likewise. [514]
[The suffix *khañ* is applied] after [a word denoting] one's own limbs when there is an extension [of those limbs].

In this context, there is the suffix *kan* as well. From words denoting one's own limbs (*svāṅga*), when they are in the locative case (*saptamī*) and signify "being occupied with" (*prasita*), the suffix *kan* occurs in this sense.
The meaning is "intent," "addicted," or "devoted to. One who is intent on hair is a *keśaka*; one who is devoted to the arrangement of hair is described in this way.
The plural number is used so that it may also apply to a word denoting a collection of one's own body parts:
*dantauṣṭhakaḥ* (having teeth and lips), *keśanakhakaḥ* (having hair and nails).
The suffix *ṭhak* is added after *udara* when it means "less than" (*ūna*).
In that case,
[the term] is *iti* itself, and also *prasita*.

From the word *udara*, when it is in the seventh case (*saptamī*), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "intent upon" (*prasita*). The term *ādhyūna* is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix; one who is not desirous of victory is called *udare-ādhyūna*.

One who is excessively tormented by hunger is called thus: *prasita* in the stomach means *audarika*, i.e., a glutton (*ādyūna*). Why [is the suffix] used in the sense of "gluttonous"? [To show the difference: *udaraka*.
It is completely covered by grain.
Only the suffix *kan* is indicated as being accented, not *ṭhak*. The third-case-competent stem is understood from the very wording of the rule itself.
The suffix *kan* occurs after the word *sasya*, when it is in the third case (instrumental) and conveys the sense of "produced from";
this word *sasya* denotes a quality (*guṇavācin*),
and the prefix *pari-* functions in the sense of "on all sides" (*sarvato bhāve*).
This is the designation for one who is born endowed with virtues and in whom there is not even the slightest deficiency.
That which is produced from grain is *sasyaka*, as in *śālika* (rice-born);
*sasyaka* means excellent;
*sasyaka* refers to a gemstone.
The meaning is "pure in its source."
One who takes a share.
Because the word *aṃśa* is specifically mentioned [in the rule], the suffix *kan* occurs after a word in the second case (*dvitīyāsamartha*) in the sense of "one who takes" (*hārī*). For example:
*aṃśaṃ hārī* = *aṃśakaḥ* (an heir).
*Aṃśakaḥ* means "son.
In the word *hārī*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*).
Since the genitive case is prohibited there, the accusative case alone is used for the object. [515]
When [the object] has been recently removed from its place. (PS 5.2.70)

By the very mention of the word *tantra*, the suffix *kan* occurs after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of "recently removed" (*acirāpahṛta*). "Recently removed" means "removed only a short time ago."
A cloth recently taken from the loom is called *tantraka*; a *tantraka* cloak is likewise so named. That which is fresh is said to be new (*nava*).
The [suffix] uṣṇika is applied after the word *brāhmaṇaka* when forming a name.
The two words *brāhmaṇaka* and *uṣṇika*, ending in the suffix *kan*, are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*) in the sense of a proper name (*saṃjñā*). An example is: *brāhmaṇaka* as a region (*deśa*).
*Uṣṇikā* is a gruel (*yavāgū*). Where there are Brahmins who live by non-combatant means, there the designation *brāhmaṇaka* is used; a gruel containing little food is called *uṣṇikā*.
[The suffix *ṇini* is applied] after [a verbal root] meaning "to cause" when used with the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa* when they denote an agent;
this suffix occurs after a word in the accusative case that functions as an adverbial modifier of an action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
One who makes cold is "śītaka," which means lazy or dull-witted;
one who makes hot is "uṣṇaka."
One who acts swiftly is called skillful.
Excessive. // PS_5.2.73 //
The word *adhika* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). It is formed by the elision of the final member of the compound *adhyārūḍha*, followed by the addition of the suffix *kan*.
Droṇa is more than a khārī;
a khārī is more by a droṇa.
The word *adhyārūḍha* is used [as a compound] with respect to both the agent and the object.
The suffixes *anuka*, *abhika*, and *abhīka* express one who desires.

The words *anuka*, *abhika*, and *abhīka* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) with the suffix *kan* in the sense of "one who desires" (*kamitṛ*). In the case of the prefix *abhi*, lengthening is also irregularly applied.
*anukāmayate* [one who desires after] becomes *anukaḥ*; likewise,
*abhikaḥ* and *abhīkaḥ*.
He seeks [the goal] by means of the side.
From the word *pārśva*, when it is in the third case (instrumental) construction, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of "seeking by means of";
*pārśva* refers to an indirect or crooked means (*anṛjur upāyaḥ*).
One who seeks wealth by such means is called a *pārśvaka*,
a deceiver, a fraudulent person, or a trickster.
The suffixes *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* are applied after the words *ayaḥśūla*, *daṇḍa*, and *ajina*.

"Seeks" (anvicchati) is used as the governing term. When "seeks" is the sense to be expressed, the suffixes *ṭhak* and *ṭhañ* are applied after the words *ayaḥśūla* and *daṇḍājina*, provided they are in the third case (instrumental) construction.

This sharp method is called a "stake" (śūla). One who seeks [gain] by means of that is an *āyaḥśūlika*, meaning one who acts with violence. Deceit (*dambha*) is the staff and antelope skin; one who seeks [gain] by means of that is a *dāṇḍājinika*.
The meaning is "hypocritical.
According to Pāṇini 5.2.77, there is optionally elision (luk) of the suffix in the expression "the *tāvatitha* taking" (*tāvatithaṃ grahaṇam*).
The ordinal number *tāvatithī* denotes the completion of that many items.
A "grahaṇa" is that by which something is grasped.
And this is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*):
the suffix *kan* occurs in its own sense after a nominal stem ending in a ordinal suffix, provided that the stem has "seizing" (*grahaṇa*) as its limiting condition;
there is also elision (*luk*) of either the ordinal suffix or the suffix itself.
By means of the second form, one grasps the text; this is the "twofold grasping":
the second [is] *dvitīyaka*, the third [is] *trikam*, [and] *tṛtīyakam*.

The suffix *kan* should be prescribed after [a word ending in] *tāvatitha* in the sense of "he seizes by that many times," and there must always be elision (*luk*) of the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*). [Examples: *catuṣkam*, *caturthakam*.
By means of the sixth form, one grasps the aggregate: Devadatta is a group of six,
a group of five,
or a group of four.
The particle *iti* serves the purpose of indicating intention (*vivakṣārtha*).
By means of it, it is understood that the reference pertains exclusively to the subject matter of the text, and not to any other subject matter.
He is their leader. (PS 5.2.78)

After a word in the nominative case (prathamāsamartha) signifying "he" (saḥ), the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the genitive (ṣaṣṭhyarthe) to form these [names], provided that the word in the nominative case is *grāmaṇī*.

*Grāmaṇīḥ* means a leader, a chief, or a principal person. *Devadattakaḥ* refers to those for whom Devadatta is the leader (*grāmaṇīḥ*). Thus, "Devadatta's followers" (*devadattakāḥ*) means those of whom Devadatta is the chief.
[The suffix] *kā* [is applied after *brahman*].
Why say "after a village head (*grāmaṇī*)"? [Consider:
"Devadatta is their enemy."
A chain is its bond for a young elephant.

From the word *śṛṅkhala* (chain), when it is used in the nominative case, the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), provided that the nominative base denotes a means of binding.
That which is indicated by "asya" (of this) is the young camel (*karabha*) if it is one;
the chain that is its bond is the *śṛṅkhalaka* (chain-bond). Young camels are called *karabhāḥ*.
A wooden shackle is fastened to their feet;
that is called a "chain" (śṛṅkhala).
Even though ropes and the like are also present there, nevertheless, because the chain is the means for making them dependent, it is called a "bond" (bandhana).
*Utka* means one whose mind is longing.
The word *utka* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) term when it signifies one whose mind is longing.
One whose mind (*manas*) has risen is "unmanāḥ.
From the prefix *ud-*, which expresses an action together with its instrument, the suffix *kan* is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) to denote the possessor of that quality;
thus, "Devadatta is elevated" (*utko devadattaḥ*).
*Utkaḥ* means a traveler;
the meaning is "eager" (*utsukaḥ*).
In the case of disease, [the use of a word may be justified] by reason of time or purpose. (PS 5.2.81)
The case-ending that conveys the sense of capability is to be understood from the context.
When a disease is to be expressed, the suffix *kan* occurs after a word denoting time or purpose, provided it is joined with the appropriate case-ending conveying capability.
Time is the primordial deity;
the purpose is the cause of the disease or its fruit.
A fever that occurs on the second day is called "second-day" (dvitīyaka).
The fourth [type] is from a specific cause: for example, a fever produced by *viṣapuṣpa* flowers is called *viṣapuṣpaka*,
and one produced by *kāśa* flowers is called *kāśapuṣpaka*.
Its effect is heat; thus there is a fever characterized by heat (*uṣṇaka-jvara*) and a fever characterized by cold (*śītaka-jvara*).
From the subsequent sūtra, the mention of "designation" (*saṃjñā*) is drawn back here [to apply to these terms].
By this, this entire rule regarding types is obtained.
Thus, in this context, the term *anna* is used in the sense of "mostly" (*prāye*). (Pāṇini 5.2.82)
The suffix *kan* occurs after a word in the nominative case (*prathamāsamartha*) in the sense of the locative (*asmin*),
provided that the nominative word is food (*anna*) and refers to what constitutes the main part of a meal.
*Prāyaḥ* means "mostly" or "abundantly.

The mention of *sañjñā* (name) is a condition (*upādhi*) for that which ends in [the suffix]. In the sense of "there is mostly molasses-cake (*guḍāpūpa*) in this full-moon day," one forms *guḍāpūpikā*.
The full moon day [is called] *tilāpūpikā*.
The suffix *ini* should be stated after the word *vaṭaka*:
[the full moon day is called] *vaṭakinī*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the word *kulmāṣa*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the word *kulmāṣa*, [forming a name] when that food constitutes the predominant part thereof, provided it is a conventional designation (*saṃjñā*). (*Pāṇini 5.2.83*)
In this sense,
the letter *ñ* is for the purpose of [indicating] the *vṛddhi* accent. *Kaulmāṣī* refers to the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) on which there is generally *kulmāṣa* (sour gruel) as food.
One who has studied the Vedic meters is called a *śrotriya*.
The word *śrotriya* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) term in the sense of "one who has studied the Veda" (*chando 'dhīte*). The letter *n* is for the sake of the accent.
A *śrotriya* is a Brāhmaṇa;
the word *śrotriya* is used for the meaning of the sentence "one who has studied the *chandas*," or it is a transformation of *chandas* into *śrotra*.
The suffix *ghan* is added [to the word *chandas*] in the sense of "one who studies that.
How is it that one says "he studies the *chandas*" (*chandaso 'dhīte*)?
It is because the term *vā* ("or") is understood from the rule *tāvatithaṃ grahaṇam iti lug vā* (Pāṇini 5.2.77). Thus, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) [of the suffix].
The suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are applied [to form adjectives] when the meaning is "this person has eaten this *śrāddha*."
"Śrāddha" is the base form (*prakṛti*);
"by this" (*anena*) is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).

The word *bhukta* (eaten) is a qualifier of the base [noun]. From the word *śrāddha*, when it is characterized by the attribute of being "eaten," the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* occur in the sense of "by means of this.
The word *śrāddha* is a name for a ritual action; it gives rise to the suffix by functioning with respect to the substance that accomplishes that action.
One who has eaten at a *śrāddha* is called a *śrāddhī* or a *śrāddhika*.
It should be understood that the suffixes *-in* and *-thañ* denote simultaneous action.
Let it not be that one who has eaten at a śrāddha today is called "śrāddhika" tomorrow.
The suffix *niḥ* is applied after [stems ending in] *pūrva* and so forth.
In the phrase "by this" (*anena*), the agent (*kartṛ*), which is the meaning of the suffix, is carried over from the previous rule.
Since an agent cannot exist without an action, one must supply some action or other and thereby apply the suffix.
The suffix *ini* occurs after the word *pūrva* in the sense of "by this.
One by whom something was previously gone, drunk, or eaten is called *pūrvī*, *pūrviṇau*, or *pūrviṇaḥ*. [518]
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after a word preceded by *sa*.
Because that which has something preceding it is "sapūrva," namely a nominal stem (*prātipadika*);
by the word "pūrva" [in the rule], there is an extension of the application (*tadantavidhi*) to that which ends with such a [preceded] element.
The suffix *ini* is applied after a nominal stem that ends in the word *pūrva* and is preceded by another word, in the sense of "by this [person]. For example:
*kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat") and *bhuktapūrvī odanam* ("one who has previously eaten rice").
Having formed the compound *sup supā*, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is produced by these two rules: *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.86) and *sapūrvāc ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.87).

Thus, two technical rules (paribhāṣā) are made known: that the treatment as if possessing a designation (vyapadeśivadbhāva) does not apply when a non-prātipadika is involved, and that there is no rule of extension to what ends with a stem (tadantavidhi) when the prātipadika is accompanied by a suffix that causes its own elision (grahaṇavat).
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after words such as *iṣṭa*.
By this very rule, the suffix *ini* is applied after nominal stems such as *iṣṭa* and others in the sense of "by this"; for example,
one who has performed a sacrifice (*iṣṭam anena*) is called *iṣṭī* with respect to the sacrifice.

In the case of *pūrta* and *śrāddha*, the locative case prescribed by the rule "the locus of that which has the sense of *kta* is [in the genitive]" (*ktasyenviṣayasya karmaṇi*) is extended [to these]. As for *iṣṭa*:
Accomplished / brought near / spoken.
Expounded,
narrated,
and fully explained.
Compiled,
recited,
and intended.
unhonored, impaired,
and well-guarded.
Fallen, recited, and conceptualized.
Honored / protected / worshipped.
Enumerated / Calculated / Scattered.
Parita / Āyukta / Āmnāta.
heard, studied, and practiced.
Set aside, conceived, or rejected.
Assisted / brought near / engaged in.
brought near,
conformed to,
recited after.
Agitated,
restrained,
desired, and so forth.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the forms *paripanthin* and *pariparin* are used in the sense of one who stands as an obstacle or an adversary.
The two words *paripanthin* and *pariparin* are prescribed as irregular forms (*nipāta*) in the domain of the Veda (*chandas*), when used to denote one who stands as an obstacle.
The one who overcomes is the antidote; he is called the adversary.
May those who lie in wait find you not; may those who surround you find you not.
One who investigates without following after [the object]. // PS 5.2.90 //
The form *anupadī* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when it denotes a seeker; [it means] "behind a footprint" (*padasya paścāt*), that is, following after a footprint.
Following after the cows; following after the camels.
When the perception [of the object] is directed toward the actual seer. (PS 5.2.91)
The indeclinable word *sākṣāt* takes the suffix *ini* when the meaning to be expressed is "a witness" (*draṣṭṛ*).
The inclusion of the term *sañjñā* is for the purpose of restricting the application [of the suffix] to its designated meaning.
One who sees directly is a *sākṣin*;
[the dual is] *sākṣiṇau*.
Witnesses:
because of the specific mention of the term *sañjñā* (name/label), only the observer is meant, not the giver or the receiver. [519]
A disease that has spread to another's field should be treated by the owner of that other field.

*kṣetriya* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātyate*) used as a complete expression for the sense of "to be treated in another's field. In this context, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the word *parakṣetra*, which stands in the locative case (i.e., ending in *-āt*), in the sense of "to be treated," and the word *para-* is elided. Thus, from *parakṣetre cikitsyaḥ*, the form *kṣetriyaḥ* is derived.

and *prativipāśam*, why is it specified that these are *avyayībhāva* compounds?

*pāramaśaraḥ*. Those [compounds] which are taught here as being understood [as such] are included for the sake of their being eternal (*nitya*). And this mention of *avyayībhāva* is intoned (*svarita*) [to apply] prior to *bahuvrīhi*.
Autumn / Vipāś / Cart.
Mind,
the upper leather thong, heaven.
himavat,
anaḍuh, diś.
dṛś, uatur,
yad.
Therefore,
for *jarā*, [the substitute] is *jara* as well;
it is similar.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *akṣi* following the prefixes *prati*, *para*, *sama*, and *anu*;
[and] *pathin* [takes the suffix *ṭac*].
Thus: *pratyakṣam*.
Out of sight; in the presence of; immediately after.
Along the path; along another's path; along the common path.
The path of following.
And [the suffix *ana* is used] after a root ending in *a*. (PS 5.4.108)
The suffix *ṭac* is added as a compound-final element after an indeclinable *avyayībhāva* compound that ends in *an*. For example: *uparājam*.
Toward each king;
internally;
individually.
After a neuter [stem], [the suffix *śas*] is optionally [used].
The word *anaḥ* alone [is the referent]. The mention of the neuter gender (*napuṃsaka*) is a qualifier of the final member of the compound (*uttarapada*).

The suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) after an *avyayībhāva* compound that ends in a neuter word having the stem-final *an*. Since the previous rule would have made this suffix mandatory, it is here made optional. Example:
*praticarmam*.
Praticarma;
upacarma, upacarma.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *nadī*, *paurṇamāsī*, and *āgrahāyaṇī*.
The suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied after an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) ending in "nadī," "paurṇamāsī," or "āgrahāyaṇī. For example:
*upanadam* or *upanadi*, meaning "near the river."
upapaurṇamāsam, upapaurṇamāsi;
upāgrahāyaṇam.
Upāgrahāyaṇī.
It is to be known. // PS_5.4.111 //
The mention of *jñayaḥ* is for the purpose of including the entire *pratyāhāra*. The suffix *ṭac* optionally occurs after an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in a word belonging to the *jña* class.
upasamimidham, upasamit;
upadṛṣadam, upadṛṣat.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *giri*. (PS 5.4.112)
The suffix *ṭac* is applied after an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in the word *giri*, according to the opinion of the teacher Senaka:
*antargiram*, *antargiri*.
Upagiram and upagiri;
the mention of Senaka is for the sake of honor;
the option indeed continues to apply. [584]
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṣac* is added after *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote one's own limbs (*svāṅga*).
The suffix *ṣac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the words *sakthi* or *akṣi* when they denote one's own limbs (*svāṅga*).
This is the intended meaning.
In the Sūtra, however, there are words with irregular case endings:
for example, *dīrghasakthaḥ* (long-thighed), meaning "one whose thigh is long," and *kalyāṇākṣaḥ* (beautiful-eyed).
*lohitākṣaḥ* (red-eyed),
*viśālākṣaḥ* (large-eyed).
Why [is the condition] "in a bahuvrīhi compound" stated?
*paramasakthiḥ*, *paramākṣiḥ*. Why [is it said] "of *sakthi* and *akṣi*"? [To exclude cases such as: *paramaśakthaḥ*, *paramākṣaḥ*.
*dīrghajānuḥ* (long-kneed), *subāhuḥ* (fair-armed).
Why [is it said] "from its own member" (*svāṅgāt*)? [To exclude cases like: *dīrghapādaḥ* (long-footed).
*Śakaṭa-* [means] "long-thighed"; *ikṣu-* [means] "thick-eyed.
Although the suffix *ṭac* was already applicable, the mention of *ṣac* is for the sake of the accent.
*Cakrasakthī* [means] "a woman with wheel-like thighs."
In the word *dīrghasakthī* (a woman with long thighs),
the rule *sakthaṃ cākrāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.198) prescribes that the final syllable of the second member is optionally acute (*antodātta*).

In that case, in the alternative where there is no acute accent (*udāttatva*), when the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, because the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara* would be absent, an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel would be heard.
However, with the suffix *ṅīṣ*, an acute accent is established everywhere.
The mention of "bahuvrīhi" continues in force until the end of the chapter.
[The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *aṅguli* when it occurs in the sense of] "wood. // PS_5.4.114 //

The suffix *ṣac* occurs as a compound-final element after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *aṅguli*, when "wood" (*dāru*) is the meaning of the compound. For example: *dvyaṅgulam dāru* ("two-finger-width wood").
A wooden piece three finger-breadths long,
or five finger-breadths long,
with parts resembling fingers, is called a wooden measure for scattering grain and other such items.

However, in the case of *dāruṇaḥ* (wood) where two fingers (*aṅguli*) are the measure, since it is a *taddhita* compound, the suffix *ac* should apply by the rule *tatpuruṣe aṅguleḥ* [Pāṇini 5.4.86]. Why say "in wood" (*dāruṇi*)? [To exclude cases like:
*pañcāṅguliḥ hastaḥ* (a hand with five fingers).
After the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *mūrdhan*, the suffix *ṣa* (which becomes *au*) is applied.
The suffix *ṣa* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *mūrdhan*, provided that it follows two or three [syllables]. For example:
*dvimūrdhaḥ*.
*trimūrdhaḥ*.
Why [is it said] "after *dvi* and *tri*"? [Consider:
*uccair mūrdhā*.
The suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of completion (*pūraṇa*) and as a standard of measure (*pramāṇa*).
Words ending in ordinal suffixes that are feminine are included by the mention of the term *pūraṇī*.
The term *pramāṇī* is used here to denote its own form (*svarūpa*).
The suffix *ap* is added as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a word denoting a full number (*pūraṇa*) or a word denoting a measure (*mānīya*). For example:
"Of these nights, the fifth is auspicious" results in *kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ*;
"the tenth is auspicious" results in *kalyāṇīdaśamā rātrayaḥ*.
"Women are the authority for these" means "householders whose authority is women," that is to say, those for whom the wife is the primary authority.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *pūraṇī* (feminine ordinal) as the primary [member of the compound] must be made.

Where the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇī*) enters into the meaning of the external member (*anyapadārtha*) and not merely into the meaning of the compound member itself, there the ordinal suffix possesses predominance;
even when the substitution of the masculine form is prohibited, it is precisely the predominant ordinal suffix that is understood.
In this case, it does not occur;
for example, "the fortnight in which the fifth day is auspicious" (kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ). There is an addition [to the rule] regarding a constellation following a leader (netaḥ). [585]
The deer is the leader of these nights; thus, "deer-eyed" (mṛganetrā) refers to the nights.
[Similarly,] "Puṣya-eyed" (puṣyanetrāḥ).
Why specify "in the sense of a lunar mansion" (nakṣatre)? [To exclude cases such as: *mṛgākṣī* ("deer-eyed woman").
[The suffix -ka is added] after words denoting a leader (netṛ). There is also an extension [of this rule] for the Vedic language (chandas) regarding a leader:
*vṛhaspatinetrā devāḥ* ("the gods led by Bṛhaspati").

Somanetrāḥ. The suffix *ṭhac* is prescribed after a word ending in *māsa* when it functions as the first member of a compound denoting wages (*bhṛti*). For example, one whose wage for five months is [five coins] is a *pañcakamāsika* laborer.

“*Daśakamāsikaḥ*. According to the rule *so ’syāṃśavasnabhṛtayaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.56), and by the rule *saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.52), the suffix *kan* is applied after a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śan*.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the words *antara* and *bahis* when followed by *loman*.
The suffix *ap* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *loman* when preceded by either *antar* or *bahis*. For example: *antarlomaḥ prāvāraḥ* ("a cloak with hair on the inside").
A garment with the hair on the outside.
In the sense of "nose," the word *nasa* is substituted for *añ*, provided that the word is not *asthūla*.
The suffix *ac* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *nāsikā*, and the word *nāsikā* does not undergo substitution.
*asthūlāt* is a qualifier of *nāsikā*, meaning that the word *nāsikā* does not follow the word *sthūla*;
*sañjñāyām* is a condition (*upādhi*) for the entire compound.
The word *druriva* means "having a nose like wood";
it is [the compound] *druṇasaḥ*. In *vādgrīṇasaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] according to the rule *pūrvapadāt sañjñāyām agaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3).
*gonasaḥ*.
Why is it said "in the sense of a name"? [Consider:
*tuṅganāsikaḥ*.
Why [is the word] *asthūla* mentioned? [To exclude cases such as:
"a boar with a thick snout" (*sthūlanāsikaḥ varāhaḥ*).
It should be stated that the suffix *naṅ* is applied after the words *khura* and *khara*.
*Khuraṇāḥ* and *kharaṇāḥ*;
in the alternative case, the suffix *ac* is also desired.
Khuraṇas, Kharaṇas,
Śitinās, Ahinas.
"Archanāḥ" is thus declared in the Veda.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after a preverb as well. (Pāṇini 5.4.119)
The suffix *ac* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *nāsikā* when it follows a prefix (*upasarga*),
and the word *nāsikā* is not elided.
The word is used for the sake of negation.
One whose nose is elevated is *unnasaḥ*; one with a prominent nose is *pranasaḥ*.
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "after a prefix, diversely" (*upasargād bahulam*, Pāṇini 8.4.28).
It should be stated that there is the substitution of *g* for *v*. One whose nose has departed is "noseless" (*vigraḥ*).
The words *suprāta*, *suśva*, *sudiva*, *śārikukṣa*, *caturaśra*, *eṇīpad*, *ajapada*, and *proṣṭhapad* [are neuter].
The bahuvrīhi compounds beginning with *suprāta* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) by means of the suffix *-ac*;
furthermore, other features such as the elision of the *ṭi*-portion are established solely through these irregular formations.
His morning is auspicious:
*suprātaḥ*. His tomorrow is auspicious: *suśvaḥ*. His day is auspicious: *sudivaḥ*.
His belly is like that of a śāri bird, thus he is Śārikukṣa; he has four corners, thus he is Caturaśra;
his feet are like those of an enī antelope, thus he is Eṇīpada.
Like the feet of a goat (aja), these are "goat-footed" (ajapada). Like the feet of a bull with a dewlap (proṣṭha), these are "dewlap-footed" (proṣṭhapada).

After the negative particle *nañ*, the word *duḥ*, or the prefix *su*, when followed by a consonant, the forms *anyatara* and *anya* optionally take the suffix *āC* (forming feminine bases in *-ā*) in the sense of "other than. (Pāṇini 5.4.121)

After the words *nañ*, *dus*, and *su*, when the words *hali* and *sakthi* follow, the suffix *ac* optionally occurs at the end of that *bahuvrīhi* compound as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). For example:
*avidyamānā haliḥ asya* results in *ahalaḥ* or *ahaliḥ*.
durhalaḥ, durhaliḥ;
suhalaḥ, suhaliḥ;
one whose thigh is non-existent is asakthaḥ, asakthiḥ.
duḥsakthaḥ,
duḥsakthiḥ; susakthaḥ, susakthiḥ.
Some read "hali-śaktyoḥ. One whose power (*śakti*) is non-existent is "powerless" (*aśakta*), [which is] *aśakti*.
One whose power is deformed is "weakly powerful" (*duḥśakta*).
*duḥśaktaḥ*, *duḥśaktiḥ*; one whose power is excellent is *suśaktaḥ*, *suśaktiḥ*.
The suffix *as* is always applied after the words *prajā* and *medhā*.

This applies specifically to the rule *nañ-dussubhyaḥ*. After the words *prajā* and *medhā*, when they follow *nañ*, *dus*, or *su*, the suffix *asic* is invariably added to the *bahuvrīhi* compound as its final member.
His offspring being non-existent:
he is childless; he has bad offspring; he has good offspring.
One who lacks intelligence is *amedhas*;
one with poor intelligence is *durmedhas*; one with excellent intelligence is *sumedhas*.
What is the purpose of including the word *nitya* (always),
given that in the preceding rule the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) is not even accented?
If this is so, then by the inclusion of *nitya*, it is indicated that [the operation] occurs elsewhere as well.
O King, like that of a dull-witted and small-minded Vedic scholar, your intellect is destroyed by mere rote recitation; it does not perceive the true meaning of reality.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *cha* is used after words meaning "having many offspring."
The form *bahuprajāḥ* is an irregularity (*nipātana*) in the Vedic language (*chandasi*); for example:
"Bahuprajā entered Nirṛti."
Why "in the Veda" (chandasi)? [Consider:
*bahuprajaḥ brāhmaṇaḥ* ("a Brahmin with many offspring").
The suffix *aniC* is applied after the word *dharma* when it occurs alone.

The suffix *anic* is applied as a compound-final element after a *bahuvrīhi* that ends in the word *dharma*, provided that *dharma* occurs alone [without being preceded by another word]. For example: one whose dharma is auspicious is *kalyāṇadharmā*.
"Priyadharma" means one who is fond of the Dharma. "Kevalāt" means from the absolute. "Paramasvadharma" means his own supreme Dharma.

If this were so, it would apply to a three-word *bahuvrīhi* such as "paramaḥ svo dharmaḥ asya" (for whom the highest is his own duty). In that case, the word "from a simple [word]" (*kevalāt*) is specified as the preceding member (*pūrvapada*).

The suffix [denoting "one who eats"] is applied after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in the word *dharma*, provided that the word *dharma* occurs as a single, independent member and not as part of a larger compound;
[this applies] after *jambha*, *suharit*, *tṛṇa*, and *soma*. (PS 5.4.125)

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when the word *jambha* follows words beginning with *su*, it is prescribed as the final member (*uttarapada*) with the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) applied; the word *jambha* denotes both that which is to be consumed (*abhyavahārya*) and a particular kind of tooth. For example: *sujambhā devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta has beautiful teeth").
One with beautiful food, or one with beautiful teeth;
likewise, one with green gums,
or one with grass-like gums.
Regarding *somajambha*—
in the case of words meaning "tooth"— the analysis (*vigraha*) should be understood as either "one whose chewing (*jambha*) is like grass" or "one whose chewing is like the Soma plant."
Why [is the rule] stated as "after *su*, *harita*, *tṛṇa*, and *soma*"? [Consider:
*patitajambhaḥ*.
One should not be greedy for the sacrificial fee. // PS 5.4.126 //

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when used in connection with a hunter (*lubdha*), the form *dakṣiṇermā* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word with the vowel lengthening (*sāman-ta*) applied; for example:
"this deer has a wound on its right side" is *dakṣiṇermā mṛgaḥ*.
*Īrma* means a wound.
The meaning is that his right limb has been wounded by a hunter. Why [is the condition] "in connection with *lubdha*" stated?
The cart is on the right side.
The suffix *ic* is used after a verbal root when there is a reciprocal exchange of action.
The suffix *ic* is added to a *bahuvrīhi* compound that expresses a reciprocal action; in this case,
it is applied according to the rule *tatra tenedam iti sarūpe* (Pāṇini 2.2.27).
Thus, this is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound:
"having seized each other by the hair, this battle proceeded"— that is,
*keśākeśi* or *kacākaci*.
Having struck with clubs (*musalaiḥ*) and pestles (*musalaiḥ*), this battle proceeded as a "club-against-club" (*musalāmusali*) fight and a "staff-against-staff" (*daṇḍādaṇḍi*) fight;
for this suffix *ic* is taught [by Pāṇini] in the rule beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu*.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *dvidaṇḍi* and so forth. (PS 5.4.128)
Words such as *dvidaṇḍi* and others, ending in the suffix *ic*, are grammatically correct.
In the expression *dvidaṇḍyādibhyaḥ*, this is a dative case (caturthī) used in the sense of "for the purpose of" (*tādarthye*), not an ablative case (pañcamī).
The suffix *ic* is introduced for the sake of forms such as *dvidaṇḍi*; the meaning is that it is so that words like *dvidaṇḍi* are successfully formed.
Furthermore, because they are established as specific compounds (*samudāya-nipātana*), they are restricted to particular meanings:
*dvidaṇḍi praharati* ("he strikes with two sticks").
One strikes with two pestles;
here [the compound] does not occur,
as in the case of "a hall with two pillars" (*dvidaṇḍā śālā*).
Even within the governing rule for *bahuvrīhi* compounds, some authorities maintain that this [suffix] is prescribed after certain *tatpuruṣa* compounds:
*nikucya karṇau dhāvati* (he runs with his ears tucked in) becomes *nikucyakarṇi dhāvati*;
*prohya pādau hastinaṃ vāhayati* (he drives the elephant after lifting its feet) becomes *prodyapādi hastinaṃ vāhayati*.
The compound is formed according to the rule for *mayūravyaṃsaka* and other such terms.
The two-staff posture; the two-club posture; the joined-palms posture.
With both hands joined in añjali; with both hands at the ears; with both hands reaching to the ears.
ubhādanti,
ubhayādanti,
ubhāhasti.
With both hands;
with both palms; with both palms.
Ubhābāhu, ubhayābāhu,
ekapadi.
prohyapadi, āḍhyapadi, sapati.

*Nikucyakarṇi* (one with ears drawn in), *saṃhatapucchi* (one with a contracted tail); in *ubhābāhu*, *ubhayābāhu*, there is the elision of the suffix *ic* due to [the rule of] irregular formation (*nipātana*).
By the definition of a *pratyaya* (suffix), the designation *avyayībhāva* is applied.
[588] After the words *pra* and *sam*, the substitute *jñu* is used for *jānu*. (Pāṇini 5.4.129)
By means of these two [prefixes], *pra* and *sam*, the word *jñu* is substituted for the final member *jānu* in a *bahuvrīhi* compound that ends in a *samāsānta* suffix; for example,
one whose knees are extended is *prajñuḥ*.
The two perceptions.
After [a word ending in] "ūrdhva," [the suffix -tasi is applied] optionally.
After the word *ūrdhva*, the substitution *jñu* optionally occurs for the word *jānu*. [Thus:
*ūrdhve jānunī asya* becomes *ūrdhvajānuḥ*.
With his knees raised.
After the word *ūdhas*, the substitute *anaṅ* is applied [in place of the final vowel and the following consonant].

The substitute *anaṅ* occurs at the end of a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose final member is the word *ūdhas*, serving as the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). For example: "she whose udder is like a jar" is *kuṇḍodhnī*.
*Ghaṭodhnī*. The mention of "feminine" (*strī*) must be made [in the rule] regarding *ūdhas-* when *anaṅ* is applied; it should not apply here: *mahodhāḥ parjanyaḥ*.
A cow that has recently calved is called *ghaṭodhnī*.
And [the same applies] to the word *dhanus*. (Pāṇini 5.4.132)
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *dhanus*, the substitute *anaṅ* occurs as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). For example:
"He whose bow is made of horn" is *śārṅgadhanvā*.
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow;
the one whose bow is made of flowers; the one whose bow has its string drawn.
Or [the suffix *khañ* is applied] after a word denoting a name (*saṃjñā*). // PS_5.4.133 //

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *dhanus*, the substitution of *an* optionally occurs when it denotes a proper name (*saṃjñā*). This is an optional rule that supersedes the obligatory application established by the preceding [sūtra].
Śatadhanuḥ,
Śatadhanvā; Dṛḍhadhanuḥ.
Dṛḍhadhanvan (the one with the firm bow).
The suffix *niṅ* is used after the word *jāyā*.
The substitute *niṅ* occurs for the word *jāyā* at the end of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For example:
"one whose wife is young" is *yuvajāniḥ*.
The word *vṛddha* is substituted for *jāni-* [in a bahuvrīhi compound].
[589] The suffix *it* is applied after the word *gandha* when it follows *ut*, *pūti*, or *su-surabhi*. (Pāṇini 5.4.135)

After these words—*ut*, *pūti*, and *su surabhi*—the word *gandha* undergoes the substitution of *i* for its final vowel when forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound; this *i* serves as the final member of the compound.
The letter *t* is for the sake of pronunciation.
Its fragrance has arisen, thus it is "fragrant" (udgandhi);
[it may be] "putrid-fragrant" (pūtigandhi) or "sweet-fragrant" (sugandhi).
"Surabhigandhiḥ.
Why [is it said] "from these"? [For example:
"tīvragandho vātaḥ" (a wind of pungent odor).
In the case of *gandha*, there is the exclusive application of that [suffix]. Therefore, one who has a beautiful fragrance is *sugandha-āpaṇikaḥ* (a merchant with a fine scent).
In the case of expressing smallness, [the suffix *kan* is applied]. (PS 5.4.136)

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when the sense is "a little," the word *gandha* undergoes the substitution of the vowel *i* as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). For example: *sūpo 'lpo 'smin* [there is little soup in this] = *sūpagandhi bhojanam* (a meal with a little soup).
In this food there is little ghee; it has the scent of ghee,
the scent of milk—
the word "scent" (gandha) is used here in a secondary sense.
And [the suffix *kalpa* is used] after a word expressing a standard of comparison. (PS 5.4.137)

When the word *gandha* follows a term used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the substitution of *i* for its final vowel occurs as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For example:
"that which has a fragrance like a lotus" is *padmagandhiḥ*.
Utpalagandhi; Karīṣagandhi.
The elision of the final syllable of the word *pāda* occurs when it follows [words] other than *hastin* and so forth.
"From a standard of comparison" (upamānāt) alone [is understood].
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is elision (*lopa*) of the word *pāda* following a standard of comparison that excludes words such as *ihasti*, and this serves as the final member of the compound.
The status of the elision as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) is understood by way of its locus [the original word]. For example:
*vyāghrapāt* ("tiger-footed") from "he whose feet are like those of a tiger," and *siṃhapāt* ("lion-footed").
Why [is it specified] "after *hasti* and so forth"? [Consider:
*hastipādaḥ*, *kaṭolapādaḥ*.
Hastin, Kaṭola, Gaṇḍola.
A female attendant, a woman, or a female slave.
A courtesan; a granary.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words ending in *kumbhapada*. (PS 5.4.139)
The words *kumbhapadī* and others, in which the [suffix] *pāda* has been elided, are taught as complete lexical items (*samudāya*). In that regard, the rule (*sūtra*) should be understood as follows.

The elision of the [first] member occurs in the case of *kumbhapadī* and so forth, as in the words *kumbhapadī* and others; they are thus established. Furthermore, the purpose of reciting them as a collective group is to restrict their scope: [the suffix applies] only in the feminine gender.
In that case, it occurs only when the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and not otherwise:
*kumbhapadī*,
*śatapadī*.

*ayodatī*.
*phāladatī*;
why [is it said] "in the sense of a name" (*sañjñāyām*)? [Consider: *samadantī*, *snigdhadantī*.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* is applied after the words *śyāva* and *aroka*.
By means of these two [words], *śyāva* and *aroka*, the word *danta* that follows them optionally takes the substitute *datṛ* when forming a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a suffix;

*Śyāvadantaḥ* and *arokadantaḥ*. [PS 5.4.145] Also after *agra*, *anta*, *śuddha*, *śubhra*, *vṛṣan*, and *varāha*.

"One whose hump has not yet grown" means one whose hump is unformed; that is to say, a fool. "One with a full hump."

Vikākut:

After the word *pūrṇa*, there is an option.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *kākuda*, when it follows the word *pūrṇa*, optionally undergoes elision. For example:

*priyasarpiṣkaḥ*,

In this regard, the purpose is that here only those ending in the singular number should be understood to be included, so that those ending in the dual and plural numbers are not [included].

A city with many parasols; a city with many masters;

The rule "śeṣadvibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 5.4.154) applies here.

The suffix *kap* is added after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *nadī* (river) and after one ending in the vowel *ṛ*. For example: "In this region there are many young women" (*bahvyaḥ kumārya asmin deśe*) becomes *bahukumārīko deśaḥ* ("the region having many young women").
It has many *brahmabandhu*s.

Regarding the statement "the *bahvṛc* hymn," since the suffix for a compound ending in *ṛṣi* or *pūḥ* is prescribed here in a general sense,

That [suffix] is desired in the sense of a specific distinction: "One who does not know the Ṛgveda is to be known as a Māṇavaka; one who knows the Bahvṛca is so called by way of his Vedic school (caraṇa).

*bahuśreyasī* [is formed] from *bahvyaḥ śreyasyaḥ asya*; there is a prohibition of the [suffix] *ṅīp* by the rule *nady-ṛtaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.153).
Nor does shortening occur, because of the rule stating that in a bahuvrīhi compound, the feminine suffix of an īyas suffix is treated as masculine.
When one's brother has been saluted. // PS_5.4.157 //

When the word *bhrātṛ* (brother) occurs in the sense of "one who is honored," the suffix *kap* is not applied to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in that word. "Honored" (*vandita*) means praised or worshipped.

One who has a wicked brother.

In the Vedic domain, the suffix *kap* is not applied to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a vowel or the letter *ṛ*. For example: *hatamātā* ("one whose mother has been killed").
One whose father has been slain; one whose sister has been slain; Suhotṛ.
The locative case endings are used for *nāḍī* and *tantrī* when they denote one's own limbs.

A pillar has many channels;
a lute has many strings.

They weave with it, thus it is called *prāvāṇī*;

The sixth chapter begins; first quarter: "The first [consonant] of a single-vowel [syllable] is doubled. (PS 6.1.1)
This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*); it applies both to this [section] and to the rule "ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.10).
It should be understood that the triad consisting of "two," "of the first," and "of the [monosyllabic root]" is the governing rule.
From this point forward, until the prescription of *saṃprasāraṇa*, whatever we shall state there should be understood as follows: "of a monosyllabic [root], two [sounds] occur for the first."

He will state [later]: "In the case of the *liṭ* suffix, for a non-reduplicated root" (*6.1.8*). In that context, two occurrences of the first *ekāc* (monosyllabic) member of a non-reduplicated root are substituted;
as in *jajāgāra*.
He cooked;
he went; he went.

The term *ekāc* is a Bahuvrīhi compound. Its analysis (*vigraha*) by way of its constituent parts is: "that which has one vowel (*ac*) is *ekāc*. In this context, the collective whole (*samudāya*) is the meaning of the compound.
And since a constituent part (avayava) exists within a composite whole (samudāya), there is reduplication of only that which consists of a single vowel (sāckasya).

Thus, in the case of *pac*, by the very same vowel (*ac*) through which the whole is "single-voweled" (*ekāc*), the constituent parts— the sound *ac* and the sound *pa*— are likewise [single-voweled].
In that case, it is not stated twice because of each individual monophthongic vowel, but rather because of the single monophthongic vowel of the entire aggregate.
For instance, by the single application of a grammatical rule, a composite whole consisting of parts is benefited.
In the case of *papāca*, the status of being "first" (*prathamatva*) arises through the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treatment as if possessing a designation).
Likewise, in the cases of *iyāya* and *āra*, the status of having a single vowel (*ekāctva*) also arises solely through *vyapadeśivadbhāva*.
And this "doubling" (dvirvacana) is a double application;
for the number two is prescribed as a repetition. Therefore, that very same word is uttered twice.
And no other word is prescribed in its place.
Of a reduplicated stem beginning with a vowel, the second syllable is reduplicated.
This is an exception to the first doubling [rule]. The doubling of the second monosyllabic member (*ekaca*) of a root beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) is now prescribed.
Of that verbal root which begins with *a*, two instances of its second *ekāc* (single-consonant) portion occur;
as in *aṭiṭiṣati* and *aśiśiṣati*.
In *aririṣati*,
the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *smi-pūṅ-rañjv-aśāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 7.2.74).
When that [substitution] has been performed, and when *r* follows [the letter], the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies by virtue of the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59).
To this, the counter-argument is stated: "in the case of an *ac* which is the cause of reduplication."
And here, the augment *iṭ* is not the cause for the doubling;
rather, it is the subject of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*).
And that which is the subject of the operation is not accepted as being the cause.

For instance, when the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* caused by suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ* is being prescribed, it does not apply in the case of *śayitā*, because the root *śīṅ*, which is the recipient of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*), does not function as the cause (*nimitta*) for that *guṇa*. Regarding this,
some maintain that the ablative case in the rule *ajādeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.2) is derived from a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Furthermore, "ajādi" means that which both begins with 'a' (aj) and is the first (ādi);
therefore, according to the rule "the single vowel following an ajādi [root] becomes doubled," one should understand that the phrase "of those, the second" is stated for the sake of clarity.
The *n*, *r*, and the first consonants of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) do not [undergo doubling]. (PS 6.1.3)

The term "of the second" (dvitīyasya) is understood [to carry over] from the preceding rule. Since the *n*, *r*, and *ṛ* sounds that constitute parts of the second monosyllable (*ekāc*) are included within it, the resulting reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would otherwise apply; this [present rule] prohibits that.
The *nakāra*, *dakāra*, and *repha* that constitute parts of a second single-consonant (*ekāc*) cluster are not doubled; for example:
*undidiṣati* and *aḍḍiḍiṣati*.
[The forms] arciciṣati and indrāḥ [are examples]; why [is it said]? Because [in the case of] īcikṣiṣate [the rule does not apply].
What is the purpose of [the mention of] "conjunctions and so forth"? [Consider:
*prāṇiṇiṣati*. Here, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rules "after *ani*" (Pāṇini 8.4.19) and "both [nasals], when there is an abhyāsa" (Pāṇini 8.4.21).
"Only [the rule] *ajādeḥ* applies," as in *diddrāsati*.
Some also maintain that *ajādeḥ* is a locative-ending *karmadhāraya* compound;
the purpose of this is as follows:
In the case of *indidrīyiṣati*,
because there is no immediate succession (*anantaratva*) following a vowel-initial element, the letter *d* is indeed reduplicated,
but the letter *n* is not reduplicated.
From the form *indra*, [the suffix] *kyac* is applied in the sense "he desires Indra" (*indram icchati*).
From that which ends in *kyac*, [the suffix] *san* is applied in the sense "he desires to act like Indra" (*indrīyitum icchati*).
It should also be stated that this prohibition applies to the letter *b* as well.

*ubjijiṣati*. When the root *ubj* is taught with the letter *b* as its penultimate (*bakaropadha*), then this prohibition applies; however, when it is taught with the letter *d* as its penultimate (*dakāropadha*), it need not be stated.
However, *batva* (the substitution of *b*) must be prescribed for the letter *d*.
It should be stated that there is no prohibition of the substitution of *r* when it follows the letter *y*.
[Thus,] *arāryate*.
The suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule "the addition of *yaṅ* for the roots *aṭ*, *arti*, and *śūrṇoti*" (Pāṇini 7.4.82).
In that context, *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule "and in the presence of *yaṅ*" (Pāṇini 7.4.30), followed by reduplication.
It should be stated that for the third [type of person], there are two [types of non-restraint].
For which third one?
Some say it is for the indeterminate (vyañjana).
*īrṣyiyiṣati*.
Others, however, explain the third [form] as having a single consonant (*ekāc*),
resulting in *īrṣyiṣiṣati*.
It should be stated that for the roots beginning with *kaṇḍū* (Pāṇini 3.1.27), the third monosyllabic portion undergoes reduplication:
*kaṇḍūyiyiṣati*,
*asuyiyiṣati*.
Alternatively, it should be stated that for nominal stems (*nāmadhātu*) beginning with a third [consonant] followed by a single vowel, the reduplication consists of two syllables:
*aśvīyiyiṣati*,
*aśiśvīyiṣati*.
Another says: it should be stated that [the application of] nominal stems and verbal roots occurs according to one's wish;
for example, *puputrīyiṣati* and *putitrīyiṣati*.
putrīyiyiṣati; puputitrīyiyiṣati; putrīyiṣiṣati.
The former practice [is the cause]. (PS 6.1.4)
The word *dve* (two), which follows in the nominative case (*prathamāntam*), is understood here by implication to be in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyantam*). Therefore,
in this context, that which is the first constituent of those two [sounds] that have been prescribed is designated as the *abhyāsa* (reduplication).
He cooked;
he desires to cook;
he cooks repeatedly.
He sacrifices (*juhoti*); he caused to cook (*apīpacat*).
However, in this context, there are rules for the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), such as "there is elision of the reduplication" (*lopo 'bhyāsasya*, Pāṇini 7.4.58).
And so forth.
Both [are called] *abhyasta* (repeated). 6.1.5.
While the word "two" (dve) is understood [from the previous rule], the mention of "both" (ubhe) is for the purpose of establishing a collective designation (*samudāya-sañjñā*).
Only those two which have been prescribed, when joined together as a pair, receive the designation of "repeated" (*abhyasta*).
He gives; giving; let them give.

What is the purpose of including the word "both" (*ubhe*)? It is so that in the case of *nenijati*, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) may apply to the entire group according to the rule "the first of reduplicated [roots] is acute," and not to each individual [syllable] alternately.
"Abhyastapradeśāḥ" refers to those rules beginning with *abhyastānām ādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.189), and so forth.
The six beginning with *jakṣ* [are also used in the present tense]. (Pāṇini 6.1.6)
The term *abhyasta* (repeated) continues [from the previous rule]. This verbal root *jakṣ* and six other roots beginning with it receive the technical designation *abhyasta*.
This designation "abhyasta" (reduplicated) is prescribed for these seven roots,
starting from *jakṣa* in the sense of eating and laughing, up to *vevīṅ*, which is equivalent to *veti*. [Thus,] *jakṣati*.
They wake;
they suffer from poverty;
they shine.
In the forms *śāsati*,
*dīdhyate*, and *vevyate*, the purpose [of this rule] is the accentuation of the initial syllable of reduplicated (abhyasta) stems.

Furthermore, in the case of *dīdhyat*, which is derived from the present participle suffix *śatṛ* by means of a transposition of elements (*vyatyaya*), the rule *na abhyastāc chatuḥ* (*Pāṇini 6.1.178*) applies.
Thus ends the prohibition regarding the *num* augment.
In the case of roots beginning with *tuj* and others, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable.
The word *ādi* in the rule *tujādīnām* indicates a class;
and what is that class?
The lengthening of the reduplication is not prescribed for *tuj* and the others, yet it is observed; those [roots] that are of such a nature as *tuj* and so forth—
for them, the lengthening of the reduplication is correct.
Exerting himself,
bestowing gifts,
the ox has sustained [the world].
He has measured out the vow;
he has supported it; he has grown strong. And this [suffix] *tū* is seen in the Veda only after a specific suffix, even when it is long.
It does not exist elsewhere than from that;
from that, the dappled bay horses were born.
In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix, reduplication occurs for a verbal root that is not already a reduplicated base.

When the *liṭ* suffix follows, two [instances] of the first or second *ekāc* (single-consonant) syllable of a verbal root—provided it is not a reduplicated root—are substituted according to the appropriate rule. For example:
*papāca*.
He recited: *prorṇunāva*.
