The word *vṛkṣāvṛśyaḥ* [is formed] for the sake of [distinguishing] its own vowel-quality (*savarṇa*) and for the sake of excluding the nasalization (*anigra*). This is the statement.
When [a suffix] occurs after [a verbal root] ending in -aplu, it is as if it were preceded by the augment -aṭ. (Pāṇini 6.1.129)
*Upasthita* refers to a non-Vedic *atikaraṇa* by which a word is extracted from a compound and established in its own form.
In that case, a protracted vowel (*pluta*) following another [vowel] behaves as if it were not protracted;
it does not undergo the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) rule which applies to a protracted vowel.
For example: *suśloka3 iti* becomes *suśloketi*.
"Sumaṅgala, O Sumaṅgala!"—
what is the purpose of including the particle *vat*?
If it were stated simply as "apluta" (non-protracted), only the protracted (*pluta*) vowel would be prohibited.
What is the fault in that?
In a case of *prakṛtibhāva* based on a *pragṛhya*, there would be no hearing of the protracted vowel (*pluta*),
as in *agnī3* and *vāyū3*.
The vowel *ī* is substituted for the final vowel of a word ending in *-cakra-vartman-* [before a case-ending]. (Pāṇini 6.1.130)
According to the opinion of the teacher Cākravarmaṇa, an *ī3*-protracted vowel followed by a vowel becomes as if it were protracted. For example:
*astu hīty abrūtām*.
"So be it," they both said. "Build this! Build this! "Build this! Build this! (hī3 idam).

The mention of *cākravarmaṇa* is for the purpose of providing an option; it serves to exclude [the application] when that [term] is present and to include it when it is not present. Thus, this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. Furthermore, this treatment as if it were not a prolated vowel (*aplutavat*) is desired even in instances other than those ending in the vowel *ī*.
This is a cow; may she be a milch-cow.
The suffix *ut* is applied after [the word] *divā*.
From the rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ati* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), the term *pada* is understood to carry over [into this sūtra].
The nominal stem *div* is understood here, not the verbal root,
because the latter possesses an indicatory letter (*anubandha*).
The substitution of *u* occurs for the word *div-* [in the locative case]. For example: *dyukāmaḥ*, meaning "one whose desire is in heaven" (*divi kāmo yasya*);
and *dyumān*.
vimaladyu dinam / dyubhyām / dyubhiḥ /
Because of the inclusion of the term "without a following suffix" (*niranubandhaka*), it does not apply here in the forms *akṣadyūbhyām* and *akṣadyūbhiḥ*.
The inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (tapara-karaṇa) is for the purpose of excluding *ūṭh*,
as in the forms *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ*.
For here, because it is subsequent, *ūṭ* would apply. Why [is there the mention of] "of a word" (*padasya*)? [Consider the examples: *divau*, *divaḥ*.

The elision of *su* (the nominative singular ending) occurs after *etad* and *tad*, provided they do not contain the vowel *a* and are not part of a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), when followed by a consonant (*hal*).

In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), when the two words beginning with *etad* and *tad* do not end in the suffix *-kāra*, the *su*-sound that occurs in them— and what is that *su*-sound in those two?
That which is connected with that [purpose], its elision occurs when it follows a consonant within the domain of *saṃhitā*. For example: *eṣa dadāti*.
He gives;
this one eats;
he eats.
Why is it said "of *etad* and *tad*"? [Consider: *yo dadāti* (he who gives), *yo bhuṅkte* (he who eats).
Why is the mention of *su* included? [Consider: *suyachati*.
These two cows are grazing. Why [is the rule] "akoḥ" stated? [Consider:
eṣako dadāti.
One gives his own [portion].

Since that which falls within something is included by the mention of that thing, even though there is a difference in form, only *etad* and *tad* with the suffix *sākacka* (i.e., *eta-* and *ta-*) occur [in this rule]. Why does it say "not in a compound with *anañ*"? [Consider: *anetad*, *anatad*.
"He gives this" (*aneṣo dadāti*) or "he gives that" (*aso dadāti*):
because the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) has the meaning of the final member as its predominant element, the word *su-* is connected here only with *etad-* and *tad-*.
Why is it said "hali"? [Consider: *eṣo 'tra*, *so 'tra*.
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *ya* for *yat*] occurs diversely.

In the Vedic language, the *s* of the particle *sya* is frequently elided when followed by a consonant (*hal*). "And that steed, bound at the neck, at the flanks, and in the mouth, speeds toward the whip. (RV 1.84.15)
This Soma of yours flows forth, O Indra;
it does not cease where it may fall.
In that case, when there is elision of *a*, it occurs if the purpose is to complete the metrical foot.
The elision of *su* occurs after the word *saḥ* when followed by a vowel, provided that by this elision a *pāda* (verse-quarter) is completed.
"He indeed rules over the people; he follows after the plants.

Why [is there] the rule "if there is elision, for the purpose of filling the meter"? [To illustrate: "He indeed rules over the people; he follows after the plants. (In this case, the *u* is not elided.)
He would be like a tiger.
The term *aci* is for the sake of clarity.
Some maintain that by the mention of "foot" (*pāda*), the quarter-verse of a *śloka* is also included here.
By this, the following is established:
"This is that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha; this is that King Yudhiṣṭhira;
this is that Karna, the great renouncer; this is that Bhīma, possessed of great strength."
The augment *suṭ* is placed before the suffix *kāt*.
This is a governing heading (adhikāra), extending as far as *pāraskaraprabhṛtīnāṃ ca sañjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.157).
From this point onward, whenever we shall state "suṭ," [it should be understood that this heading applies].
It should be understood that "kātpūrvaḥ" (that which precedes *kā*) is also governed by this [rule].
As he will say: "After *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*, when used with the root *kṛ* in the sense of adorning" (*samparyupebhyaḥ karotau bhūṣaṇe*, Pāṇini 6.1.137); for example, *saṃskartā*.
To form; that which is to be formed. The mention of "prior to *kā*" (*kāt pūrva*) is for the purpose of making known that *suṭ* is not a part of the suffix.

For instance, in the forms *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa* and *saṃskriyate*, the augment *iṭ* and the guṇa substitution do not occur due to the presence of the prefix *sam*; this is because of the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28).
In that case, would not the *nighāta* (elision of accent) also fail to apply because it is separated by the *suṭ* augment?
No, because of the rule stating that in the application of accentual rules a consonant is as if non-existent; thus there is no separation, as in *saṃcaskaratuḥ*.

How is there guna in the form *saṃcaskaruḥ*? [The answer is: "That which falls within [the scope of] a rule is included by the mention of that [rule]. Furthermore, the mention of "having a conjunct as a penultimate" (in Pāṇini 7.4.10: *ṛtaśca saṃyogāder guṇaḥ*) applies here.
This is what must be done here:
the addition of the marker *ṭ* is for the purpose of qualifying [the root] in the rule *suṭ-stu-svañjām*.
[The substitution of *na* for *n* occurs] even when there is an intervention by the suffix *aṭ* or by a reduplicated syllable.
Even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* or an intervention by the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the augment *suṭ* occurs before the root-initial consonant (*kātpūrva*). Example: *saṃskaroti*.
He prepared;
he prepared thoroughly; he prepared around.
But for what purpose is this stated—

that first the root is joined with a prefix— given that in that case the operation of the root and the prefix is *antaraṅga* (internal), so that *suṭ* would be applied first, and afterwards the *aṅga* and the reduplication?
For it has been stated that *suṭ* is not a part (*abhakta*) [of the root].

Consequently, if the augment *aṭ* and reduplication were to follow after the letter *s*, they would occur in an undesired location. However, because of this very statement [of the rule], once *aṭ* and reduplication have been applied according to reality, even when there is an intervention by those two, the *suṭ* augment is placed before the *k* sound; thus the desired result is established.
The prefix *sam* [and its variants] are used with the root *kṛ* when it means "adornment."
After the prefixes *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*, when followed by the root *kṛ* in the sense of adorning (*bhuṣaṇa*), the augment *suṭ* is inserted before the final consonant of the root; for example,
*saṃskartā*.
To refine (*saṃskartum*);
that which is to be refined (*saṃskartavyam*).
Here, by the rule "there is *s*-substitution for *sam*, *puṃs*, and *kān*," the *m* of *sama* becomes *s*.
The nasalized form of the preceding vowel [is used]:
*pariṣkartā*,
*pariṣkartum*.
It should be adorned.
By the rule *suṭ-stu-svañjām*, there is the substitution of *ṣ*. Thus:
*upaskartā*.
In the sense of "adorned" (*bhūṣaṇa*), [the forms] *upaskartum* and *upaskartavyam* [are used]. Why [is this stated]? [Because otherwise it would apply to] *upakaroti* [in the sense of "to assist"].
The augment *suṭ* is desired after the prefix *sam-* in some cases even when it does not signify ornamentation, as in *saṃskṛtam annam* ("seasoned food").
And [it occurs] in the sense of "coming together" (*samavāya*). (Pāṇini 6.1.138)

A collection (*samavāya*) is a multitude (*samudāya*); when the root *kṛ* (to do/make) has this sense, the augment *suṭ* is placed before the letter *k* following the prefixes *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*.
There we have been refined; there we have been adorned; there we have been prepared.
The meaning is "arisen together."
The prefix *upa* [is used] in the senses of effort (*pratiyatna*), modification (*vaikṛta*), and ellipsis (*vākya-adhyāhāra*). (Pāṇini 6.1.139)
Pratiyatna is the effort toward the addition of another quality to an existing thing for the sake of improvement, or toward the maintenance of the state of that which has already grown.
That which is modified is called *vaikṛta*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied because [the root] begins with *prajña*.
The "supplying of a sentence" (*vākyādhyāhāra*) refers to the formal employment of a sentence whose meaning is already implied.
When these meanings are implied, the augment *suṭ* is inserted before the final consonant of the verbal root *kṛ* when it follows the prefix *upa*.
First, regarding *pratiyatna* (improvement): "He improves the fuel for the water";
"he improves the quality of the arrow-shaft.
Regarding *vaikṛta* (transformation): "He eats the prepared food."
He goes having prepared [the meal].
In the case of supplying words from the context: he prattles having prepared [it];
he studies having prepared [it].
What is the purpose of [specifying] "in these"? [To exclude cases such as: "he helps" (*upakaroti*).
The [suffix] *kvip* is applied after the roots *kṛtī* and *lavan*.
By the rule "after *upa*" alone:
when the root *kṛ* (kirati) follows *upa*, provided the context is that of cutting (*lavana*), the suffix *suk* is added, and the preceding [root] becomes *kat*.
The Madrakas cut with a side-thrust; the Kāśmīrakas cut with a side-thrust;
the meaning is that they cut by tossing [the blade] aside.
The suffix *ṇamul* should be stated here [in this context]. Why [is it said] "in the sense of cutting" (*lavane*)? [Consider: "Devadatta scatters [the grain]. (In this case, *ṇamul* is not applied.)
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after the root *prati* when it signifies injury (*hiṃsā*).
The same applies to the root *kṛ* (kirati).
When preceded by *upa* and *prati*, the augment *suṭ* is inserted before the *k* of the root *kṛ* (*kirati*), provided that the sense is one of injury.
"May it be scattered upon you, O low-born one! May it be scattered against you, O low-born one!
May your agitation, O low-born one, be such that it results in injury"—this is the meaning.
What is the purpose of the condition "in the case of violence"? [Example:
*pratikīrṇam* (scattered).
In the case of quadrupeds, birds, and drawings, [the rule applies] from the rear.
The rule "kiratau" (in the case of the root *kṛ* meaning 'to scatter') applies here as well.
When the root *kṛ* follows *apa*, in the sense of drawing out quadrupeds or birds, the augment *suk* is placed before the suffix *kā*.
The bull leaps up in joy;
the cock leaps up seeking food;
the dog leaps up seeking a place of shelter.
The meaning is that one draws [something] and then scatters it.
Why specify "among quadrupeds and birds"?
[Consider: *apakirati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta scatters").
It should be stated: "in the cases of joy, livelihood, and making a nest.
Let it not be so here: "The dog, having eaten, scatters the lump of boiled rice.
The addition [to the rule] is that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *kṛ* (to scatter) applies only in the cases of joy, livelihood, and making a nest.
The word *kustumburu* denotes the *jāti* (genus). PS_6.1.143.
The suffix *suṭ* is prescribed as an irregular form (*nipātana*) in the word *kustumburūṇi* when it refers to a genus (*jāti*).
*Kustumburu* is the name of a species of medicinal herb, namely coriander (*dhānyaka*).
In the rule concerning *kusumburuṇi* as the fruits thereof, the neuter gender is not intended [to be restrictive].
Why [is the word] *jātiḥ* mentioned? [To exclude cases such as:
*kutumburūṇi*, meaning "inferior *tumburu* fruits."
By the word *tumburu*, the fruits of the *tindukī* tree are meant; it is a compound expressing contempt for them.
The term *aparaspara* is used in the sense of continuous action.
The *suṭ* augment is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for *aparaspara* when the continuity of an action is implied: "The caravans go one after another."
The meaning is that they go continuously without interruption.
Why [specify] "in the continuity of action"? [Consider:
"Successive caravans are going."
The meaning is that others and those beyond go at one and the same time;
here, a continuous succession of movement is not intended. What, then, is this "continuity"?
The state of being constant is "constancy" (*sātatyam*).
How is it constant?
The elision of the letter *m* is prescribed when [the word] is in the locative case (*samaste*) by means of an alternative rule (*vikalpena*).
The suffix *vaś* is necessarily applied after the roots *lup*, *pad*, and *damś*, even when the agent is desirous (*kāma*) or mental (*mānasa*);
likewise, it is optionally applied after the roots *hi*, *tan*, *pac*, and *ci*, as well as after the root *māṃs* with the suffixes *ṇyuṭ* and *ghañ*.
The term *goṣpada* [is used] in the senses of that which has been frequented, that which has not been frequented, and as a measure. (PS 6.1.145)

The form *goṣpada* is derived by the irregular application (*nipātana*) of the augment *suṭ*, and its *ṣ*-sound occurs when the referent is either frequented (*sevita*), not frequented (*asevita*), or a measure (*pramāṇa*).
A "cow-path" (*goṣpada*) is a place;
that place in which cows tread is a place frequented by cows, and is thus called a cow-path. In the case of what is not frequented, one speaks of "non-cow-paths," such as forests.

The term *agoṣpada* is a nipātana (irregular formation) because the word *goṣpada* cannot occur when [the ground] has not been traversed by cattle; thus, its meaning is established through this irregularity.
If that is so, there is no purpose served by this [nipātana], for *agoṣpada* could simply result from the negation of *goṣpada*.
This is true; however,
it is only where there is the possibility of being frequented that there can be "not a footprint of a cow" (agoṣpada),
whereas where there is absolute impossibility [of such frequency], it would not apply.

Regarding the expression "forests without the tracks of cattle" (*agoṣpadāny araṇyāni*), it applies there as well because of the inclusion of the term "unfrequented. For those great wildernesses where the presence of cattle is absolutely impossible are described in this way.
Regarding measure: "the field is the size of a cow's footprint" (goṣpamātraṃ kṣetram); "it has rained until the cow's footprints are filled" (goṣpadapūraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ).
Here, the term "cow's footprint" (goṣpada) is not employed for the purpose of conveying its own literal meaning.
What then?
It is for the purpose of determining the extent of the field and the rain. What is meant by "in the measures of what has been cultivated and what has not been cultivated"?
*gopada* means "the footprint of a cow"; *āspada* is used in the sense of "a foundation" or "a standing place. (Pāṇini 6.1.146)
A *sthāna* is a place for sustaining oneself; the suffix *suṭ* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) in the sense of "having one's footing" (*āspada*) in that [place].
The word *āspada* is formed by this [rule].
Why is it said "in the sense of a standing place" (*pratiṣṭhāyām*)? [To show that it does not apply here:
*ā padāt āpadam*.
It is a marvel that [the self] is impermanent. // PS 6.1.147 //
Here, wonder (*adbhutatva*) is indicated by impermanence (*anityatā*) as the object;
the suffix *ācarya* is applied to that [object].
When the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *careś cāgurau*, the augment *suṭ* is inserted by way of a formal exception (*nipātana*).
"It would be a marvel if he were to eat";
"it would be a marvel if he were to study."
"Citram" means wonderful or marvelous. Why [is the word] "anitye" used? [To exclude cases such as: "āścaryam karma śobhanam" (a beautiful deed is wonderful).
The word *avaskaraḥ* is used in the sense of excrement.
*Avaskaraḥ* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātana*) when it denotes "contemptible feces," that is, the impurity of food (*annamala*).
From the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *ava*, the suffix *ap* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.57 (*ṛdorap*). By means of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the augment *suṭ* is added.
That which is scattered (*avakīryate*) is called *avaskara*, meaning "food refuse."
Due to that connection, the place is also called by that name. Why "in the case of excrement"? [Consider: "avakaraḥ" (a heap of refuse).
*Apaskara* is a term for a part of a chariot.

The word *apaskaraḥ* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) term when it denotes a part of a chariot. It is derived from the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *apa*, with the suffix *ap* according to Pāṇini 3.3.57 (*ṛdorap*).
Thus, by virtue of this irregular derivation (nipātana), there is the insertion of *suṭ*.
*Apaskara* refers to a component of a chariot; why say "a part of a chariot"? [To show the distinction: *apakaraḥ* [is not so used].
The words *viṣkiraḥ*, *śukumnaḥ*, and *vikiraḥ* [are used for a bird that scatters grain].
Regarding the word *viṣkira*: when the suffix *ka* is prescribed after the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-*— by the rule *ig-upadha-jñā-prī-kiraḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.135)—
the augment *suṭ* is introduced as an irregularity (*nipātana*) provided that it refers to a bird (*śakuni*).
Or, the term *vikiro* refers to a bird.
All birds are edible, except for the *viṣkira* (the chicken);

however, since the optional application of the augment *suṭ* is already established by the very mention of the word *śakuni* in the rule "or *śakuni* [is used] in the sense of *viṣkira*," the specific mention of *vikiro* here is so that its usage as a bird-name does not occur elsewhere.
In a mantra, when *candra* follows as a final member of a compound, [the preceding vowel] is short.
When the word *candra* is the second member of a compound, the augment *suṭ* is added after a short vowel in the domain of Vedic mantras. Example:
*suścandraḥ yuṣmān*.
Why [is it specified] "after a short vowel"?
[As in: *sūryācandramasāv iva*. Why [is it specified] "in a mantra"?
The term *sucandrā* refers to the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).
It is well known that [the compound] *uttarapada* occurs only within a compound; therefore, it does not apply here.
"śukram asi" and "candram asi"; [the suffix *kan* is applied after the root *kaś* in the sense of] "pratiṣkaśa. (Pāṇini 6.1.152)

From the root *kaś*, meaning "to go" or "to teach," when the prefix *prati-* is added and the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) is applied, the augment *suṭ* is prescribed as a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*), and for that very [augment], the substitution of *ṣ* is also prescribed.
"I shall enter the village today; be my scout,
my messenger, and my companion."
The term *pratiṣkaśaḥ* is said to mean "one who goes before" (*puroyāyī*).
Why [is the root] *kaśi-* mentioned? [To show that] *pratikaśaḥ* means "a horse that has gone toward the whip."
In this case, although the word *kaśā* is derived from *kaś* alone, the root *kaś* is nevertheless mentioned in order to indicate its prefix *prati*;
consequently, it does not apply to prefixes of other roots.
Praskaṇva and Hariścandra are the two seers.
The suffix *suṭ* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) in the words *praskaṇva* and *hariścandra* when they refer to sages (*ṛṣi*). For example:
*praskaṇva ṛṣiḥ*.
Hariścandra is a seer (ṛṣi). The mention of Hariścandra is for the purpose of excluding those who are not seers. Why say "seers"? [To exclude: Prakaṇva is a region.
The young brahmin Haricandra.
The forms *maskara* and *maskarin* are used for a bamboo staff and a wandering mendicant, respectively.
The forms *maskara* and *maskarin* are established as irregular derivations (*nipātana*) for "bamboo" and "wandering mendicant" respectively.
For the word *makara* is an underived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*).
When *veṇu* is the object to be expressed, *suṭ* is substituted [for the prefix *pra-*], whereas when *parivrājaka* is the object, *ini* is also applied; thus,
*maskaraḥ* means "flute."
In the case of *maskarī parivrājakaḥ* and *veṇuparivrājakayoḥ*, what [is the purpose]?
[It is to show that] *makaraḥ* means a crocodile (*grāhaḥ*).
The ocean is *makarī*.

Furthermore, some here also derive the form *maskara* from the root *kṛ* with the prefix *māṅ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), applying the suffix *ac* by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), as well as the shortening of *māṅ* and the augment *suṭ*.
That bamboo by which [the sound] is produced and thereby prohibited is a *maskara* bamboo.
The mention of the *veṇu* (bamboo) is for the sake of illustration; it also occurs elsewhere, as in the case of *maskara* meaning "staff.

Furthermore, even in the case of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), the suffix *ini* is prescribed after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the prefix *māṅ* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).
The word *māṅ* undergoes shortening and likewise takes the prefix *suṭ*.
One whose habit is "do not" (*mā*) is a *maskarī*; because he censures action (*karman*), he is called a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).
For he says thus: "Do not perform actions; tranquility is better for you."
In the city of Rājastunda, there is Kāstīra. // PS_6,1.155 //
The two words *kāstīra* and *ajastunda* are established as irregular forms (*nipātana*) when denoting a city;
[the former is derived from] "that which has slightly sloping banks" (*īṣattīram asya*).
The etymological derivation is made simply as "the belly (tunda) of one who is unborn (aja)," yet the actual referent (*vācya*) of these two words is the city named Kāstīra.
"Ajastunda" is the name of a city.
Why "in a city"? [To show that it does not apply to] "Kātīra" or "Ajatunada."
The word *kāraskara* denotes a tree.
The form *kāraskara* is derived with the irregular insertion of the suffix *suṭ*, provided that it refers to a tree. [The derivation is as follows:
from the sense "he makes a sound" (*kāram karoti*), the suffix *ṭa* is applied according to the rule *divāvibhāniśāprabhābhāskarānta*.
*Kāraskara* is a tree.
Why [is] "tree" mentioned? [To exclude] *kārakara*.
Some do not study this [sūtra].
In the list beginning with *pāraskara*, they read "the *kāraskara* tree"; and the rule states:
"The words *pāraskara* and so forth are used as proper names (*sañjñā*). (Pāṇini 6.1.157).
The forms beginning with *pāraskara* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when they function as proper names; for example,
*pāraskara* is a country.
*Kāraskara* is a tree;
*rathaspā* is a river;
*kiṣku* is a measure of length.
*Kiṣkindhā* means a cave.
After the words *bṛhat* and *karapatya*, when they mean "thief" and "deity" respectively, the suffix *suṭ* is added and the final *t* is elided.
Thus, *taskara* means a thief.
The deity is Vṛhaspati.
Why [is it said] "of the two deities, Caura and Devatā"? [Consider: tatkaraḥ;
bṛhatpatiḥ.

Since the inclusion of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is already established by the mention of the term "notion" (*sañjñā*), the specific mention of "thieves" (*cora*) and "deities" (*devatā*) in the list is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*).
Regarding the rule *pra attumpatau gavi kartari*:
when the root *tumpati* follows the prefix *pra*, the augment *suṭ* occurs before it when "cow" (*go*) is the agent.
The word *go* [undergoes the substitution of *o* for *au*] in the form *prastumpati gauḥ*.
Why [is it specified] "in *go*"? [Consider:
*pratumpati vanaspatiḥ*.

The group beginning with *pāraskara* is a class based on form (*ākṛtigaṇa*). The augment *suṭ*, though not prescribed by a specific rule, should be understood as applying to the words in the *pāraskara* group,
such as in *prāyaścitta*.
Regarding *prāyaścittiḥ*:
what was stated—that there is either the addition of *suṭ* to *prāya* and *citi* or to *prāya* and *cit*—is here summarized.
A word is unaccented, with the exception of a single [vowel].
This is a *paribhāṣā* concerning the rules for accents (*svaravidhi*). Where another accent— either the acute (*udātta*) or the circumflex (*svarita*)— is prescribed, [this rule applies].
In this context, one should understand that the rule "a word becomes [anudātta] with the exception of a single [accented syllable]" is present.
An *anudātta* word is one consisting of *anudātta* vowels.
But which single [syllable] is excluded?
That accent which is prescribed for it will be stated: "The final syllable of a verbal root is udātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.162).
In the roots *gopāyati* and *dhūpāyati*,
with the exception of the final vowel of the root, the remainder becomes unaccented (anudātta).
The *śnā* affix, which possesses the sound *ś*, supersedes the *dhātu* vowel:
*lunāti*,
*punāti*.
The substitution of *śna* for *t* occurs in *lunītaḥ* and *punītaḥ*.
His voice was more resonant;
he cut more thoroughly;
he purified more thoroughly.

The accent of a word (padasvara) occurs when [the final vowel] is alone, for the purpose of excluding the independent accent (svarita) belonging to the augment (āgama), the modification (vikāra), the base (prakṛti), or the suffix (pratyaya).
Regarding the *āgama*: "After the stems *catur* and *anaḍuh*, the augment *ām* is added, and it is udātta. Examples:
*catvāraḥ*;
*anaḍvāhaḥ*.
The accent of the substitute (*ādeśasvara*) overrides the accent of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*). For example, in *asthani* and *dadhani*,
the accent of the *anaṅ* substitute overrides the accent of the original form.
From the root *prakṛ*: *gopāyati*, *dhūpāyati*.
The accent of the base (*prakṛtisvara*) overrides the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Regarding the suffix: [the action] is to be done, [the object] is to be taken away;
the accent of the suffix (pratyayasvara) supersedes the accent of the base (prakṛtisvara).

The determination [of accentuation] is established by means of exceptions that are subsequent, permanent, internal, and irregular, as well as by what remains after others have been applied (*satiśiṣṭa*).
For when one thing remains while another is present, the former becomes the sublater of the latter.
Thus, for example, in *gopāyati*, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) is an exception to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*).

By that very same principle of the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), the accent of a root ending in an affix is set aside, because the latter is *satiśiṣṭa* (more residual). Furthermore, in the example *kārṣṇottarāsaṅgaputraḥ*, the *bahuvrīhi* accent—which is an exception to the accent of a compound—is set aside by the *satiśiṣṭa* oxytone accent of the compound as a whole.
However, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* (conjugational sign), even though it is *satiśiṣṭa*, does not set aside the accent of the *sārvadhātuka* (present-system) affix.
In the case of *lunītaḥ*, the accent belongs to that very [suffix].
It should be stated that the accent of the negative particle (*nañ*) is stronger than the accent of a case ending;
thus, in *atisraḥ*, [the accent is governed by] *tisṛbhyaḥ jasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.166).
This being the case, even though the accent of the case-ending is prescribed later, it is superseded by the accent of the negative particle *nañ*.
It should be stated that the accent of *nañ* is stronger than the accent caused by a case-ending,
as in *acatvāraḥ* and *ananḍvāhaḥ*.
For that [word] whose case-ending is the cause of the āmantrita designation, its udātta accent is superseded by the anudātta accent.
Why is the word *pada* mentioned?
For in the sentence "Devadatta, bring the white cow" (*devadatta gām abhyāja śuklām*), the accent of each individual word (*pratipada*) is distinct.
And this mention of "word" (*pada*) is for the purpose of defining its measure; it effects the cessation of the governing topic (*adhikāra*) of "word.
Consequently, even before the designation of a "word" occurs, at the very time the rule for accentuation is being applied, the remainder [of the word] becomes *anudātta* (unaccented).
And thus, in the case of *kauvalam*—meaning "a derivative of *kuvalī*"—the suffix *añ*, characterized by having an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*), is established.

Similarly, the word *garbhiṇī* is listed among the *bhikṣā*-group [of words] for the purpose of overriding the suffix *añ* that would otherwise be prescribed by the rule regarding initial low-pitched vowels;
for the words *kuvala* and *garbha* have their first syllable acutely accented (*ādyudātta*).
In a *ghañ*-derived noun, the final syllable following a root ending in /r/ or a long vowel (ā) is acute-accented.
The final syllable of the verbal root *karṣ* and of a *ghañ*-derived stem containing the vowel *ā* is udātta. For example: *karṣaḥ*.
Cooking;
relinquishment; attachment.
*dāyaḥ* / *dhāyaḥ*.
By the rule *ñnityādir nityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.197), [the udātta accent is applied to the first syllable].
This is an exception [to the preceding rule].

The irregular form *karṣaḥ* is specified in order to exclude the root *kṛṣ* belonging to the *tud*-class; for the word *karṣaḥ*, derived from that root with the suffix *ghañ*, remains acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) alone.
And [the same applies] to *ucchā* and the others. (PS 6.1.160)
In words such as *uccha* and others, the final syllable is udātta; for example,
*uñchaḥ*, *mlecchaḥ*.
In *jañjaḥ* and *jalpaḥ*, since these end in the suffix *ghañ*, the accent on the *ñi*-affix (*ñitsvara*) would apply; however,
in *japaḥ* and *vyadhaḥ*, they end in *ap*.
The accent of the root applies to these two;
however, some read it as *vadhaḥ*.
[Also] *yugaḥ*.
Because of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the noun ending in *ghañ* from the root *yuj*, there is an absence of *guṇa*; furthermore, this irregularity is intended for specific objects.
The word *yuga* is used in reference to a particular time and to equipment such as a chariot; otherwise, it remains simply *yoga*.
The word *gara*, meaning "poison," ends in the suffix *ap*.
The word *gara*, ending in the suffix *ap*,
is necessarily oxytone;
*gara* means poison.
Otherwise, it is necessarily udātta at the beginning.
These words— *veda*, *vega*, *veṣṭa*, and *bandha*— ending in the suffix *ghañ* according to Pāṇini 3.3.121 (*karaṇe halaś ca*), are udātta at the end when they denote an instrument (*karaṇa*).
In the case of verbal roots (*bhāve*), they are indeed *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). The rule "stuyudruvaḥ chandasi" (in the Veda, the roots *stu*, *yu*,
and *dru* [are *ādyudātta*]) is for the purpose of including those preceded by prefixes (*upasamasta*).
Praised all around;
joined together; run around.
The word *vartani* [is used] for "praise" (*stotra*). When that word *vartani* occurs in the sense of "praise" (*sāman*), it is udātta on the final syllable.
In other cases, it has the udātta accent on the middle syllable.
Regarding the word *dara* in the sense of "chasm":
when the word *dara* denotes a chasm, it has the udātta accent on the final syllable.

The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after the roots *īḍ*, *vanda*, *vṛ*, *śaṃs*, and *duh*.
The first syllable of a word ending in the suffix *ṇyat* is acute-accented when following these roots: *īḍ*, *vand*, *vṛ*, *śaṃs*, and *duh*. Example:
*īḍyam*.
To be revered; to be warded off; to be praised.
The word *dohyā* [is derived from] *dhenu*. Because it has two *anubandhas*, the suffix *ṇyat* is not included by the mention of *yat*; thus, the rule *tit svaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185) would apply.
In the word *vārya*, this suffix *ṇyat* belongs to the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "to choose" (*sambhaktau*);
for in the rule prescribing the suffix *kyap*, it is intended that only the root *vṛñ* be understood.
The substitution of *vi* for *ve* occurs optionally before the words *veṇu* and *indhana*.
In the case of these two [verses], "veṇu indhāna" and so forth, the first syllable is optionally acute (udātta):
*veṇuḥ*, *veṇuḥ*.
*indhānaḥ*, *indhānaḥ*, *indhānaḥ*.
This word *veṇu* would have been expected to be always acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *ṇu* according to the rule *ajivṛrībhyo nicca*;
however, the word *indhāna*—when it ends in the suffix *cānaś*—is acutely accented on the final syllable because it possesses the designation *cit*.

Now, when [the suffix] is in the *śānac* form, once the *anudātta* status of the *lasārvadhātuka* has been applied, the middle syllable becomes udātta by the rule of "the accent of the cessation of the udātta" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*).
Thus, in the case of *indhāne*, an udātta accent—which was not applicable in any way—is prescribed as an alternative.
When the word *veṇu* is used as a comparison, as in "like a bamboo," and functions as a proper name (*sañjñā*), [the following applies].
Then, by the rule *sañjñāyām upamānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.204), a constant initial udātta accent is desired. [PS 6.1.216: [The first syllable of the following is udātta when they form a name:
*tyāga*, *rāga*, *hāsa*, *kuha*, *śvaṭha*, and *kratha*.
In the case of these words—*tyāga*, *rāga*, *hāsa*, *kuha*, *śvaṭha*, and *kratha*—the first syllable is optionally acute (*udātta*). For example:
*tyāgaḥ* or *tayāgaḥ*.
*rāgaḥ*, *rāgaḥ*;
*hāsaḥ*, *hāsaḥ*. These end in the suffix *ghañ*.
According to their view, by the rule *karṣātvato ghaño 'nta udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.159), the final syllable of the suffix *ghañ* is indeed acute;
thus [the forms] are *kuhaḥ*, *kuhaḥ*.
Śvaṭhaḥ, śvaṭhaḥ; krathaḥ, krathaḥ. These are derived from the *pacādi* group with the suffix *yañ*.
The penultimate vowel is called *ṛt* [in the context of the rules concerning *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*]. (Pāṇini 1.1.51)

In a word ending in *ṛ*, the penultimate syllable is acute (*udātta*). Among words consisting of three or more syllables, the last is called the final (*uttama*); that which is near it is the penultimate (*upottama*).
That which is to be done;
that which is to be taken away;
one who is naturally quick-witted.
It belongs to the soft category;
this is an exception to the rule concerning the vowel of the suffix.
The suffix *caṅ* is optionally applied [after a root] when it is preceded by a prefix.
In a form ending in *caṅ*, the penultimate syllable is optionally acute (*udātta*):
*mā hi cīkaratām*.
Let us not perform [the action].

Since the augment *aṭ* is prohibited by the rule *na māṅyoge* (Pāṇini 6.4.74), and since the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent applies by the rule *hi ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.34), and since the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes would otherwise be unaccented by the rule *anudāttau suppitau* (Pāṇini 3.1.4) following the designation of the root as *adupadeśa*, the accent of the *caṅ* itself would normally prevail; however, in this instance, the vowel of the verbal root optionally becomes udātta.
Because of the inclusion of the term "upottama" (penultimate), it does not apply to a word consisting of two syllables, as in *mā hi dadhat*.
The suffix *matup* is applied after a word denoting a male ancestor, provided that the resulting name refers to a female.
In a word ending in the suffix *mat*, the vowel preceding the *mat* is acute (*udātta*) if that word ending in *mat* is a feminine technical term (*sañjñā*). Example:
*udumbarāvatī*.
Puṣkarāvatī, Vīraṇāvatī, Śarāvatī.
The vowel lengthening occurs by the rule "śarādīnāṃ ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.120). Why [is it specified] that the final vowel must be *āt*? [Consider] *ikṣumatī*.
[The suffix] -vatī [is applied after a word ending in -a] when it denotes a name; why [is this said]? [Because in the case of] *khaṭvāvatī*, [the suffix -matup is used].
Why is it specified "in the feminine"? [Consider: *śarāvān*. Why is it specified "of the suffix *mat*"? [Consider: *gavādinī*.
The suffix *at* is applied after the word *avati*.
Only with reference to a name (*sañjñā*).
A word ending in *avatī* has its final syllable acute-accented when it denotes a name.
Ajiravatī, Khadiravatī, Haṃsavatī.
In *kāraṇḍavatī*,
the suffix *ṅīp* would have been anudātta by virtue of being marked with *p*. Why, then, is it said "of *avati*"?
Could it not be said that [the word] is *navatī*?
It cannot be so; for here too [the form] *rājavatī* would result.
Because the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) in the application of rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), this is not the word *avatī*.
Furthermore, the nature of the entity is established by virtue of its basis.
[The suffix] īvatī [is applied after a word ending in the sixth case]. // PS_6.1.221 //
A word ending in *īvatī* has its final syllable acute-accented when used as a feminine proper name. Example: *ahīvatī*.
The suffix *matup* is applied after words ending in *kṛṣi* and *muni*.
The word *cau* refers to the root *añc-* with its nasal elided;
when this follows, the final syllable of the preceding word becomes udātta.
O Dadhīca! To Dadhīca!
Behold Madhūca!
*madhūcā* and *madhūce*:
this is an exception to the rule concerning the accent of the *udāttanivṛtti*.
It should be stated that this applies even when a taddhita suffix follows:
*dādhīcaḥ*,
*mādhūcaḥ*.
In this case, only the accent of the suffix occurs.
[The substitution of *ṣat* occurs] for the final member of a compound. (Pāṇini 8.3.47)
The final syllable of a compound becomes udātta (acute-accented). For example:
*rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man).
The sound of a Brahmin's blanket;
the sound of a maiden's voice; the sound of a drum.
nadīghoṣaḥ (river-sound), rājapṛṣat (king-spotted), brāhmaṇasamit (Brāhmaṇa-assembly).
In the rule for accentuation, a consonant is treated as if it were non-existent; thus, even in the case of words ending in consonants, the final syllable retains its udātta accent.
This is an exception to the accentuation rules governing multiple-word compounds.
Thus ends the first quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikāvṛtti*.
Now begins the second quarter of the sixth chapter:
"In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the preceding member retains its original accent. (PS 6.2.1)
The mention of the "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) here refers to an accent— either acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*)— situated in that prior member.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, whatever accent belongs to the prior member remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*).
It remains in its own nature and does not undergo the modification of becoming unaccented;
for if there were the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound, then by the rule "a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]" (Pāṇini 6.1.158), it would become unaccented.
Thus, it would be unaccented; therefore, this rule is commenced as an exception to the general rule of the final acute accent of a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*). [Example: *kārṣṇottarāsaṅgāḥ*.
[Derivation: *kṛṣṇa* is a black deer; its derivative product is *kārṣṇa*.
By the rule *prāṇi-rajata-ādibhyo ’ñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.154), the word ending in the suffix *añ* is acute on the first syllable due to the accentuation of the *ñit* suffix; for example,
*yūpavalajaḥ*.
The word *yūpa* ends in the suffix *ap*, according to the rule *kusuyubhyaś ca* in the *Uṇādi* list;
and since the rules for *dīrghaḥ* and *nid* apply there, it is consequently acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). [The term] *brahmacāripariskandaḥ* [is likewise explained].
The word *brahmacārin* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of the rule regarding the original accent of the second member in a *kṛt*-derivative compound. *Snātakaputra*:
the word *snātaka* ends in the suffix *-kan* and is accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the rule regarding *nit*-suffixes.
The son of a teacher (*adhyāpakaputra*):
by the accent of the *lit* suffix, the word *adhyāpaka* has its acute accent on the middle syllable.
The son of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyaputra*).
The word *śrotriya* has its first syllable accented acute because it is a *nit* [ending in a *t* or *n*].
It is the lord of men. The word *manuṣya* has its middle syllable circumflex according to Pāṇini 6.1.185.
Thus ends the section on [compounds] ending in a svarita.
The terms "udātta" and "svarita" are carried over (anuvartate) here;
therefore, since there is no rule at all when the preceding member is entirely unaccented (sarvānudātta), the final syllable of the compound becomes udātta.
Regarding the term *samābhyāgaḥ*: for the word *sama* is entirely unaccented (*anudātta*).

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the first member consists of words having the sense of "equal to," words in the third case, seventh case, or used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), indeclinables, words in the second case, or gerundives (*kṛtya*). (Pāṇini 2.1.30)

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the first member—whether it ends in the third case, the seventh case, or the second case, or is an indeclinable expressing a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or ends in a gerundive (*kṛtya*)—retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples of those having the meaning of "equal" (*tulyārtha*): *tulya-śvetaḥ*.
Equal in redness;
equal in greatness;
similar in whiteness.
"Sadṛśamahān":
these are *karmadhāraya* compounds formed by the rule "kṛtya-tulya-ākhyā ajātyā" (Pāṇini 2.1.68).
In that context, the word *tulya* is accented on the first syllable by the rule *tulyārthair atulopamābhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.213);
the word *sadṛś* ends in the *kvin* suffix by the rule *samānānyayoś ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.137).
By the rule of the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative compound, it is oxytone (*antodātta*).
The word *sadṛśa*, ending in the suffix *kañ*, is also middle-accented (*madhyodātta*);
thus, they have the same meaning.
The third [example]: *śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ* becomes *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ*;

*kiriṇā kāṇaḥ* becomes *kirikāṇaḥ*. Alternatively, the word *śaṅkulā* ends in the suffix *ka*, according to the rule "the suffix *ka* is prescribed after the root *lā* preceded by *śaṅku* in the sense of *ghan*"; thus, it is oxytone (*antodātta*).
The word *kiri* is also derived from the root *kṝ* (to scatter) with the *ik* suffix added according to the rule *kṝ-gṝ-śṝ-pṝ-kuṭi-bhid-chidibhyaś ca*;
thus, it has an udātta accent on its final syllable. It is used here in the instrumental case.
The seventh [case]: *akṣeṣu śauṇḍaḥ* (skilled at dice) forms *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*;
likewise *pānaśauṇḍaḥ*.
According to the rule *aśer devane*, the word *akṣa* ending in the suffix *sa* is oxytone.

The word *pāna* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ* and is acute-accented on its first syllable by the rule regarding the suffix *lit*. It is used in the locative case. [653] The example for the "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*) is *śastrīśyāmā*.
Her complexion is like that of the kumuda lily;
her voice is as sweet as a swan's;
and her body is well-proportioned like a banyan tree.
"Dark as a blade of dūrvā grass;
white as a stalk of śara reed"—
[these are examples of] "standard objects [compounded] with words expressing common properties" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.55).
This is the compound analysis.

The word *śastrī* ends in the suffix *ṅīṣ* and is oxytone (accented on the final syllable). The word *kumuda* also ends in the suffix *ka*, derived from the root *mud* with the prefix *ku-* according to the rule for roots such as *mūlavibhuja*.
Alternatively, [the word *nabhi*] is acutely accented on the first syllable because it is not a *viṣaya* (a specific domain) and does not end in an *ani* suffix.
The word *haṃsa* ends in the suffix *sa*, according to the rule "from the roots *vṛ*, *tṝ*, *vidi*, *hani*, *kami*, and *kaśi*, [the suffix] *sa*.
[The word *nyagrodha* is derived as follows: it grows downwards, thus it is *nyagrodha*.

Because it belongs to the *pacādi* group, it ends in the suffix *ac*; furthermore, by the rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*) stating "and of that [word] *nyagrodha* alone" (*Pāṇini 6.1.148*), the letter *ha* is replaced by *dha*, and it has the middle-acute accent (*madhyodātta*).
The words *dūrvākāṇḍa* and *śarakāṇḍa* are genitive *tatpuruṣa* compounds with the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*).
Upamāna (comparison):
*avyaya* (indeclinable) — *abrāhmaṇaḥ* (one who is not a Brāhmaṇa),
*avṛṣalaḥ* (one who is not a Vṛṣala).
A bad Brahmin; a bad Vṛṣala; one who has departed from Kauśāmbī.
nirvārāṇasiḥ (one who has gone beyond Vārāṇasī),
atikhaṭvaḥ (one who has surpassed the couch),
atimālaḥ (one who has surpassed the garland).

These indeclinables (avyaya) have their initial syllable accented (ādyudātta). It should be stated that this applies to the negative particle *nañ*, the particle *ku*, and the indeclinables (*nipāta*); it should not apply here, as in the case of *snatvākālakaḥ*.
Indeclinable:
accusative case – *muhūrtasukham* (pleasure for a moment),
*muhūrtaramaṇīyam* (delightful for a moment).
*sarvarātrakalyāṇī* (beautiful throughout the entire night), *sarvarātraśībhanā* (auspicious throughout the entire night);
[this occurs] in the sense of continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). (*Pāṇini 2.1.28*)
Thus ends the second section on compounds.
The word *muhūrta* belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group and has its accent on the final syllable.
The word *sarvarātra* also ends in the suffix *ac*.
The second [type of compound]:
kṛtya— *bhojyoṣṇam* (palatable and hot),
*bhojyalavaṇam* (palatable and salty).
*pānīyaśīta* (cold water),
*haraṇīyacūrṇa* (powder to be taken away);
the word *bhojya* ends in the suffix *ṇyat* and has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on its final syllable.
In the words *pānīya* and *haraṇīya*, the vowel *ī* is acute (udātta) according to the rule "the penultimate [vowel] is acute in a word ending in *ri*" (*Pāṇini 6.1.217*).
A quality [is used] for qualities, except in the case of *aneta*.
The phrase "the preceding word [retains its accent] by its original nature" (*prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*) and "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound" (*tatpuruṣe*) both continue to apply.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when a word denoting color stands as the prior member and words denoting color—excluding the word *eta*—stand as the subsequent members, the accent remains that of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples:
*kṛṣṇasāraṅgaḥ*, *lohitasāraṅgaḥ*.
*Kṛṣṇakalmāṣaḥ* (black-spotted) and *lohitakalmāṣaḥ* (red-spotted). In the sense of "color," the word *kṛṣṇa* ends in the suffix *na* and is oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable).
The word *lohita* is also derived from the root *ruh* with the suffix *itac*, where *ra* is replaced by *la*; thus, it is acutely accented on the first syllable.
Why [is the word] *varṇaḥ* mentioned?
[To exclude cases such as] *paramakṛṣṇaḥ*.
Why "among castes" (*varṇeṣu*)? [Consider:
*kṛṣṇatilāḥ* (black sesame seeds). Why "not denoting a person" (*anete*)? [Consider: *kṛṣṇaitaḥ* (a black-haired man).
The suffix *itaC* is applied after the words *lohita* and *eta*, as well as after *gādha* and *lavana*, when they denote a measure (*pramāṇa*). [PS 6.2.4]
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound expressing a measure, when the words *gādha* or *lavaṇa* are the final members (*uttarapada*), the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Example:
*śambagādham udakam*.
"Water deep enough for a boat" means its depth is that much;
[this refers to] salt from cow-dung.
*Aśvalavaṇa* / *aśvalavaṇa*. The meaning is: as much as is given to a horse.
These are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Among them, because the word *śamba* ends in the suffix *-ban* according to the rule *śamer ban*, it is acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
The word *aritra* ends in the suffix *-itran* according to the rule *artilūdhūsū*, and is acute-accented on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*).

The word *go* ends in the suffix *ḍo* and is udātta on the final syllable. The word *aśva* ends in the suffix *kvan*—according to the rule *aśū-pruṣi-laṭi-kaṇi-khathi-viśibhyaḥ kvan*—and is udātta on the initial syllable.
Here, "measure" (*pramāṇa*) should be understood as the mere determination of quantity, and not as length alone.
And these [words] have as their specific object of cognition that which is manifested by accent (*svaravyaṅgya*).
Why "in a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇe*)? [Consider:
*paramagādham*.
It is extremely salty.
The inheritance [is used] for the heir.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the word *dāyāda* follows as the final member (*uttarapada*) and denotes an inheritance, the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Example:
*vidyādāyādaḥ* (“an heir to learning”).
The word *dhanadāyādaḥ* [is formed with the suffix *kyap*]. In the rule *sañjñāyāṃ samajaniṣada*, the word *vidyā* ends in the suffix *kyap*;
and the term *udāttaḥ* also applies there.
Therefore, this word is oxytone (antodātta).

By the rule *kṛpṛvṛjimandinidhāñbhyaḥ kyuḥ*, due to the use of the term "bahulam" (diversely), the suffix *kyu* is applied even after the root *dhāñ* alone; consequently, the word *dhana* is udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Now, in the expression *vidyādāyādaḥ*, by which rule is the genitive case applied?
It is by the rule *svāmīśvarādhipatidāyāda*.

If that is so, does it not follow that there would be a prohibition of compounding, because of the rule stating that a genitive case prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not compounded?
If that is so, then the genitive here is indeed one characterized as "residual" (śeṣa);
however, lest it be understood that the locative being prescribed would override it, it is authorized once again.
What is the purpose of [the term] "dāyādya"?
*Paramadāyādaḥ*:
here, there is only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
The suffix *pratibandhi* is used in the sense of "long duration" (*cira*) and "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*).
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when the final members are *cira* or *kṛcchra*, the preceding member, provided it denotes an obstacle, retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Example:
*gamanacira*.
The difficulty of walking; the protracted nature of speech;
the difficulty of speaking.
The words *gamana* and *vyāharana* end in the suffix *lyuṭ*; their accent is that of the *lit* suffix.
Furthermore, this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of *gamana* and *yat ciraṃ*.
Or rather, this should be regarded as belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group [of compounds].
For movement, due to a deficiency in its causes, becomes obstructed—either by occurring at an improper time or by being associated with difficulty.
What is meant by "obstructed"?
Dysuria.
In the case of *apadeśa*, [the suffix *kha* is applied]. // PS 6.2.7 //
Apadeśa means a pretext;
in a tatpuruṣa compound expressing that meaning, when the word *pada* is the final member (*uttarapada*), the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
He set out on the path of urine; he set out on the path of excrement. The word *mūtra* ends in the suffix *ṣṭran*, according to the rule *sivimucyoṣṭerū ca*.
Alternatively, *mūtrayateḥ* is derived from the root with the suffix *ghañ*, and thus has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
The word *uccāra* is also derived with the suffix *ghañ*; according to the rule *tha-atha-ghañ-kta-aj-ab-itra-kāṇām* (Pāṇini 6.2.144), it has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

This is either a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) or one belonging to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*. Why does it say "in the sense of a pretext" (*apadeśe*)? [Consider:
*viṣṇoḥ padam* (the foot of Viṣṇu) = *viṣṇupada*. [655]
In a place sheltered from the wind, free from drafts.

When the word *nivāta*—meaning "protection from wind"—is the second member of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). For example: *kuṭī-nivātam*, meaning "a hut that serves as protection from the wind. (Just like a hut is a shelter.)
"Shielded from wind" means sheltered by a *śamī* tree or sheltered by a wall; "sheltered from wind" (*nivāta*) is the absence of wind.

*Arthābhāvaḥ* is an *avyayībhāva* compound. *Nivātam*—meaning "that in which the wind is obstructed"—is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. In that case, when walls and the like, which are the causes [of the absence of wind], exist in a windless place (*nivāte*), they are compounded with the word *nivāta*, which stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
The words *kuṭī* and *śamī*, ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* from the *gaurādi* group, are oxytone.

Regarding the word *kuḍya*, some maintain that it is derived from the root *kav-* with the suffix *yat* (which is treated as having the *ḍit* marker), making it a *yat*-derivative and thus ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable);
others hold that it ends in the suffix *ḍyak* and is therefore antodātta (accented on the final syllable).
Why "in the sense of protection from wind" (*vātatrāne*)? [Examples where it does not apply:
*rājanivāte vasati* (he lives in a king's shelter); *sukhaṃ mātṛnivātam* (a comfortable mother's shelter).
This word *nivāta* is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) denoting "side" (*pārśva*); in both cases [of its usage], it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
In the autumn, when it is not the proper season. // PS_6,2.9 //

*Ārtava* means "occurring in the season. When the word *śarada* (autumn), which does not signify *ārtava*, is the final member (*uttarapada*) in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
"Water fresh from the rains" (*rajjuśārada*);
"barley flour fresh from the rains" (*dṛṣatśārada*).
This word *śārada* signifies that which is newly produced.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, the word *kumāra* as the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Example:
*kumāra-śramaṇā*.
*Kumārakulaṭā* and *kumāratāpasī*:
the word *kumāra* has its accent on the final syllable.

In this regard, some— by the paribhāṣā rule "between that which is taught by a technical definition and that which is taught by its actual wording, only the latter is to be taken"— desire this accent only in the specific compound *kumāraḥ śramaṇādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.70).
Others, however, [desire it] without distinction in every case of the karmadhāraya compound.
The initial [vowel] is elided before a word beginning with *pratyenas*.
The term "in a *karmadhāraya* compound" continues [from the previous rule]. [The word] *pratīta* means "gone toward sin."
Alternatively, one whose sin (*enas*) has departed is *pratyenāḥ*.
When this forms the second member of a *karmadhāraya* compound, the first syllable of *kumāra-* becomes udātta. For example: *kumārapratyenāḥ*.
In this context, it should be understood by implication that the word *udāttaḥ* [is understood];

for it is precisely the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member that is here taught as being acute on the initial syllable. [PS 6.2.28] *pūgeṣv anyatarasyām* (in the case of *pūga* compounds, optionally).
In a *karmadhāraya* compound, when a word denoting a *pūga* or *gaṇa* (an association or group) follows as the second member, the first syllable of *kumāra* is optionally acute (*udātta*). Example:
*kumāracātakāḥ*.
Young Cātakas, young Cātakas!
Young Lohadhvajas!
Kumāralohadhvajas, Kumāralohadhvajas;
Kumārabalāhakas.
The young Balāhakas, the young Balāhakas;
the young Jīmūtas.
Kumārajīmūtas, Kumārajīmūtas;

From those [words], the suffix *ñya* is applied by the rule *tebhyaḥ pūgāññyo 'grāmaṇīpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 5.3.112);
then, by the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaiva striyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.62), there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix].

In this regard, when the acute accent on the first syllable does not occur, some apply the rule *kumāraś ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.26), which prescribes the preservation of the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).

However, for those who maintain that the term [in 6.2.26] refers specifically to the word as stated in the sūtra itself (*pratipadokta*), there occurs only the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*).
In a *dvigu* compound, the feminine suffix is applied after words ending in *i*, as well as after *kāla*, *kapāla*, *bhagāla*, and *śarāva*.
When the final member of a compound ends in *iK* and denotes time, [the first member takes the acute accent on its final syllable].
In these compounds—*kapāla*, *bhagāla*, and *śarāva*—when forming a *dvigu* compound, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Examples:
*pañcāratniḥ* (five cubits long) and *daśāratniḥ* (ten cubits long).
"Pañcāratni" means "that whose measure is five cubits," and "daśāratni" means "that whose measure is ten cubits"; this is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
According to the rule "laḥ pramāṇe dvigornityam," there is the obligatory elision of the suffix *mātrac*.
The suffix *ig* is applied after a word ending in *kāla* [meaning time] when followed by the suffixes *-pañcamāsya* and *-daśamāsya*. For example: *kālapañcamāsyaḥ* and *kāladaśamāsyaḥ*.

In the sense of a secondary derivative (taddhita), the suffix *yaP* is applied after a *dvigu* compound ending in *māsa*, provided that the meaning is "hired for," "has been hired for," or "will be hired for" five months; thus,
*pañcavarṣaḥ* ("hired for five years") and *daśavarṣaḥ* ("hired for ten years").
By the rule *varṣāl luk ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.88), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ*; thus,
*kāla*.
*Kapāla*: one with five skulls (*pañcakapālaḥ*), one with ten skulls (*daśakapālaḥ*),

Bhagāla: five bhagālas, ten bhagālas,

A preparation made with one *śarāva* measure [is called] *ekasarāva*, with five *śarāva* measures [is called] *pañcaśarāva*, and with ten *śarāva* measures [is called] *daśaśarāva*.
These are prepared foods (*bhakṣāḥ*). (Pāṇini 4.2.16)

Thus, these compounds, having the sense of a secondary derivative (taddhita), are to be understood as having the suffix *aṇ* elided by the rule "there is elision of the [suffix] after a *dvigu* when no patronymic is intended" (*4.1.88*).

"Purchased for five horses" is *pañcāśvaḥ*; "purchased for ten horses" is *daśāśvaḥ*. Why [is the rule] stated as "in a *dvigu* compound"? [To exclude cases such as: *pañcabhir aśvaiḥ krītaḥ*.
In the cases of *paramāratniḥ*, *paramaśarāvam*,

When the word *bahu* occurs, [the suffix *śas*] is optionally used in either case.

In a *dvigu* compound, the word *bahu*, when it constitutes the first member (*pūrvapada*), optionally retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) before second members (*uttarapada*) beginning with a vowel (*iganta*) and so forth.
Since the preceding rule would have made this accent obligatory, this [rule] provides an option.
One who has many cubits;
one whose face is of the earth.

one who has many skull-bones, one who has many skull-bones.
bahubhagālaḥ, bahubhagālaḥ;

*bahuśarāvaḥ*.
The word *bahu* has its final syllable accented (antodātta).

When its original accentuation is applied, wherever there is a *yaṇ*-substitution, the rule "for an unaccented vowel following a *yaṇ* that results from an acute or circumflex vowel, a circumflex [is substituted]" (*Pāṇini* 8.2.4) applies.
Such is this tone.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the words *diṣṭi* and *vitasti*.
In a *dvigu* compound, when the words *diṣṭi* or *vitasti* follow as the final members, the preceding member optionally retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). For example:
*pañcadiṣṭiḥ*.
Five *diṣṭis*;

The locative case ending is applied after words other than those denoting time when they are used in connection with *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *pakva*, and *bandha*. (Pāṇini 2.3.32)

When a word ending in the locative case is the first member of a compound and is followed by the subsequent members *siddha*, *śuṣka*, *pakva*, or *bandha*, it retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), provided that the locative case does not denote time. For example:
*sāṃkaśyasiddhaḥ*.
One perfected at Sāṃkāśya; one perfected at Kāmpilya,
one perfected at Kāmpilya.
The words *sāṃkāśya* and *kāmpilya*, ending in the suffix *ṇya*, have the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
However, in the *Phiṭ-sūtras* it is recited: "In the case of *sāṃkāśya*, *kāmpilya*, *nasikya*, and *dārvāghāṭa*, the accent falls on the final syllable or the preceding one.
According to that rule, they may also have the acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*) in the alternative view.

*śuṣka-ūkaśuṣkaḥ* / *nidhanaśuṣkaḥ*. By virtue of the rule allowing for various suffixes (*bahulavacana*), the word *ūka* is derived from the root *ava-* with the suffix *-ka*, and it is oxytone (*antodātta*).

The word *nidhana* is derived from the root *dhā* with the suffix *kyap*, and it has the acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*). Examples include *kumbhīpakva* (cooked in a pot) and *kalasīpakva* (cooked in a jar).
*bhrāṣṭrapakvaḥ*.
The words *kumbhī* and *kalasī*, ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, have the acute accent on the final syllable.
The word *bhrāṣṭra*, ending in the suffix *ṣṭran*, has the acute accent on the first syllable.
*bandha*: *cakrabandhaḥ* (binding of a wheel), *cārakabandhaḥ* (imprisonment).
The word *cakra* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
The word *cāraka*, ending in the suffix *ṇvul*, is udātta on its first syllable. Why [is it specified] "after a non-time word"? [Consider:
*pūrvāhṇasiddhaḥ*.
Established by the *aparāhṇa* rule, this *saptamīsvara* is overridden by the *kṛtsvara* rule; therefore, it is prescribed once again.

The words *pari*, *prati*, *upa*, and *apa*, when functioning as the first members of a compound, retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) when the second member denotes that which is excluded or avoided, or when it denotes a part of the day or a part of the night. For example:

parisauvīram, parisārvaseni,

At every afternoon;

Toward the latter part of the night:

In that context, the prefixes *apa-* and *pari-* function in the sense of exclusion; therefore, for these two alone, the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) is that which is being excluded, and not for the other two [prefixes].

Thus, this occurs.

In a dvandva compound consisting of words denoting Kṣatriyas ending in the plural number, which refers to the Andhakas or the Vṛṣṇis, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Example:
*śvāphalkacaitrakāḥ*.
The descendants of Caitra are the Andhakas;

Why [is the term] *rājanya* mentioned? [Consider: *dvaipyahaimāyanāḥ*. [In this case, the suffix] *yañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.10: *dvīpād anusamudraṃ yañ* ("the suffix *yañ* is applied after *dvīpa* when it means 'born on an island'"). Thus, *dvīpe bhavāḥ* ("those born on an island") results in *dvaipyaḥ*. From that, the patronymic suffix *aṇ* is applied. However, because the word *dvīpa* ends in *a*, the subsequent rule 4.1.158 (*yasyeti ca*) causes the elision of the final vowel and the following consonant (*taddhiteṣvacām ādeḥ*), which would result in the form *dvaiyaḥ*. To prevent this, the mention of *rājanya* is made. Since *rājanya* is a *rājanyādi-gaṇa* (a class of words beginning with *rājanya*), the suffix *yañ* is applied by 4.1.178 (*rājanyādibhyo vun*), resulting in *rājanya-yañ* = *rājanya-ya*. This *yañ* is subsequently elided by 6.4.148 (*yaño ṅyāpprātipadikāt*), and finally, the patronymic suffix *aṇ* is applied to form *rājanya-aṇ* = *rājanya*. Because the word *rājanya* ends in *a*, the rule 4.1.158 applies once again, causing the elision of the final vowel and the following consonant (*taddhiteṣvacām ādeḥ*), which would result in the form *rājñaḥ*. To prevent this, the mention of *rājanya* is made. By the rule 1.1.59 (*yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe*), the elision does not apply to the *a* of *rājanya* itself. Therefore, the form *rājanya* is established. Consequently, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to *dvaipya* to form *dvaipyāṇ* = *dvaipya*, and from that, the plural *dvaipyāḥ* is derived. Then, the patronymic suffix *aṇ* is applied to *dvaipya* to form *dvaipyā-aṇ* = *dvaipya*, and from that, the plural *dvaipyāḥ* is derived. Subsequently, the suffix *phak* is applied to *dvaipya* to form *dvaipyaphak* = *dvaipyāyani*, and from that, the plural *dvaipyāyanayaḥ* is derived. Thus, the compound *dvaipyahaimāyanāḥ* is formed. In this way, the mention of *rājanya* serves to exclude the application of the rule 4.1.158 (*yasyeti ca*). Furthermore, the mention of *rājanya* is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule 4.1.158 (*yasyeti ca*) in cases such as *vaidhryaḥ* and *vaidhryāyaṇiḥ*. Haimāyana is the young descendant of Haima.
These [groups] are Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, but they are not *rājanyas*.
The mention of *rājanya* here is for the purpose of including those Kṣatriyas who belong to consecrated lineages.
And these do not belong to the lineage of those who have been consecrated.
What is the purpose of employing the plural number?
[To include] Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva.
Why specify "in a dvandva compound"? [Consider:
*vṛṣṇīnāṃ kumārāḥ* (the youths of the Vṛṣṇis) = *vṛṣṇikumārāḥ*. Why specify "among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis"? [Consider: *kauravyamallāḥ*.
The Kurus and Pañcālas; [this is the section on] numbers. PS 6.2.35.
In a *dvandva* compound, a preceding member that expresses a number retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). For example:
*ekādaśa*.
Twelve;
thirteen, thirteen.
The word *eka* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it is formed with the suffix *kan* by the rule *iṇbhīkāpāśalyatimarcibhyaḥ kan*, and this suffix is marked with the *ṇi*-indicator.
The form *trestrayaḥ* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) word with an udātta accent on the final syllable.
And a pupil is subordinate to his teacher. (PS 6.2.36)
In a *dvandva* compound consisting of pupils preceded by their teacher, the initial member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
The followers of Āpiśali and Pāṇini;
the followers of Pāṇini and Rauḍhi;
the followers of Rauḍhi and Kāśakṛtsna.
The teacher Āpiśali is the descendant of Apiśala; thus, by [Pāṇini 4.1.95], the suffix *iñ* is applied.
That which was taught by him is called *Āpiśalam*; here, by [Pāṇini 4.2.112], the suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in *iñ*.
Those who study that [work] are also called Āpiśalas;
by the rule "proktāl luk" (Pāṇini 4.2.64), there is elision of that taddhita suffix prescribed for one who studies [a work] taught by such a person.
The students of Āpiśali are "Āpiśalāḥ";
thus, in both cases, the pupil has the teacher as a subordinate member [of the compound].
The mention of "having the teacher as a subordinate member" is for the purpose of qualifying the *dvandva* [compound].
The entire compound is intended to be understood as having "the teacher" (*ācārya*) as its subordinate member (*upasarjana*), so that it may not occur here: *pāṇiniya-devadattau*.
Why [is it specified] "with the teacher as the subordinate member"?
[The term refers to] Vedic grammarians.
Why [is it said] "a pupil"?
[To exclude cases such as] the *Āpiśala* and *Pāṇinīya* treatises.
And [the names] Kārta, Kaujapa, and so forth. (PS 6.2.37)

In those *dvandva* compounds beginning with *kārtakaujapa*, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Thus, *kārtakaujapādayaḥ* are those *dvandvas* whose first members have their original accent.
The recitation of words ending in case-terminations is for the purpose of indicating the intended number (vacana).
The particle *ca* is for the purpose of continuing the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *dvandva* compounds. Example:
*kārtakaujapau*.
*Kṛtasyāpatyam* and *kujapasyāpatyam*— these two end in the suffix *aṇ*;
[they refer to] Sāvarṇi and Māṇḍūkeya.
The Sāvarṇis are those ending in -iñ;
the Avantyas and Aśmakas are the many descendants of Avanti.
The country inhabited by them is Avanti;
likewise the Aśmakas and the Pailaśyāparṇeyas.
This is a case of the dual suffix *yuvan*.

[The derivation is as follows: Paila is the offspring of Pīlā; his offspring who is a youth is [called] *paila-yuvana*, according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.156: *aṇo dvyacaḥ* ("the suffix *aṇ* [is elided] after a *dvyac* [stem] ending in *aṇ*").
Thus, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *phiñ* prescribed by the rule "pailādibhyaś ca" (Pāṇini 2.4.59).
The word *śyāparṇa* belongs to the *bidādi* group; its female descendant is *śyāparṇī*.
The descendant of that [Śyāparṇa] who is a youth is Śyāparṇeya;
the use of the plural number is not restrictive,
and therefore the form "Paila-Śyāparṇeyau" also occurs here.
The descendants of Kapi are the Āparṇeyas. *Kapi* is oxytone; its offspring in the plural [is formed by adding *iñ*] according to Pāṇini 4.1.107: *kapi-bodhāṅgiro-aṅgirasām anyatarasyām*.
Thus, by the rule *yañaś ca yañañoś ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *yañ* and *yaññ*; therefore, plurality is indeed resorted to here:
*śaitikākṣapāñcāleyāḥ*.
There is a sage named Śitikākṣa; his descendant is formed by the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*.

For that descendant who is a youth, the suffix *iñ* is applied; however, by the rule "the elision of *ṇya*, *kṣatriya*, and *ārṣa* [suffixes] ending in *it*, as well as of *ṇya* and *iñ*, occurs when a youth is denoted" (Pāṇini 2.4.58), there is elision (*luk*) of both *ṇya* and *iñ*.
The feminine descendant of Pāñcāla is *pāñcālī*; her youthful male descendant is *pāñcāleya*.
Here too, the plural number is not intended to be expressed; thus, in the case of "the two [descendants], Śaitikākṣa and Pāñcāleya," the dual form also occurs.

*kaṭukavārcaleyaḥ*: [The derivation is as follows: *kaṭuka* + suffix *iñ* (by Pāṇini 4.1.95, meaning "the offspring of Kaṭuka"), then [the substitution of *vārcaleya* by] Pāṇini 2.4.66: "In the case of a patronymic suffix *iñ* preceded by more than two syllables, [the final vowel and consonant are elided] when the descendants are among the Easterners or the Bharatas."
Thus, there is elision (*luk*) in many cases.
