The compound *śuna itva śepaḥ asya* is a *bahuvrīhi*. In that context, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case ending according to the rule *śunaḥ sañjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.21), which applies to the words *śepa*, *puccha*, and *lāṅgūla* when used in a name.
Both [words] have the udātta accent on the first syllable:
śaṇḍāmarkau.
The words śaṇḍa and marka, being formed with the suffix ghañ, have the udātta accent on the first syllable.
In the copulative compound of those two, the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137); thus,
it is *tṛṣṇāvarūtrī*.
The word *tṛṣṇā* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
The word *varūtrī*, being listed in the *grasitādi* group of sūtras, is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
In this case, the lengthening [of the vowel] in the *dvandva* compound follows the previous rule.
*Bambāviśvavayasau*:
the word *bamba* has its accent on the final syllable;
the word *viśvavayas* also [has its accent on the final syllable] because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound governed by Pāṇini 6.2.106: *viśvaṃ sañjñāyām*.
Thus, the word *viśva* has its accent on the final syllable.
In the *dvandva* compound of those two, the lengthening is as before:
*marmṛtyuḥ*.
The word *mar* is derived from the root *mṛñ* with the suffix *vic*.
The word *mṛtyu* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

Regarding compounds consisting of two deities, their inclusion in the list beginning with *vanaspati* is for the purpose of signifying a dual deity and for the case where the second member begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*).
And [the first vowel retains its original accent] in a dvandva compound of deities.
In a *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting deities, both the preceding and the following members retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) simultaneously; for example:
*indrāsomau*.
In *indrāvaruṇau*,
*indrābṛhaspatī*,
and *ṛjrendrāgraḥ*, the word *indra* is prescribed as having its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).
The word *soma* ends in the suffix *man*;
*varuṇa* ends in the suffix *unan*, and by that rule it is acute on the first syllable. In the word *bṛhaspati*, because it belongs to the *vanaspati*-class, there are two acute accents.
Therefore, in the case of *indrābṛhaspatī*, there are three acute accents (*udātta*).
Why is the mention of "deities" (*devatā*) included?
[For example,] *plakṣanyagrodhau* [does not have this].
What is the purpose of mentioning "dvandva" (copulative compounds)? [Consider the example:
*agniṣṭomaḥ*.

The first syllable of the word *vṛtra* is not acute when followed by a word beginning with an unaccented initial vowel in a compound, except when the subsequent member is *pṛthivī*, *rudra*, *pūṣan*, or *manthin*.

In a *devatā-dvandva* (compound of divine names) where the first member begins with an unaccented vowel and the second member is not *pṛthivī*, *rudra*, *pūṣan*, or *manthin*, both members do not simultaneously retain their original accents (*prakṛtisvara*). For example:
*indrāgnī*.
The words *indravāyū* and *agnivāyu* have their accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

The mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is intended as a qualifier for the subsequent member, so that [the rule] applies when the subsequent member begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*).
This is so that it may not serve as a qualifier for the *dvandva* compound itself.
The phrase "beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*anudāttādau*) is for the purpose of distinguishing the respective domains of the positive injunction and the prohibition.
Why [is the restriction] "not in the case of *pṛthivī* and so forth" (*apṛthivyādiṣu*) stated?
Regarding *dyāvāpṛthivyau*:
the word *dyāvā* is prescribed as having its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*);
the word *pṛthivī*, because it ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
Regarding *rudra*: in the case of *somārudrau*, the word *rudra* ends in the suffix *rak* and is oxytone according to the rule *roder ṇiluk ca*.
Regarding *pūṣan*: [in the case of] *indrāpūṣaṇau*.
In the word *svannukṣanpūṣan*, *pūṣan* is prescribed as an exception (nipātana) with the acute accent on the final syllable.
Regarding *manthin*: *śukrāmanthinau*; one who has "churning" (*mantha*) is called *manthī*. Because it ends in the suffix *-in*, it has the acute accent on the final syllable.
In the case of *pṛthivī* and the others, however, both [accents] indeed occur simultaneously as the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
The suffix *anta* [is applied after a verbal root] to form a word expressing the completion of an action.
The word *antaḥ* ("end") is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).
It should be understood that whatever we shall explain hereafter applies to the final syllable of the second member of a compound (*samāsottarapada*), which becomes acute-accented (*udātta*).
He will state [the rule]: "After verbal roots ending in *thā*, *tha*, *ghañ*, *ktā*, *ac*, *ap*, *tra*, *ka*, and *aṇ*...
(Pāṇini 6.2.144). Examples: *sunīthaḥ* and *avabhṛthaḥ*.
The substitution of *u* for the final vowel of a verbal root occurs before the suffixes *tha*, *atha*, *ghañ*, *kta*, *ac*, *ap*, *itrac*, and *kān*.

Now, when the final members of a compound end in *ghañ*, *kta*, *ac*, *ap*, *itra*, or *ka*, provided they follow a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada*, the penultimate syllable of the final member becomes acute (*udātta*). For example: *sunīthaḥ*.
*Avabhṛthaḥ*:

These two words end in the suffix *kthan*, according to the rules "after the roots *han*, *kuṣ*, *ni*, *ram*, and *kāś*, [the suffix] *kthan*" and "after the root *bhṛ* with the prefix *ava*, [the suffix] *kthan*".
In that case, by the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), the final member would be udātta on its first syllable.
Now, *āvasatha* and *upavasatha*:

in the sense of "dwelling" (*vaseḥ*) with a prefix (*upasarge*), there is the suffix *athan*; [alternatively], there is the suffix *ghañ*, as in *kāṣṭhabheda* ("splitting wood") and *prabheda* ("division").
The breaking of a rope;
the suffix *kta*— as in "come from afar" (*dūrādāgataḥ*) and "dried by the sun" (*ātapaśuṣkaḥ*).
*viśuṣkaḥ* (dried up);
*ac-* [as a suffix] in *prakṣayaḥ* (destruction) and *prajayaḥ* (conquest).

The words *kṣaya* and *jaya*, being respectively [governed by] Pāṇini 6.1.201 (*kṣayo nivāse*) and 6.1.202 (*jayaḥ karaṇam*), cause them to be used as having the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
*ap*: *pralavaḥ*, *prasavaḥ*;
*itra*: *pralavitram*.
To the Impeller.
Ka— the bull of the cow, the bull of the female donkey.

In the expressions *gāṃ varṣati* (it rains on the cow) and *kharīṃ varṣati* (it rains on the she-ass), the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *mūlavibhuja* (Pāṇini 3.2.5).
[The resulting form is] *pravṛṣ*.

The root *prahṛṣ* [forms the word *prahṛṣṭa*]. The suffix *kap* is applied because it has *i* as its penultimate vowel (Pāṇini 3.1.135). And [the word *prahṛṣṭa* belongs to] the *vṛṣādi* group (Pāṇini 6.1.203).
Thus, the word *vṛṣan* has its initial syllable accented; this is by the rule "after a prefix, a kāraka, or an upapada," as in *sustutam bhavatā*.
In the case of a *karmapravacanīya*, only the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) occurs.
The suffix *kta* is applied after a word that serves as a good point of comparison.
After the prefix *su* and after a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the final member ending in the suffix *-kta* has its final syllable accented acute. For example: *sukṛtam*.
"well-eaten," "well-drunk";
from a comparison— as in "devoured by a wolf."
*śaśapluta*, *siṃhavinardita*,
and after a word with a good sound (*suśabda*), the following [term] becomes a *gati*. (Pāṇini 6.2.49)

This being the case, the following is an exception [to the previous rule]: "The third case ending is also used for the object when it follows a word denoting comparison" (Pāṇini 2.3.48). This applies specifically to words that follow a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada*.
It has been well praised by you.
In a compound denoting a name, the elision of *an* does not occur for words beginning with *acita*.

In the domain of a technical name (*sañjñā*), a final member ending in *kta* following a preceding member that is either a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada* becomes oxytone, with the exception of *ācita* and others. Example:
*sambhūto rāmāyaṇaḥ*.
Śākalya was invited;
Kauṇḍinya was devoured;
[he] was produced—thus, by virtue of the respective meanings, the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of the object.
For in the rule *gatir anantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.49), the term *karmaṇi* (in the sense of the object) is understood from the preceding context; this [present rule] is intended to set that aside.
A river dug by an archer;
a city excavated by a spade;
ground trampled by an elephant.
The application of the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.4.48) is here set aside. Why [is it said] "of words other than *ācita* and so forth"? [Consider: *ācitam*.
Not requested;
tasted; accepted.
Etymologically analyzed,
understood,
and thoroughly integrated.
"Upahatam," "upasthitam," and "saṃhitā" [occur] in the sense of "not in a cow."
When the word *saṃhitā* is a name for something other than a cow, it does not have an udātta accent on the final syllable;
however, when it is the name of a cow, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable precisely.
And [the same applies] to those who have increased [their practice], and so forth. (PS 6.2.147)
In the case of *pravṛddha* and other such words, the final member ending in a *kta*-suffix is udātta-accented on its last syllable:
*pravṛddhaṃ yānam*.
The low-born man has grown great;
barley-meal has been prepared for the gambling-match;
he is intent upon his enjoyments.
"Khaṭvārūḍhaḥ" (one who has mounted the bed) and "kaviśastaḥ" (one censured by poets);
the inclusion of these vehicles and so forth in this list is for the purpose of illustrating common usage.
It is not for the purpose of restricting the scope;
even outside of the *yāna* group and others, they still possess the quality of having an udātta accent on the final syllable.
Some, however, maintain that it is indeed for the purpose of restricting the scope.
This undertaking has the purpose of [establishing] the absence of a fixed rule; and the *pravṛddha* group should be understood as an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
By this, a garment that has been mended again is to be given.
Thus, forms such as *punarniṣkṛto rathaḥ* are established. [PS 6.2.148:
After a word denoting an agent (*kāraka*), the suffixes *datta* and *śruta* are used only in the sense of benediction (*āśis*).
The terms *sañjñāyām* (in the sense of a name) and *ktaḥ* (the suffix *kta*) carry over from the previous rule.

When a name is being formed and a benediction (*āśis*) is implied, the final syllable of the words *datta* and *śruta*, which end in the suffix *kta* and follow a *kāraka* (participant in an action), becomes acute-accented (*udātta*).
He to whom the gods would give [wealth] is Devadatta;
he who is heard by Viṣṇu is Viṣṇuśruta. Why [is it said] "from a kāraka"?
Let there be no restriction regarding the grammatical case (kāraka). [Example:
*sambhūto rāmāyaṇaḥ* ("the Rāmāyaṇa has been produced").
Why say "of *datta* and *śruta*"? [Because it would otherwise apply to other cases as well.]

Devapālita: By this rule, the word-final acute accent (antodāttatva) prescribed by Pāṇini 6.2.146, "In this [section], for the purpose of forming a compound name, [the first member retains its original accent] except for *ācita* and the others," does not apply here.
In this case, only the rule "the third [case ending occurs] when there is an object" (*Pāṇini 2.3.48*) applies.
What is the purpose of employing the particle *eva*?
The restriction [applies] to the *kāraka* so that there may be the restriction of the *datta* and *śruta* [terms]; let there not be a restriction of the *datta* and *śruta* [terms].
Even from a non-*kāraka*, the final syllable of *datta* and *śruta* becomes acute (*udātta*).
In the case of *saṃśrutaḥ* and *viśrutaḥ*,
why [is it] said "in the sense of a benediction" (*āśiṣi*)?
Let there be no restriction regarding the absence of a benediction (*anāśiṣi*). [For example:
*devakhātā*, "dug by the gods.
It is intended that this restriction applies here only when a word denoting an agent (*kāraka*) precedes the words *datta* or *śruta* in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).
Therefore, in the case of *tena āhato nadati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta, struck by him, sounds"), [the rule] does not apply;
for "Devadatta" is the name of a certain conch shell.
In that instance, the third case ending occurs in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) according to Pāṇini 2.3.2.
Thus, there is indeed the preservation of the original accent of the preceding member.
And [the suffix *ṇamul* is used] after a word meaning "done by one who is in such a state. (PS 6.2.149)
When a compound occurs in the sense of "having attained this state" (*itthambhūta*)—
that is, "done by one who has reached such a condition"— the final member ending in a *kta* suffix is udātta-accented on its last syllable.
The ravings of one asleep; the ravings of one insane;
the songs of one intoxicated.
"Vipannaśrutam" (one whose learning has perished).
The verb *kṛ* occurs in the sense of action in general, and not solely in the sense of the manifestation of what was previously non-existent.
By that [rule], even the act of prattling and so forth is accomplished;
this is an exception to the rule "the third case is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.48).
But when [the words] such as *pralapita* occur in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve*), then their final acute accent is established by the rule for *thā-thādi* suffixes.
The [term] *bhāva* expresses the object of the action (*karma*). (PS 6.2.150)

A final member of a compound that ends in a suffix other than *an*, expresses a state (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*), and follows a word denoting an agent (*kāraka*), is udātta on its final syllable. For example:
*odanabhojanam sukham* ("the eating of rice is pleasant").
Drinking milk is pleasant;
anointing with sandalwood and priyaṅgu is pleasant.
An example of a verbal compound (karmavacana) is: "śāli rice fit for the king's meal."
The garments are the royal coverings.

Regarding the rule "and [the word denoting] the object [is in the accusative when it is that] by contact with which there is pleasure for the body of the agent" (Pāṇini 3.3.116), this grammatical application is explained in both ways.

The suffix *lyuṭ* occurs when *karman* (object) is the upapada, meaning that *lyuṭ* occurs when the object is to be expressed. Regarding these two meanings of the sūtra, the following are examples for the first sense, where it expresses an abstract state (*bhāva*).
Below are examples of the use of the term *karman*. Why [is the word] *anaḥ* mentioned? [Consider:
"buttermilk to be carried by hand" (*hastahāryam udaśvit*).
Why [is it specified] "expressing the agent and the object"?
[Consider] *dantadhāvanaṃ* ("tooth-cleaning");
here the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
The rule "after a kāraka" applies here as well. Examples:
*avalekhanam* (the act of scraping).
In all these counter-examples, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) prevails.

[PS 6.2.151: Words ending in the suffixes *man* and *ktin*, as well as those meaning "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*), "bed" (*śayana*), "seat" (*āsana*), "place" (*sthāna*), "priest" (*yājaka*), and so forth, and words ending in *krīta*, retain their original accent.

A word ending in *man*, a word ending in *ktin*, and these specific words—*vyākhyāna*, *śayana*, *sthāna*—as well as the group beginning with *yājaka* and the word *krīta* when they form the second member [of a compound], have their final syllable unaccented (*anudātta*). Example: *rathavartma* (the path for a chariot).
The path of a cart (*śakaṭavartma*);
the feminine suffix *ktin*: the work composed by Pāṇini (*pāṇinikṛtiḥ*), the work composed by Āpiśali (*āpiśalikṛtiḥ*).
Vyākhyāna: the exposition of the Ṛgveda;
the exposition of prosody.
Śayana: the royal bedchamber.
The bed of a brahmin;
the seat— the royal seat,
the brahmin’s seat.
Place: a cow-pen, a horse-stable; a priest and so forth: a Brāhmaṇa who performs sacrifices.
One who performs sacrifices for Kṣatriyas; one who honors Brāhmaṇas;
one who honors Kṣatriyas.
Those very meanings of the genitive compound taught in [Pāṇini 2.2.9], "those who are priests and so forth, and by means of those who are priests and so forth," are what are understood here.
Example: *krītagotrītaḥ* ("one who has been bought by his lineage").
*aśvakrītaḥ*. This rule is an exception to [the suffix] *kṛt-svara*. However, in the word *krīta*, the third case ending occurs in the sense of the object [of the action], according to Pāṇini 2.3.48.
This is its exception (apavāda).
The mention [of the word *kāraka*] is for the purpose of excluding the non-existence of the action (*abhāva-karma*) in the case of explanations, beds, seats, and places.
It is simply from a *kāraka*, namely, the base form (*prakṛti*).
The striking.
The merit [accrues] from the seventh [case]. (PS 6.2.152)
When the word *puṇya* follows a word ending in the locative case, this final member is udātta on its final syllable. For example:
*adhyayane puṇyam* → *adhyayanapuṇya*.
"Vedapuṇya" means "merit pertaining to the Veda. The compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) regarding the locative case (*saptamī*).

Since a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in a word meaning "equal to" would normally result in the accent of the first member (*pūrvapadakṛtisvara*), the rule here prescribes that the final syllable (*antodātta*) should be accented instead.

However, according to the view that the *uṇādi* suffixes are derivational (*vyutpattipakṣa*), the word *puṇya* would be acute-accented on the first syllable by the rule governing the accent of *kṛt* suffixes. Why is the locative case used [in the rule]? [Consider: "merit through the Veda" (*vedapuṇyam*).
From the third [case-ending], there is the sense of deficiency and quarrel.
Words meaning "deficient" (*ūnārtha*) and the word *kalaha* (quarrel), when they follow a word ending in the third case, become non-udātta; for example:
*māṣona*.
Less than a kārṣāpaṇa;
deficient by a māṣa;
deficient by a kārṣāpaṇa.
*Kalaha*— such as *asi-kalahaḥ* (a sword-fight) or *vāk-kalahaḥ* (a verbal quarrel)—
is a rule that sets aside the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the third case as the preceding member.
In this regard, some maintain that the word *arthe* (in the sense of) is intended to denote the actual form [of the word]. Thus, *dhānyena arthaḥ* becomes *dhānyārthaḥ*.

However, since the inclusion of those words whose meaning is "wanting" (*ūna*) is already established by the very mention of the word *artha* itself for the purpose of indicating the meaning, and since the formation of the third-case compound is already accomplished through that very specific mention (*pratipadokta*), the explicit mention of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is for the sake of clarity.
And a *miśra* [particle] that is not a prefix (*anupasarga*) [is called *gati*], provided there is no *saṃdhi*. (PS 6.2.154)

The term "third case" (tṛtīyā) continues [to apply]. When the word *miśra* follows a word ending in the third case and is not a prefix (*anupasarga*), it becomes udātta on its final syllable, provided that no elision (*asandhi*) is understood to have occurred.
Mixed with molasses;
mixed with sesame seeds;
mixed with clarified butter.
What is the purpose of [the rule] "mixed" (*miśra*)? [Example:
*guḍadhānāḥ* (molasses and grains).
What is the purpose of [the rule] "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarga*)?

"Guḍasaṃmiśrāḥ. Here, the mention of the prefixless form (*anupasarga*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in other instances where *miśra* is mentioned, the form with a prefix (*sopasarga*) is also intended. Consequently, in the rule *miśraślakṣṇaiḥ*, a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyāsamāsa*) occurs even with the word *miśra* when it includes a prefix.
Why is it said "in the absence of compounding" (asandhau)? [Consider:
*brāhmaṇamiśro rājā* ("a king mixed with Brahmins").
Here, he is joined together (*saṃhitaḥ*) with the Brahmins, having attained a single purpose (*aikārthyam*).
For "sandhi" (junction) is said to be the state of having a single purpose through a formal agreement (*paṇabandha*).
Others, however, say that *sandhi* is proximity (*pratyāsatti*) in which a specific distinction is perceived.

In this regard, even though there is spatial proximity between a king and Brahmins, a distinction of form is perceived; thus, the counter-example "the king mixed with Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇamiśraḥ rājā*) is cited. [690]
In the examples, the very attainment of non-distinction is expressed by the phrase "mixed with molasses."

When there is a negation of a quality (*guṇapratiṣedha*), the negative particle *nañ* [is compounded] with taddhita suffixes having the meanings of “to be accomplished” (*sampādya*), “deserving” (*arha*), “beneficial” (*hita*), or “sufficient for” (*alam*). Pāṇini 6.2.155.

The secondary (taddhita) suffixes having the meanings "suitable" (*sampādī*), "worthy" (*arha*), "fitting" (*hita*), and "sufficient" (*alam*), when they follow a word ending in *nañ* used in the sense of negating a quality, cause the final syllable of the subsequent member to be udātta. For example:
*kārṇaveṣṭakikam*, meaning "a face suitable for two ear-rings."
Not made of black bricks, nor not made of black bricks.
Worthy of cutting—*cheda*; one who deserves it is *chaidika*; one who does not deserve it is *acchaidika*.
Beneficial to calves is "vatsīya"; not more beneficial is "avatsīya.
That which is capable of causing excessive distress is "sāntāpika."
*sāntāpikaḥ* means "one who causes distress," while *asāntāpikaḥ* means "one who does not cause distress.
Why [is there] the mention of *nañ*? [Consider:
"one who deserves a donkey-cart" (*gardabharatham arhati*).
*gārdabharathikaḥ* (one who rides a donkey-cart);
*vigārdabharathikaḥ* (one who does not ride a donkey-cart).
Why is it said "in the negation of a quality"? [To illustrate:]...
"Other than a donkey-cart" is *agārdabharathikaḥ*.

"Quality" (*guṇa*) refers to that which serves as the basis for the application of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), such as being produced and so forth. This rule applies where its negation is expressed in a compound, as in the case of *karṇaveṣṭakābhyām*.
Regarding the rule "sampādi mukham":
what is the purpose of the statement that the suffix *yat* has the senses of "fit for," "deserving," "beneficial," and "sufficient"? [Example:
*pāṇinīyam adhīte pāṇinīyaḥ* ("one who studies the work of Pāṇini").
*pāṇinīyaḥ* means "a follower of Pāṇini"; *apāṇinīyaḥ* means "one who is not a follower of Pāṇini.
Why [is the category] "taddhita" mentioned? [Consider:
*kanyāvoḍhā*, meaning "one who is fit to marry another girl."
*voḍhā* means "one who carries" or "one who has carried";
the suffix *tṛc* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.169: *arhe kṛtyatṛcaś ca*.
And [the suffixes] *ya* and *yata* are used when the sense is not that of the object itself. (PS 6.2.156)

When the two taddhita suffixes *ya* and *yat* occur in a sense other than that of the base itself, the final syllable of the subsequent member ending in those suffixes becomes acute (udātta) when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, provided the context concerns the negation of a quality (*guṇapratiṣedha*). For example:
a collection of *pāśas* is *pāśyā*.
It is not bound by fetters, nor is it free from fetters;

in its place, the substitute *pada* is prescribed as being acutely accented on the final syllable even at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśa*).
Therefore, in the expression *padopahataḥ*, the third case ending is used in the sense of the object (Pāṇini 2.3.2).
Thus, by virtue of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member, there is an udātta on the final syllable.
In the case of *padājiḥ*, *padātiḥ*, and *padagaḥ*, however, by the accent rule for *kṛt*-affixes (*kṛtsvara*), the compound itself has the udātta on its final syllable.
A word [ending in the genitive] is used with another word that does not have that as its referent. (PS 6.3.53)
When the suffix *pratya* follows, the word *pāda* is replaced by *pad*, provided that the sense is not "foot" itself. For example:
*padyāḥ śarkarāḥ* ("gravel that strikes the feet").
*Padya* means "thorns. Why [is it specified] "not for that purpose"? [Consider:
water for the feet is *pādya*.

*tripādyam*.

Kāṣin—now they go as foot-travelers; hati—this is the path.

Or [it occurs] in words mixed with sounds. // PS 6.3.56 //

In the sense of naming, the word *udaka* is replaced by *uda*. (Pāṇini 6.3.57)
In the domain of technical names (*saṃjñā*), the word *udaka* undergoes the substitution *uda* when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

[Udaka] becomes [uda] before [vah], as in *udavāha*, whose son is *audavahi*. Why [is it said] "in the sense of a name"? [Consider] *udakagiri* (the water-mountain).
It should be stated that when *sañjñā* [is the governing condition], the word *udaka* is replaced by *uda* as the final member of a compound; for example,
*lohitodaḥ*.

And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the verbal roots *piṣ*, *vas*, *vah*, and *dhā*.
In the case of these subsequent members—*peṣam*, *vāsam*, *vahana*, and *dhi*—the word *udaka* undergoes the substitution *uda*. For example:
*udapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi* ("he grinds with water").
The suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *snehane piṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.38).
*Vāsa-udaka* becomes *vāsa-udavāsaḥ*;
*vāhana-udaka* becomes *vāhana-udavāhanaḥ*.
It is called the "ocean" (udadhi) because water is held within it.
When a single syllable at the beginning of a word is to be lengthened, it may optionally be so done.

The term *udaka* continues [from the previous rule], with the word *uda* being understood. "Single" (*eka*) means without a companion, that is, not followed by a similar class of consonant such as a *hal* (consonant) and so forth.

When the second member of a compound begins with a single consonant (*ekahal-ādi*), the word *udaka* may optionally undergo the substitution *uda* when it signifies something that is to be filled. For example:
*udakumbhaḥ*.
*udakakumbhaḥ*,
*udapātram*, *udakapātram*.
Why [is the rule] "after a single consonant" (*ekahalādau*) stated?
"Water-vessel.
To what does "should be filled" apply? To "water-mountain. [714]
And [the locative case is used] in the senses of "churning," "boiled rice," "flour-meal," "a drop," "a thunderbolt," "a burden," "a carrier," "a load," and "plunging. // PS_6.3.60 //

When *mantha*, *odana*, *saktu*, *bindu*, *vajra*, *bhārahāra*, *vīvadha*, or *gāha* follow as the second members of a compound, the word *udaka* may optionally take the substitute *uda*. For example:

rice with water is *odana-udaka*, [which becomes] *udaudana* or *udakaudana*.

A drop of water.
Regarding *vajrodaka*: *vajra* is [the term] for water; thus it is *udavajra*, or *udakavajra*.

According to Gālava, a short vowel is substituted for a long vowel, except in the case of the word *aṅga*.

*grāmaṇiputraḥ* or *grāmaṇīputraḥ*.
*brahmabandhuputraḥ*, *brahyabandhūputraḥ*.

What is the purpose of the term "aṅga" [in the rule]?
[Examples: *khaṭvāpādaḥ* (the leg of a bed), *mālāpādaḥ* (the foot of a garland). Why is it necessary?
Gārgīputra; Vātsīputra;
the mention of Gālava is for the sake of honor.
For the term "anyatarasyām" (optionally) is understood [to apply here], and this is an option restricted by specific conditions;

In the case of *kārīṣagandhīputraḥ*, and for indeclinables that undergo the substitution of *iyan* and *uvan*, [the suffix *ṅīp*] does not occur; for example,

The lineage of the brow has become like a reed-stalk; it has become like a low-caste woman.

The frown.

In a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) when it is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the word *eka* undergoes shortening. For example:

For here, that which is being grasped as a vowel is qualified [by the following consonant], and not, conversely, that which is being grasped as a consonant by the vowel.
In technical terminology (sañjñā) and in Vedic literature (chandas), the substitution of *ṅ* and *y* for *i* and *u* occurs diversely (*bahulam*).
In names and in Vedic usage, the final vowel of words ending in *ṅī* or *ap* is frequently shortened.
As an example of a word ending in *ṅī* used as a name: *revatiputraḥ*.
The son of Rohiṇī;
the son of Bharaṇī;
yet he does not exist.
Nāndīkara, Nāndīghoṣa, and Nāndīviśāla.
In the Vedic language, there is [the substitution] of *kumārīdā* for *chandasi*;

*jagatīchadaḥ* (roof-covering the earth). Regarding a word ending in *ā* when it is a proper name (*sañjñā*): *śilavaham*, *śilaprastham*.

When the suffix *tva* follows, the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are frequently shortened. Thus,

The state of being Rohiṇī is *rohiṇitva*, or *rohiṇītvam*.
Because this is impossible in the case of a proper name (*sañjñā*), these are examples only within the Vedic language (*chandas*).
In the case of bricks, reeds, and garlands, [the suffix -maya is used] when they are piled up, made of cotton, or worn as a burden.

In the case of *iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānām*, when followed by the subsequent words *cita*, *tūla*, and *bhārin* respectively, a short vowel occurs [in place of the final vowel of the first member]. For example:
*iṣṭakacitam*.

The suffix *taddhita* is also understood after words such as *iṣṭakā* (brick), even when it forms part of a compound ending in that word.
A structure built of baked bricks; cotton from the *muñja* and *iṣīkā* reeds;
a maiden bearing a garland of blue lotuses.
In the case of *khiti*, [the substitution of *u* for the final vowel of the preceding stem] does not apply when the suffix is indeclinable (*anavyaya*).

When *khida* occurs as the final member of a compound, the short vowel is substituted for the penultimate vowel of the preceding word, provided it is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Example: *kāliṃmanyā*.

the rule for shortening [the penultimate vowel] by the suffix *mum* is not superseded;

The augment *mum* is added after a stem ending in *ar*, *dviṣat*, or a vowel, before a case-ending beginning with a consonant.

In the case of the two words *arus* and *dviṣat*, as well as those ending in the suffix *-jan*, when followed by a verbal root (*khidanta*) as the second member of a compound, the augment *mum* is inserted before the final vowel of the first member, provided that it is not an indeclinable (*anavyaya*). For example:
*aruntudaḥ*.
*dviṣantapaḥ* (one who torments enemies).
Regarding those ending in vowels: *kālimmanyā* (one who considers herself black).

Regarding "one who considers himself learned":
this applies only to that which is not indeclinable;
for example, *doṣāmanyam ahaḥ* ("the day considered as evening").

Therefore, when [the vowel] has been shortened, *mum* is substituted.

The two words *vācaṃyama* and *purandara* are treated as irregularly formed (nipātita). For example:

When the word *kāra* follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the augment *mum* is inserted after the words *satya* and *agada*. [Thus:
*satyaṃ karoti*.

*bhakṣaṃ karoti*.

The suffix *mum* should be stated [as an augment] after the word *dhenu* when followed by *bhavyā*: *dhenumbhavyā*. The suffix *mum* should be stated [as an augment] after the word *loka* when followed by *pṛṇe*.

*Timiṅgilagila* is formed [from *timiṅgila*].

In the case of *tailampātā*, what is the purpose of the word *ñe*? [It serves to exclude forms such as] *śyenapātaḥ*.
The suffix *kṛt* is optionally applied after the word *rātri*.
When a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix follows as a final member, the augment *mum* optionally occurs after *rātri*. For example: *rātriñcaraḥ*.
*rātricaraḥ*,

This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) that applies when [the suffix] has not been previously established.

as in *ratrimmanyaḥ*.
There is elision of the *n* of the negative particle *nañ*.

Therefore, the augment *nuṭ* is inserted before a vowel. (Pāṇini 6.3.74)

*anajaḥ*.
"Anaśvaḥ. Why [is the word] "tasmāt" used? For otherwise, it would apply only to the negative particle (nañ).

The words *nabhrāj*, *napāt*, *naveda*, *nāsatya*, *namuci*, *nakula*, *nakha*, *napuṃsaka*, *nakṣatra*, *nakra*, and *nāka* remain in their original form [before a following vowel].

In the following words— *nabhrāṭ*, *napāt*, *navedāḥ*, *nāsatyāḥ*, *namuci*, *nakula*, *nakha*, *napuṃsaka*, *nakṣatra*, *nakra*, and *nāka*— the negative particle *nañ* retains its original form (*prakṛti*).

"Nāsatyāḥ"—those who are virtuous among the good are "satyāḥ."

neither unreal nor not unreal;

Neuter (napuṃsaka): it is neither female nor male; thus it is neuter. The state of being neuter is applied to both female and male through grammatical irregularity (nipātana). The word *kṣiyaḥ* is derived from the root *kṣarati*; alternatively, *kṣatram* is formed as an irregular derivative (*nipātyate*).

the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *kram* by way of irregular derivation (*nipātanāt*).
*nāka* means "that in which there is no suffering (*aka*). [718] According to Pāṇini 6.3.76, the suffix *āduK* is applied after *eka* and its derivatives.
The negative particle *nañ* and the word *eka-* remain in their original form (*prakṛti*), and the augment *ād-uk* is inserted before the word *eka*.
"By one, not twenty" means nineteen; "not thirty by one" means twenty-nine. The compound is formed through a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) of the third [sūtra].
This is introduced from the beginning so that the nasalization characterized by the end of a word may optionally occur here.
The word *naga* may optionally [be treated as a bahuvrīhi compound] when it does not refer to living beings.
The negative particle *nañ* optionally retains its original form (*prakṛti*). [Examples:
*nagā vṛkṣāḥ* (trees that do not go), *agā vṛkṣāḥ* (trees that do not go).
Nagas are mountains;
agas are mountains.

In the domain of technical names (*sañjñā*), the word *saha* undergoes the substitution of *sa*. For example:
*sāśvattham*.
*sapalāśam* (with palāśa trees), *saśiṃśapam* (with śiṃśapā trees).

In *sahayudhvā* and *sahakṛtvā*,
the vowel of the prefix *sa-* is prescribed as udātta by way of a nipātana.

elsewhere, it is indeed set aside by the rule that the final syllable of a compound is acute.

At the end of a book (*granthānta*) and when used in the sense of "more" (*adhika*), the word *saha* undergoes the substitution *sa*. Example:
*sakalaṃ jyautiṣam adhīte* ("He studies the entire science of astronomy").
For a short duration;
they study grammar together with its compendium,

The term *saṅgrahāntam* is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed according to the rule *antavacane*. In that regard, because of the rule *avyayībhāve cākāle*, a compound would not be obtained when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) denotes time; thus, this [present rule] is commenced. Weightiness; weightier; elder; most aged.
Varṣīyān;
tṛpra-trapiṣṭhaḥ; trapīyān.
Long—longest; length; longer.
*vṛndāraka*, *vṛndiṣṭha*,
and *vṛndīyān*.
The words *priya*, *uru*, *guru*, *bahula*, and *dīrgha* are recited in the *pṛthv-ādi* group.
Therefore, since this does not apply to other cases, it is not cited as an example. [768] *PS 6.4.158*: There is elision of the final vowel of *bahu*, and *bahu* is replaced by *bhū*.
In the case of the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, and *īyasun* following *bahu*, there is elision (*lopa*) of these suffixes, and in place of that *bahu*, the substitute *bhū* occurs.
*bhūmā* and *bhūyān*: the word *bahu* is recited among the *pṛthu*-class [of adjectives].
The repetition of the word *bahoḥ* is for the purpose of establishing its status as a substitute;
otherwise, the substitution of *bhū* would apply only to the suffixes.
[PS 6.4.159] *iṣṭhasya yiṭ ca*. (And *yiṭ* is added to *iṣṭha*).
The augment *yiṭ* is added after the suffix *iṣṭha* when it follows *bahu*,
and *bahu* undergoes the substitution of *bhū*.
The augment *yiṭ* is a general exception to elision;
in it, the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.
The [final] vowel of *jya* is elided before the suffix *īyas*.
In place of the suffix *īyas* when preceded by *jya*, the substitution of the vowel *ā* occurs; thus,
*jyāyān*.
Because the elision (*lopa*) is separated from the *yiṭ* augment, it is stated that [the rule] applies "after *ā*.
For when the elision occurs, the form *jyāyān* is established through the lengthening prescribed by the rule *akṛd-yakārāt*.
The substitution of *ra* occurs for *ṛ*, when it is followed by a consonant beginning with a *hal* (consonant) and is light.
The substitution of the sound *ra* occurs for the light vowel *ṛ* at the beginning of a consonant, when followed by the suffixes *iṣṭha*, *im*, or *īyas*. For example:
*prathiṣṭhaḥ*.
Broadness; broader;
most soft.
Why [is it said] "mradimā, mradīyān, ṛtaḥ"? [To show that the rule applies only when the word ends in ṛ.]
Most capable: *paṭiṣṭhaḥ*,
*paṭimā*,
*paṭīyān*.
Why [is it said] "after *hal* etc."? [Consider: *ṛjiṣṭhaḥ*, *ṛjimā*, *ṛjīyān*.
Why is it stated "of a light vowel"?
[Consider: *kṛṣṇa*—*kṛṣṇiṣṭhaḥ*, *kṛṣṇimā*.
It should be smaller than black.
An enumeration should be made here:
broad, soft, intense, thin, and firm.
One should remember these six—pari, pūrva, vṛḍha, and the others—in the rule for the letter ra.
Consequently, it does not occur here:
*kṛtam ācaṣṭe* becomes *kṛtayati*;
*mātaram ācaṣṭe* becomes *mātayati*.
He causes [them] to tremble.
In the Vedic language, there is optionally the substitution of *ūṭh* for the vowel *ṛ* before a suffix beginning with *j*.
In the Vedic domain, when the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, or *īyasun* follow, the letter *r* is optionally substituted for the *ṛ* of the word *ṛju*. As an example:
*rajiṣṭham anu neṣi panthām*.
The word *ṛjiṣṭha* is [formed with the suffix -iṣṭhan] by its very nature when it consists of a single vowel. (Pāṇini 6.4.163)

A monosyllabic stem that bears the designation *bha* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, or *īyasun*. Thus, from this stem *sragvin* ending in the suffix *vin*, [the comparative] *srajiṣṭhaḥ* is formed.
From *sraj* we have *srajīyān* and *srājyati*;
from the word *sruc*, ending in the suffix *mat* (*srugvat*), we have *sruciṣṭhaḥ*,
*srucīyān*, and *srucayati*.
Why [is the condition] "ending in a single vowel" (ekāc) specified? [To exclude cases such as:

*vasumat* becomes *vasiṣṭhaḥ* or *vasīyān*. [In these cases, the rule] "the *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan* [suffixes] remain in their original form (*prakṛtyā*) when followed by the suffix *aka*" applies.
Before the suffix *ya*, these bases—*rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan*—remain in their original form (*prakṛti*). For example:
*rājanyakam*, meaning "a collection of *rājanyas*";
*mānuṣyakam*, meaning "a collection of *manuṣyas*."

By the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite ’nāti* (Pāṇini 6.4.151), the elision of *ya* does not occur due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Thus, "the state of a youth" is *yauvanikā*.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *manojña*-class;
the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) does not occur by virtue of the rule *tasya naḥ taddhite* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.144).
In the case of the word *anya*, when it does not mean "offspring," [the suffix *cha* is applied].
A stem ending in *inn* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when the suffix *aṇ* follows in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). Example:
*sāṅkūṭina*.
*sāṃrāviṇaṃ* (the act of making a general noise),
*sāṃmārjinaṃ* (the act of sweeping thoroughly);
[these are formed] by the suffix *inuṇ* in the sense of "pervasive action" (*abhividhau bhāve*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.44.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *aṇinuṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.15).
Thus, "this belongs to one who possesses a garland" (*sragviṇa idam*) becomes *srāgviṇam*.
Why is it specified "before *aṇ*"? [Consider: a collection of staff-bearers (*daṇḍinām samūhaḥ*) is *dāṇḍam*, [which does not take *aṇ*].
The suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anudāttāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44). Why is it specified "not denoting a descendant" (*anapatye*)?
The offspring of Medhāvin is a Maidhāva.
And [the suffix *ini* is applied after] *gāthin*, *vidathin*, *keśin*, *gaṇin*, and *paṇin*.
Gāthin, vidathin, keśin, gaṇin, and paṇin— these also remain in their original form before the suffix *aṇ*.
The descendant of Gāthin is a Gāthin.
The Vaidathinas, the Kaiśinas, and the Gāṇinas.
[The suffix] *pāṇin* [is applied].
This rule is commenced for the purpose of expressing offspring (*apatya*).
And conjunction and so forth [are also included]. (PS 6.4.166)
A consonant cluster (saṃyoga) at the beginning of a word remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*) before the suffix *iñ*, except for the suffix *aṇ*. For example:
the descendant of Śaṅkhin is Śāṅkhinaḥ.
Of Mādrin;
of Vajrin.
The word *annantamaṇi* is by nature used both with respect to offspring and without respect to offspring; for example:
*sāmanaḥ*.
vaimanaḥ, sautvanaḥ, jaitvanaḥ.
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after a verbal root denoting non-existence (*abhāva*) or an action (*karman*).
And before a taddhita suffix beginning with *y*, when it does not signify the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) or "action" (*karman*), the stem remains in its original form (*prakṛti*). For example:
*sāmanyaḥ*, meaning "one who is good at the *sāmans*."
Why is it said "vemanyaḥ abhāvakarmaṇoḥ"?
[The answer is: *rājyam* (sovereignty) is the state (*bhāva*) or the action (*karman*) of a king (*rājan*).
The word *rājan* is listed among the *purohita*-group [in Pāṇini 5.1.128].
Therefore, this is the suffix *yak*.
The self and the path are in the void. (PS 6.4.169)
The words *ātman* and *adhvan* retain their original form when followed by the suffix *kha*. For example:
*ātmane hitaḥ* (beneficial for oneself) becomes *ātmanīnaḥ*.
One who travels along a path is called *adhvanīna*.
Why [is it said] "in the sense of *kha*"? [To exclude cases such as] *pratyātmam* and *prādhvam*.
In *pratyātmam*, the compound-final suffix *ṭac* is applied according to *avyayībhāve 'naś ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.108).
In *prādhvam*, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] according to *upasargād adhvanaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.85).
Thus ends the section on the *ac* suffix.
The suffix *mayaṭ* is not applied to form a word for offspring when it follows a stem ending in *man*, provided the stem does not end in *varman*.

A word preceded by *m* does not retain its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by an *aṇ* suffix in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), provided it is not *varman*. For example: the offspring of Suṣāman is *Sauṣāmaḥ*.
The word *cāndrasāmaḥ* [is formed with the suffix *aṇ*]. Why is it specified that it must be preceded by *m*? [Consider] *sautvanaḥ*.
Why is it specified that it refers to "descendant" (*apatya*)?
A chariot covered with leather is *cārmaṇaḥ*.
Why [is the rule] "not after *avarman*" stated?
[Because] the descendant of *cakravarman* is *cākravarmaṇaḥ*.
Alternatively, when prohibiting [the suffix] *map* for the first time, it should be stated that this applies to names ending in *hita*:
the descendant of one whose name ends in *hita* is *haitanāmaḥ* or *haitanāmanaḥ*.
The suffix *brāhma* is applied after the word *ajāti*.
A separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) is made here:

even though *brāhma* occurs under the heading of "descendant" (*apatya*), by virtue of its specific force, it is treated as an irregular form (*nipātana*) for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the final vowel) when applied to meanings other than "descendant."
The womb of Brahmā;
the weapon of Brahmā;
the oblation of Brahmā.

Consequently, [the suffix] *ajāti* applies; that is, only when there is a descendant (*apatya*). When a descendant is denoted by the suffix *āt* or *aṇ*, the elision of the *ṭi* of *brahman* does not occur.
The offspring of Brahmā is a Brāhmaṇa;
[the rule] "in the sense of offspring" applies here as well:
*brāhmī* is a medicinal herb.
The suffix *kārman* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).
In the word *kārmaḥ*, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix is prescribed in the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlye*).
One whose nature is action (*karmaśīlaḥ*) is a *kārmaḥ*.
The suffix *ṇa* [is applied] by the rule *śīlam, chatrādibhyo ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.61).
If this is so, for what purpose is this [present rule]?
Is the elision of *ṭi* not already established by the rule "in a *taddhita*" (Pāṇini 6.4.144)?
True, this is so.

But it is for the purpose of indication (*jñāpaka*); this indicates that in the case of a *ṇa*-suffix used in the sense of "having the habit of" (*tācchīlika*), the operations prescribed for an *aṇ*-suffix take place.
Consequently, forms such as *caurī* and *tāpasī*, which end in a *ṇa*-suffix, are established with the feminine suffix *īkāra*.
Why is it said "in the sense of habitual action" (*tācchīlye*)? [Because otherwise,] *kārmaṇam* would mean "this belongs to the action" (*karmaṇaḥ idam*).
[The rule] *aukṣam anapatye* (PS 6.4.173) applies when there is no offspring.
In the form *aukṣam*, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is prescribed by rule when the suffix *aṇ* does not denote offspring; thus, *aukṣam padam*.
Why "when not denoting offspring"? [Consider: *aukṣakaḥ*.
The offspring of an *ukṣan* is *aukṣṇaḥ*;
there is elision of the final vowel by the rule *ṣapūrvahandhṛtarājñām aṇi* (Pāṇini 6.4.165).

The forms *dāṇḍināyana*, *hāstināyana*, *ātharvaṇika*, *jaihmāśineya*, *vāsināyani*, *bhrauṇahatya*, *dhaivatya*, *sārava*, *aikṣvāka*, *maitreya*, and *hiraṇmaya* [are derived with the suffix *yañ*]. (Pāṇini 6.4.174)

The following forms are derived as irregularly formed (*nipātana*): Dāṇḍināyana, Hāstināyana, Ātharvaṇika, Jaihmāśineya, Vāsināyani, Bhrauṇahatya, Dhaivatya, Sārava, Aikṣvāka, Maitreya, and Hiraṇmaya.
These are formed from *daṇḍin* and *hastin*, which are listed in the *naḍādi* group.
In the sense of "their path" (*tayor āyane*), the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed [by the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak*].

However, for some authorities, since *hastin* is not listed among the *naḍādi* group, they maintain that the suffix *phak* also occurs for them precisely because of this specific prescriptive rule (*nipātana*).
The offspring of Daṇḍin is Dāṇḍināyana;
the offspring of Hastin is Hāstināyana.
Furthermore, "Atharvan" is recited among the [Vedic branches] beginning with Vāsanta.
The text proclaimed by Atharvan is also called "Atharvan" by way of metaphorical designation;
one who studies that is an *ātharvaṇika*. In the formation of this term, the original stem (*prakṛti*) is retained as an irregularity (*nipāta*) before the suffix *-ika*.
*jihmāśin* is listed among the *śubhra*-type words; when the suffix *ṇya* follows it, its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed by rule. Thus, the offspring of *jihmāśin* is *jaihmāśineya*.
The offspring of those who dwell [there] is [denoted by the suffix] *phiñ*,
according to the rule *jīdāṃ vṛddhād agotrāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.157).
In that case, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātyate*).
In the case of *vāsināyani* and *bhrūṇahan*, as well as *dhīvan*, the substitution of *t* for the final syllable is prescribed when the suffix *ṣyañ* follows. Thus,
the state (*bhāva*) of a *bhrūṇahan* is *bhrauṇahatyam*.

The state of being a *dhīvan* is *dhaivatya*. Regarding the rule "the substitution of *t* for *n* occurs before a suffix beginning with a vowel, except for *ciṇ* and *ṇal*" (*Pāṇini* 7.3.32), since that substitution applies only to a verbal root and its suffix, [the form] is *bhrauṇaghnaḥ*.
In the case of *vārtraghna*, [the substitution] does not occur;
therefore, in *bhrauṇahatya*, the preservation of the original form (*tattva*) is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
In *sārava*, the substitution of *va* for the syllable *yū* of the word *sarayū* is prescribed as an irregularity when the suffix *aṇ* follows.
In the word *sarayvām*, the water is "sāravam" (abounding in essence).

The term *aikṣvākaḥ* is recited with a single accent (*ekaśruti*) by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) that retains its own inherent accent; consequently, this [word] is prescribed as being both acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) and acutely accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

The word *aikṣvāka* is derived from *ikṣvāku*; by the rule *janapada-śabdāt kṣatriyād-añ* (Pāṇini 4.1.166), the suffix *añ* is applied, and therein the elision of the vowel *u* is prescribed as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
*Aikṣvākaḥ*:
one who exists among the *Ikṣvāku* territories; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.132, *kopadhādaṇ*.
"Aikṣvāka," "Maitreya":
the word *mitrayu* is listed among the *gṛṣṭi*-type words.

Then, when the suffix *ḍhañ* has been applied, the elision of the word *yu* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *iy* for the initial vowel and following consonant. Thus, from *mitrayoḥ apatyam*, we derive *maitreyaḥ*.
Now, for what purpose is the word *mitrayu* not simply listed among the *bidādi* group?

In that case, once the augment *aṇ* has been applied, the desired form is already established by the substitution of *iy* according to the rule *yāder īt* (Pāṇini 7.1.2). Furthermore, it would not be necessary to formulate a special rule (*nipātana*) for the elision of *yu*,
nor would it be necessary to include [the word] in the *yaskādi* group for the sake of its elision.
Is it not the case that [the elision] is already established by the rule *mitrayava ity año yaññoś ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.64)?
This is not so.

In the case of *mitrayūṇāṃ saṅghaḥ*, the suffix *vuñ* prescribed after [names of] lineages (*gotra*) and schools (*caraṇa*) is set aside; however, in the case of *maitreyakaḥ saṅghaḥ*, the suffix *añ* applies by the rule *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣv añ*. Furthermore, by the rule *yañ-iñām aṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.127), the suffix *aṇ* would be expected to apply.
In the word *hiraṇmayam*, when the suffix *mayaṭ* follows *hiraṇya*, the elision of the initial *y* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
That which is a modification of gold is *hiraṇmaya*.
In the Vedic language, the forms *ṛtvya*, *vāstvya*, *vāstvam*, *mādhvī*, and *hiraṇyayā* [are used]. (PS 6.4.175)
The forms *ṛtvya*, *vāstvya*, *vāstva*, *mādhvī*, and *hiraṇyaya* are established as irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) within the domain of Vedic literature (*chandasi*).
In these cases, the substitution of *yaṇ* for the semivowel *y* in the words *ṛtu* and *vāstu* is established as an irregularity.
That which exists in the season (*ṛtu*) is *ṛtvyam*;
that which exists in the dwelling (*vāstu*) is *vāstvyam*.
In the case of the word *vastu*, the substitution of *yaṇ* [for the final vowel] is prescribed when the suffix *aṇ* follows.
The suffix *vāstva* means "existing in a dwelling" (*vastuni bhavaḥ*).
In the case of the word *madhu*, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* is prescribed for the feminine;
thus: *mādhvīr naḥ santvoṣadhīḥ*.
The elision of the syllable *ma* of the suffix *mayaṭ*, which is prescribed after the word *hiraṇya*, is irregularly applied;
thus, [the form] *hiraṇyayam*.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikā* commentary composed by the venerable Vāmana.
Seventh Chapter, First Quarter:
*yu* and *vu* are replaced by *ana* and *aka*, respectively. (Pāṇini 7.1.1)
When the suffixes *yu* and *vu*— which have abandoned their specific qualifiers and consist of the semivowel *yaṇ* with a nasal— are employed, these two are understood;
in their place, the substitutes *ana* and *aka* respectively occur.
The suffix *ya* replaces *ana*, and *va* replaces *aka*. From roots such as *nandi*, the suffix *lyu* is applied: *nandanaḥ*, *ramaṇaḥ*.
From *sāyaṃ* and others, the suffixes *ṭyu*, *ṭyul*, and *tuṭ* [are applied]: *sāyantanaḥ* (belonging to evening), *cirantanaḥ* (long-standing).
By the rule for *ṇvul* and *tṛc*: *kārakaḥ* (an agent).
The suffix *vun* is applied after the words *hāraka*,
*vāsudeva*, and *arjuna* (Pāṇini 4.3.98): *vāsudevakaḥ*.
Arjunaka: [The question is] regarding "anunāsikayaṇoḥ" (before a nasalized vowel and a semi-vowel): what is the purpose? [Consider:
*ūrṇāyā yus* (Pāṇini 5.2.123) — *ūrṇāyuḥ*.
When joined with *bhuj* and *mṛj*, [the suffix] *u* becomes *ū*: *bhujyuḥ* and *mṛtyuḥ*.
For in such cases, the nasality (*anunāsikatva*) of the *yaṇ* is not admitted; indeed, the followers of Pāṇini admit the nasality [of certain sounds].

Here, because of the specific mention of *yuvoḥ*, the augment is not applied under the view that a copulative compound (*dvandva*) takes a singular form, based on the principle that "the teaching regarding augments is not mandatory.
Alternatively, the neuter gender does not apply, according to the principle that "gender is not prescribed by grammar, as gender depends upon worldly usage.
However, in the case of the *itaretara-dvandva* (mutual pair), the elision of the vowel should be understood as being Vedic (*chāndasa*).
If there is a dual designation for the two [words], then the *yaṇ* substitution would apply to the duality;
but if there is a singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*), how could this [form] be like the masculine?
In the case of duality, there would be elision according to the Vaigamikas; in the case of singularity, the augment *num* would be non-obligatory.
For since gender is not subject to formal prescription (*aśiṣyatva*), the masculine gender is here relied upon.
The suffixes beginning with *ph*, *ḍh*, *kh*, *ch*, and *gh* take the augment *āyan*, *ey*, *īn*, *īy*, or *iya* respectively.

The substitutes *āyan*, *ey*, *īn*, *īy*, and *iy* occur respectively in place of the initial elements of suffixes, namely *pha*, *ḍha*, *kha*, *cha*, and *gha*. For the element *pha*, the substitute *āyan* occurs.
The suffix *phak* is added after [patronymic bases] beginning with *naḍa* (Pāṇini 4.1.99)— for example, *nāḍāyanaḥ* and *cārāyaṇaḥ*.
The substitute *ey* takes the place of the suffix *ḍha*.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after feminine stems [to form patronymics] (Pāṇini 4.1.120):
*sauparṇeyaḥ*, *vainateyaḥ*.
The substitution of *īn* occurs for *kha* after the word *kula* (Pāṇini 4.1.139):
*āḍhyakulīnaḥ* ("born of a wealthy family"),
*śrotriyakulīnaḥ* ("born of a family of Vedic scholars").
The suffix *cha* is substituted for [the patronymic suffix *ya*]. According to Pāṇini 4.2.114, *cha* follows a *vṛddha* [stem]: *gārgīyaḥ*, *vātsīyaḥ*.
The substitution of *iy* occurs for this [root] *gha*.
From *kṣatra*, the suffix *dhak* is applied—*kṣatriyaḥ*. Why is there a mention of "an affix" (*pratyaya*)? [Observe: *phakkati*.
He approaches; he digs; he cuts.
It wavers.
Why is the word "ādi" (and so forth) included?
[To provide examples such as] *ūrudaghnam* (reaching the thighs).
*jānudaghnam* (reaching the knee).
These suffixes, beginning with *āyan*, occur at the very time of the instruction of the suffix itself.
Once these have been applied, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the initial syllable of the suffix.
And thus, the assignment of the *cittva* (acute accent) to the suffixes *ghac* and *cha* in the rule *ghacchau ca* (Pāṇini 4.4.117) becomes meaningful;
for in the case of words such as *śaṅkhaḥ* and *ṣaṇḍhaḥ*, the substitutes [prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.52] do not apply due to the mention of the term *bahulam* in the rule *uṇādayo bahulam*.
The rule *ṛter īyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.29), which includes the word "optionally" (*vā*), is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that substitutes do not apply to verbal roots and suffixes.
However, in rules such as *ejeḥ khaś* (3.2.28) and *padarujaviśaspṛśo ghañ* (3.3.16), the designation *it* must indeed apply.
For, among the *taddhita* suffixes, the prescription of the substitutes *kh* and *gh* has a scope of application; thus, it is not capable of overriding the designation *it*.
When the designation *it* would apply to the letter *n* in *āyan*, *īn*, and *īna*, a counter-measure must be taken, for an operation dependent on being *nit* is possible. [774]
The *jha* group [of consonants] is final. (PS 7.1.3)
The term *pratyaya* (suffix) is understood to carry over,
while the term *ādi* (beginning) has ceased to apply.
The substitute *anta* is applied in place of the *jh* that is a member of a suffix; for example:
*kurvanti*, *sunvanti*.
They gather [the wood], thinking, "Today or tomorrow we shall be awakened; we shall lie down with our husbands.
From the roots *jṛ* and *viś*, the suffix *jhac* is applied: thus, *jarantaḥ*.
*veśantaḥ*; by the rule "of the suffix" (*pratyayasya*) alone, *ujjhitā*,
*ujjhitum*.
It must be abandoned;
